effects.title: 1-Bit Dithering
effects.name: 1-bit dithering
effects.dating: Older algorithms. Personal computer look with MacPaint from 1984 onwards.
effects.caption: MacPaint, 1984: Susan Kare's 1-bit bitmap based on a Japanese template.
effects.credit: Apple / Susan Kare; Image: Computer History Museum. Copyright protected; Source image courtesy of the Computer History Museum

body.label: Identify
body.text: A black and white dot pattern merges from a distance into apparent shades of gray and soft gradients.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Limited colors are spatially distributed to approximate intermediate tones. Error diffusion passes rounding errors to neighboring pixels.

body.label: Example
body.text: Bill Atkinson's MacPaint for the Macintosh (1984) shaped monochrome computer graphics.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Convert a gradient to threshold black and white and dithering. Compare the gradations and dot structure.

context: Algorithmic prehistory before 1980; iconic personal computer look with MacPaint (1984).
Intermediate tones are approximated by the spatial distribution of lighter and darker pixels. In error diffusion, the quantization error of one pixel is passed on to neighboring pixels.
Bill Atkinson's MacPaint for the first Macintosh (1984); dithering is also discussed in the preserved developer oral history.
Image: Historical original / source image. Black and white pixel and pattern areas simulate grayscale, textures and shading with only two tonal values.
effects.distinction: Pixelation reduces the resolution; dithering distributes a limited number of colors for tonal simulation. Both can be combined. Do not confuse this with the invention of the halftone screen in printing and photography. This refers to digital tonal simulation with a limited number of colors.
effects.aftermath: The technical limitation to a few colors became a distinct graphic aesthetic: home computers, early desktop publishing, and later retro graphics.
effects.funFact: In 1984, MacPaint created a surprisingly diverse visual language from just black and white.

margin.note: A method that passes a pixel’s brightness mismatch to nearby pixels, balancing light and dark dots across an area.
Using one color or one color family. In this example the image has only black and white pixels.

effects.title: 2.5D Parallax
effects.name: 2.5D parallax / 3D photo
effects.dating: 2020: 3D Photo Inpainting as a research milestone; layer animation older
effects.caption: 3D Photo Inpainting: two frames from Moon Swing, 2020.
effects.credit: Meng-Li Shih, Shih-Yang Su, Johannes Kopf and Jia-Bin Huang.

body.label: Identify
body.text: A photograph appears to move spatially, even though the depth is limited.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Image planes or depth values are shifted; hidden areas must be filled in.

body.label: Example
body.text: Shih and Team: 3D Photography, CVPR 2020.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Animate three depth levels at different speeds.

context: The term 2.5D describes spatial movement based on limited image and depth information. Manual layer animation is older; the CVPR work by Shih et al. in 2020 serves as a documented milestone. It transforms an RGB-D image into a layered depth representation and adds previously hidden color and depth areas. When the camera is moved laterally, near and far parts shift differently. Where this reveals new background behind a foreground object, information is missing in the original photo. The method estimates these areas. Therefore, pay particular attention to contours in the exercise. Small movements usually work more convincingly because less hidden space needs to be invented.
effects.distinction: A depth photograph is not a fully captured three-dimensional object with freely accessible back sides.
effects.aftermath: Parallax is the relative difference in motion, not a simple zoom. The depth of field must remain plausible so that the subject doesn't appear flat.
effects.funFact: A sideways-moving virtual camera needs image parts that were hidden behind the foreground in the original photo.
highlights: hidden areas must be filled in

margin.note: Flat image layers placed at different simulated distances. Moving them at different rates can suggest depth.
Groups of image content treated as being at different distances, such as foreground, middle ground, and background.

sources.label: Shih et al.: 3D Photography using Context-aware Layered Depth Inpainting, 2020

effects.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting
effects.name: 3D Gaussian splatting
effects.dating: 2023: SIGGRAPH work by Kerbl and team
effects.caption: 3D Gaussian Splatting: Research result Bicycle, 2023.
effects.credit: Bernhard Kerbl, Georgios Kopanas, Thomas Leimkühler and George Drettakis / Inria.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Photorealistic spaces with cloudy, floating transitions at uncertain points.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Optimized three-dimensional Gaussian distributions are quickly rendered as overlapping image contributions.

body.label: Example
body.text: Kerbl and team: 3D Gaussian Splatting, 2023.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare a good view with the edge of the recorded space.

context: In 2023, Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkühler, and Drettakis presented a method for high-quality, real-time view synthesis. It begins with calibrated cameras and a sparse point cloud, then optimizes spatial Gaussian distributions with extent and other properties. An efficient visibility-dependent renderer projects these contributions onto the image. Their work reports high-quality rendering at a minimum of 100 frames per second at 1080p for their tests. This performance figure applies to the research environment, not to any subsequent tool. Unlike a simple point cloud, the elements possess a spatial shape and overlapping effect. Edge artifacts indicate where the underlying views provide little information.
effects.funFact: The SIGGRAPH 2023 study reported real-time views at a minimum of 100 frames per second at 1080p.

margin.note: Smooth, bell-shaped mathematical profiles. In this technique, each describes a soft 3D element with position, extent, color, and opacity.
Converted from a scene representation into a viewable image. Many soft elements are combined to form each view.

sources.label: Kerbl et al.: 3D Gaussian Splatting, SIGGRAPH 2023

effects.title: 360° Panorama
effects.name: 360° Panorama
effects.dating: 2013, the release of the Ricoh Theta consumer 360° camera
effects.caption: 360° panorama of a snowy mountain top building. A snowy mountain landscape with a small building is shown as a flat, wrapped image.
effects.credit: Capricorn4049 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a fully interactive sphere of vision wrapped around a central viewing point. When viewed flat, it looks heavily distorted at the top and bottom poles.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Software stitches multiple wide-angle photographs together into an equirectangular projection. This flat map maps spherical coordinates to a rectangular grid.

body.label: Example
body.text: Chris Milk: Clouds Over Sidra, 2015.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Open a flat equirectangular image and notice how straight lines curve dramatically near the top and bottom edges.

context: Creating full spherical panoramas once required complex rigs and tedious manual stitching. In the 2010s, consumer cameras with dual fisheye lenses made instant 360-degree capture accessible. These devices record overlapping ultra-wide fields of view. Built-in processors instantly merge the edges to form an unbroken sphere. The final file is typically saved as an equirectangular projection. This standard format stretches the top and bottom regions severely to fit a 2:1 rectangle. Dedicated software or web players then wrap this flat image onto a virtual sphere around the viewer's perspective. You can then look in any direction.
effects.distinction: Unlike a traditional cylindrical panorama, a 360° spherical panorama includes the zenith and nadir. This means you can look straight up and straight down.
effects.aftermath: It reveals how mathematical map projections are essential for translating three-dimensional viewing space onto two-dimensional digital screens.
effects.funFact: The equirectangular projection was actually invented by Marinus of Tyre around AD 100 for mapmaking.

margin.note: A standard map projection mapping longitude to horizontal lines and latitude to vertical lines. It creates heavy distortion at the poles.
Ultra-wide-angle camera lenses that produce strong visual distortion intended to create a wide panoramic or hemispherical image.

effects.title: Active Contour Snake
effects.name: Active Contour Snake
effects.caption: Atlas demonstration: the free source photo and the computed Active Contour Snake. A grand, symmetrical palace with central domes and tall minarets stands shrouded in a soft morning mist. The evolving curve demonstrates high precision as it conforms to the distinct architectural silhouettes of the domes and the horizontal rooflines.
effects.credit: Image: Varshesh Joshi varshesh · CC0 (via Wikimedia Commons), processed for the Atlas

body.label: Identify
body.text: A smooth contour traces an estimated object boundary in the photograph.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An initial curve moves to reduce an energy function that balances internal tension and bending against attraction to image edges. The result depends on the starting curve and can settle on the wrong boundary.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Vary the starting curve and stiffness to see which edges the snake follows.

body.label: Classification
body.text: Calculated image processing result.

effects.funFact: Michael Kass, Andrew Witkin, and Demetri Terzopoulos introduced snakes as active contour models.

margin.note: A mathematical score assigned to each curve shape and position. The algorithm seeks a lower score, not necessarily the lowest possible.
A force within the curve that resists stretching and tends to shorten it. A separate bending penalty discourages sharp turns.

effects.title: Aerial Photography
effects.name: Aerial Photography
effects.dating: 1858, Nadar’s balloon photographs near Paris
effects.caption: Oval Aerial View of a Waterfront City. An oval sepia photograph shows dense city rooftops, winding streets, and a waterfront from above.
effects.credit: Black, James Wallace, 1825-1896 · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: An elevated viewpoint reveals rooftops, street patterns, and land divisions that are hard to see from the ground. Oblique views show building sides, while downward views flatten the scene into map-like shapes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A camera above the ground records reflected light through a lens; height and viewing angle determine the visible layout. Early wet collodion plates required exposure and chemical development while their coating remained wet.

body.label: Example
body.text: James Wallace Black: Boston, as the Eagle and the Wild Goose See It, 1860.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph a model street from its side, then from directly above; compare visible roofs, hidden walls, and street shapes.

context: In 1858, Nadar made balloon photographs near Paris, establishing an early milestone in aerial photography. Those photographs do not survive. In 1860, James Wallace Black photographed Boston from a balloon; his famous view is the earliest surviving aerial photograph. These experiments used wet collodion plates, which demanded preparation, exposure, and development before the coating dried. Carrying photographic equipment into a balloon made that sequence difficult. The aerial viewpoint revealed urban patterns rather than merely enlarging familiar street views. Later photographers used kites, aircraft, and other elevated platforms.
effects.distinction: Unlike a drawn bird’s-eye view, an aerial photograph records light from an actual scene through a camera. It is not automatically a map: tilted views and terrain height can distort scale.
effects.aftermath: Aerial photography teaches how changing the camera’s position can reveal spatial relationships hidden at ground level.
effects.funFact: Nadar’s pioneering aerial photographs are lost, but Black’s Boston view survives.

margin.note: Views taken at a slant rather than straight down.
Glass plates coated with collodion and made light-sensitive using silver salts. They had to be exposed and developed before drying.
The stage when light reaches the sensitive surface and forms a latent image. Chemical development then makes that image visible.

effects.title: Affine Texture Warping
effects.name: Affine Texture Warping
effects.dating: 1990s; strongly associated with Sony’s PlayStation, launched in Japan in 1994.
effects.caption: AI illustration: Warped Brick Textures in a Low-Fidelity 3D Environment.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Surface patterns stretch and skew as the camera moves, producing wobbly textures on walls and floors. Nearby polygon edges may show vertex jitter, a separate but often accompanying artifact.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Affine texture mapping interpolates texture coordinates across screen-space triangles without perspective correction, distorting patterns on surfaces that recede into depth. Vertex jitter instead comes from limited coordinate precision, including snapping projected vertices to whole-pixel positions.

body.label: Example
body.text: Core Design: Tomb Raider, 1996.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch original PlayStation Tomb Raider footage during a slow camera turn; compare sliding floor patterns with stepping polygon edges.

context: Affine mapping predates the PlayStation, but its artifacts became familiar through 1990s real-time 3D games. The console’s graphics hardware mapped textures without perspective correction. This reduced calculation demands, but textures could distort across tilted polygons. Developers could divide large surfaces into smaller polygons to make the error less noticeable. Separately, whole-pixel vertex positions made geometry jump slightly during motion. Together, these limitations produced the characteristic unstable appearance. Modern renderers usually correct perspective and retain finer coordinate precision, while retro graphics sometimes deliberately recreate both artifacts.
effects.distinction: Perspective-correct texture mapping accounts for depth, keeping a surface pattern consistent under projection. Vertex jitter moves polygon boundaries; affine warping distorts the texture within them.
effects.aftermath: It shows how shortcuts in rendering can become recognizable visual styles, even when they began as unwanted errors.
effects.funFact: A perfectly stationary scene can contain affine distortion; movement simply makes the changing distortion easier to notice.

margin.note: Numbers that specify which part of an image belongs at a point on a surface.
A depth-aware calculation that keeps mapped images consistent with the apparent shrinking of distant surfaces.
Polygon corners restricted to integer pixel coordinates, rather than positions between them.

effects.title: Airbrush Illustration
effects.name: Airbrush Illustration
effects.dating: 1920s commercial prominence; nineteenth-century origins
effects.caption: Firefighter Helmet with Mirrored Visor. A firefighter’s red helmet and mirrored visor are rendered with luminous highlights and intricate reflected street scenery.
effects.credit: Fabio pastori · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Smooth gradients shape idealized faces, rounded objects, and glossy surfaces with few visible brush marks. Soft transitions meet crisp masked edges, often around lettering or chrome highlights.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Compressed air breaks liquid paint or ink into fine droplets, which build tone through overlapping spray passes. Masks block selected areas, while spray distance, paint flow, and hand movement control coverage and softness.

body.label: Example
body.text: Philip Castle: A Clockwork Orange film poster, 1971.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare a sprayed edge beside a paper mask with an unmasked edge, using washable paint and following equipment ventilation instructions.

context: Airbrush tools existed before the 1920s, when commercial artists used sprayed shading alongside the geometric forms of Art Deco. The technique deposits pigment onto a surface; it does not expose or develop photographic material. Artists build shadows through repeated passes and preserve highlights by leaving areas unpainted or adding lighter paint. Removable masks help separate smooth shading from sharp outlines. Later advertising, pin-up illustration, and record sleeves extended this polished vocabulary. By the 1970s, airbrushed skin and exaggerated chrome reflections were familiar features of commercial illustration.
effects.distinction: A blended brush painting can also have smooth shading, but an airbrush deposits sprayed droplets rather than spreading paint with bristles. Photographic retouching may use the same tool, but modifies an existing photograph rather than necessarily creating an illustration.
effects.aftermath: Airbrush illustration shows how controlled shading and selective sharp edges can make flat pigment suggest volume, gloss, and idealized perfection.
effects.funFact: An airbrush can paint without its nozzle ever touching the picture surface.

margin.note: Air held under pressure supplies the force that turns liquid paint into a spray.
Paper, film, or other barriers protect parts of the picture from sprayed paint.
A decorative style associated with geometric shapes, streamlined forms, and luxury materials, especially during the 1920s and 1930s.

effects.title: Albumen Print
effects.name: Albums print
effects.dating: Introduced in 1850; dominant withdrawal of the later 19th century
effects.caption: H.M.S. Herald in Sydney Harbour, 1857. Albums print. State Library of New South Wales.
effects.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author / Public domain; Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Fine details, smooth surface and often warm image tones.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Protein binds the light-sensitive silver salts to paper.

body.label: Example
body.text: H.M.S. Herald, Sydney Harbour, 1857.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare albumin and salt paper: Where do details appear clearer?

context: In 1850, Louis Désiré Blanquart-Evrard introduced the albumen process. The protein layer holds the silver image to the paper surface, enabling detailed reproduction. Together with glass negatives, albumen prints became the basis of large portrait and view print markets. The process of taking the photograph on the negative and the subsequent paper print remain two distinct steps.
effects.distinction: The typical warm tone is not evidence of a sepia filter. During scanning, gloss and paper texture are partially lost. A screen reproduction therefore better explains the image effect than the complete material surface.
effects.aftermath: The substrate and its coating also contribute to the overall shape of the image.
effects.funFact: Albumin, which gives the substance its name, is actually egg white.
highlights: Protein binds the light-sensitive silver salts

margin.note: Here, the egg-white material used to coat paper and hold the image-forming chemicals near its surface.
Silver-containing compounds that react to light. They provide the light-sensitive ingredients used to create the photographic image.

effects.title: Aliasing Jaggies
effects.name: Aliasing Jaggies
effects.caption: Atlas demonstration: the free source photo and the computed Aliasing Jaggies. A vehicle drives across a vast, dusty landscape beneath a sunset sky. The horizontal horizons and the vehicle's body display harsh, staircase edges caused by the coarse grid sampling.
effects.credit: Image: FORREST CAVALE forrestcavale · CC0 (via Wikimedia Commons), processed for the Atlas

body.label: Identify
body.text: Smooth contours become staircase edges, with blocky diagonals and broken fine detail across the photograph.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The image is sampled on a coarser pixel grid without low-pass filtering, then enlarged using nearest-neighbor interpolation. Fine details can become false patterns because the grid cannot represent them accurately.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Vary the grid spacing and watch diagonal edges become increasingly stepped.

body.label: Classification
body.text: Calculated image processing result.

effects.funFact: The wagon-wheel illusion in film is a related form of aliasing across time.

margin.note: This smooths fine detail before reducing resolution. It helps prevent details smaller than the new grid can capture from becoming misleading patterns.
Each output pixel copies the closest source pixel rather than blending nearby colors. Enlarging this way makes individual pixels appear as blocks.

effects.title: Ambient Occlusion
effects.name: Ambient occlusion / AO
effects.dating: 2000s: widespread in rendering and subsequently real-time graphics.
effects.caption: AO/Accessibility Shading, GPU Gems, Fig. 17–3.
effects.credit: Pharr / Green, GPU Gems / NVIDIA; official technical demonstration.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Corners, gaps and contact zones receive a soft, dark densification.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Fewer free surrounding directions mean less ambient lighting.

body.label: Example
body.text: GPU Gems: Ambient Occlusion Comparison.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare two touching objects with and without AO.

context: In 2004, GPU Gems documented ambient occlusion as a practical complement to material and lighting models. For each surface point, it estimates what proportion of its surroundings is obscured by geometry. This makes shape relationships and contacts more legible, even under simple lighting conditions. Later real-time versions calculate approximations from screen data or geometry. The 2000s mark this documented phase of widespread adoption, not an exclusive point of invention.
effects.distinction: AO is a visibility approximation for ambient light, not a complete global illumination. Excessive intensity produces dirty edges and dark halos.
effects.aftermath: A subtle contact shadow can explain spatial relationships more clearly than more texture.
effects.funFact: AO can show how open a point is to its surroundings.

margin.note: Light arriving from the surrounding environment rather than just a single direct source.
Short for ambient occlusion: an estimate of how nearby surfaces block surrounding light.

body.label: Identify
body.text: A glass portrait lies against a dark background.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A thin negative appears as a positive image against a black background.

body.label: Example
body.text: Man with book, 1850s–60s, hand-colored.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Hold a transparent negative over white and black. Which one flips?

context: In 1854, James Ambrose Cutting patented a variant of the collodion positive on glass in the USA. Ambrotypes were unique, direct camera prints and a more affordable alternative to the daguerreotype. Their principle utilizes the perception of a faint silver negative against a dark surface. In the case, this creates an apparently positive portrait, even though the plate was exposed and developed as a negative.
effects.distinction: The positive impression depends on the dark background. A normal positive scan does not show this optical change. The depicted object contains applied paint; the colorization is an additional intervention.
effects.aftermath: The background can reverse the perception of an image.
effects.funFact: The supposed positive image is technically a weak negative against a dark background.
highlights: positive image against a black background

margin.note: An image whose light and dark values are reversed. In an ambrotype, a faint negative looks positive when backed by something dark.

effects.title: Anaglyph Stereo
effects.name: Anaglyph stereo
effects.dating: 1850s: early color stereoscopy; science and design to this day
effects.caption: NASA: Typhoon Nepartak as an anaglyph and comparison views, 2016.
effects.credit: NASA / GSFC / LaRC / JPL-Caltech, MISR team.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Red and cyan double contours; spatially visible through filter glasses.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Two perspectives are separated by color and each is directed to one eye.

body.label: Example
body.text: NASA: Stereo view of a typhoon.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare true stereo shifting with simple RGB shift.

context: Color stereoscopic experiments date back to the 1850s; Rollmann described a color stereoscope in 1853. The anaglyph is a special form of stereoscopic representation: Two views are placed in different color channels, and specially filtered glasses separate them again for the two eyes. NASA demonstrates how this can be used to spatially examine cloud heights and landscape features, for example. Red-cyan is a common combination, but not the only one. The comparison with RGB shift is crucial: A decorative color shift replicates the same perspective. A true stereo anaglyph requires two matching views with spatially different shifts. The NASA example shown is a modern scientific application.
effects.distinction: Simply shifting the color channels of a photograph does not create correct, different perspectives.
effects.aftermath: Stereoscopy refers to spatial vision from two perspectives; anaglyph here refers to their color-separated encoding. The terms are not interchangeable.
effects.funFact: NASA also uses anaglyphs to spatially study clouds and terrain.
highlights: Two perspectives are separated by color
each is directed to one eye

margin.note: A blue-green color. In red-cyan stereo, colored glasses separate the two encoded views so each eye receives mainly one.
An offset between the red, green, and blue channels of an image. It creates colored edges but does not necessarily encode genuine depth.

sources.label: NASA: What on Earth is an Anaglyph?

body.label: Identify
body.text: Horizontal light streaks, colored reflections and washed-out contrasts make the reaction to bright light sources visible.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Light is reflected or scattered in the lens. Anamorphic lenses produce characteristic bands. Digital effects imitate them.

body.label: Example
body.text: Star Trek (2009): Abrams and Mindel create flares on set.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Move a light source to the edge of the image. Do real flares and digital overlays react differently?

context: Optical origin much older; strong, deliberate stylistic wave around Star Trek (2009).

Bright light is reflected or scattered within a lens. Anamorphic lenses can create striking horizontal light bands and other reflection patterns. The effect can be triggered on set or added digitally.
Star Trek (2009), J. J. Abrams and cinematographer Dan Mindel: deliberately created anamorphic flares.
Regarding the illustration: Historical original / source image. Bright light sources reflect in the lens. Anamorphic optics stretch the reflections into characteristic horizontal stripes.
effects.distinction: A halo around a bright object is glow/bloom; a horizontal streak can mimic lens flare, but doesn't necessarily have to be optically generated. Not invented in 2009. This case shows how a long-known lens aberration is being repurposed as a sign of the future and authenticity.
effects.aftermath: The visible reaction of the camera makes even an artificial future world physical and unpredictable; the optics become part of the visual language.
effects.funFact: The flares in Star Trek 2009 were deliberately created on set, not just added later.
highlights: reflected or scattered in the lens

effects.title: Animated GIF
effects.name: Animated GIF
effects.dating: 1987, CompuServe introduces GIF; 1989, GIF89a adds animation controls.
effects.caption: AI illustration: Bouncing ball animation frames on CRT monitor.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: A short sequence repeats, often with stepped motion, hard pixel edges, and a limited palette. Flat colors or speckled shading are common.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A player displays stored image frames in sequence, using timing instructions to create apparent motion. Each frame uses a color table of at most 256 entries; a looping extension requests repetition.

body.label: Example
body.text: Chris Torres: Nyan Cat, 2011.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Open a looping GIF in a frame viewer. Compare adjacent frames, then check whether they have equal display times.

context: CompuServe introduced GIF in 1987 for exchanging color images across computer systems. The original format could hold multiple images. GIF89a followed in 1989, adding controls for frame delays, transparency, and how previous frames are retained or cleared. Continuous looping came through a later Netscape application extension, not the original GIF89a specification alone. Each image can have its own color table, so an animation can contain more than 256 colors overall. Small files and broad browser support helped animated GIFs spread through early websites, then online jokes and reaction images.
effects.distinction: Unlike a static GIF, an animated GIF changes its displayed image over time. Unlike most web video formats, GIF has no standard audio track.
effects.aftermath: Animated GIFs show how carefully chosen frames and timing can make restricted color and simple repetition expressive.
effects.funFact: A frame can update only a small rectangle instead of replacing the whole picture.

margin.note: A stored list of colors. Pixel values point to entries in this list rather than storing full color values themselves.
Extra instructions that tell compatible players to repeat an animation, either a set number of times or indefinitely.
GIF can mark one color-table entry as transparent, letting the background show through. It does not support partially transparent pixels.

effects.title: Animatronics
effects.name: Animatronics
effects.dating: 1970s film prominence; earlier Disney Audio-Animatronics
effects.caption: Transparent Cowboy Animatronic. A cowboy-hatted humanoid stands above a crowd, its transparent body revealing mechanical joints, wiring, and linkages.
effects.credit: Michael Barera · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Physical creatures or figures move through articulated joints, with blinking eyes, turning heads, or opening jaws. Their solid bodies cast real shadows and interact with water, props, and performers.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Hidden mechanisms use motors, cables, or fluid pressure to move a constructed figure beneath its outer skin. Operators or programmed controls coordinate the movements during filming or live display.

body.label: Example
body.text: Steven Spielberg: Jaws, 1975.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a mechanical shark shot from Jaws without sound; track the jaw movement, water displacement, and shadows.

context: Animatronics combines puppet construction with controlled machinery to give physical figures lifelike movement. Disney developed Audio-Animatronics for attractions before the technique gained particular visibility in 1970s cinema. These figures could synchronize movement with recorded sound. In Jaws, mechanical sharks brought a dangerous animal into the same photographed space as actors and seawater. Flexible coverings concealed rigid frames, while powered mechanisms moved selected body parts. Operators coordinated actions rather than relying on an autonomous robot. The camera recorded an actual moving object, so lighting, splashes, and contact were physical rather than drawn.
effects.distinction: Unlike stop-motion, animatronics moves a physical figure continuously while the camera records. Unlike computer-generated animation, its visible body exists on set.
effects.aftermath: Animatronics shows how coordinated mechanical movement and physical interaction can make a constructed body appear alive.
effects.funFact: The mechanical sharks built for Jaws were nicknamed Bruce.

margin.note: Connections that let separate body parts bend or rotate relative to one another.
Pressurized liquid or gas can push a piston, which moves a connected part.
Disney's name for its animated mechanical figures and their control technology, often coordinating movement with sound.

effects.title: Anthotype
effects.name: Anthotype
effects.dating: 1842, Sir John Herschel's experiments with plant juices
effects.caption: Pale purple leaf anthotype photogram. A pale purple silhouette of a leaf is visible against a faded background.
effects.credit: Hutschi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a soft, monochromatic image in natural hues like pale pink, purple, or green. The picture often looks faded, lacking sharp contrast or deep blacks.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Sunlight slowly destroys the color of a plant-based dye coated on paper. The covered areas keep their original color, creating a positive image.

body.label: Example
body.text: Sir John Herschel: Experimental anthotype of an engraving, 1842.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Leave a dark piece of construction paper partly covered in bright sunlight for a week to see the uncovered dye fade.

context: In 1842, Sir John Herschel experimented with using crushed flower petals and plant juices to make photographs. He coated paper with alcohol-extracted pigments from poppies, violets, or spinach. He then placed an object or positive transparency over the dried paper. Leaving it in direct sunlight for days or weeks destroyed the unprotected pigment. This fading process left a visible image. However, the technique was entirely impractical. The images could not be chemically fixed to stop the fading. Any further exposure to ambient light gradually erased the picture completely. Consequently, very few original anthotypes survive today.
effects.distinction: Unlike cyanotypes which use iron salts to create stable blue images, anthotypes use unstable plant dyes. Anthotypes cannot be fixed and remain forever sensitive to light.
effects.aftermath: This delicate technique highlights the fundamental challenge of early photography: making an image permanent.
effects.funFact: Alcohol or water was originally used to extract the colorful, light-sensitive juices from crushed flower petals.

margin.note: A picture where the light and dark areas naturally match the original scene or object.
An image on clear material where the light and dark tones look normal, not reversed like a negative.
Treating a photograph with a chemical solution to remove unexposed light-sensitive material, making the image permanent.

context: Large consumer wave with Snapchat Lenses from September 2015.

The software estimates facial features or a facial model and tracks its movement. Deformations, masks, materials, and 3D objects are superimposed in real time, matching the facial expressions and camera perspective.
Snapchat introduced Lenses on September 15, 2015; the official 2017 retrospective mentions puppies, rainbows, and Face Swap.

Image shown: Later technical demonstration. Facial positions are captured and digital elements are attached to them. This is a current public product preview, not an original image from the Lenses launch in 2015.
effects.distinction: A color filter changes pixel values ​​across the entire image. An AR face filter must track the shape, position, and movement of the face. Face tracking and AR are older technologies. 2015 marks an important product and distribution milestone, not the invention of facial recognition itself.
effects.aftermath: Visual effects became an everyday form of social expression. The viewer simultaneously became both performer and operator of the effect.
effects.funFact: Snapchat introduced Lenses on September 15, 2015; puppies, rainbows, and Face Swap became prominent applications.
highlights: follow head movements and facial expressions

margin.note: Recognizable parts or landmarks of a face, such as eye corners and the outline of the mouth.

context: The visual world of early computer terminals and printers transformed text itself into visual material. ASCII was standardized in 1963; the method of drawing with characters has further, even pre-digital, histories. In today's software, the brightness of an image cell is assigned to a character shape. A digital image editor allows for modifiable character sets, raster density, and color. This slide discusses this principle without claiming a single inventor of all ASCII art.

effects.title: Astrophotography
effects.name: Astrophotography
effects.dating: 1840, John W. Draper's daguerreotype of the Moon
effects.caption: Milky Way Reflected in a Mountain Lake. The Milky Way rises above silhouetted mountains and trees, with stars reflected in a still lake.
effects.credit: Giles Laurent · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Images show a cratered lunar disk, scattered star points, or faint nebular clouds against dark space. Untracked long exposures can turn stars into curved trails.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A lens or telescope gathers celestial light onto a light-sensitive surface during exposure. Chemical development makes the recorded image visible on historical plates; tracking Earth's rotation helps keep stars sharp.

body.label: Example
body.text: John W. Draper: Daguerreotype of the Moon, 1840.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph stars from a fixed tripod with several exposure lengths, then compare how their points stretch into trails.

context: In 1840, John W. Draper made a successful daguerreotype of the Moon through a telescope. Its silver-coated copper plate recorded light chemically and required development to reveal the image. Early materials needed substantial exposure, making astronomical photography difficult. Later glass photographic plates supported systematic surveys of stars and recordings of faint nebulae. Longer exposures gathered more light, but Earth's rotation moved celestial images across an untracked plate. Tracking mounts compensated for that motion. Photography also preserved records that astronomers could measure and compare across years.
effects.distinction: Unlike an astronomical drawing, astrophotography records incoming light rather than an observer's interpretation. False-color processing is optional, not a defining feature.
effects.aftermath: Astrophotography shows how accumulated light can reveal celestial structures too faint for unaided vision.
effects.funFact: Astronomers still study old photographic plates to investigate how stars changed over decades.

margin.note: An early photographic process producing a unique image on a silver-coated copper plate.
Treatment after exposure that makes a recorded photographic image visible.
Supports that move a camera or telescope to follow the sky's apparent motion.

Recognize: Bright, slightly grainy colors; a soft, pointillist impression.
Mechanism: Microscopically colored starch grains form a color filter on a glass plate. When the developed positive image is illuminated, a color picture is produced.

effects.title: Autostereogram
effects.name: Autostereogram
effects.dating: 1990s popularization; English-language Magic Eye book, 1993
effects.caption: Blue Water-Pattern Autostereogram. A blue, waterlike texture repeats across the picture, with localized distortions interrupting its rhythm.
effects.credit: Nevit Dilmen (talk) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: A dense repeating pattern covers a flat picture, often resembling colorful wallpaper or visual noise. With the right gaze, a hidden three-dimensional shape appears within it.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Small changes in horizontal spacing encode depth within the pattern. When your eyes match different repetitions, binocular disparity makes the brain interpret those differences as depth.

body.label: Example
body.text: N. E. Thing Enterprises: Magic Eye: A New Way of Looking at the World, 1993.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: View a parallel-view autostereogram as though looking through the page; notice whether a shape emerges, and stop if uncomfortable.

context: Autostereograms became a popular visual puzzle during the 1990s, especially through Magic Eye books and posters. Their roots lie in stereoscopic research and computer-generated random-dot images. Christopher Tyler developed the random-dot autostereogram in 1979. Unlike paired stereo pictures, one image supplies matching features for both eyes. A depth map guides small horizontal shifts in repeated texture. These shifts create disparities when the eyes pair neighboring repetitions rather than identical positions. The surface remains flat, but the brain reconstructs an apparent arrangement of nearer and farther regions.
effects.distinction: A conventional stereogram presents separate left-eye and right-eye pictures. An autostereogram combines the necessary depth cues in one patterned image, without colored filters or a stereoscope.
effects.aftermath: It shows that perceived depth depends on how the eyes match visual information, not simply on the picture's physical surface.
effects.funFact: A hidden shape can remain invisible to either eye alone, even when you know where it is.

margin.note: The difference between a feature's positions in the two eyes' views. The brain uses this difference to estimate depth.
An image or data grid that assigns a depth value to each location.
Pictures built from seemingly random dots. Carefully arranged relationships between dots can provide depth cues without recognizable outlines.

effects.title: Beauty Filter
effects.name: Beauty Filter
effects.dating: 2010s, with smartphone beautification apps expanding from 2013 onward
effects.caption: AI illustration: Comparison of skin smoothing and freckle removal.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Faces show smoother skin, fewer visible pores, and sometimes larger eyes or narrower jaws. Strong settings can produce a waxy complexion while leaving eyelashes unusually crisp.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Software locates facial landmarks, then selectively smooths skin texture while preserving important edges. Geometric warping can enlarge eyes or reshape the jaw without changing the camera's optics.

body.label: Example
body.text: Meitu: BeautyCam, 2013.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare filtered and unfiltered selfies under identical lighting; inspect pores, eyelash edges, eye size, and background lines beside the cheeks.

context: Beauty filters brought older portrait-retouching practices into everyday smartphone photography during the 2010s. Meitu released BeautyCam in 2013, offering a recognizable example of this shift. Unlike manual airbrushing, automated processing finds faces and applies adjustments with little user effort. Skin smoothing reduces local texture differences, while facial landmarks guide changes to eyes and contours. Later systems increasingly used machine learning to estimate facial structure and separate skin from other image regions. Live previews made altered faces visible before capture, encouraging debate about beauty standards and photographic credibility.
effects.distinction: Soft-focus optics spread light and soften detail across the image. A beauty filter can target skin alone and change facial proportions digitally.
effects.aftermath: Beauty filters show how a photograph can preserve someone's identity while quietly changing the features viewers use to judge appearance.
effects.funFact: Digital jaw reshaping can accidentally bend background lines beside a face.

margin.note: Reference points marking features such as eye corners, the nose tip, and the mouth.
Moving image positions to change shapes or proportions, rather than merely changing brightness or color.
Methods that learn patterns from examples rather than relying entirely on hand-written rules.

effects.title: Ben-Day Dots
effects.name: Ben-Day dots / Benday dots
effects.dating: 1879: Ben-Day trial; 1961–1962: Lichtenstein's appropriation
effects.caption: Roy Lichtenstein: In the Car, 1963.
effects.credit: Photography Antonia Reeve; © Estate of Roy Lichtenstein / DACS. National Galleries of Scotland.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Evenly spaced dots in flat comic colors.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Predefined dot patterns fill areas; overlaps create color mixtures.

body.label: Example
body.text: Roy Lichtenstein: In the Car, 1963.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Construct the same area using constant and variable point sizes.

context: In 1879, Benjamin Day developed a process for creating pre-made dot patterns on printing plates. The National Galleries of Scotland explicitly distinguish this from photographic halftones with varying dot sizes. In the early 1960s, Roy Lichtenstein made these patterns a defining element of his painting. From 1962 onward, he used a perforated metal screen for dots that he had previously painted by hand. This painterly appropriation is therefore not an automatic mechanical enlargement of a comic strip. In this exercise, you will first keep the dot size constant and then deliberately change its size depending on the brightness. This will make the difference between surface patterns and photographic tonal modulation visible.
effects.distinction: Ben-Day dots are not simply another name for photographic halftone screen.
effects.funFact: Lichtenstein's seemingly machine-made dots were initially painted by hand; from 1962 onwards, a perforated metal sieve was used.

margin.note: Ready-made arrangements of dots used to fill printed areas with tone or color rather than drawing every dot individually.
Equal-sized dots produce a uniform pattern; varying dot size can create lighter or darker tones.

context: Bevel means chamfering. In digital layer styles, an edge is simulated along a shape using light and shadow. Photoshop 6.0 documented the expanded use of such layer effects around the year 2000; this point in time is the specific software reference point here. The chrome look complements the edge with strong changes in reflection, often with light and dark bands. This explains why a smooth gradient can appear more plastic, while a more sharply defined one resembles reflective metal. In this exercise, the outline and text remain the same. Only change the contrast of the reflections. This allows you to separate the shape modeling effect of the bevel from the material effect of the reflection, and to control both more precisely.
effects.aftermath: Strong silhouettes are easier to read even with a metallic texture. The effect should support the letterforms and respect their internal spaces.
effects.funFact: Bevel describes the chamfered edge; the chrome effect is additionally created by the simulated reflection.

margin.note: An angled edge between surfaces. Simulated shading can make flat lettering appear to have this edge.
Gradual or sharp changes in brightness and color that imitate a reflected environment on a shiny surface.

context: Robert W. Wood was one of the pioneers of infrared photography. The Wood effect, named after him, describes the striking brightness of vegetation in such images. body.label: Identify
body.text: Less color, stronger contrast, often dense shadows.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Some of the silver remains in the film in addition to the dyes.

body.label: Example
body.text: Demonstration of the desaturated skip bleach look.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Slightly desaturate an image and increase the contrast. Check skin tones and shadows.

context: Bleach bypass encompasses several laboratory techniques in which silver is partially or completely retained. The added silver alters density, contrast, and color saturation. Kodak describes distinct differences between its application on camera negatives and projection prints. The approach is part of historical cinema and later became a common digital style term. Crucially, it involves the ratio of color to black, not simply a gray filter.
effects.distinction: A digital look is an approximation. Chemical bleaching has different effects depending on whether the negative, intermediate, or positive is affected. Therefore, black shadows are not a universal rule for every variant.
effects.aftermath: Silver and dyes can simultaneously form a colored image.
effects.funFact: The same procedure produces different visible effects on the negative than on the finished film print.

margin.note: Developed metallic silver forms a black-and-white image in film. Bleaching normally removes it during color processing.
Reduce the intensity of colors, moving them toward gray.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Blurry lights appear as soft discs or characteristic shapes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Lens, aperture and distances determine the reproduction outside the plane of focus.

body.label: Example
body.text: Lindsay Silverman: blurred lights, Nikon tutorial.

body.label: Try it out

context: Lens culture discusses not only sharpness but also the character of out-of-focus areas. Round or angular light sources, soft transitions, and hard contours all influence the effect. In 2013, Nikon explicitly introduced the 58mm f/1.4G with its bokeh characteristics. This dated product example is not the origin of the phenomenon or the Japanese term. For a proper experiment, compare the same scene with the camera in the same position.
effects.distinction: Bokeh refers to the quality of the blur rendering, not simply any blurry image. Increasing the distance from the background also alters the effect. Artificial smartphone portrait mode can produce similar images, but additionally uses depth estimation.
effects.aftermath: Blurriness can be shaped and has its own character.
effects.funFact: The shape of blurry light points can reveal the shape of the aperture.

margin.note: The lens opening that controls incoming light. Its size and shape affect the appearance of blurred highlights.
The distance at which objects are rendered sharpest for a particular focus setting.

effects.title: Bromoil Print
effects.name: Bromoil print
effects.dating: Developed in 1907; Pictorialism of the 1910s and 1920s
effects.caption: Joseph Woodson “Pops” Whitesell: Old Arsenal, 1930s. Bromooil printing.
effects.credit: Historic New Orleans Collection, 1978.122.5 / Joseph Woodson Whitesell

body.label: Identify
body.text: Painterly surfaces, grainy structure and controllable tonal values.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A bleached silver print is colored with oil paint via gelatin that swells to different degrees.

body.label: Example
body.text: Whitesell: Old Arsenal, 1930s, bromoil print.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Translate a photo into three large clay areas.

context: Bromoil printing originated in 1907 as a further development of oil printing. The starting point is an enlarged silver bromide print. After bleaching and tanning, the gelatin sections react differently to water and oil-based printing ink. The photographer can significantly influence the image effect using a brush. A bromoil transfer transfers the inked image onto a different paper; this transfer is a separate technique.
effects.distinction: Oil prints and bromoil prints are related but technically different. A pictorialist photograph with a painterly effect should not automatically be labeled as a bromoil print. The specific museum object must demonstrate the process.
effects.aftermath: The photograph becomes an editable print matrix.
effects.funFact: In bromoil printing, the original silver image is removed before the oil paint forms the visible image.
highlights: gelatin that swells to different degrees

margin.note: A protein coating that absorbs water. In bromoil, differently hardened areas swell differently and accept oily ink selectively.
A photographic print whose silver image has been chemically removed or converted during preparation. The process leaves differences in the gelatin that guide subsequent inking.

effects.title: Brûlage
effects.name: Brûlage
effects.dating: 1930s-1940s, Raoul Ubac's surrealist experiments
effects.caption: Blistered Portrait in an Ornate Frame. An ornate frame surrounds a monochrome portrait whose head dissolves into swollen, flowing forms and a band of blister-like cells.
effects.credit: Jindřich Heisler (1914-1953) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see distorted, flowing, and blistered photographic images. The subjects appear to melt, warp, or dissolve into chaotic bubbles and ripples.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Heat is carefully applied directly to a photographic negative before printing. This physically melts the gelatin emulsion, shifting the silver particles inside.

body.label: Example
body.text: Raoul Ubac: La Nébuleuse, 1939.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a melting ice cube or candle wax and imagine a face stretched across its shifting, bubbling surface.

context: Brûlage emerged as a surrealist technique to disrupt the reliable reality of a photograph. Artists like Raoul Ubac sought to introduce chance and destruction into their creative process. By exposing a glass or film negative to controlled heat, they altered the image physically. The gelatin emulsion layer would soften, bubble, and warp. This shifted the light-sensitive silver particles, destroying the original likeness. When this ruined negative was finally printed onto paper, the resulting photograph showed a haunting, fluid distortion. It merged the original captured scene with the physical marks of heat.
effects.distinction: Unlike solarization, which uses light to reverse tones during development, brûlage uses physical heat to distort the actual negative.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that a photograph is a fragile physical object, not just a clear window into reality.
effects.funFact: The word brûlage translates directly from French as burning or scorching.

margin.note: A clear, jelly-like layer on photographic film that holds the light-sensitive chemicals.
Tiny grains of metal that form the visible dark areas of a developed black-and-white photograph.
An art movement focused on dreams, chance, and the unconscious mind to challenge ordinary reality.

body.label: Identify
body.text: The action is almost stationary while the focus flies around the body.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Spatially distributed cameras take photographs simultaneously or at different times. Combined, digitally smoothed views create the illusion of a camera movement.

body.label: Example
body.text: The Matrix (1999): John Gaeta's team uses up to 120 cameras.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Arrange views of a frozen moment one after the other. Compare the change in perspective with ordinary slow motion.

context: Pop cultural breakthrough: The Matrix (1999).

A series of spatially distributed cameras captures a moment simultaneously or with a time delay. The sequence of images jumps between viewpoints. Interpolation and digital backgrounds smooth the apparent camera movement around the slowed-down action.
The Matrix (1999), VFX team led by John Gaeta: Arrays with up to 120 cameras for the famous slow-motion sequences.

Regarding the image: Historical original / source image. Several cameras are positioned on the ground along the action sequence. This production shot shows the setup, not the finished, seemingly slow-motion footage with free camera movement.
effects.distinction: Super slow motion slows down time from a single camera perspective. Bullet time adds a deliberate change in spatial perspective. Multi-camera techniques and earlier experiments are older. The Matrix made this variant a widely recognizable film look.
effects.aftermath: Time and camera movement could be decoupled. An impossible perspective became a sign of superhuman perception.
effects.funFact: For The Matrix, the team used camera arrays with up to 120 cameras in 1999.

margin.note: Calculating intermediate views between captured images to make the sequence look smoother.
Groups of cameras arranged to record a subject from multiple viewpoints.

effects.title: Bump Mapping
effects.name: Bump mapping
effects.dating: Jim Blinn: Simulation of Wrinkled Surfaces, 1978.
effects.caption: Jim Blinn: Leather Donut, 1978. Original illustration by the author.
effects.credit: Jim Blinn, Author Archive.

body.label: Identify
body.text: A smooth base shape appears rough, grained, or wrinkled.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Changes to a height function change the simulated surface normal.

body.label: Example
body.text: Jim Blinn: Leather Donut, 1978.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare the same body with color, bump, and displacement textures.

context: Jim Blinn's own publication list explicitly identifies SIGGRAPH's 1978 "Simulation of Wrinkled Surfaces" as the introduction of bump mapping. His "Leather Donut" illustrates how roughness becomes visible without a correspondingly fine model geometry. Modern shaders evaluate a height function and translate its changes into a modified normal. Normal mapping, on the other hand, can read directions directly from an RGB map.
effects.distinction: Bump mapping alters the shading, not the actual geometry. It loses its illusion on silhouettes and at shallow viewing angles.
effects.aftermath: The impression of material complexity does not always require a complex form.
effects.funFact: The early demonstration object was a leather-like textured donut.

margin.note: A direction perpendicular to a surface, used to calculate lighting. Bump mapping changes this direction without changing the actual shape.
Maps that move the actual surface geometry, unlike bump maps, which only alter how light is calculated.

effects.title: Busby Berkeley Top Shot

effects.dating: 1930s, Busby Berkeley’s Hollywood musical numbers

body.label: Identify
body.text: Seen directly from above, dancers form concentric circles, radiating spokes, and flower-like patterns. Synchronized movement makes these human mosaics expand, rotate, and dissolve.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An overhead camera looks straight down, reducing visible depth and emphasizing the dancers’ arrangement across the floor. Repetition and radial symmetry create the kaleidoscopic appearance through choreography, rather than mirrors.

body.label: Example
body.text: Busby Berkeley (musical numbers): Footlight Parade, 1933.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Arrange twelve paper figures around a circle, then compare photographs taken from directly above and from table height.

context: Busby Berkeley made overhead dance formations a signature of Hollywood musicals during the 1930s. His musical numbers in 42nd Street helped establish his reputation in 1933. Footlight Parade, released that same year, includes elaborate aquatic formations in its “By a Waterfall” number. These designs depended on precise spacing, synchronized gestures, and a camera position unavailable to ordinary theater audiences. From above, individual performers become parts of a larger geometric image. The effect comes primarily from staging and viewpoint, not from a special lens or chemical treatment of film.
effects.distinction: A mirror kaleidoscope multiplies images through reflections; Berkeley’s formations usually contain many actual performers arranged for the camera. A merely elevated shot can retain depth without revealing a complete geometric pattern.
effects.aftermath: The technique shows how camera position can turn choreography into moving graphic design.
effects.funFact: Some of Berkeley’s most elaborate geometric formations used swimmers rather than dancers on a dry floor.

margin.note: Circles of different sizes that share the same center.
A pattern whose similar parts spread around a central point, like petals around a flower’s center.
The planned arrangement of performers’ movements and positions.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Soft contours, matte paper texture, and calm tonal areas. The paper fibers can influence the image.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A developed paper negative serves as a template for several positive contact prints. The image information is contained within the paper.

body.label: Example

body.label: Try it out

context: Talbot patented the calotype in February 1841. 1840s–1850s; early negative-positive workflow. Detailed mechanism: The camera image is created as a developed paper negative. Several positive contact prints can be made from this; paper fibers affect the detail. One negative can produce many positive images: the early starting point of reproducible photography.
effects.distinction: One negative can provide many positive images: the early starting point of reproducible photography.
effects.aftermath: Paper texture and low microcontrast as design elements.
effects.funFact: Talbot's paper negative made several positive images from one photograph: Reproducibility became the crucial principle.

margin.note: A paper image with light and dark reversed. Light passing through it can expose another sheet to produce a positive image.
Small differences in brightness between neighboring details. Reducing it makes fine texture and edges appear softer.

effects.title: Carbon Print
effects.name: Carbon Print
effects.dating: 1864, Joseph Swan's perfected transfer process
effects.caption: Carbon Print of Classical Greek Sculptures. A photograph captures classical Greek sculptures resting on pedestals.
effects.credit: Adolphe Braun · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a rich, highly detailed photographic print. It often features deep charcoal, sepia, or warm brown tones without any fading.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Light hardens a mixture of gelatin and pigment mixed with potassium dichromate. Unexposed, soft gelatin washes away in warm water.

body.label: Example
body.text: Thomas Annan: The Old Closes and Streets of Glasgow, 1868.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at a vintage photograph's darkest shadows; a true carbon print shows a slight physical relief.

context: In the 1850s, early silver photographs faded quickly. Photographers urgently needed a permanent alternative. Alphonse Poitevin discovered that dichromated gelatin hardens when exposed to light. In 1864, Joseph Swan perfected the carbon process. He coated paper with gelatin, potassium dichromate, and permanent carbon pigment. After exposure beneath a negative, he transferred the image to a new base. Warm water washed away the unhardened gelatin. The remaining pigment formed a stunning, fade-resistant image. This complex method created durable, richly toned prints that survive perfectly today.
effects.distinction: Unlike albumen or silver prints, carbon prints do not rely on light-sensitive silver. Therefore, they never yellow or fade over time.
effects.aftermath: It proves that utilizing chemically stable pigments can preserve photographic history indefinitely.
effects.funFact: Carbon prints can be made in any color simply by mixing different pigments into the gelatin.

margin.note: A chemical compound used to make gelatin sensitive to ultraviolet light.
A clear, natural protein derived from animal collagen, widely used to hold photographic chemicals.
A highly stable, dark powder made from soot, used to color the image permanently.

effects.name: Carte de Visite
effects.dating: 1854, André-Adolphe-Eugène Disdéri's patented portrait format

body.label: Identify
body.text: A small photographic portrait sits on a rectangular card mount, often showing a full-length figure against a studio backdrop. Warm brown tones and printed studio names are common.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A multi-lens camera and a moving plate holder could record eight small negatives on one glass plate through successive exposures. Paper prints were then cut apart and mounted on cards.

body.label: Example
body.text: John Jabez Edwin Mayall: Queen Victoria, 1860.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare three historical cards, noting repeated furniture, poses, and mount sizes that reveal a standardized studio process.

context: Disdéri patented his carte de visite process in Paris in 1854. A four-lens camera and a shifting plate holder allowed eight portraits on one plate, reducing material costs. The wet collodion process required preparing, exposing, and developing the glass negative while its coating remained wet. Studios commonly made albumen prints from these negatives, then trimmed and pasted them onto cards about the size of visiting cards. Customers exchanged portraits with relatives and collected famous faces in albums. The format became especially popular during the 1860s.
effects.distinction: Unlike a daguerreotype, a carte de visite is a paper photograph mounted on card, usually printed from a reusable negative. Later cabinet cards used a similar presentation but were substantially larger.
effects.aftermath: The carte de visite shows how repeatable production and a standard physical format helped turn portraits into widely exchanged objects.
effects.funFact: Collectors placed portraits of royalty beside family members in the same album.

margin.note: Separate moments when light reaches the sensitive plate, one after another.
A glass plate carries a coating made light-sensitive with silver salts. It must remain wet through exposure and development.
Paper photographs with an egg-white coating that holds light-sensitive silver salts. The coating gives a smooth, detailed surface.

effects.title: Cel Animation
effects.name: Cel Animation
effects.dating: 1914, Earl Hurd's patent
effects.caption: Hand-Painted Monkey King Animation Cel. A painted monkey character crouches over a textured, painted underwater background.
effects.credit: Unknown · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see moving, painted characters interacting seamlessly with static, detailed backgrounds. The moving figures often have distinct outlines and flat colors.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Artists paint moving elements on transparent celluloid sheets. They stack these sheets over a single painted background to photograph them.

body.label: Example
body.text: Earl Hurd: Bobby Bumps, 1915.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Pause an old animated cartoon and look closely at a character's painted edges. You might see a faint shadow where the clear plastic sits above the background.

context: Before cel animation, early animators drew every single frame completely from scratch. This meant redrawing the exact same backgrounds thousands of times. In 1914, Earl Hurd patented a new method using transparent sheets made of celluloid. Artists could now draw only the moving characters on these clear sheets. They placed these transparent layers over a single painted background. A camera then photographed the stacked setup one frame at a time. This saved massive amounts of labor and allowed for highly detailed backgrounds. It became the absolute standard process for 2D animation for nearly a century.
effects.distinction: Unlike direct animation where artists scratch or paint directly onto the physical film strip, cel animation photographs layered drawings beneath a camera.
effects.aftermath: It teaches us that separating static and dynamic visual elements fundamentally optimizes complex visual production.
effects.funFact: Cel paint was applied to the reverse side of the plastic to keep the front linework perfectly sharp.

margin.note: An early, slightly flammable transparent plastic used to make photographic film. It provided the clear base for these animation frames.
Clear sheets stacked together so you can see through them. This lets the bottom artwork remain entirely visible.

effects.title: Cel Shading
effects.name: Cel Shading
effects.dating: 2000, Sega's Jet Set Radio
effects.caption: Combining Shading and Edge Lines. A three-part diagram combines a colored village scene with a separate black-line rendering to produce an outlined composite.
effects.credit: Donniedeboer · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see 3D computer graphics that look like flat, hand-drawn 2D animation. Colors feature stark, unblended shadows and sharp black outlines.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Lighting values are quantized into a few discrete steps rather than a smooth gradient. A specialized shader renders bold edge lines around the 3D models.

body.label: Example
body.text: Smilebit: Jet Set Radio, 2000.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a cel-shaded character and notice how shadows jump instantly from light to dark without any smooth transitions.

context: Before the year 2000, most 3D games pushed for realistic, smooth lighting to mimic the physical world. Developers then realized they could manipulate rendering calculations to mimic traditional animation cels. Instead of calculating continuous light on curved surfaces, engines map lighting to a small palette of flat colors. This creates distinct bands of highlight, base color, and shadow. Programmers often combine this flat shading with inverted backface rendering to generate thick black ink lines around characters. The style exploded in popularity during the early 2000s, keeping aging 3D graphics looking timeless.
effects.distinction: Unlike standard photorealistic 3D rendering which uses smooth lighting gradients, cel shading forces harsh, stepped transitions between light and dark areas.
effects.aftermath: It proves that artistic stylization often ages much better than attempts at pure graphical realism.
effects.funFact: The name comes from clear celluloid sheets historically used by traditional animators to paint 2D frames.

margin.note: This means converting a continuous range of values into a limited number of fixed, distinct steps.
Transparent sheets originally used in traditional hand-drawn animation, where characters were painted on separate layers.
A graphics trick where the inside of a 3D model is drawn slightly larger and black to create outlines.

effects.title: Chemigram
effects.name: Chemigram
effects.dating: 1956, Pierre Cordier's chemical paintings
effects.caption: Abstract Chemigram With Mesh Resist. Abstract, high-contrast black blobs are scattered across a light background featuring a subtle, dotted mesh pattern.
effects.credit: Paolo Monti · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see abstract, painterly shapes and textures on photographic paper. These images often feature organic blobs and sharp geometric lines.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Chemicals used to develop photographs are applied directly onto light-sensitive paper. Resists like wax or varnish control where the chemicals react.

body.label: Example
body.text: Pierre Cordier: Chemigram 1/5/70 II, 1970.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a chemigram and try to spot where the artist painted the chemical directly versus where a resist blocked it.

context: Pierre Cordier invented the chemigram in 1956 while writing a dedication with nail polish on photographic paper. Unlike traditional photography, this technique uses no camera, no lens, and no enlarger. It combines the physics of painting with the chemistry of photography. Artists apply darkroom chemicals directly onto the paper in full room light. Developer creates black areas, and fixer creates white areas. Artists also use resists, such as wax or varnish, to block the chemicals. As these resists slowly lift or crack, the chemicals seep in. This creates unpredictable, intricate textures and organic patterns.
effects.distinction: A photogram uses objects to block light from hitting paper during an exposure. A chemigram applies chemicals directly to paper in broad daylight.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that photographic materials can be used purely as a physical medium for abstract painting.
effects.funFact: Cordier discovered the technique when he wrote a dedication using nail polish as a chemical resist.

margin.note: Substances like wax or varnish used to protect a surface from a chemical reaction.
A darkroom chemical that turns exposed silver halide crystals black to reveal an image.
A chemical solution that removes unexposed silver halides from photographic paper, leaving white areas intact.

effects.title: Chroma Key
effects.name: Chroma key
effects.dating: Bluescreen since 1940. Real-time tool wave from Ultimatte in 1976.
effects.caption: Chroma key principle: Shot, background and composite image: Example from 2010.
effects.credit: Imyzc. CC BY-SA 3.0

body.label: Identify
body.text: People or models appear in separately generated environments. Errors are revealed by color fringing.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A background color acts as a mask. It separates the foreground so that another image can be placed behind it.

body.label: Example
body.text: Star Wars (1977): models filmed separately in front of a bluescreen are combined.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare the green image, the black and white mask, and the composite. Check the hair, transparency, and light direction.

context: Prehistory in the 1930s/1940s; refined color masks in the 1950s/1960s; important expansion phase of real-time technology from 1976 onwards.

A defined background color is translated into a mask. The mask separates the foreground and background; hair, transparencies, and color bleed are corrected at the edges. Then another image is inserted.
Star Wars (1977): separately filmed models in front of a bluescreen; Ultimatte (from 1976) as an important real-time compositing milestone.

Regarding the image: A later technical demonstration. On the left, the original image against a uniform green background; in the middle, the clipping mask; on the right, the composite image on a new red background. This is a later demonstration, not an original from the 1970s.
effects.distinction: Blue/greenscreen is not synonymous with all compositing. A mask can also be painted, rotoscoped, or created using other methods. The 1970s classification refers to the wave of its widespread use and the development of the necessary tools. The Thief of Bagdad (1940) already employed an early bluescreen process; Ultimatte was founded in 1976.
effects.aftermath: Places and characters no longer had to coexist in front of a single camera. News broadcasts, weather reports, music videos, and fantasy films became combinable visual layers.
effects.funFact: Color coding was already an analog film technique; it wasn't invented with Photoshop.
highlights: Errors are revealed by color fringing
background color acts as a mask

margin.note: Unwanted colored edges around a cut-out subject, often left by the original screen or an imperfect mask.
A finished image assembled from separately recorded or generated elements.

effects.title: ChromaDepth 3D
effects.name: ChromaDepth 3D
effects.dating: 1990s, commercial color-coded 3D glasses
effects.caption: Rainbow Branches for ChromaDepth Viewing. A luminous network of twisting branches shifts from red and yellow through green to blue against a nearly black background.
effects.credit: Paweł Janczewski · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Through special glasses, red shapes appear forward, while blue shapes appear farther back, especially against black backgrounds. Without the glasses, you see a flat, brightly colored image.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The glasses use optical dispersion to shift different colors sideways by different amounts in each eye. These color-dependent offsets create binocular disparity, which the brain interprets as depth.

body.label: Example
body.text: KISS: Psycho Circus (music video), 1998.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: View red, green, and blue circles on black through ChromaDepth glasses, then remove them and compare their apparent distances.

context: ChromaDepth became commercially available in the 1990s, offering depth from a single color image rather than two separately photographed views. Its transparent lenses use tiny optical structures to redirect light according to wavelength. The resulting differences between the eyes make colors occupy apparent depth layers. Designers typically place red subjects in front and blue backgrounds behind, with other colors between them. The method works with printed pictures and screens. However, color and depth are linked, so choosing a realistic surface color can conflict with placing an object.
effects.distinction: Unlike red-and-cyan anaglyphs, ChromaDepth does not filter two overlaid views into separate eyes. It derives apparent depth from colors within one image.
effects.aftermath: ChromaDepth shows how controlled differences between the eyes can turn color choices into spatial cues.
effects.funFact: A flat rainbow can become a staircase of apparent depth.

margin.note: Light of different wavelengths is redirected by different amounts. Here, that separates colors sideways.
This is a difference in an object's position between the two eyes' views. The brain uses it to judge depth.
The distance between successive peaks of a light wave. Different visible wavelengths correspond to different spectral colors.
