effects.title: Chromolithography
effects.name: Chromolithography
effects.dating: 1870s, the golden age of mass colour printing
effects.caption: Chromolithograph Portrait of Toussaint L'Ouverture. A detailed portrait with rich, overlapping colors and smooth gradients that lack a mechanical halftone grid.
effects.credit: DeBaptiste, George, 1815-1875, publisher; DeBaptiste, George, 1815-1875, copyright clai… · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see rich, vibrant, opaque colours that often overlap. Up close, you see irregular dots called stippling rather than a mechanical grid.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Oil and water do not mix. Printers draw separate colour layers onto flat limestone using greasy crayons, which attract oily ink.

body.label: Example
body.text: Louis Prang: Yellowstone National Park portfolio, 1876.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at a vintage poster or cigar box label with a magnifying glass to spot the irregular, crayon-like colour dots.

context: Chromolithography revolutionized visual culture in the late nineteenth century. Before this, colour prints were mostly hand-painted and very expensive. This chemical process made mass colour printing possible. An artist analyzed an original painting and broke it down into different colour layers. They drew each layer onto a separate heavy limestone block using a greasy substance. The stone was wet with water, which repelled the greasy ink. Only the drawn areas held the coloured ink. Pressing paper against multiple aligned stones built up a full-colour image. Some elaborate prints required up to twenty different stones to achieve realistic shading.
effects.distinction: Halftone printing uses a strict, uniform grid of mechanical dots to mix colours. Chromolithography uses overlapping solid colours and irregular stippling.
effects.aftermath: It democratized art by bringing affordable, high-quality colour images into everyday homes and advertising.
effects.funFact: Prints mimicking oil paintings were called "oleographs" and were sometimes stamped with artificial canvas textures.

margin.note: A drawing technique using small dots to create shading or texture without solid lines.
A heavy, flat piece of special porous stone used as the printing surface.

effects.title: Chronophotography
effects.name: Chronophotography
effects.dating: 1882, Étienne-Jules Marey's moving subjects
effects.caption: Chronophotograph of a white bird in flight.. A single photographic frame shows several overlapping phases of a white bird flying across a dark background.
effects.credit: Étienne-Jules Marey · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see multiple overlapping phases of a single moving subject captured within one single image frame. The subject appears as a stroboscopic sequence against a dark, stationary background.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A camera lens is left open while a slotted disk spins rapidly in front of the photographic plate. Each slot passes, briefly exposing the plate to the bright moving subject.

body.label: Example
body.text: Étienne-Jules Marey: Pelican in Flight, 1882.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Wave your hand rapidly under a strobe light in a dark room to see overlapping motion trails.

context: Étienne-Jules Marey wanted to study human and animal movement scientifically. Earlier methods required multiple cameras to capture motion phases. Marey invented the photographic gun, and later a fixed-plate chronophotographic camera. He dressed subjects in bright white clothes and placed them against deep black backgrounds. A rotating shutter disk spun in front of a single glass photographic plate. The shutter rapidly blocked and unblocked the light. Because the background reflected no light, only the moving subject exposed the plate. The result was a continuous overlapping graph of motion on one plate. This subtractive background technique ensured clear exposures.
effects.distinction: Unlike Eadweard Muybridge's separate sequential frames, Marey recorded all overlapping motion phases onto one single photographic plate.
effects.aftermath: It proves that complex, rapid motions can be decomposed and mapped onto a single spatial plane.
effects.funFact: Marey once attached lights to a walker's joints to create glowing stick figures.

margin.note: A visual effect where continuous motion appears as a series of short, frozen flashes of light.
A flat sheet of glass coated with light-sensitive chemicals used before flexible film was invented.

effects.title: Cinemagraph
effects.name: Cinemagraph
effects.dating: Beck and Burg coined the term in 2011. Selective loops are older.
effects.caption:
Jamie Beck & Kevin Burg: Stir, 2011: two real frames of the same cinemagraph.
Temporal effect: still image or image sequence.
effects.credit: Jamie Beck & Kevin Burg / Cinemagraphs.com; Image: CBS News 2011. © Jamie Beck & Kevin Burg

body.label: Identify
body.text: The photo appears frozen. Only smoke, water, or clothing move endlessly.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A frozen image is overlaid on video. A mask releases selected movement. The transition is looped seamlessly.

body.label: Example
body.text: Jamie Beck and Kevin Burg develop their Fashion Week practice in 2011.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Film a static shot. Freeze a frame and mask a moving detail as a loop.

context: Concept and known working practice of Jamie Beck and Kevin Burg from 2011 onwards.
A single still image is superimposed on a short video. A mask reveals only the moving part. The beginning and end are joined as seamlessly as possible.
Jamie Beck and Kevin Burg, the first so-called cinemagraphs, were created in 2011, among other things from their fashion and New York Fashion Week environment.

For illustration: Historical original frames, mounted side by side. Only the spoon and hand in the coffee area are moving, while the rest remains photographically still. Original frames 0 and 5 are shown side by side; no movement has been added later.
effects.distinction: GIF is a possible file format, cinemagraph a visual style. A standard video loop can move the entire image. Selective animation and loops are older concepts. Beck and Burg coined the term, not every form of partially moving image.
effects.aftermath: The photo acquired a subtle temporal dimension that worked particularly well for fashion, advertising, and social media loops.
effects.funFact: Jamie Beck and Kevin Burg coined the term Cinemagraph in 2011 for their selectively moving image loops.

margin.note: An image or selection controlling where a layer is visible, allowing movement to appear only in chosen areas.
A sequence that repeats. A seamless loop hides the transition from its last frame back to its first.

effects.title: Cinerama
effects.name: Cinerama
effects.dating: 1952, Fred Waller's widescreen process
effects.caption: Niagara Falls in Three-Panel Cinerama. A panoramic view of Niagara Falls fills a deeply curved cinema screen, with vertical joins dividing the landscape.
effects.credit: Chemical Engineer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see an extremely wide, immersive moving image wrapping around your peripheral vision. Faint vertical lines or seams often appear where the picture is divided into three equal panels.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Three synchronized cameras film a scene from slightly different angles simultaneously. In theaters, three separate projectors cast these films onto a deeply curved louvered screen.

body.label: Example
body.text: Merian C. Cooper and Robert L. Bendick: This Is Cinerama, 1952.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Stand close to a large TV and notice how much of the room you still see. Cup your hands around your eyes to mimic a curved screen blocking the room.

context: Cinerama debuted in 1952 to lure audiences away from early televisions. Fred Waller invented the system using three synchronized 35mm cameras with 27-millimeter lenses. Each camera captured one-third of a massive 146-degree field of view. In special theaters, three projectors fired images crosswise onto a deeply curved screen made of hundreds of vertical strips. These overlapping projections created an illusion of deep space without 3D glasses. However, keeping the three projectors perfectly synchronized was difficult. The seams where the three images overlapped were nearly impossible to hide completely.
effects.distinction: Unlike CinemaScope, which squeezes a wide image onto one film strip, Cinerama uses three completely separate films projected side-by-side.
effects.aftermath: It shows how early mechanical complexity pushed the boundaries of immersive theater experiences before single-lens wide formats took over.
effects.funFact: The system used a completely separate 35mm magnetic film reel to deliver pioneering seven-channel surround sound.

margin.note: Made to operate at the exact same time and speed, which was necessary so the three separate film reels stayed aligned.
A projection surface made of overlapping vertical strips rather than a solid sheet, designed to prevent light from bouncing across a deep curve.
The total extent of the observable world that can be seen at any given moment by a camera or a human eye.

effects.title: Cliché Verre
effects.name: Cliché Verre
effects.dating: 1853, popularized by Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot
effects.caption: Energetically Scratched Tree Landscape Print. You see a landscape featuring trees rendered with highly energetic, chaotic scratched lines.
effects.credit: Jean-Baptiste Camille Corot · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see an image resembling a fluid ink drawing or delicate etching. However, the lines often show a slightly soft, photographic blur.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An artist scratches lines through an opaque coating on a glass plate. Light shines through these scratches to expose photographic paper underneath.

body.label: Example
body.text: Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot: The Woodcutter of Rembrandt, 1853.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Examine a cliché verre print under magnification to find soft, diffused edges that distinguish it from the sharp bite of acid etching.

context: In 1853, three Frenchmen developed the cliché verre technique. They convinced famous painters like Corot and Millet to try it. The artist takes a glass plate covered with an opaque coating, usually collodion or white lead. They draw onto the plate with an etching needle, removing the coating to reveal clear glass. This creates a handmade photographic negative. The plate is then placed onto light-sensitive paper and exposed to the sun. Because the glass has thickness, the drawn lines cast slightly diffused shadows. This gives the final print its characteristic soft, atmospheric quality.
effects.distinction: Unlike traditional etching into metal, cliché verre uses light to expose hand-drawn lines onto photographic paper. It requires no ink or mechanical printing press.
effects.aftermath: It bridges printmaking and photography, proving that photosensitive paper can capture direct hand-drawn gestures.
effects.funFact: The term "cliché verre" translates directly from French as "glass negative" or "glass plate."

margin.note: A layer of material, like soot or paint, that completely blocks light from passing through.
To allow light to hit a treated surface, causing a chemical reaction that forms an image.
A syrupy liquid mixture used in early photography to bind chemicals or opaque layers to glass.

effects.title: Collotype
effects.name: Collotype
effects.dating: 1868, Joseph Albert's refined gelatin process
effects.caption: Collotype Glass Printing Plate Medium. A thick glass plate featuring a faint grid and an image matrix used for printing.
effects.credit: User:CatOnMars · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a printed image with smooth tonal transitions, deep shadows, and delicate highlights. Close inspection reveals a microscopic, worm-like reticulated grain instead of standard printing dots.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A glass plate is coated with light-sensitive gelatin and baked. Exposure hardens the gelatin, making it absorb greasy ink in proportion to the light received.

body.label: Example
body.text: Eadweard Muybridge: Animal Locomotion, 1887.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Magnify a high-quality vintage postcard from the early 1900s to look for random, cracked-mud textures instead of organized dots.

context: Alphonse Poitevin invented the basic process in 1855, but Joseph Albert perfected it in 1868. He replaced a fragile stone base with a glass plate. The process relies on dichromated gelatin. When exposed to light under a negative, the gelatin hardens. Baking the plate creates microscopic wrinkles in the gelatin. During printing, the plate is dampened. Soft, unexposed areas absorb water and repel greasy ink. Hardened, exposed areas repel water and hold the ink. This allows for incredibly smooth, photographic gradients. Collotype became the premier method for reproducing fine art and high-quality postcards.
effects.distinction: Unlike halftone printing, which uses a regular grid of distinct dots, collotype uses a random, continuous-tone wrinkle pattern.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how exploiting the physical limits of a chemical binder can create reproductions of unmatched photographic fidelity.
effects.funFact: A single collotype plate usually breaks down after producing only a couple of thousand printed impressions.

margin.note: This is a random, web-like pattern of tiny cracks. It forms when the gelatin layer dries and shrinks.
Gelatin treated with a chromium salt. It becomes sensitive to light and hardens when exposed to ultraviolet rays.
A photographic image where light and dark areas are inverted. It acts as a stencil during light exposure.

effects.title: Combination Printing
effects.name: Combination printing
effects.dating: Artistic debates since the late 1850s
effects.caption: Oscar Gustav Rejlander: The Two Ways of Life, 1857. Historical combination print.
effects.credit: Oscar Gustav Rejlander / Wikimedia Commons. Public domain / faithful reproduction on Commons.

body.label: Identify
body.text: A carefully arranged scene appears seamless, even though its components may have been created at different times.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Masks expose parts of several negatives successively onto one sheet of paper. The individual exposures form a single composition.

body.label: Example
body.text: Rejlander: The Two Ways of Life, 1857, over thirty negatives.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Create a simple montage from two images. Use the same perspective, lighting, and edges so that the combination holds together.

context: Used by several photographers in the 1850s, most notably Rejlander and Robinson. Artistic photography gained attention and sparked debate from the late 1850s onward. Detailed mechanism: Several negatives are successively copied onto a single sheet of paper using masks. Parts of different photographs form a seemingly coherent scene. Photographic compositing existed long before digital image processing.
effects.distinction: Photographic compositing existed long before digital image editing.
effects.aftermath: Layers, masks, photobashing, and digital composites.
effects.funFact: Rejlanders' The Two Ways of Life from 1857 combines over thirty negatives into a single image.
highlights: Masks expose parts of several negatives
individual exposures form a single composition

margin.note: Opaque barriers that block selected areas during printing, allowing other areas to receive light.
Photographs with reversed light and dark values. Several can supply different parts of one final print.

effects.title: Composite Portraiture
effects.name: Composite Portraiture
effects.dating: 1878, Francis Galton's published composite portraits
effects.caption: Collected Family and Group Composite Portraits. A photographic display brings together family, sibling, and group composites, with several faces surrounded by hazy hair and jaw contours.
effects.credit: Francis Galton · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: A single face has softly blurred contours, while shared features appear comparatively sharp. Faint overlapping outlines can surround the hair, ears, and jaw.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Aligned source portraits receive successive partial exposures on one photographic plate, which is then developed. Accumulated exposure reinforces matching features, while differences spread into ghostly edges.

body.label: Example
body.text: Francis Galton: Composite Portraits, 1878.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Align three consented portrait photographs by their eyes in transparent layers; compare the stable eyes with the blurred outer contours.

context: Galton presented composite portraiture in 1878 as a way to investigate shared facial characteristics. He aligned existing portraits at a common scale, using the eyes as reference points. Each portrait contributed only part of the total exposure on the same plate. Development then revealed their combined image. Galton hoped these pictures would reveal group types, including supposed criminal types. Such claims were entangled with his eugenic thinking and did not establish reliable links between appearance and character. The result depended strongly on selection, alignment, and exposure.
effects.distinction: Unlike ordinary double exposure, composite portraiture deliberately aligns comparable faces to suggest an average rather than juxtaposing separate subjects. It is not a cut-and-paste photomontage.
effects.aftermath: It shows how photographic combination can make a constructed average look like evidence of a natural human category.
effects.funFact: The finished face can look like a real sitter who never existed.

margin.note: Separate exposures made one after another, each supplying only part of the light needed for the final image.
A rigid support carrying a light-sensitive coating, commonly glass in this period.
The belief that controlling human reproduction could improve inherited population traits. It supported discriminatory hierarchies and coercive policies.

effects.title: Computational Night Mode
effects.name: Computational Night Mode
effects.dating: 2010s; Google introduced Night Sight in 2018
effects.caption: Tree Beneath a Brightened Night Sky. A tall tree rises above dark rooftops beneath a softly luminous, star-speckled sky.
effects.credit: The wub · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Dark scenes show brighter shadows, clearer colors, and less visible grain than ordinary low-light snapshots. Moving people may look blurred or leave faint ghosts.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Software aligns and merges many short exposures, reducing random noise while preserving shared scene detail. Tone mapping and color correction make the merged image easier to read.

body.label: Example
body.text: Google: Night Sight demonstration photographs, 2018.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph a dim room with night mode on and off; compare shadow detail, colored objects, and a moving hand.

context: Combining exposures predates smartphones, notably in astronomical imaging. During the 2010s, mobile cameras made this approach practical for handheld photographs. Google introduced Night Sight in 2018, bringing it to Pixel phones. Instead of relying on one long exposure, it captures a sequence and aligns corresponding details before merging them. Random noise varies between frames, so combining measurements can reveal faint detail more reliably. Exposure choices depend on available light and detected motion. Color correction and tone mapping then shape the visible result. Moving subjects remain difficult because their positions change during capture.
effects.distinction: Unlike a single long exposure, computational night mode combines separate captures and can compensate for some camera movement. Simply brightening one photograph also amplifies its existing noise.
effects.aftermath: It shows that a photograph can represent measurements gathered across time, rather than one uninterrupted exposure.
effects.funFact: A handheld night photograph can combine moments when the camera pointed in slightly different directions.

margin.note: Separate captures that each collect light for a limited time. Their duration varies with lighting and movement.
Unpredictable variations in recorded brightness or color. These become especially noticeable when little light reaches the sensor.
Adjusting recorded brightness values to fit a viewable image. It can lift shadows without making every bright area equally brighter.

effects.title: Conway's Game of Life
effects.name: Conway's Game of Life
effects.dating: 1970, John Conway's cellular automaton
effects.caption: AI illustration: Block Still Life Pattern Sequence.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: On a square grid, small clusters form blinking patterns, stationary blocks, and shapes that seem to crawl. These moving shapes can collide, disappear, or generate expanding streams.

body.label: Principle
body.text: This cellular automaton updates every cell simultaneously, using only its current state and its eight neighbors. Fixed rules determine which cells remain alive, die, or become alive; apparent motion comes from successive grid states.

body.label: Example
body.text: Bill Gosper: Gosper glider gun, 1970.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Mark three adjacent squares in a horizontal row on graph paper, leaving surrounding squares empty. Apply the rules twice and observe the alternation.

context: John Conway devised Life in 1970. Martin Gardner introduced it to Scientific American readers that October. Its square grid contains cells labeled alive or dead. Each cell has eight neighbors, including diagonal ones. A live cell survives with two or three live neighbors; otherwise, it dies. A dead cell becomes alive with exactly three live neighbors. All changes happen simultaneously, based on the previous generation. The standard model uses an infinite grid, though screens show finite regions. Simple starting arrangements can settle, oscillate, travel, or keep producing new patterns.
effects.distinction: Unlike a randomly flickering pixel display, Life produces the same sequence whenever the starting arrangement and boundary conditions match. Its moving patterns are changing cell states, not objects sliding between squares.
effects.aftermath: Life shows how simple local rules can produce complex behavior without a central controller.
effects.funFact: The Gosper glider gun emits a new glider every 30 generations.

margin.note: A system of cells that change in discrete steps according to fixed rules involving nearby cells.
One complete grid state in the sequence. Updating every cell produces the next generation.
Repeat a sequence of patterns in the same location.

effects.title: Crash Zoom
effects.name: Crash Zoom
effects.dating: 1960s, popularized in genre cinema
effects.caption: AI illustration: Triptych of a dramatic psychological crash zoom.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see the camera's view suddenly rocket forward or backward in a fraction of a second. This rapid change creates a jarring, dynamic leap to a close-up or wide shot.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A camera operator violently turns the zoom ring on a variable focal length lens. This rapidly magnifies the image without moving the physical camera.

body.label: Example
body.text: Sergio Leone: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, 1966.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch an old martial arts film and count how many times a quick zoom emphasizes a sudden realization.

context: The crash zoom emerged in the 1960s as zoom lenses became lighter and more practical. Directors like Sergio Leone and Hong Kong martial arts filmmakers fully embraced the technique. They used it to add sudden energy, emphasize dramatic moments, or highlight violent impacts. Mechanically, the camera operator twists the lens barrel as fast as possible. This instantly shifts the optical focal length. Because it was cheaper and faster than setting up a camera track, it became a staple of low-budget cinema. Today, it remains a beloved stylistic homage to that era.
effects.distinction: Unlike a dolly shot where the physical camera moves through space, a crash zoom only changes the lens magnification. It flattens the background rather than shifting the perspective.
effects.aftermath: It teaches us that manipulating optical magnification can create intense psychological impacts without moving the camera.
effects.funFact: Quentin Tarantino frequently uses crash zooms paired with a swoosh sound to mimic 1970s films.

margin.note: The optical distance inside a lens. Changing it alters how large the subject appears.
A rotating mechanical band on a lens barrel. Twisting it moves internal glass elements.

effects.name: Cross processing / X-pro
effects.dating: 1990s and 2000s: experimental fashion and Lomography aesthetics
effects.caption: Lomography teaching example for cross-processing: Slide film developed in C-41.
effects.credit: Lomography / Community Photography; Credits on source page

body.label: Identify
body.text: Unusual color casts coincide with altered contrast.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The film is developed using chemicals intended for a different type of film.

body.label: Example
body.text: Lomography: Slide film with C-41 color shifts.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Shift the color channel curves differently. Pay particular attention to neutral areas.

context: The combination of slide film and color negative chemistry was particularly associated with experimental color aesthetics. Often, slide film designed for E-6 is processed in C-41. This results in negatives with sometimes strong, film-dependent color shifts. The reverse combination is also possible, but produces a different character. Digital X-Pro presets transfer a selection of these results without actually performing the chemical reversal.
effects.distinction: Cross-processing is a chemical process, not a uniform shade of green. Film type, exposure, development, and scanning determine the result. In analog experiments, the lab needs to know in advance which film is to be processed differently.
effects.aftermath: A supposed mistake can become a consistent stylistic device.
effects.funFact: Slide film in C-41 produces a negative, even though the material was originally intended for slides.
highlights: chemicals intended for a different type

margin.note: The standard chemical process for developing color negative film.

effects.title: Crowd Simulation
effects.name: Crowd Simulation
effects.dating: 2001, The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring
effects.caption: Crowd Agents in a Wireframe Town. Colored block-like agents populate streets between wireframe buildings in a simplified digital town.
effects.credit: Paul Donnellan · CC BY 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see thousands of digital characters moving together in complex scenes like battles or cities. Instead of moving exactly alike, each individual acts uniquely, reacting to its surroundings.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Computers use rule-based artificial intelligence to guide digital agents. Each agent responds to neighboring agents, terrain, and built-in logic independently.

body.label: Example
body.text: Stephen Regelous and Wētā Digital: The Lord of the Rings, 2001.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a modern CGI battle scene and track one background soldier to see if they react uniquely to obstacles.

context: Before the 2000s, large film crowds were mostly live extras or copy-pasted digital clones. This changed when software like MASSIVE introduced agent-based simulation. Programmers gave individual digital models basic senses like sight and hearing. They also provided a set of rules, like running toward enemies or avoiding cliffs. When the scene played, the computer calculated each agent's decisions in real time. This created highly realistic, chaotic motion without hand-animating every person. The technique revolutionized epic cinema, making massive, dynamic digital armies possible for the first time.
effects.distinction: It differs from simple digital compositing or crowd cloning. Cloned crowds repeat the exact same animation loops, while simulated crowds make independent choices.
effects.aftermath: It shows how programming logic can generate highly natural, unpredictable visual complexity.
effects.funFact: Early Lord of the Rings agents ran away from battles because their self-preservation rules were too strong.

margin.note: A branch of computer science where machines mimic human logic. In this case, it helps characters make simple choices.
Individual computer-generated characters within a simulation. They are programmed to act independently based on specific rules.
A digital model that lets independent entities interact in a shared environment. It is widely used to study complex systems.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Fine horizontal bands of brightness structure the entire image.

body.label: Principle

body.label: Example
body.text: Digital effect: TV/CRT demonstration.

body.label: Try it out

context: The line structure is part of the display on cathode ray tubes and is distinct from the content of the recorded video. The 1980s represent the everyday experience with television and computer monitors. Current tools elevate this to an aesthetic level. The digital process describes its TV effect as a combination of scanlines, pixel grid, color distortion, noise, and warping. For comparison, it is helpful to activate these components one after the other.
effects.distinction: The CRT look additionally includes luminance, phosphor structure, or curvature. A uniform striped overlay is merely a simplified imitation.
effects.aftermath: Display features become a graphic texture once the original device disappears.
effects.funFact: Scanlines and interlacing are not interchangeable terms.

margin.note: A stream of electrons that strikes a light-emitting coating inside a tube display to draw the image.
Cathode-ray tube: a display that creates light by scanning electron beams across a coated screen.

effects.title: Crystoleum
effects.name: Crystoleum
effects.dating: Popular in the 1880s
effects.caption: Boy in a Sailor Collar. A boy wearing a sailor collar appears beneath reflective glass, with gently coloured cheeks and a softly fading background.
effects.credit: Rijksmuseum · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: A softly coloured photograph appears beneath convex glass, with fine photographic detail and a glossy, painting-like finish. Colours can seem suspended behind the surface.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An albumen print is pasted image-side against the glass’s concave inner surface; its paper backing is rubbed thin and made translucent. Colour applied from behind shows through the photographic image, combining painted colour with photographic shading.

body.label: Example
body.text: No famous individual example can be named here with confidence.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Place a monochrome image printed on transparent film over coloured paper, then under glass; observe how shading and colour combine.

context: Crystoleum became a popular decorative photographic technique during the late nineteenth century, including the 1880s. Makers used an existing albumen print, rather than exposing a photographic image directly on the curved glass. After attaching the image face-down, they carefully removed much of the paper backing. Oil or wax could make the remaining paper more translucent. Fine colour was applied behind this image. A second glass could carry broader areas of background colour. The assembled picture combined photographic detail with hand painting and was commonly displayed in a decorative frame.
effects.distinction: Unlike ordinary hand-colouring, crystoleum places colour behind a thinned photograph viewed through glass. Unlike an ambrotype, it uses a paper print attached to glass.
effects.aftermath: Crystoleum shows how a photograph’s support and added colour can change its appearance without changing its original exposure.
effects.funFact: Some crystoleums contain two glass sheets, separating fine painted details from broader background colours.

margin.note: A photographic paper print whose image-bearing coating contains egg white and light-sensitive silver compounds.
Curving inward, like the inside of a bowl.
Allowing light through without being fully clear.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Prussian blue areas with light silhouettes and delicate transitions through semi-transparent objects.

body.label: Principle
body.text: UV light alters iron salts on paper. After washing, a blue print appears, either from the negative or as a contact print.

body.label: Example
body.text: Anna Atkins: Himanthalia lorea, around 1853. Project started in 1843.

body.label: Try it out

context: John Herschel's process from 1842. Anna Atkins used it from 1843 onwards for botanical illustrations; later disseminated as a blueprint. Detailed mechanism: Iron salts react with UV light. After washing, Prussian blue areas and lighter areas remain; possible as a photogram or from a negative. Cyanotype refers to the chemical process; photogram refers to the application of objects. An image can be both.
effects.distinction: Cyanotype refers to the chemical process; photogram refers to the placement of objects. An image can be both.
effects.aftermath: Botanical prints, blueprint aesthetics, experimental textiles.
effects.funFact: Starting in 1843, Anna Atkins published a photographically illustrated book about algae – with real plants on light-sensitive paper.

margin.note: A deep blue iron-based pigment formed by the cyanotype process.
An image made with an object or negative resting directly against light-sensitive paper, without an enlarging lens.

effects.title: Cymatics
effects.name: Cymatics
effects.dating: 1967, Hans Jenny’s first volume of Cymatics
effects.caption: Sand Nodes at 1010 Hz. Pale sand traces stacked, rounded cells across a centrally fastened metal plate beside a 1010 Hz inscription.
effects.credit: Hladnison · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Sand forms branching lines and symmetrical grids on vibrating plates. Liquids display rippling cells, rings, and shifting surface patterns.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Mechanical vibration drives these patterns; standing waves can organize the motion. On vibrating plates, sand typically gathers along nodal lines, where the surface moves least.

body.label: Example
body.text: Hans Jenny: Cymatics, volume 1, 1967.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Stretch plastic wrap tightly over a bowl, sprinkle a few salt grains, and gently tap the rim to observe vibration moving them.

context: Swiss physician Hans Jenny introduced the term cymatics for his studies of visible vibration patterns. His first volume of Cymatics appeared in 1967, documenting experiments with powders, liquids, and other materials. The work extended earlier demonstrations by Ernst Chladni, who made sand patterns on vibrating plates. A plate’s shape, supports, and driving frequency determine which vibration modes appear. Sand often collects where motion is weakest, outlining the mode rather than tracing sound travelling through air. Liquid patterns also depend on depth, viscosity, and surface tension.
effects.distinction: Chladni figures specifically describe patterns formed by particles on vibrating surfaces, especially plates. Cymatics includes these figures but also investigates liquids and other vibrating materials.
effects.aftermath: Cymatics shows how invisible vibration becomes visible through its interaction with matter, rather than revealing one universal shape for each sound.
effects.funFact: The clearest sand lines often mark the parts of a plate that move least.

margin.note: Wave patterns whose quiet and strongly moving regions stay in fixed positions.
Lines on a vibrating surface where motion is minimal or absent within a particular vibration mode.
A fluid’s resistance to flowing. Honey has higher viscosity than water.

body.label: Identify
body.text: A sharp, small image on a reflective surface. The light-dark contrast changes with the viewing angle.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A silver-plated copper plate creates a unique photographic image. The highly polished substrate also influences the visual impression.

body.label: Example

context: Publicly presented in 1839; Daguerre had been working on it before then. Internationally widespread in the 1840s–1850s, especially for portraits. Detailed mechanism: A direct, unique print on highly polished, silvered copper. Light-sensitive plate, exposure, development, and fixing produce the finest details. Daguerreotype is not simply sepia. The substrate is part of the visible effect.
effects.distinction: Daguerreotype does not simply mean sepia. The substrate is part of the visible effect.
effects.aftermath: Metallic photo look, unique pieces, reflective print surfaces.
effects.funFact: A daguerreotype is a direct unique item: It lacks the negative for any number of prints.

margin.note: The physical support carrying an image. Here, polished silver on copper contributes to its mirror-like appearance.
A one-off image made directly on the plate, without a separate negative for producing copies.

body.text: File structure appears as unexpected offsets, bands, and color breaks.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Image data is modified using unsuitable tools or directly as bytes.

body.label: Example
body.text: Doctor Popular: modified PSD, 2014.

context: Databending exploits the gap between data and its intended interpretation. For example, an image can be altered with a hex editor or processed as audio data. Nick Briz and Rosa Menkman document this practice and its cultural significance; Doctor Popular presents a concrete PSD and JPEG comparison. The era refers to the documented glitch art scene, not the first discovery of intentional data errors. The file format influences the type of visible distortion that results.
effects.distinction: Databending refers to the general practice of processing data for purposes other than those intended. The slide "JPEG Glitch" isolates JPEG-specific codec errors. Corrupted critical file structures can render the entire image unreadable; work with copies.
effects.aftermath: The codec becomes the material itself, and not just an invisible means of transport.
effects.funFact: The same data gesture can look completely different in PSD and JPEG.
highlights: unexpected offsets, bands, and color breaks

margin.note: Small units of digital data. Changing them can alter an image or make the file unreadable.

effects.title: Datamoshing
effects.name: Datamoshing
effects.dating: Experimental background. A significant wave of music videos and online activity occurred in 2009.
effects.caption:
Lee Brenton: My first datamosh, November 15, 2009: Original video still.
Temporal effect: still image or image sequence.
effects.credit: Lee Brenton. CC BY 3.0

body.label: Identify
body.text: Pixel blocks become fluid. Foreign textures follow body movements. One scene seems to melt into the next.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Video compression stores motion data. Modified reference images cause this data to be applied to unsuitable image content. For example, Welcome to Heartbreak and Evident Utensil spread the look in 2009.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare blending, morphing, and Datamosh. Do the transparency, shape, or the relationship between movement and texture change?

context: Experimental prehistory; significant music video/online wave in 2009.

Temporal video compression doesn't save every frame completely, but also captures change and motion information, among other things. If reference frames are missing or motion data is used inappropriately, the texture of one scene can bleed into the motion of another.
Kanye West, Welcome to Heartbreak (2009, directed by Nabil Elderkin), and Chairlift, Evident Utensil (2009, directed by Ray Tintori). Earlier art reference: Takashi Murata, Monster Movie (2005).

Image: Historical original / source image. Color and macroblock areas smear across the subject. Still image from a real datamoshing sequence; the video shows how motion data further distorts the old image.
effects.distinction: Datamoshing is a specific subgenre of glitch aesthetics, not a name for every RGB shift or screen noise. Compression errors predate the term. The 2000s are marked by their deliberate artistic use and popularization.
effects.aftermath: The normally invisible codec becomes an image engine. A technical defect appears as a painterly transition.
effects.funFact: Welcome to Heartbreak and Evident Utensil made datamoshing particularly visible in music videos in 2009.

margin.note: Reducing video data, often by storing changes from earlier frames instead of complete new pictures.
Frames used as starting points for reconstructing other frames. Wrong references can carry unrelated textures along with motion.

effects.title: Decalcomania
effects.name: Decalcomania
effects.dating: 1936, Óscar Domínguez's surrealist experiments
effects.caption: Surrealist Landscape Made With Decalcomania. A painted landscape features towering, pillar-like rock formations with intricate, spongy textures against a yellow and orange sky.
effects.credit: H. Grobe · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see unpredictable, spongy textures in paint or ink. These patterns often resemble organic shapes, strange vegetation, or alien landscapes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Thick ink or paint is pressed between two smooth surfaces. When peeled apart, the suction creates branching, vein-like ridges and random pools.

body.label: Example
body.text: Max Ernst: Europe After the Rain II, 1940-1942.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Squeeze wet watercolor or gouache between two sheets of smooth paper, press down, and pull them apart to see the textures.

context: Decalcomania started as an 18th-century decorative craft for transferring engravings to ceramics. In 1936, surrealist artist Óscar Domínguez adapted it to create spontaneous art. He spread dark gouache on smooth paper, covered it with another sheet, and pressed them. Peeling them apart revealed strange, random textures. Surrealists loved this because it removed conscious control, letting the subconscious find meaning in the random shapes. Max Ernst later used oil paint on canvas to create highly detailed, ruined landscapes. The technique relies on fluid dynamics and suction, forming complex ridges as the wet medium splits.
effects.distinction: Unlike a Rorschach inkblot, which folds paper for perfect symmetry, decalcomania creates asymmetrical, highly detailed surface textures.
effects.aftermath: It shows how giving up control to physical forces can spark human imagination.
effects.funFact: The word 'decal' comes directly from decalcomania, though today it means a printed sticker.

margin.note: The physics of how liquids and gases move. Here, it explains how the wet paint flows and separates.
A type of opaque watercolor paint. It stays wet and sticky long enough to press and transfer easily.
The vacuum-like pull created when two wet, stuck surfaces are forced apart. It pulls the paint into ridges.

effects.title: Deep Focus
effects.name: Deep-focus photography

effects.caption: Citizen Kane (1941): several distinct plot lines.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Foreground, middle ground and background remain in focus simultaneously and tell the story in parallel.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Short focal length, small aperture, strong light, and precise staging increase the depth of field. Some shots also use compositing.

body.label: Example
body.text: Orson Welles and Gregg Toland: Citizen Kane, 1941.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: First describe the plot at the beginning, then at the very end. Decide which level deserves your attention first.

context: Long history; further developed by Gregg Toland in the 1930s. 1941: Citizen Kane as a famous milestone. No added special effect and not invented in 1941. Deliberate photographic composition; greater depth of field alone does not explain a good composition.

recognize: Foreground, middle ground and background tell the story simultaneously; the distance remains legible.
Mechanism: Short focal length, small aperture, strong light and precise staging keep near and far planes in focus; some shots also use compositing.
example: Orson Welles / Gregg Toland: Citizen Kane, 1941.
Practice: In a still image, first describe the action in the foreground, then the action in the background. Then decide for yourself on which level the most important information lies and what draws your eye there.

Short focal length, small aperture, strong light and precise staging keep near and far planes in focus; some shots also use compositing.
Foreground, middle ground and background tell the story simultaneously; the distance remains legible.
In the still image, first describe the action in the foreground, then the action in the very back.
No added special effect and not invented in 1941. A deliberate photographic composition; greater depth of field alone does not explain a good composition.
effects.distinction: Not a post-processing special effect and not invented in 1941. A deliberate photographic composition; greater depth of field alone does not explain a good composition.
effects.aftermath: Influence on multi-layered image staging to this day.
effects.funFact: Some famous deep-focus images in Citizen Kane combine optical depth of field with compositing.

effects.title: Deep-Fried Meme
effects.name: Deep-Fried Meme
effects.dating: 2010s; widely circulated by 2017
effects.caption: Deep-Fried Face with Glowing Eyes. A recognizable face emerges from dense orange-yellow speckling, crushed shadows, and brilliant red glowing eyes with horizontal flares.
effects.credit: Lord Belbury · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Images show harsh saturation, blocky compression artifacts, and glaring highlights, often with glowing eyes or added lens flares. Captions and faces may remain recognizable despite severe distortion.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Editors combine extreme contrast, saturation, sharpening, and low-quality JPEG encoding to exaggerate digital damage. Added flare graphics imitate optical glare rather than recording light scattered inside a lens.

body.label: Example
body.text: Anonymous internet users: Lord Farquaad “E” meme, 2018.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Save an image as a low-quality JPEG, boost saturation and contrast, then compare its edges and shadows with the original.

context: Deep-fried memes became a recognizable internet style during the 2010s, with widespread circulation by 2017. They deliberately exaggerated the damage associated with copying, editing, and reposting images. JPEG compression discards information, producing blocks and ringing around sharp edges at low quality. Strong contrast crushes shadow detail and clips highlights, while saturation adjustments intensify colors. Added flares and glowing eyes push the result beyond ordinary compression damage. The visual abuse becomes part of the joke, sometimes making a familiar image nearly unreadable. No single creator securely defines the style’s origin.
effects.distinction: An ordinary low-quality image may show compression damage without deliberate exaggeration. Deep-frying combines that damage with aggressive tonal changes and often added graphic effects.
effects.aftermath: The technique shows how digital defects can become a shared visual language rather than merely unwanted errors.
effects.funFact: Copying a JPEG file without re-encoding it does not progressively damage its image.

margin.note: A process that stores an image using compression. Lower quality settings discard more visual information.
Faint ripples or halos near sharp edges. Heavy compression can make them conspicuous.
Pushes bright values to the maximum the image can represent. Different bright details then become the same flat tone.

effects.title: DeepDream
effects.name: DeepDream / neural style transfer
effects.dating: Two different neural imaging approaches will become publicly visible in 2015.
effects.caption: Google Research: Inceptionism / DeepDream, 2015: Input at the top, neural reinterpretation at the bottom.
effects.credit: Google Inc.; Alexander Mordvintsev, Christopher Olah & Mike Tyka. CC BY 4.0

body.label: Identify
body.text: DeepDream displays recurring eyes and animal shapes. Style Transfer overlays photographic images with painting-like textures.

body.label: Principle
body.text: DeepDream enhances detected network features. Style Transfer combines content features of a source image with style statistics of a second image.

body.label: Example
body.text: Google: DeepDream (2015). Gatys, Ecker, Bethge: Neural Style Transfer (2015).

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare both using the same image. What is added, what is retained, which textures are carried over?

context: Two defining public approaches in 2015.

DeepDream enhances features that a trained image network already believes it recognizes. Neural Style Transfer seeks an image version that combines the image content of a source image with the texture and style statistics of another image.
Google, Inceptionism/DeepDream (June/July 2015); Gatys, Ecker and Bethge, A Neural Algorithm of Artistic Style (August 2015).

Image: Historical original / source image. A neural network amplifies recognized image patterns. This historical example shows DeepDream; Neural Style Transfer is a related, technically different approach.
effects.distinction: Style transfer is not simply an oil paint filter. DeepDream is not the same as today's text-to-image diffusion technology. DeepDream and Neural Style Transfer are different methods. Treat them as a learning family, but clearly distinguish their functionality; no equals sign.
effects.aftermath: Not only image values ​​or geometry, but also the learned feature spaces of a network could control the visible transformation.
effects.funFact: DeepDream and Neural Style Transfer both became known in 2015, but pursue different image goals.
highlights: style statistics of a second image

margin.note: Patterns learned by a neural network, from simple edges to complex shapes. DeepDream amplifies patterns the network detects.
Numerical summaries of patterns such as textures and colors, used to transfer an image’s visual style without copying its scene.

effects.title: Deepfake
effects.name: Deepfake / face swapping
effects.dating: 2010s: rapid visibility; FaceForensics++ benchmarked several methods in 2019
effects.caption: FaceForensics++: Research illustration of various facial manipulations, 2019.
effects.credit: Andreas Rössler, Davide Cozzolino, Luisa Verdoliva, Christian Riess, Justus Thies and Matthias Nießner.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Identity or facial expression is replaced in existing image sequences.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Facial models, warping, or neural synthesis are integrated into the target image.

body.label: Example
body.text: FaceForensics++ compares four manipulation families in 2019.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare eyes, mouth edges, light, and temporal stability.

context: Face swapping predates the term "deepfake." In the 2010s, neural approaches increased its public visibility; research responded with data and detection methods. FaceForensics++ from 2019 compares deepfakes, face-to-face, face swaps, and neural textures. This distinction is particularly helpful for learning: identity swapping, facial expression transfer, and neural rendering are not identical. The image is taken from the research presentation and shows several types of manipulation. A plausible single image can still become unstable when moved. Therefore, pay attention to contours, occlusions, and the temporal relationship. However, visible artifacts alone are not reliable general proof for or against manipulation.
effects.distinction: Face swapping is a specific task; deepfake is a broader term and not every method works the same way.
effects.funFact: FaceForensics++ investigated four different families of facial manipulation in 2019.

margin.note: Geometrically stretching or moving image parts so facial features align with another face.
Consistency from one video frame to the next. Unstable edits may flicker or shift as a face moves.

effects.title: Depth-Map Portrait
effects.name: Depth-map portrait / computational portrait mode
effects.dating: 2017: Pixel 2 portrait mode as a vivid milestone
effects.caption: Google Research: Estimated depth map and derived uncertainty, 2017.
effects.credit: Google Research, technical illustration of the photo by Sam Kweskin.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Face in focus, background blurred depending on estimated distance.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Segmentation and depth mapping control artificial defocusing.

body.label: Example
body.text: Pixel 2: Portrait mode, 2017.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Test hair, eyeglasses, and objects in front of your body.

context: In 2017, Google explained the Pixel 2 portrait mode as a combination of image processing, person masking, and depth estimation. The main camera is particularly illustrative: Split sensor pixels provide two slightly different views through different parts of the same lens. A depth map is then estimated from this. Together with segmentation, this determines how much individual image areas are blurred. The process is therefore more than simply isolating a person from a generally blurred background. In the example explained, a pastry in front of the person must be treated differently than the more distant surroundings. In the exercise, look for similar borderline cases. These will help you determine whether a portrait filter actually takes depth of field into account.
effects.distinction: A person mask is not a depth map; both pieces of information can be used together.
effects.aftermath: The look refers back to optical depth of field, but its flaws also arise from masks and estimated geometry.
effects.funFact: Pixel 2 estimated depth using split sensor pixels, even though the main camera only had one lens.

margin.note: Dividing an image into meaningful areas, such as a person and the background.
Estimating how far different parts of a scene are from the camera. These distances help determine how much blur to apply.

sources.label: Google Research: Portrait mode on Pixel 2, 2017

effects.title: Digital Color Grading
effects.name: Digital Color Grading
effects.dating: 2000, color correction of O Brother, Where Art Thou?
effects.caption: Moody Forest Path with Blue Shadows. A dark forest path is illuminated by a warm central highlight surrounded by deeply blue-tinted shadows.
effects.credit: SavidgeMichael · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a movie where colors look stylized, uniform, or artificially enhanced across entire scenes. Shadows might be tinted blue while highlights are warm, creating distinct visual moods that defy natural lighting.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Film negatives are scanned into a computer, turning chemical images into digital pixels. Software then mathematically adjusts the color values of specific areas before printing back to film.

body.label: Example
body.text: Joel and Ethan Coen: O Brother, Where Art Thou?, 2000.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a modern film and look for scenes where every object is bathed in the exact same unnatural green or orange hue.

context: Before the 2000s, filmmakers changed movie colors chemically. They used color filters and varied light exposure when copying negatives. This process was called color timing. It only allowed broad changes to the entire frame. In 2000, O Brother, Where Art Thou? changed the industry. The directors wanted a dry, sepia-toned autumn look, but they filmed during a green summer. They scanned the original film into a computer, creating a digital intermediate. Using software, they digitally isolated green leaves and turned them brown. Then, they printed the digital files back onto physical film. This provided unprecedented control over individual colors.
effects.distinction: Photochemical color timing alters the whole image globally by adding colored light during physical printing. Digital color grading uses software to alter specific targeted colors or objects within the frame.
effects.aftermath: It teaches us that digital intervention can completely rewrite the atmospheric reality of a filmed physical space.
effects.funFact: The digital files for O Brother, Where Art Thou? required a massive 2.5 terabytes of disk space.

margin.note: A high-resolution digital copy of a movie made by scanning physical film. It is used for digital editing and color correction.
The traditional, photochemical method of adjusting a movie's color. It relies on physical filters and light manipulation during film duplication.
The tiny squares of visual data that make up a computer image. Each pixel holds specific mathematical color information.

effects.title: Digital De-Aging
effects.name: Digital De-Aging
effects.dating: 2010s, widespread adoption in major film franchises
effects.caption: AI illustration: Side-by-side digital de-aging comparison on monitor.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see an older actor appearing remarkably younger on screen. Their skin is smooth, and their facial structure matches older photographs.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Visual effects artists digitally alter high-resolution footage frame by frame. They warp facial geometry and replace skin textures using 3D models.

body.label: Example
body.text: Lola VFX: Ant-Man (Young Michael Douglas), 2015.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at the mouth and eyes of a de-aged character; notice if the lip movements feel slightly stiff or weightless.

context: While early digital makeup existed before, digital de-aging became a standard tool in the 2010s. Studios like Lola VFX pioneered a technique often compared to digital plastic surgery. Artists use reference photos from an actor's youth to guide their work. They take the live-action footage and meticulously adjust sagging skin, wrinkles, and bone structure. Sometimes, a younger double performs the scene alongside the veteran actor. The effects team then blends the older actor’s performance onto the younger body. This technique allows aging stars to reprise iconic roles in prequels without casting new actors.
effects.distinction: Unlike deepfakes which use artificial intelligence to swap faces automatically, digital de-aging relies on manual, frame-by-frame 3D sculpting by human artists.
effects.aftermath: It reveals our enduring desire to freeze time and preserve beloved screen icons indefinitely.
effects.funFact: Actors often wear dots on their faces during filming to help computers track their exact expressions.

margin.note: The mathematical 3D shape and proportions of a person's face.
Virtual objects created in computer software that possess width, height, and depth.
Video or film recorded with real people and cameras, rather than being completely computer-generated.

effects.title: Digital Video Effects
effects.name: Digital Video Effects
effects.dating: 1980s broadcast television; Ampex ADO introduced in 1981
effects.caption: AI illustration: Picture-in-picture news broadcast composition.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Television pictures shrink into floating panels, rotate through space, or appear as picture-in-picture windows. Page turns and flying cubes make moving images behave like flexible sheets or solid surfaces.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Digital processors store video frames in memory, then remap their pixels to change size, position, shape, and apparent perspective. Compositing places the transformed picture over another image.

body.label: Example
body.text: Ampex: ADO (Ampex Digital Optics), 1981.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a television transition frame by frame, checking whether the picture changes shape while movement continues inside it.

context: Digital video effects became a familiar part of television during the 1980s, building on digital equipment developed in the previous decade. Ampex introduced ADO in 1981, helping establish electronically positioned and rotated video pictures as a broadcast design tool. A frame store held sampled images while processors calculated new pixel locations. Operators could move pictures across backgrounds without moving a camera or a physical screen. Different systems offered different capabilities; elaborate page turns and cubes were not universal features. These transformations became common in sports coverage, station promotions, and music television.
effects.distinction: A conventional wipe reveals one picture by moving a boundary across another; it need not distort either image. DVE transforms the picture itself, although a production can combine both techniques.
effects.aftermath: DVE shows how storing video as numerical samples lets the screen become a movable object within another screen.
effects.funFact: A picture could keep playing while its entire rectangular frame seemed to tumble through space.

margin.note: Combining separate images into one output picture, with control over which parts remain visible.
Electronic memory that holds a video image so equipment can read and manipulate its samples.
A simulated sense of depth, created by changing the picture's outline and the spacing of its details.

effects.title: Diorama Light Change
effects.name: Diorama Light Change
effects.dating: 1822, Louis Daguerre and Charles Bouton's Diorama theatre
effects.caption: Bry-sur-Marne Diorama in Chapel Light. An altar stands before a painted Gothic nave, flanked by sculpted figures and decorative chapel walls.
effects.credit: Pierre Tribhou · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: A massive landscape painting seems to magically transform from day to night. Colors shift, shadows move, and hidden figures appear seamlessly.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The canvas is painted on both sides using translucent and opaque paints. Changing the lighting from front to back reveals hidden details.

body.label: Example
body.text: Louis Daguerre: The Ruins of Holyrood Chapel, 1824.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a daytime scene on paper, add a moon on the back, and shine a flashlight behind it in darkness.

context: Louis Daguerre and Charles Bouton opened the Diorama theatre in Paris in 1822. Audiences sat in a dark auditorium viewing massive paintings. These canvases were painted on thin calico cloth. Artists applied opaque paints to the front and translucent tints to the back. A complex system of skylights and shutters controlled the illumination. By slowly blocking front light and increasing backlight, the scene shifted seamlessly. A sunny cathedral could suddenly host a midnight mass. This optical illusion thrilled crowds long before cinema existed.
effects.distinction: Unlike magic lanterns projecting onto a blank screen, a Diorama manipulates light passing through a massive painted fabric.
effects.aftermath: It shows how manipulating light transmission through painted media can create powerful, time-based visual storytelling without moving parts.
effects.funFact: Daguerre later used his deep understanding of light to invent the daguerreotype, an early photographic process.
highlights: magically transform from day to night

margin.note: A material that allows some light to pass through, but diffuses it so objects behind are not clearly visible.
A plain-woven textile made from unbleached, often not fully processed cotton.
Pigments that completely block light, hiding anything underneath or behind them on the canvas.

effects.title: Direct Animation on Film
effects.name: Direct Animation on Film
effects.dating: 1930s, pioneered by Len Lye and Norman McLaren
effects.caption: Mothlight Hand-Painted Film Title. Rough black brushstrokes spell “Moth Light” across a warm, translucent field, with uneven edges and visible smears.
effects.credit: Stan Brakhage · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see rapidly shifting, jittery colors and frantic lines dancing on screen. The visuals often look textured, raw, and highly energetic.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Artists apply paint directly onto the transparent film base, or they scratch imagery into the dark emulsion of developed film. This bypasses the camera entirely.

body.label: Example
body.text: Len Lye: A Colour Box, 1935.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a flipbook using a thick marker. Notice how hard it is to keep the shapes stable between pages.

context: Standard animation requires a camera to photograph individual drawings. Direct animation skips the camera phase. Instead, creators manipulate the physical celluloid strip itself. They paint, ink, or stencil shapes onto clear film stock. This is an additive process. Alternatively, they use a subtractive method. They take black, exposed film and scrape away the dark emulsion layer to let light through. The film strip is tiny, making precise drawing difficult. When projected at 24 frames per second, these small, physical marks become large, kinetic bursts of color and light.
effects.distinction: Unlike traditional cel animation, direct animation puts the artwork physically on the projection film itself. There are no cameras or separate background layers.
effects.aftermath: It shows that moving pictures only require a physical medium and a projector to create the illusion of life.
effects.funFact: Stan Brakhage once glued dead moths and leaves directly onto a film strip for his movie Mothlight.

margin.note: This is the light-sensitive chemical coating on film. When scratched away, it leaves a clear spot for light to pass through.
This is the flexible, transparent plastic material that makes up the physical film reel.
This refers to creating an image by adding material, like painting colors onto a clear surface.

context: Displacement is a principle with various implementations. It involves the 2D shifting of horizontal and vertical image coordinates using a control layer. Software often distinguishes between actual geometry changes and bump mapping. The 1990s mark the learning phase for desktop deformation filters, not the origin of all displacement techniques. Today, digital image editors offer texture scaling, curves, and map blurring in a directly visible preview.
effects.distinction: In compositing, image coordinates are shifted; in 3D, true displacement can change the geometry. Bump and normal mapping primarily alter the light response.

context: Columbia cites Méliès's Cendrillon from 1899 as a possible early use and describes its creation through rewinding and re-exposure. In classic cinema, the dissolve effect was frequently used to signify a change of location, the passage of time, or memory. Citizen Kane also uses it to shift between narrative levels. The date indicates an early example; its priority is not presented as definitively established.
effects.distinction: A dissolve is a temporal transition, while a double exposure can permanently combine several subjects. Its duration and the image content determine the effect.
effects.aftermath: Similar image overlays can have very different functions.
effects.funFact: In Great Britain, the crossfade is also called a "mix".

margin.note: Both shots remain visible at the same time during the transition. One gradually replaces the other rather than switching in a single cut.

effects.title: Dissolving Views
effects.name: Dissolving Views
effects.dating: 1830s-1840s, Henry Langdon Childe's magic lantern shows
effects.caption: AI illustration: Victorian bi-unial lantern projecting a seasonal dissolving view.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see one painted image slowly fade away. At the exact same time, a new image slowly fades in.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Two projectors overlap their light perfectly onto one screen. A mechanical shutter slowly blocks one lens while opening the other.

body.label: Example
body.text: Henry Langdon Childe: Various Royal Polytechnic Institution shows, 1840s.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Use two phone flashlights in a dark room. Cover one slowly with your hand while uncovering the other.

context: Dissolving views became highly popular in the 1840s. Showmen used a specialized magic lantern with two or three optical tubes. They called this a biunial or triunial lantern. The operator carefully aligned the lenses so the projected images overlapped completely. A special comb-like shutter, called a dissolver, moved in front of the lenses. It reduced the light from the first slide while revealing the second. This crossfade effect hid the clumsy changing of glass slides. It allowed smooth transitions between daytime and nighttime scenes or changing seasons. Audiences found the gentle blending of large, luminous paintings deeply magical.
effects.distinction: Unlike a standard slideshow where the screen goes black between slides, dissolving views never interrupt the picture. The screen remains constantly illuminated.
effects.aftermath: It introduced the crossfade, a transition technique that became foundational in modern film editing.
effects.funFact: Limelight, the intense gas illumination used for these shows, coined the phrase 'in the limelight'.

margin.note: An early type of image projector that used lenses and a light source to show painted glass slides.
A projector built with two completely separate lens systems stacked on top of each other.
A visual transition where one picture gradually disappears while another appears, blending the two briefly.

effects.title: Distance Fog
effects.name: Distance Fog
effects.dating: 1990s real-time 3D games; Turok: Dinosaur Hunter, 1997
effects.caption: AI illustration: Jungle landscape showing depth-based color blending.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Distant scenery loses contrast and fades toward a uniform fog color. Nearby objects stay clear, while faraway silhouettes merge into a hazy background.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The renderer blends surface colors with a fog color, using camera depth to control the blend. This approximates atmospheric scattering without simulating light traveling through actual mist.

body.label: Example
body.text: Iguana Entertainment: Turok: Dinosaur Hunter, 1997.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch outdoor gameplay from Turok: Dinosaur Hunter, and track how one distant rock gains contrast as the player approaches.

context: Distance fog became familiar in 1990s games as developers balanced outdoor scenery against limited rendering power. The Nintendo 64 supported fog blending, and Turok: Dinosaur Hunter used conspicuous haze around its environments. A short draw distance meant distant geometry could be omitted. Fog helped conceal that boundary by making approaching scenery blend into the background before its disappearance became obvious. Fog itself did not remove geometry or automatically improve performance. Its practical value came from disguising a restricted visible range while also suggesting humid air, depth, and isolation.
effects.distinction: Unlike depth of field, distance fog changes color and contrast rather than blurring edges. Unlike volumetric fog, basic depth fog cannot represent localized shafts or pockets of mist.
effects.aftermath: Distance fog shows how a visible hardware compromise can also become an expressive part of a game's atmosphere.
effects.funFact: Game fog can hide missing scenery without blurring a single edge.

margin.note: An object's position along the camera's viewing direction. This is not necessarily its straight-line distance from the camera.
Air molecules and suspended particles redirect light. Over long distances, this can weaken contrast and add a visible haze.
The distance limit beyond which a game stops drawing certain scenery. Different object types may have different limits.

effects.title: Distortion Photography
effects.name: Distortion Photography
effects.dating: 1930s; André Kertész's Distortions, 1933

body.label: Identify
body.text: Bodies appear as stretched limbs, swollen curves, and compressed shapes, while skin and lighting remain photographically detailed. Familiar anatomy becomes strange and sometimes almost abstract.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A curved mirror redirects reflected light, producing uneven magnification across the image. The camera records this warped reflection during exposure; development does not create the deformation.

body.label: Example
body.text: André Kertész: Distortions, 1933.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph your reflection in a shiny spoon, then change its angle and watch which features expand or shrink.

context: In 1933, André Kertész photographed nude models reflected in distorting mirrors in Paris. His Distortions series turned familiar bodies into unstable combinations of recognizable details and sweeping curves. The pictures belong to a wider interwar interest in experimental photography and unfamiliar views of ordinary things. Mirror curvature changes the apparent scale and position of different body parts. Moving the model, mirror, or camera changes the result before exposure. The photographic process preserves these optical transformations rather than inventing them during development. Smooth tonal detail makes the impossible-looking anatomy especially convincing.
effects.distinction: Unlike a double exposure, this method does not require overlapping separate exposures. Unlike motion blur, its stretched forms can retain sharply defined edges.
effects.aftermath: It shows that a photograph can record light faithfully while presenting radically misleading proportions.
effects.funFact: A household spoon can produce related distortions without any special camera lens.

margin.note: Different areas appear enlarged or reduced by different amounts.
The period when light reaches the camera's light-sensitive film or sensor.

effects.title: Dot-Matrix Printout
effects.name: Dot-Matrix Printout
effects.dating: 1970s, widespread use in computer terminals and printers
effects.caption: AI illustration: Pear rendered with low-resolution dot-matrix grid.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Text and images break into round dots arranged in regular rows. Coarse dot grids give curves stepped edges, while uneven ink makes some dots faint.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An impact printhead drives selected pins against an inked ribbon, transferring small ink marks onto paper. Printhead movement and paper feeding position these marks to build letters and pictures.

body.label: Example
body.text: Digital Equipment Corporation: LA36 DECwriter II, 1974.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Examine an impact-printer receipt with a magnifier, then copy one letter onto squared paper using only dots.

context: Dot-matrix impact printing became common in the 1970s as computers needed affordable paper output. Unlike printers with fixed letter shapes, these machines assembled characters from individually selected dots. A moving printhead struck an inked ribbon while the paper advanced between printed lines. Continuous stationery often had perforated edges that helped feed it through the machine. Graphics-capable models could also place dots to form diagrams and pictures. More pins and overlapping passes could improve detail, but printing took longer. The visible grid records both the printer's mechanical spacing and its instructions.
effects.distinction: Halftone printing uses dot patterns to reproduce tones, often by varying dot size. Impact dot-matrix printing builds marks with pin strikes, including the letters themselves.
effects.aftermath: The printout shows how a visible image can emerge from discrete marks constrained by mechanical movement.
effects.funFact: Pin strikes can produce several copies at once through multipart forms.

margin.note: The printing assembly contains pins that physically strike a ribbon against paper.
A long connected strip of paper, usually folded into a stack. Perforations allow individual sheets to be separated.
The printhead travels across an area more than once. Additional dots can fill gaps or darken existing marks.

context: Multiple exposures were an early photographic technique; spirit photography was marketed in the USA in the 1860s. Spiritualist portraits appeared in the 19th and early 20th centuries; later, it became an independent art technique. Detailed mechanism: An image carrier is exposed more than once. A less exposed subject can appear transparent in a second exposure. The visible effect is a form of image manipulation, not proof of ghosts. The exact technique used in some historical images remains partially unconfirmed.
effects.distinction: The visible phenomenon is a manipulation of the image, not proof of ghosts. The exact method used in some historical images remains partially unproven.
effects.aftermath: Double-exposure portraits, blend modes, experimental music visuals.
effects.funFact: Manipulated ghost photography was already being sold as a service in the 1860s.
