effects.title: Dunning Process
effects.name: Dunning Process
effects.dating: 1927, Carroll Dunning's colour-separation process
effects.caption: AI illustration: Shipboard actor composited against storm footage.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Live actors appear inside a separately filmed setting, with moving silhouettes revealing the background around them. The finished composite is black and white, sometimes with visible edge fringes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Yellow-lit actors stand before a blue backing, while a yellow-dyed background positive runs against unexposed negative film inside the camera. The positive filters blue light according to its image, while passing yellow foreground light to expose the negative.

body.label: Example
body.text: Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack: King Kong, 1933.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look through transparent yellow film at blue and yellow patches on a screen; compare how strongly each patch darkens.

context: Carroll Dunning introduced this process in the 1920s, and Roy Pomeroy helped develop it for studio use. It combined actors with previously photographed scenery during exposure, rather than joining two finished images afterward. The camera carried two film strips together, an arrangement called bipack. A yellow-dyed positive supplied the background image, while a fresh negative recorded the combination. Yellow light illuminated the actors, and blue light came from the backing. Their different transmission through the dyed positive separated foreground from background. Careful lighting was essential, especially around hair, shadows, and reflective costumes.
effects.distinction: Unlike modern blue-screen compositing, Dunning combined the images photographically inside the camera rather than extracting a digital mask afterward. Its coloured lighting produced a black-and-white result.
effects.aftermath: It shows how colour separation can control where an image forms, even when the finished picture contains no colour.
effects.funFact: The camera ran an already developed background print beside fresh film.

margin.note: A film image with normal light and dark relationships, unlike a negative. Here, its image was carried by yellow dye.
Two film strips running together through a camera. One can filter the light reaching the other.
The stage when light reaches sensitive film and creates a latent image. Chemical development makes that image visible later.

body.label: Identify

body.label: Principle

context: The term originates from printing: Two printing inks expand or shape the tonal range of a grayscale image. Each color can have its own tone curve and printing plate. The digital revival is anchored here with Spotify's Year in Music 2015; the participating Stink Studios documented gradients and duotone shaders for this purpose. This is a documented application example, not a date of invention. A modern browser filter, on the other hand, usually distributes RGB colors across brightness. This makes the image appear two-tone, but technically it often contains many mixed color tones. Therefore, check before printing whether two separate separations have actually been created.
effects.distinction: RGB two-color look and printable duotone are different production methods.
effects.aftermath: Recognizable image families are created through fixed color pairs. The subject and its light distribution continue to determine the contrast.
effects.funFact: Photoshop's duotone mode even includes one-, three- and four-color variations.
highlights: Brightness levels retain shadow and light colors
true duotone prints two separate colors

context: The Dutch angle is a camera technique, not a digitally invented filter. The tilted coordinate system can suggest instability or a subjective state. Columbia illustrates the concept with Bertolucci's *The Constructive Mistake*. The film noir of the 1940s provides a relevant point of reference, while similar compositions appear earlier and later. Crucially, it relates to the scene, movement, and recurring visual language.
effects.distinction: Tilting a camera is not an automatic guarantee of meaning. It can signal restlessness, humor, or simply an established cinematic language. An intentionally tilted camera must be distinguished from an accidentally uneven composition.
effects.aftermath: The audience also interprets the orientation of the image space.
effects.funFact: “Canted angle” is another technical name for the tilted camera.

margin.note: The imaginary line running through the center of the lens toward the scene. Rotating around it tilts the whole picture.
A style associated with shadowy crime stories, moral uncertainty, and dramatic lighting, especially in mid-century cinema.

effects.title: Dynamation
effects.name: Dynamation
effects.dating: 1950s, Ray Harryhausen; demonstrated in 20 Million Miles to Earth, 1957.
effects.caption: Ymir Among Fleeing City Crowds. A towering reptilian creature strides through a city street among fleeing people, overturned vehicles, and foreground wreckage.
effects.credit: Columbia Pictures · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Stop-motion creatures appear among live actors in photographed locations. Foreground scenery hides parts of their bodies, while slightly stepped movements distinguish them from surrounding action.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Rear projection places filmed action behind an animated model, with both photographed frame by frame. Complementary mattes reserve separate image areas for successive exposures, allowing foreground action to appear in front of the model.

body.label: Example
body.text: Ray Harryhausen: 20 Million Miles to Earth, 1957.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a creature pass behind scenery, pausing frequently; trace the boundary where the photographed foreground conceals the animated model.

context: Harryhausen developed this approach to combine miniature creatures with filmed people and places without building complete miniature sets. He used it before Dynamation became a promotional name for The 7th Voyage of Sinbad in 1958. A projector advanced the live-action footage one frame at a time behind the model. The animator adjusted the model between camera exposures. A matte blocked the foreground area during this pass. After rewinding the camera film, a complementary matte protected the recorded area while the missing foreground was exposed. This placed the creature between photographed background and foreground.
effects.distinction: Ordinary rear projection places performers or models in front of a projected background. Dynamation adds split-screen masking and additional exposures so photographed foreground elements can also overlap the model.
effects.aftermath: Dynamation shows how carefully controlled overlap can make separately photographed subjects appear to occupy one continuous space.
effects.funFact: The Dynamation name arrived after Harryhausen had already used the underlying technique.

margin.note: Film is projected onto a translucent screen from behind. A camera on the opposite side records it together with the model.
Paired masks block opposite areas of the image. Each exposure fills an area left unexposed by the other.
Intervals when light reaches the camera film and records an image. Chemical development happens afterward.

effects.title: Emboss
effects.name: Emboss / relief filter
effects.dating: 2000s: established standard filters in image software
effects.caption: Emboss: modern digital demonstration.
effects.credit: Digital effect demonstration.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Image edges appear as raised or embossed relief.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Local differences in brightness are represented as directed light and shadow edges.

body.label: Example
body.text: Embossed paper or metal surfaces as a filter look.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Rotate the lighting direction by 180 degrees.

context: Digital emboss filters translate differences in adjacent image values ​​into apparent surface height. A chosen lighting direction creates light and dark edges, which our eyes interpret as relief. The reference to the 2000s refers to the established toolkit: GIMP's documentation from that time lists emboss as a standard filter. Adobe also describes the gray base effect with preserved or highlighted contours. This differs from true paper embossing, where a tool physically deforms the material. In this exercise, simply rotate the light angle without changing the subject. Often, the impression shifts from raised to recessed. This reversal demonstrates how strongly we infer form from lighting.
effects.distinction: The filter creates an optical relief impression, not an actually deformed printed surface.
effects.aftermath: Emboss is suitable for learning surface perception. For actual embossing, you will subsequently need separate production data and a suitable process.
effects.funFact: The same edge can suddenly appear recessed instead of raised due to a reversed direction of light.

margin.note: A surface design that appears to project above or sink below its background.
The angle from which simulated light arrives, determining which edges appear bright or dark.

effects.dating: 1960s aerial and experimental color photography; earlier technical precursors

body.label: Identify
body.text: Vegetation often appears red or magenta.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Near-infrared light is assigned to a visible color channel.

body.label: Example
body.text: Yann Philippe: digital IR-chrome false-color landscape.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Explain: What information does red convey when it is not the color of a real object?

context: False-color infrared combines measurement and design. Film types for aerial photography translate spectral differences in such a way that vegetation appears striking. Later, this unusual color world was also used artistically. Kodak describes different reactions of healthy plants and various vegetation types. Digital full-spectrum cameras and special filters can produce related looks. The decade assignment refers to the established application in aerial photography and visual culture, not to a single date of invention.
effects.distinction: Red here is a representational color and not a temperature indicator. Analog infrared color film, digital channel mapping, and a conventional color filter are different methods. A red tree alone does not prove an infrared photograph. The modern digital example shown approximates the Aerochrome color world; it is not a historical Aerochrome film print.
effects.aftermath: An unnatural color can convey real, invisible information.
effects.funFact: Infrared false color can reveal differences that are barely noticeable in a normal color photo.
highlights: Vegetation often appears red or magenta

margin.note: Light just beyond visible red. Healthy leaves often reflect it strongly, so it can make vegetation stand out.

effects.title: Film Colorization
effects.name: Film Colorization
effects.dating: 1983–86, expanding computer colorization; Ted Turner becomes a prominent advocate
effects.caption: Colorized Silent-Film Character. A silent-film character appears with softly tinted skin, light brown hair, and dark clothing against a muted interior.
effects.credit: Bink111 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Black-and-white footage gains added hues while retaining its original light and shadow. Early versions often show muted skin tones and broad color areas.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Operators assign colors to selected regions in digitized frames, then software helps carry those choices across successive frames. The original brightness information supplies shading; the added colors are interpretations, not recovered records of the scene.

body.label: Example
body.text: Hal Roach Studios: It's a Wonderful Life, 1986 (computer-colorized version).

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Color a grayscale photograph using a transparent digital layer, then compare how two different skin colors preserve the same shading.

context: Computer colorization became commercially prominent during the 1980s, building on much older practices of coloring finished film images. Operators selected colors and outlined regions, such as faces, clothing, and backgrounds. Software helped transfer these assignments between frames, while technicians corrected movement and boundaries. The resulting versions circulated through television and home video, rather than changing the original camera negatives. Ted Turner championed colorized versions of older films, provoking opposition from filmmakers and preservationists. Critics argued that adding color could alter deliberate artistic choices, even when the black-and-white source survived.
effects.distinction: Unlike photography on color film, colorization adds color after the original image has been recorded. Unlike uniform tinting, it can give different objects different colors within one frame.
effects.aftermath: Colorization shows how an image can preserve recorded shading while replacing important parts of its visual meaning.
effects.funFact: Colorists can give the same gray costume several plausible colors without changing its shading.

margin.note: Individual film images converted into numerical data that a computer can process.
The recorded pattern of light and dark. It helps preserve shadows and surface detail when colors are added.
The film exposed inside the camera and then developed. Later colored copies need not alter this source material.

effects.title: Film Grain
effects.name: Film grain
effects.dating: 1960s reportage aesthetics; film grain has existed since earlier emulsions.
effects.caption: Kodak Tri-X 400: Section of a real negative scan to show the grain. Evenly exposed test area.
effects.credit: Wiley.andrew.r / CC0; Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Irregular fine structure becomes visible under magnification.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Developed silver particles or dye clouds form the granular texture.

body.label: Example
body.text: Enlarged scan of a Kodak Tri-X negative.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare the grain at 100 percent and as a small overall picture.

context: Visible graininess depends on factors such as film type, format, development, and enlargement. Highly sensitive 35mm film combined mobility and low-light capabilities with a clearly visible texture. Later digital image processing adopted grain as a marker of material, reportage, and memory. A good reproduction takes image size and brightness into account, rather than simply applying the same fixed layer of noise.
effects.distinction: Film grain is not the same as digital sensor noise or JPEG blockiness. Scan sharpening and compression can alter its appearance. The decade chosen here describes an aesthetic use, not an invention of the emulsion.
effects.aftermath: Texture should match the image size and exposure.
effects.funFact: In color film, the visible graininess is caused by dye clouds, not by remaining image silver.

margin.note: Tiny colored dye formations in developed color film that contribute to its visible texture.

effects.title: Film Noir Lighting
effects.name: Film Noir Lighting
effects.dating: 1940s, American crime and detective films
effects.caption: Venetian Blind Shadows Cast Across A Face. Harsh light filters through venetian blinds, casting distinctively striped, high-contrast shadows across a young man's face.
effects.credit: Robby McKee · CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see stark contrasts between blinding white light and pitch-black shadows. Distinctive patterns, like venetian blinds, often fall across faces.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Cinematographers use hard, undiffused light sources placed at harsh angles. They intentionally block most light to leave deep, unlit shadows.

body.label: Example
body.text: Billy Wilder: Double Indemnity, 1944.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Shine a harsh flashlight through a slotted object in a dark room to cast sharp striped shadows on a wall.

context: In the 1940s, Hollywood studios needed to produce cheap crime films rapidly. To save money on building detailed sets, directors hid empty backgrounds in deep shadows. German expressionist filmmakers, fleeing Europe, brought over this moody visual style. They adapted high-contrast theater lighting to black-and-white film stock. By relying on a single hard light source, technicians created sharp edges. This subtractive approach actively blocked light using flags or blinds. It perfectly matched the pessimistic, morally ambiguous themes of the postwar era.
effects.distinction: Unlike standard three-point lighting, noir lighting removes the soft fill light. This leaves shadows completely dark instead of gently brightening them.
effects.aftermath: It shows how hiding details in shadow creates more psychological tension than revealing everything.
effects.funFact: Low-key lighting actually requires bright, intense lamps to blast through heavy shadow modifiers.

margin.note: Window coverings made of horizontal slats that can be tilted to control light. They create distinct striped shadow patterns.
Light that travels directly from a bulb without passing through a softening material. It produces very sharp, crisp shadows.
Opaque panels placed in front of a light source on a film set. Technicians use them to block light from hitting specific areas.

effects.title: Film Tinting
effects.name: Film Tinting
effects.dating: 1890s, early silent cinema
effects.caption: Yellow-Tinted Aviation Scene. Two men stand beside an aircraft in a film sample with golden-yellow highlights and deep dark shadows.
effects.credit: Eastman Kodak · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: The entire film frame is bathed in a single, uniform color. The light areas take on this bright hue, while the darkest shadows remain mostly black.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Developed black-and-white film strips are soaked in liquid aniline dyes. The dye chemically bonds to the gelatin emulsion on the film base.

body.label: Example
body.text: Robert Wiene: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, 1920.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a tinted silent film scene and note how the single color dictates the overall emotional mood.

context: Early filmmakers quickly realized black-and-white images lacked emotional impact and narrative clarity. By the 1900s, they began soaking entire film rolls in colored dye baths. This technique changed the lighter parts of the printed image to a specific color. Studios standardized these colors to signal specific times or settings to the audience. Blue always meant night, while yellow or amber indicated bright daylight. Red signaled fire, danger, or passion, and green represented nature or eerie situations. This cheap, effective method dominated silent cinema until the late 1920s.
effects.distinction: Unlike film toning, which replaces the dark silver shadows with color, tinting only dyes the lighter gelatin areas. Hand-coloring paints individual objects, whereas tinting washes the whole frame.
effects.aftermath: It shows how early cinema used clever chemical workarounds to solve narrative and emotional storytelling problems.
effects.funFact: Some projectionists had to manually change glass color filters over the lens during untinted film screenings.

margin.note: Synthetic organic dyes originally derived from coal tar. They dissolve easily in water to create bright, transparent colors.
A light-sensitive layer painted onto the plastic film strip. It holds the image and absorbs liquid dyes perfectly.

context: Fisheye lenses had precursors in scientific and meteorological applications. In 1962, Nikon offered a corresponding lens for the 35mm system with the Fisheye-Nikkor 8mm f/8. effects.title: Flash Powder Photography
effects.name: Flash Powder Photography
effects.dating: 1887, invention of Blitzlicht; 1888, Jacob Riis's tenement photos
effects.caption: Flash-Lit Lodging in a Cellar. A man rests on bedding laid across barrels in a rough brick cellar, his face and clothing sharply illuminated against dark recesses.
effects.credit: Jacob Riis · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see stark, high-contrast scenes with harsh, frontal lighting. Backgrounds often fall into deep black shadows. Subjects may look startled, frozen, or have harsh outlines.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Igniting a mix of magnesium powder and potassium chlorate creates a sudden, intense burst of artificial light. This brief flash exposes the photographic plate before subjects can move.

body.label: Example
body.text: Jacob Riis: Lodgers in a Crowded Bayard Street Tenement, 1889.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Shine a harsh, unshaded flashlight directly into someone's face in a dark room and notice the flat, stark shadows.

context: Before the 1880s, photographers relied entirely on sunlight or very long exposures. Dark interiors and night scenes were nearly impossible to capture. In 1887, German scientists invented a reliable flash powder using magnesium and an oxidizing agent. This powder burned in a fraction of a second, producing a blinding white light. Social reformers like Jacob Riis quickly adopted this dangerous technique. He carried a frying pan of powder into dark New York tenements. The sudden explosion captured poverty in places sunlight never reached. This harsh, artificial illumination revolutionized documentary photography, exposing hidden social realities to the public.
effects.distinction: Unlike modern electronic flash, flash powder was an open, explosive chemical reaction. It produced a massive cloud of thick white smoke and posed a serious fire hazard.
effects.aftermath: It proves that portable, instant artificial light fundamentally changed what kind of stories photography could tell.
effects.funFact: Photographers often caused severe burns or set rooms on fire when using unstable flash powder.

margin.note: A highly flammable metallic dust that burns with a brilliant, blinding white light when ignited.
A chemical compound used to provide extra oxygen, making the magnesium burn much faster and brighter.
A substance that releases oxygen during a chemical reaction, fueling rapid combustion or explosions.

effects.title: Flat Design
effects.name: Flat Design
effects.dating: 2010s; Windows 8, 2012, and iOS 7, 2013
effects.caption: Football in Solid Colour. A brown American football is reduced to a broad silhouette, white stripes, white laces, and thin seam lines.

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see solid colour fields, simplified icons, and clear typography arranged with generous spacing. Strict examples avoid gradients, textures, bevels, and cast shadows.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Uniform colour fills replace simulated lighting and material surfaces. Visual hierarchy comes from contrast, size, alignment, and spacing rather than rendered depth.

body.label: Example
body.text: Microsoft: Windows 8 Start screen, 2012.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a button with a gradient and shadow, then redraw it using one solid colour; compare how clearly each suggests clicking.

context: Flat design became prominent in digital interfaces during the early 2010s, drawing on older traditions of geometric graphics and orderly typography. Microsoft's Metro design language shaped Windows Phone and the Windows 8 Start screen. Apple's iOS 7 helped popularise the broader shift in 2013, although it retained gradients, translucency, and depth effects. Strict flat design replaces simulated materials with solid fills and simplified shapes. Designers use scale, spacing, and colour contrast to organise information. Removing familiar button edges can, however, make interactive controls harder to recognise.
effects.distinction: Unlike skeuomorphism, flat design generally avoids imitating physical materials and objects. Unlike minimalism, it specifically reduces depth cues, not necessarily content or colour.
effects.aftermath: Flat design shows how typography and spacing can organise a screen, but decoration sometimes provides useful clues about interaction.
effects.funFact: Despite its reputation for flatness, iOS 7 included a wallpaper effect that suggested depth as the phone tilted.

margin.note: The arrangement that helps viewers notice important elements first and understand what belongs together.
Sloping edges, often drawn with highlights and shading to make a shape look raised or recessed.
Partial visibility through a surface, often simulated by blending or blurring the content behind it.

effects.title: Flicker Film
effects.name: Flicker Film
effects.dating: 1960s; Tony Conrad’s The Flicker, 1966
effects.caption: AI illustration: Sequential representation of a flicker film screening.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: The screen pulses through alternating black and white frames, often without recognizable objects. Viewers may perceive illusory colors or shifting patterns.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Rapid changes in projected light stimulate the visual system, producing sensations beyond the recorded images. The timing of light pulses shapes the experience.

body.label: Example
body.text: Tony Conrad: The Flicker, 1966.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Arrange black and white paper squares into different sequences; compare their rhythms without flashing lights, which can trigger seizures.

context: During the 1960s, experimental filmmakers made projected light itself a subject, rather than simply a carrier of photographed scenes. Tony Conrad’s The Flicker used sequences of black and white frames to organize darkness and brightness over time. Clear areas of the film print transmit light, while dense black areas largely block it. Changing the sequences changes the rhythm, even when the projector runs at a fixed speed. Some viewers perceive colors or patterns absent from the film. These responses vary, and flashing light can trigger photosensitive seizures.
effects.distinction: Unlike ordinary projector flicker, flicker film deliberately organizes brightness changes within the film’s frames. A still image cannot reproduce this temporal effect.
effects.aftermath: Flicker film shows that perceived images can arise from timed light changes, not just pictures recorded on film.
effects.funFact: The Flicker begins with a warning about possible physical effects on viewers.

margin.note: Colors perceived by a viewer even though those colors are not present in the projected frames.
The physical strip of film run through a projector to show a movie.
Seizures triggered by certain flashing lights or visual patterns in susceptible people.

effects.title: Flip Book
effects.name: Flip Book
effects.dating: 1868, John Barnes Linnett’s kineograph patent
effects.caption: Antique Fencing Flip Book. A small antique picture booklet rests partly outside its brown sleeve, with two fencing figures visible on the exposed page and layered paper edges below.
effects.credit: SunOfErat · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: A stack of small pictures becomes a moving scene when its pages are released rapidly under the thumb. Slight changes between successive pictures create a short action, often with visible flicker.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Each page carries a separate frame, showing a different stage of movement. Rapid sequential viewing produces apparent motion: the visual system interprets changing still images as movement.

body.label: Example
body.text: John Barnes Linnett: Kineograph patent illustrations, 1868.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a ball at slightly different heights across twenty page corners, then compare slow and fast flipping.

context: John Barnes Linnett patented the kineograph in Britain in 1868. It placed successive images in a bound sequence rather than around a rotating drum or disc. The viewer bent the pages and released them with a thumb, briefly revealing each picture. Page order supplied the sequence, while the viewer’s hand controlled its speed. Drawings or photographs could provide the images. This compact format helped establish animation as something people could handle directly. Its mechanism needed neither projection nor a separate viewing machine.
effects.distinction: A zoetrope presents images inside a rotating drum, viewed through slits. A flip book replaces the drum and slits with sequentially released pages.
effects.aftermath: It shows how image order, spacing, and viewing speed shape perceived movement.
effects.funFact: Flipping through the pages in reverse order can make the action run backward.

margin.note: One still image within a sequence that represents movement.
Movement perceived when separate still images appear in succession. No pictured object actually travels across the paper.
Using light and lenses to display an image on a separate surface.

effects.title: Fluid Simulation
effects.name: Fluid Simulation
effects.dating: Late 1990s to 2000s
effects.caption: 3D fluid simulation splashing over colored spheres. Highly realistic 3D rendered fluid is shown splashing dynamically over brightly colored molecular spheres.
effects.credit: Nbrawand · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see highly realistic water, smoke, or fire moving naturally on a screen. It splashes, flows, and swirls just like physical matter.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Computers calculate the physics of millions of tiny digital particles interacting with each other. These calculations create an underlying grid that mimics natural fluid dynamics.

body.label: Example
body.text: Industrial Light & Magic: The Perfect Storm, 2000.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a real splash of water in slow motion. Compare its chaotic droplets to a 2000s CGI movie wave.

context: Before the late 1990s, animators had to draw or sculpt water effects by hand. This was tedious and rarely looked realistic. In the 2000s, computers became powerful enough to run complex mathematical equations. They used physics formulas, like the Navier-Stokes equations, inside 3D software. Instead of animating the surface, artists created volumes filled with interacting particles. The software calculated gravity, density, and collision for every single frame. Once the math was done, the particles were wrapped in a digital skin. This allowed water to crash, foam, and break apart naturally.
effects.distinction: It differs from traditional animation because the computer simulates physical laws automatically. Older methods required an artist to manually draw every changing shape.
effects.aftermath: It shows how advanced mathematics can perfectly replicate the chaotic beauty of nature.
effects.funFact: Some early movie fluid simulations took multiple days to calculate a single second of footage.

margin.note: The branch of physics that studies how liquids and gases move.
A set of mathematical formulas used to describe the flow of fluid substances.
A continuous 3D surface generated around scattered particles to make them look like a solid liquid.

effects.title: Focus Stacking
effects.name: Focus Stacking
effects.dating: 2000s, growing use of digital focus stacking in macro photography
effects.caption: Golden Bee Face in Extended Focus. A bee’s face fills the frame, revealing finely textured eyes, segmented antennae, and dense golden hairs.
effects.credit: USGS Bee Inventory and Monitoring Lab from Beltsville, Maryland, USA · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Tiny subjects show sharp detail across several depths, from nearby antennae to distant wings. This extended sharpness can coexist with a blurred background.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Software aligns separate exposures taken at different focus distances, then blends their sharp regions. The composite extends apparent depth of field without increasing the optical sharpness of any individual exposure.

body.label: Example
body.text: Levon Biss: Microsculpture, 2016.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph a stationary flower at three focus distances, then compare which parts are sharp before blending the images.

context: Focus stacking became more accessible during the 2000s as digital cameras and specialist software spread. It addressed a familiar macro problem: high magnification leaves very little depth of field. Photographers record successive focus slices by adjusting focus or moving the camera along a rail. Software aligns these images and combines their sharp regions after capture. Earlier microscopy methods also combined information from different focal planes. Stacking does not require a smaller aperture, which can soften fine detail through diffraction. Moving subjects and overlapping edges can produce blending errors.
effects.distinction: Stopping down increases depth of field within one exposure, but can introduce diffraction blur. Focus stacking combines multiple exposures, so subject movement can disrupt the result.
effects.aftermath: Focus stacking shows that a photograph's apparent sharpness can come from combining observations rather than from one optical view.
effects.funFact: A sharply rendered insect can be assembled from thousands of photographs.

margin.note: The range of distances that appears acceptably sharp in an image.
Images that each record a different thin zone of the subject in sharp focus.
Light spreads as it passes through an aperture. Very small apertures make this spreading visibly soften fine detail.

context: Disney's Darby O'Gill is a striking example of cinematic illusions of scale. Characters and set pieces are actually at different distances; the camera angle and focus make them appear as a single world. The 1950s represent this famous example, not an invention. Modern productions supplement the method with digital manipulations but retain its geometric foundations.
effects.distinction: The same perspective does not necessarily mean the same distance. A camera pan, changing eye level, or incorrect viewing angles can reveal the spatial illusion.
effects.aftermath: Size in the image depends on object size and camera distance.
effects.funFact: 649 lamps illuminated the huge stage for Darby O’Gill.

margin.note: Scenery built or chosen at a different size to make subjects appear larger or smaller relative to their surroundings.

effects.title: Fractal Flames
effects.name: Fractal Flames
effects.dating: 1992, Scott Draves's fractal flame algorithm
effects.caption: Blue Filament Vortex. Blue and violet filaments sweep through looping fans around a luminous central knot against black.
effects.credit: “Jon Zander (Digon3)" · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Glowing filaments curl into translucent ribbons, branching fans, and tangled spirals against dark backgrounds. Fine structures repeat at different scales, with smooth color transitions and bright knots.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A randomly chosen sequence of nonlinear transformations moves a point repeatedly, building a density map of its visited positions. Logarithmic brightness mapping reveals faint structures alongside dense regions, while transformation histories guide color.

body.label: Example
body.text: Scott Draves: Electric Sheep, 1999.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Magnify a fractal flame image and trace one ribbon, noting where fine strands merge into brighter knots.

context: Scott Draves developed fractal flames in 1992, extending iterated function systems with nonlinear transformations and a distinctive rendering method. Instead of drawing continuous luminous curves, the algorithm records many successive point positions. Frequently visited areas accumulate more samples. Logarithmic brightness mapping compresses this density range, preserving faint wisps without letting dense regions dominate. Color follows the sequence of transformations rather than representing physical temperature. Draves later used these methods in Electric Sheep, launched in 1999. This distributed computing artwork generates animated flames, with viewer votes influencing their evolution.
effects.distinction: Unlike a Mandelbrot image, a fractal flame usually maps the density of sampled point visits rather than escape behavior. Its glow is computed, not photographed fire or simulated light scattering.
effects.aftermath: Fractal flames show how repeated mathematical rules and density rendering can produce intricate forms that resemble luminous natural structures.
effects.funFact: Electric Sheep lets viewers influence the evolution of its animated fractal population by voting.

margin.note: Mathematical operations that can bend or warp coordinates, rather than only shifting, rotating, or uniformly scaling them.
A record of how many sampled points land in each image region.
Sets of mathematical transformations applied repeatedly, often producing detailed patterns from simple rules.

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see computer-generated mountains and valleys with jagged, repeating details. As the view zooms in, smaller shapes look identical to the larger shapes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An algorithm repeatedly divides flat triangles into smaller triangles. It offsets their center points randomly to create infinite, natural-looking roughness.

body.label: Example
body.text: Loren Carpenter: Vol Libre, 1980.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at rugged mountains in a video game. Notice how small rocks echo the shape of the whole peak.

context: In the late 1970s, computer graphics struggled to create realistic nature. Smooth polygons looked artificial and plastic. Mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot published theories on fractals, describing shapes with self-similarity across different scales. Loren Carpenter applied this math to 3D computer graphics. He wrote software that split large triangles into smaller ones, randomly shifting their heights. This simple recursive division generated highly detailed, irregular mountains very quickly. Carpenter debuted an animated flight through these mountains at a 1980 conference. The stunning realism revolutionized visual effects, soon leading to the Genesis Effect in Star Trek II.
effects.distinction: Unlike hand-painted matte paintings, fractal landscapes are true 3D models that a virtual camera can physically fly through.
effects.aftermath: It teaches that complex natural structures can be built rapidly from very simple mathematical rules.
effects.funFact: Carpenter's presentation was so impressive that Lucasfilm immediately hired him for their new computer division.

margin.note: A step-by-step set of mathematical instructions that a computer follows to solve a problem or generate an image.
A property where a small part of an object looks exactly like a miniature version of the whole object.
A process that repeats itself, breaking a geometric shape into smaller pieces using the exact same rule each time.

effects.name: Freelensing
effects.dating: 2010s popularization in digital photography and video; not a securely dated invention.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Narrow patches of selective focus drift through soft blur, sometimes crossed by pale light leaks. In video, brightness and sharpness can pulse as the lens moves.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A detached lens is held near the camera mount and tilted, changing the plane of focus. Stray light entering the open mount during exposure can wash out contrast or create flare.

body.label: Example
body.text: James Miller: Lens Whacking, 2012.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: In a clean indoor space, hold a detached manual lens near the mount without touching internal parts; gently tilt and observe focus.

context: Freelensing became conspicuous in digital photography and independent video during the 2010s, although moving lenses independently of cameras has much older precedents. Photographers hold an interchangeable lens just outside its mount rather than locking it into place. Tilting changes how the plane of focus intersects the subject. Moving the lens farther from the sensor also changes the available focusing range, often favoring nearby subjects. The open gap can admit stray light during exposure, producing flare and reduced contrast. Video makers often call the practice lens whacking, despite no actual striking being required.
effects.distinction: A tilt-shift lens provides controlled movements while remaining attached, normally excluding light from the mount. Freelensing adds an open gap and less repeatable movement; light leaks are possible, not essential.
effects.aftermath: Freelensing shows how lens alignment and stray light can change an image before any digital processing.
effects.funFact: Despite the name lens whacking, the lens should never strike the camera.

margin.note: An idealized flat surface in the scene where objects are focused most sharply. Tilting the lens changes its orientation.
Unwanted light reaching the image can create bright patches or a veil that reduces contrast.
The interval when light is recorded by the sensor or film. These light effects happen then, not during film development.

effects.title: Freeze Frame
effects.name: Freeze Frame
effects.dating: 1959, ending of The 400 Blows
effects.caption: AI illustration: Duplicated film frames of a boy running.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Moving film footage suddenly halts on a single, motionless image. The scene transforms instantly from dynamic motion into a still photograph.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An optical printer repeatedly duplicates a single frame of film onto a new negative. This creates a continuous strip of identical pictures.

body.label: Example
body.text: François Truffaut: The 400 Blows, 1959.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Pause a movie during a fast action scene to see how motion blur affects a single frozen frame.

context: Filmmakers used an optical printer to create the freeze frame effect. This large machine contained a projector linked to a camera. Technicians loaded the original film into the projector. They chose one specific frame to freeze. The camera photographed this exact frame over and over onto new film. When played back, the identical frames create the illusion of time stopping. François Truffaut famously used this in 1959 for The 400 Blows. The frozen image left the protagonist's fate ambiguous and suspended. It quickly became a popular narrative tool in modern cinema.
effects.distinction: A freeze frame is printed directly onto the film strip itself. In contrast, a paused video is a playback function controlled by the viewer.
effects.aftermath: It shows how stopping time can force an audience to dwell on a character's unresolved emotion.
effects.funFact: Early freeze frames often suffered from noticeable dust because the exact same specks were copied repeatedly.

margin.note: A mechanical device linking a film projector and a camera, used by technicians to re-photograph film strips for visual effects.
A strip of photographic film where light and dark areas are inverted, which is used as a master to print viewable copies.
The psychological and visual effect created when a continuous reel of moving pictures suddenly presents an unchanging image.

body.label: Example
body.text: 2001: A Space Odyssey, 1968.

context: For the Dawn of Man sequence from 2001, photographed landscapes were projected onto a special screen. Light preferentially returns to its source; the camera therefore sees a bright background image. A beam splitter brings the projection and camera close to the same axis and hides the shadow behind the foreground subject. Kubrick's production made the technique famous in 1968; rear projection remains a technically different setup.
effects.distinction: Front projection here refers to the historical combination technique using a retroreflective screen. Just any projector placed in front of a wall will not automatically produce the same image integration.
effects.aftermath: The position of the light source determines where shadows become visible in the recorded image.
effects.funFact: In 2001, large photographic banners were used for the landscape backgrounds.

margin.note: An optical surface that reflects some light and transmits the rest, allowing camera and projector paths to align.
A setup that projects a background onto a screen from behind, rather than from the actors’ side.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Glossy aqua bubbles, translucent glass panels, and vivid green landscapes appear against bright skies. Rounded icons and white highlights suggest clean, polished surfaces.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Digital gradients, simulated reflections, and transparency create the appearance of glass, water, and shiny plastic. Compositing combines these surfaces with photographs or rendered scenes.

body.label: Example
body.text: Microsoft: Windows Vista Aero interface, 2007.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a blue circle, add a pale oval highlight, and compare its apparent depth before and after the highlight.

context: Frutiger Aero is a retrospective label for a visual style common in 2000s interfaces, advertising, and digital illustration. Its name connects the Frutiger typeface with Microsoft's Aero interface. Designers paired technological surfaces with grass, water, clouds, and other reassuring natural imagery. Gradients and highlights suggested curved objects without requiring physically accurate rendering. In Windows Vista, desktop compositing enabled translucent window borders with blurred backgrounds. The broader style also appeared in static images, where transparency and reflections were simply painted or rendered. It describes a shared visual vocabulary, not one standardized technique.
effects.distinction: Skeuomorphism makes digital objects resemble familiar physical tools, such as a calculator or leather notebook. Frutiger Aero overlaps with it but emphasizes glossy surfaces and idealized nature.
effects.aftermath: It shows how simulated materials and natural imagery can make digital technology feel tangible and approachable.
effects.funFact: The name combines a typeface reference with a Microsoft interface name.

margin.note: Smooth changes between colors or brightness levels. They can suggest curved surfaces, lighting, or depth.
Combining separate visual layers into one image. Layers may include photographs, interface elements, and rendered objects.
Combining separately drawn windows into the final screen image. This allows effects such as transparent borders and background blur.

effects.title: Fumage
effects.name: Fumage
effects.dating: 1937, Wolfgang Paalen's surrealist technique
effects.caption: Four Smoke Plumes on Paper. Four dark, tapering plumes spread into a translucent gray veil across pale paper.
effects.credit: Edgar Degas · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see swirling, translucent gray and black patterns on a light background. These shapes often resemble clouds, ghosts, or organic textures.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Soot from a lit candle or lamp is deposited onto a surface like paper or canvas. The artist then fixes or alters this carbon layer.

body.label: Example
body.text: Wolfgang Paalen: Dictated by a Candle, 1938.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Hold a piece of sturdy paper safely above a burning candle and watch the black soot gather into strange shapes.

context: Fumage was popularized in 1937 by Wolfgang Paalen, a Surrealist artist seeking new ways to bypass conscious control. It relies on an additive process where a flame's carbon residue forms unpredictable, delicate marks. Paalen moved a blank canvas or paper over a lit candle, letting the rising smoke dictate the initial forms. Later, he often used a brush to manipulate the soot or painted over it to reveal hidden figures. This technique fit perfectly with the Surrealist goal of tapping into the subconscious. The delicate soot layer remains fragile until sprayed with a fixative varnish.
effects.distinction: Unlike sfumato, which uses soft brushstrokes to blur painted edges, fumage builds actual physical layers of burnt carbon. Sfumato is an optical blending technique, while fumage relies on direct soot deposition.
effects.aftermath: It shows how unpredictable natural elements like fire can become collaborative tools in art.
effects.funFact: Salvador Dalí later adopted the technique, calling his personal soot-based variations by the classical name sfumato.

margin.note: A method where material is added to a surface, rather than being carved or washed away.
The black soot left behind by incomplete burning, consisting mostly of pure carbon particles.
A clear liquid spray used to seal delicate drawings so the dry particles do not smudge.

effects.title: Fur Simulation
effects.name: Fur Simulation
effects.dating: 2001, Pixar's Monsters, Inc.
effects.caption: Big Buck Bunny Character Fur. A Big Buck Bunny DVD cover presents a large rabbit and smaller animal characters with visibly soft, strand-textured coats.
effects.credit: Film: Blender Foundation | www.bigbuckbunny.orgScreenshot: User:Toni Grappa · CC BY 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see realistic computer-generated hair or fur that moves naturally on a digital character. The hair catches light, casts soft shadows, and clumps together realistically.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Special software treats each hair as a flexible line of connected points. A physics engine calculates how these points move with wind or motion.

body.label: Example
body.text: Pixar Animation Studios: Monsters, Inc., 2001.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at a digital furry creature in a modern movie. Watch how the fur parts and reacts when the creature moves or shakes.

context: Before the 2000s, computer-generated characters had smooth, plastic-like skin. Animating millions of individual hairs was too computationally expensive. Early attempts used flat textures that merely looked like fur. Then, studios developed new physics programs to handle complex hair dynamics. These systems grouped hairs into clumps guided by a few master strands. This saved computing power while keeping realistic movement. Rendering engines also improved, calculating how light scatters through dense fur. Pixar's Monsters, Inc. became a major milestone. They created a custom program to simulate millions of hairs reacting to gravity.
effects.distinction: Fur simulation calculates individual moving strands using physics. This differs from texture mapping, which simply paints a flat image of fur onto a smooth surface.
effects.aftermath: It shows how managing massive data allowed computers to mimic the complex, organic chaos of nature.
effects.funFact: Sulley from Monsters, Inc. had exactly 2,320,413 individual hairs rendered for his body.

margin.note: Software that simulates real-world physical laws like gravity and momentum. It calculates how digital objects naturally fall or bend.
Programs that turn 3D data into a final 2D image. They calculate how virtual light bounces off digital surfaces.

effects.title: GAN Portraits
effects.name: GAN Portraits
effects.dating: 2014, Ian Goodfellow's Generative Adversarial Networks
effects.caption: Synthetic Smiling Man. A smiling young man appears in a tightly cropped portrait against a softly blurred outdoor setting.
effects.credit: StyleGAN2 · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see highly realistic, photographic portraits of human faces. Look closely to spot subtle distortions like melted backgrounds or asymmetrical earrings.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Two neural networks compete to generate and evaluate images. They repeat this until the artificial image passes for a real photograph. The system learns visual rules from real photos but lacks actual 3D understanding.

body.label: Example
body.text: Tero Karras et al. (NVIDIA): A Style-Based Generator Architecture for Generative Adversarial Networks (StyleGAN), 2018.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Visit the website 'This Person Does Not Exist'. Look at the edges of hair or glasses for blurry glitches.

context: In 2014, researcher Ian Goodfellow invented Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). A GAN uses two computer programs playing a game. The generator tries to forge an image, while the discriminator tries to spot the fake. They train together, improving rapidly. By 2018, NVIDIA engineers released StyleGAN. This system could produce incredibly high-resolution, photorealistic human faces. It analyzed thousands of celebrity photos to learn the statistical arrangement of human features. It did not copy any specific person. Instead, it mathematically combined learned features to invent entirely new, non-existent people.
effects.distinction: Traditional 3D CGI models are built manually by artists using actual spatial geometry. In contrast, GAN portraits are generated entirely by statistical algorithms mapping 2D pixels.
effects.aftermath: It teaches us that computers can convincingly fake reality by mapping mathematical patterns rather than understanding physical space.
effects.funFact: The first GAN concept was invented by Ian Goodfellow during a late-night argument at a pub.

margin.note: A type of computer program inspired by the human brain. It uses layers of connected nodes to process data.
An AI system where two algorithms compete against each other. One creates fake data, and the other tries to catch it.
The part of a GAN that evaluates images. It tries to determine if the generated image is real or fake.

effects.title: Generative Inpainting
effects.name: Generative inpainting
effects.dating: 2021–2022: LaMa research and more widely accessible generative image processing
effects.caption: DALL·E 2: documented inpainting demo example, 2022.
effects.credit: OpenAI / DALL·E 2, historical product example.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Masked image areas are filled with newly synthesized content.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A model fills in the gap based on the environment and, if necessary, text.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Replace an object; check shadows and continuous patterns.

context: Inpainting fills in missing or selected areas within an image. Classical methods existed before generative AI; this slide focuses on machine learning-based augmentations from the early 2020s. LaMa was presented as a preprint in 2021 and at the WACV conference in 2022. The method uses Fourier convolutions for large-scale spatial context and also demonstrates periodic structures. DALL·E 2 made describable image changes with appropriate surroundings, shadows, and textures publicly visible in 2022. The illustration is a documented demo from that time, not a newly created historical reconstruction. The key learning question is which cues are preserved. A local exchange must match the perspective, light, and material of the surrounding image.
effects.distinction: A plausible addition does not necessarily reconstruct the original content that was actually concealed.
effects.aftermath: Inpainting works within the chosen image area. Unlike repair by copying, it can invent new objects and structures.
effects.funFact: LaMa was trained on 256x256 pixel images and also demonstrated significantly higher resolutions.

margin.note: Parts of a picture marked for replacement or repair. The mask tells the model where it may generate new content.
New image material created by a model rather than directly photographed. It should fit the surrounding scene but need not reflect real events.

context: Outpainting extends an image area beyond its original boundaries. It is closely related to inpainting: a model fills in new areas while existing parts of the image serve as context. OpenAI publicly demonstrated a corresponding DALL·E function on August 31, 2022, including an extension of Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring. effects.title: Go Motion
effects.name: Go Motion
effects.dating: 1980, Phil Tippett and Industrial Light & Magic
effects.caption: AI illustration: Miniature dinosaur featuring photographic motion blur.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see an animated miniature creature or vehicle moving smoothly across the screen. Its fast-moving parts show a natural, streaky motion blur.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A computer controls motors connected to the puppet. The motors move the puppet slightly while the camera shutter is open.

body.label: Example
body.text: Phil Tippett: Dragonslayer, 1981.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Pause a go-motion scene and a standard stop-motion scene during fast action. Notice how go-motion frames look blurry while standard frames remain sharp.

context: Standard stop motion looks jerky because each frame captures a perfectly still puppet. In the late 1970s, Industrial Light and Magic needed smoother animation. Phil Tippett and his team developed go motion. They attached metal rods to the puppet and linked them to computer-controlled motors. As the camera exposed the film, the motors shifted the puppet slightly. This recorded a true motion blur directly onto the physical film. Later, animators combined these computer-driven rods with traditional hand animation for highly complex creature movements.
effects.distinction: Standard stop motion photographs a stationary object, resulting in a jerky, strobe-like sequence. Go motion actively moves the object during the photograph, creating natural optical blur.
effects.aftermath: It shows that copying physical camera limitations, like motion blur, helps artificial elements look completely real to the human eye.
effects.funFact: Go motion was used for Jurassic Park's dinosaurs before CGI fully replaced the technique.

margin.note: The visual streak captured when an object moves while a camera is actively taking a picture.
The exact moment when light is allowed to hit photographic film to record a picture.

effects.title: Gouraud Shading
effects.name: Gouraud Shading
effects.dating: 1971, Henri Gouraud's continuous shading method
effects.caption: Blue Torus with Gouraud Shading. A blue polygonal torus carries smoothly blended shadows and a bright, angular highlight.
effects.credit: Maarten Everts · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a 3D computer model with smooth, gradient-like surfaces instead of blocky facets. The colors blend seamlessly across the shape.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Software calculates lighting only at the corners of a flat polygon. It then blends these colors evenly across the surface.

body.label: Example
body.text: Henri Gouraud: Sylvia's Face (first smooth-shaded 3D facial model), 1971.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at an older 3D video game character. Notice how surfaces seem curved until you spot the straight, jagged outer edges.

context: In the early days of computer graphics, 3D objects were built from flat triangles or polygons. Early rendering simply colored each polygon with a single flat shade. This created very blocky, faceted shapes. In 1971, Henri Gouraud invented a faster way to make these faceted objects look smoothly curved. His method calculated the light bouncing off the vertices, which are the corners of each shape. The computer then smoothly blended those colors across the flat face. This optical trick saved immense computing power. It became a standard hardware feature in 3D graphics cards throughout the 1990s.
effects.distinction: Flat shading gives every polygon a single solid color. Phong shading calculates light at every single pixel, capturing precise glossy highlights that Gouraud shading misses.
effects.aftermath: It reveals how clever mathematical approximations can fool the human eye while saving massive amounts of computing power.
effects.funFact: Gouraud's wife, Sylvia, provided the physical face model used to demonstrate this famous smooth shading technique.

margin.note: A flat, closed geometric shape with straight sides. In 3D graphics, models are usually built from thousands of these flat shapes.
The automated process of using a computer program to generate a 2D image from a 3D model.
The singular corner points where the edges of a polygon meet. A triangle has exactly three vertices.

effects.title: Gradient Map
effects.name: Gradient map
effects.dating: Documented in Photoshop CS6 in 2012; digital precursors older.
effects.caption: Gradient mapping: modern digital image editor demonstration.
effects.credit: Digital effect demonstration.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Brightness levels appear as a freely selectable color sequence.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A color gradient replaces the tonal values of the original image.

body.label: Example
body.text: Multicolored editorial portraits and psychedelic posters.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Set three color stops; move only the middle one.

context: Gradient mapping treats brightness as an address within a color gradient. Dark areas of the image are assigned colors from the beginning, light areas from the end; additional color stops create the intermediate tones. The method is established in the official Photoshop CS6 documentation and is categorized here within the documented CS6 tool set of 2012, without claiming an unconfirmed year of invention. Unlike a geometric gradient overlay, the same brightness value receives the same assignment everywhere. Therefore, two widely separated areas can be assigned the same color. In this exercise, move a single color stop and observe how suddenly different facial features or landscape areas stand out. Tonal order and color order can be deliberately separated in this way.
effects.distinction: Gradient map follows brightness; a gradient overlaid on top follows its spatial position.
effects.aftermath: Duotone is the simple two-color relationship. With further stops, complex false colors, banding, or deliberately unnatural tonal jumps result.
effects.funFact: A gradient map colors according to brightness, not the position of a pixel.
highlights: tonal values of the original image

margin.note: The lightness or darkness of image areas, independent of their original hues.
Chosen colors at specific positions along a gradient. Moving one changes how the colors are distributed.

effects.title: Graduated Filter
effects.name: Graduated Filter
effects.dating: 1970s, popularized by the Cokin square filter system
effects.caption: Circular Graduated Color Filter. A circular screw-in filter transitions smoothly from nearly clear glass to a violet-gray tint.
effects.credit: Esquilo · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a photograph where one half is noticeably darker or differently colored than the other. The transition between the two halves is smooth and seamless.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A glass or resin filter is placed in front of the camera lens. It is tinted on one side and fades to clear on the other.

body.label: Example
body.text: Galen Rowell: Rainbow over the Potala Palace, 1981.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a bright sky through half-tinted sunglasses to see how the ground becomes easier to view.

context: Before digital editing, capturing a bright sky and a dark landscape in one shot was difficult. Film could not record both extremes at once. If the sky looked good, the ground was pitch black. If the ground was visible, the sky turned completely white. Photographers solved this by placing a graduated filter over the lens. The dark half covered the sky, reducing its brightness. The clear half covered the ground, letting in full light. This optical trick balanced the exposure directly on the film. In the 1970s, square filter systems made it easy to slide the gradient up or down.
effects.distinction: Unlike a polarizing filter, which darkens skies based on the sun's angle, a graduated filter darkens any physically covered area.
effects.aftermath: It shows how physical optical tools solved dynamic range limits long before digital software existed.
effects.funFact: Some early photographers used a moving black card during exposure to achieve a similar effect.

margin.note: A tough, transparent synthetic plastic often used instead of glass to make lightweight camera filters.

effects.title: Grunge Typography
effects.name: Grunge Typography
effects.dating: 1990s; David Carson’s art direction for Ray Gun, launched in 1992
effects.caption: Distressed Multicolor Festival Typography. Oversized festival lettering fills the composition in blue, orange, yellow, white, and black, with speckled gaps and overlapping forms.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Letters show broken edges, uneven spacing, and overlapping layers. Scratches, stains, mixed sizes, and abrupt changes of direction make text look worn or unstable.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Photocopy degradation, physical abrasion, or digital masks interrupt letter shapes. Layering and irregular placement disrupt the reading order without necessarily damaging the type itself.

body.label: Example
body.text: David Carson: Ray Gun magazine art direction, 1992.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photocopy a printed headline several times, using each copy as the next original; compare its edges with the first print.

context: Grunge typography became prominent in 1990s music magazines, record packaging, and alternative publishing. It drew on punk graphics, photocopied zines, collage, and earlier experiments with fragmented text. David Carson’s work for Ray Gun helped make disrupted reading order widely recognizable. Designers combined damaged source material with desktop publishing, scanning, and digital manipulation. Some roughness came from repeated copying; other marks were deliberately drawn or digitally imposed. The result challenged the idea that typography should always be clean and immediately readable. Its visual disorder was often carefully composed.
effects.distinction: Distressed typography describes damaged-looking letters, even within an orderly layout. Grunge typography also includes disruptive composition, so intact letters can contribute to the effect.
effects.aftermath: It teaches that typography communicates mood through texture and arrangement, sometimes at the expense of easy reading.
effects.funFact: Carson famously set a Bryan Ferry interview in Zapf Dingbats, replacing readable letters with symbols.

margin.note: Repeated copying can lose fine details, thicken marks, and introduce specks. Results depend on the copier and its settings.
These control which parts of an image or letter remain visible. They can create gaps without erasing the original shape.
Computer software used to arrange text and images into pages ready for printing.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Grainy, chalky, or painterly surfaces. Brushstrokes and pigments significantly alter the character of a photograph.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A light-sensitive pigment layer made of gum arabic forms the print. Washing and hand-finishing control the visible tonal values.

context: Invented in 1855, revived in the 1890s; Demachy influential from 1894 onwards. Pictorialist art photography around 1900. Detailed mechanism: Pigment, gum arabic, and light-sensitive dichromate are applied to paper, exposed through a negative, and developed in water. Manual processing alters the print. The painterly effect can arise in the printing material itself; it does not necessarily have to be a manipulated photograph.
effects.distinction: The painterly effect can occur in the printed material; it does not have to be a manipulated photograph.
effects.aftermath: Painterly filters, texture overlays, and alternative photographic printing processes.
effects.funFact: Gum printing was developed in 1855 and experienced an artistic revival about forty years later.

margin.note: A natural tree gum that binds pigment in the coating. With a light-sensitive dichromate added, exposed areas become less soluble in water.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Bright light sources develop colored, often red, fringes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Light is reflected back in the film carrier or at the pressure plate.

body.label: Example
body.text: CineStill-800T night shot with bright highlights.

body.label: Try it out

context: Antihalation coatings are intended to reduce disruptive back reflections in photographic material. If they are not used or function differently, a characteristic halo can appear around overexposed light sources. Since the 2010s, CineStill has associated this visible characteristic with a popular analog night look. This association describes the current revival; the technical phenomenon was already known in older black-and-white and specialty photography.
effects.distinction: Halation is not a general blurring effect, and not every halo is halation. Lens scattering and digital bloom effects can have a similar appearance. Color and intensity depend on the specific film stock and exposure.
effects.aftermath: A local material defect can become a trademark.
effects.funFact: Halation can also occur with a sharply focused light source.

margin.note: The transparent base that supports a film’s light-sensitive layers. Reflected light can pass back through these layers.

effects.title: Harmonograph
effects.name: Harmonograph
effects.dating: 1840s; invention often attributed to Hugh Blackburn in 1844
effects.caption: Harmonograph Tracing a Green Mesh. A green pen traces a fine, overlapping mesh on paper suspended by chains beneath a wooden mechanism.
effects.credit: Exhibit made by Estes Objethos Atelier photo by Rodrigo Tetsuo Argenton · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Fine lines form nested loops, woven meshes, and narrowing spirals. Repeated crossings create dense bands as the drawing gradually contracts.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Combined pendulum motions move a pen relative to paper, producing curves related to Lissajous figures. Mechanical damping reduces the swings, so successive loops shrink.

body.label: Example
body.text: Anthony Ashton: Harmonograph: A Visual Guide to the Mathematics of Music, 2003.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Suspend a leaking sand cup over a tray, start an elliptical swing, and watch successive loops shrink as the motion fades.

context: The harmonograph emerged in the nineteenth century, with its invention often attributed to Hugh Blackburn in 1844. Later makers developed several arrangements of pendulums, pens, and moving tables. Some machines move the pen in two directions; others also move the paper. Pendulum lengths help determine the frequency ratio, which shapes the pattern. Simple ratios can produce orderly, repeating loops. Friction and air resistance gradually drain energy, drawing those loops inward. These machines connected demonstrations of vibration with decorative drawing, making relationships between rhythmic motions visible without photography.
effects.distinction: A Spirograph uses gears to constrain a tracing point, rather than freely swinging pendulums. Ideal Lissajous figures have constant amplitudes; harmonograph drawings usually show shrinking amplitudes.
effects.aftermath: The harmonograph shows how simple oscillations can combine into intricate patterns while recording the gradual loss of mechanical energy.
effects.funFact: Some harmonographs move the paper as well as the pen.

margin.note: Curves formed by combining two perpendicular back-and-forth motions. Their shapes depend on the motions' frequencies and relative timing.
The loss of motion as mechanical energy is dissipated, often through friction or air resistance.
A comparison of how often two motions repeat. A ratio of 2:1 means one repeats twice for every cycle of the other.

effects.title: HDR Imaging
effects.name: HDR imaging / tone mapping
effects.dating: Research 1997. Photo editing wave of the 2000s, around CS2 2005.
effects.caption: HDR tone mapping: exposure series above, composite representation below: Cody Pope, 2007.
effects.credit: Cody Pope. CC BY-SA 2.5

body.label: Identify
body.text: Bright windows and dark rooms retain detail. Extreme variations overemphasize clouds, structures, and edges.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Exposure bracketing provides a greater dynamic range. Tone mapping translates this data into a displayable image.

body.label: Example
body.text: Debevec/Malik: important method 1997. Photoshop CS2: Merge to HDR 2005.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare normal exposure, natural HDR, and extreme tone mapping. When does shadow information become a stylistic device?

context: Important research work in 1997; particularly visible for photo editing in the 2000s, e.g. Photoshop CS2 (2005).

Several differently exposed photographs are combined to create an image with a wider dynamic range. Tone mapping translates this range into a displayable version. Strong local tone mapping can overemphasize textures and contrast.
Debevec and Malik, Recovering High Dynamic Range Radiance Maps from Photographs (SIGGRAPH 1997); Merge to HDR in Photoshop CS2 (2005).

Regarding the illustration: Example image. Nine exposures capture scene areas with varying brightness. The combined, wide range of brightness is compressed for visual display. This example demonstrates the basis of the HDR look; extreme local contrast enhancement would be a possible additional stylistic choice.
effects.distinction: HDR data, HDR display, and the popular HDR photo look are not the same thing. Tone mapping can be very subtle. HDR is not a 2000s invention and does not automatically result in an over-sharpened HDR look. Capture/reconstruction and display are two separate steps.
effects.aftermath: A motif could be shown closer to the wide brightness range of the scene or deliberately hyperrealistically; the technical rescue process became a style in its own right.
effects.funFact: An important HDR research paper was published in 1997; Photoshop CS2 introduced Merge to HDR in 2005.

margin.note: Taking several photographs of the same scene at different exposure settings.
The span between the darkest and brightest detail an image or device can represent.
Compressing a wide range of brightness into a range a display can show while preserving useful detail.

context: Niépce's experiments began in the 1810s; the first surviving camera photograph dates from 1827. This is a historical starting point, not a mass-produced look of the time. The detailed mechanism: Light hardens a thin layer of bitumen on a tin plate. The coated plate records the camera image over a very long period. Before every filter, the question arises: What is image information, and what is the inherent property of the material?
effects.distinction: Before every filter, the question arises: What is image information, what is the nature of the material?
effects.aftermath: Distinguish between materiality, exposure time, and subsequent contrast enhancement.
effects.funFact: Niépce's surviving camera image from 1827 was taken on metal, not photographic paper.
highlights: Light hardens a layer of bitumen

margin.note: A dark, tar-like material that becomes less soluble after exposure to light. Washing away the unhardened areas leaves an image.
The period during which light reaches a light-sensitive surface. Heliography required exceptionally long exposures.

effects.title: Hollywood Glamour Lighting
effects.name: Hollywood Glamour Lighting
effects.dating: 1940s studio glamour, developed during the preceding decades
effects.caption: Butterfly Shadow and Sculpted Cheekbones. A monochrome portrait presents a woman with waved hair, bright cheekbones, and a compact shadow beneath her nose.
effects.credit: George Hurrell · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Sculpted cheekbones, luminous skin, and a butterfly-shaped shadow beneath the nose define a common version of this look. Bright hair highlights and deep backgrounds often accompany a soft glow around facial highlights.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A key light placed above the camera and aimed downward creates the central nose shadow; separate lights can outline the hair. Optical diffusion spreads bright light into neighboring image areas, while negative retouching can smooth skin without changing the lighting pattern.

body.label: Example
body.text: George Hurrell: Portrait of Jane Russell, 1941.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Aim a desk lamp downward from above your phone camera, then move it sideways and watch the nose shadow shift.

context: Hollywood studios used carefully lit portraits to shape stars’ public identities during the 1930s and 1940s. George Hurrell became closely associated with this dramatic portrait style. Butterfly lighting, also called Paramount lighting, was one arrangement within a broader vocabulary, not a requirement for every glamour portrait. A high frontal lamp emphasized cheekbones and placed a small shadow beneath the nose. Fill light controlled shadow depth, while additional lamps separated hair from the background. Optical diffusion and negative retouching could soften the result, even when the original lighting produced crisp shadows.
effects.distinction: Rembrandt lighting places the main light farther to one side, producing a small illuminated triangle on the shadowed cheek. Butterfly lighting instead centers the nose shadow; neither arrangement automatically creates a soft glow.
effects.aftermath: This style shows how light placement shapes facial form, while diffusion and retouching separately shape the appearance of skin.
effects.funFact: The “butterfly” is a nose shadow, not a special lamp or lens.

margin.note: The main light that establishes the direction and shape of illumination on a subject.
Scattering light during image formation softens detail and can spread highlights. It differs from simply moving the lens out of focus.
Physical alteration of a photographic negative to change the resulting print. Portrait retouchers could reduce visible blemishes and wrinkles.
