effects.title: Holography
effects.name: Holography
effects.dating: 1962, Emmett Leith and Juris Upatnieks' first laser transmission holograms
effects.caption: Red Laser Reconstructing a Transmission Hologram. A brilliant red laser beam illuminates a glass plate, revealing a fully three-dimensional scene of a Smurf standing before a clock.
effects.credit: Tomasz Kawalec · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a fully three-dimensional image trapped on a flat surface. As you move your head, the perspective changes, revealing different sides of the object.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A laser beam is split in two to record the interference pattern of light waves bouncing off an object. When illuminated later, this microscopic pattern bends light to perfectly reconstruct the original 3D light field.

body.label: Example
body.text: Emmett Leith and Juris Upatnieks: Train and Bird, 1964.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at a holographic sticker on a credit card. Tilt it back and forth to see how the image has depth and changes perspective, unlike a regular flat print.

context: Hungarian-British physicist Dennis Gabor first proposed holography in 1947 to improve electron microscopes. However, practical 3D holography required a pure, coherent light source. The invention of the laser in 1960 changed everything. By 1962, researchers Emmett Leith and Juris Upatnieks successfully created the first high-quality 3D laser holograms. They achieved this by splitting a single laser beam. One part hit a photographic plate directly, while the other bounced off an object first. The meeting of these two beams created an interference pattern. This captured not just the intensity of light, but its physical phase. Developing the plate locked this microscopic wave record in place permanently.
effects.distinction: Lenticular prints use tiny plastic lenses over sliced images to fake depth from specific angles. Holography uses microscopic wave interference to recreate a continuous, true 3D light field.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that light behaves as a physical wave, and its phase can be frozen and replayed.
effects.funFact: You can cut a hologram in half and still see the entire whole object.

margin.note: A complex web of bright and dark spots created when two waves of light collide and overlap.
Light where all the electromagnetic waves are perfectly synchronized in frequency and phase, like a marching band.
The exact position of a wave within its cycle at a given moment. Capturing this provides the depth information.

effects.title: Hyperlapse
effects.name: Hyperlapse
effects.dating: 2012, term popularized by Shahab Gabriel Behzumi's videos
effects.caption: AI illustration: Spatial translation sequence toward an urban landmark.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a fast-paced video moving smoothly across vast physical distances. The camera travels through a city while time accelerates rapidly.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A camera captures still photos at set intervals while moving across space. Software then aligns these frames to create smooth continuous motion.

body.label: Example
body.text: Shahab Gabriel Behzumi: Berlin Hyper-Lapse, 2012.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Walk down a street, stopping every three steps to take a photo of the same distant building, then flip through them.

context: A traditional time-lapse keeps the camera strictly locked in one place. A hyperlapse breaks this rule by moving the camera over long distances. Photographers historically achieved this manually by shifting a tripod inches at a time. This manual method required intense precision to keep the target centered. In the 2010s, digital image stabilization software changed everything. Creators could walk with a camera, taking photos continuously. Algorithms then smoothed out the bumpy path by tracking fixed points. This created a floating, cinematic journey through time and space.
effects.distinction: A standard time-lapse relies on a stationary camera watching a changing scene. A hyperlapse moves the camera significantly over large physical distances.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how combining spatial movement with compressed time creates an entirely new perspective on urban environments.
effects.funFact: Early creators calculated precise camera movements using measuring tape on the ground.

margin.note: The fixed amount of time or physical distance between each captured photograph.
Software techniques that reduce blurring and shaking in a sequence of images.
Software identifies high-contrast pixels on a building to keep it centered in every frame.

effects.title: Image Morphing
effects.name: Image morphing
effects.dating: Cinema milestone Willow (1988). Pop wave of the early 1990s.
effects.caption:
Willow, 1988: original intermediate images of the MORF transformation.
Temporal effect: still image or image sequence.
effects.credit: Industrial Light & Magic / Lucasfilm; VFX Voice. © 1988 Lucasfilm Limited

body.label: Identify
body.text: Eyes, mouth, and outlines flow continuously from one figure into another.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Corresponding image features are assigned. Geometric distortion and simultaneous blending create a controlled transition between the shapes.

body.label: Example
body.text: Willow (1988): Fin Raziel transforms back into a human via animal forms.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Highlight identical features in two portraits. Compare the blending and morphing effects. Observe shifting contours.

context: cinematic milestone 1988; particularly visible pop wave in the early 1990s.

Matching features of two images are assigned to each other. Both images are geometrically distorted and simultaneously blended. In this way, the shape shifts, instead of simply replacing one image with the other.
Willow (1988): Fin Raziel transforms through several animal forms back into a human. Later pop reference: Michael Jackson, Black or White (1991).

Regarding the illustration: Historical original / source image. Eight successive image states show how animals transition into one another through fluid changes in form; reproduced original image sequence.
effects.distinction: Dissolve = change in transparency. Morph = change in shape plus transition. Generative AI morphs do not need to use explicit point correspondences. Form interpolation already existed. Willow is a breakthrough for convincing digital morphing in popular film, not an invention of every type of transformation.
effects.aftermath: The digital transformation itself became an attraction and later the familiar effect of music videos, advertising and apps.
effects.funFact: Willow showcased digital morphing in 1988 – three years before Michael Jackson's Black or White.
highlights: flow continuously from one figure into another

margin.note: Matching points or regions, such as the eyes in two portraits, that guide a smooth transformation.
Moving or warping image positions to align shapes, rather than merely fading one image into another.

effects.title: Image-Based Lighting
effects.name: Image-Based Lighting
effects.dating: 1999, Paul Debevec's film "Fiat Lux"
effects.caption: AI illustration: Reflective chrome light probe in a cathedral interior.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see computer-generated 3D objects that look remarkably real because they reflect their exact surroundings. The virtual shadows and highlights perfectly match the lighting of the real-world background.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A 360-degree photograph captures all incoming light in a real location. Software uses this high dynamic range image as a giant spherical light source to illuminate virtual models.

body.label: Example
body.text: Paul Debevec: Fiat Lux, 1999.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Hold a shiny metal ball bearing outdoors and observe how it catches the entire sky and ground. Notice how the sun creates a blindingly bright spot compared to the clouds.

context: Image-based lighting revolutionized visual effects in the early 2000s. Before this, artists manually placed hundreds of virtual lamps to mimic real sunlight. Paul Debevec popularized a new method using a mirrored chrome ball. By photographing the ball at different exposures, he captured all real-world light data. This created a high dynamic range image, or HDRI. Software then wraps this HDRI around a virtual scene like a glowing dome. Every pixel in the photograph acts as a tiny spotlight. This ensures virtual objects cast realistic shadows and reflect their environment flawlessly. It seamlessly blends fake objects into real footage.
effects.distinction: Unlike simple environment mapping which only mimics reflections on shiny surfaces, IBL actually uses the image pixels to calculate realistic light and shadows. Standard 3D lighting relies on artificial point lamps instead of photographic data.
effects.aftermath: It proved that capturing actual real-world light data is far more convincing than trying to recreate it manually.
effects.funFact: Chrome balls used on movie sets are often hollow garden gazing spheres bought from local hardware stores.

margin.note: A digital picture containing extreme levels of brightness and darkness, holding much more data than a standard photo.
A virtual dome of light that surrounds a 3D scene, casting illumination inward from all directions.

context: Ink bleed initially describes a material behavior of ink and paper. A digital simulation is placed in the 2020s here because modern digital filter techniques allow the spread to be controlled in real time with masks, direction, and grain. A simple blur distributes values ​​more evenly and therefore has a different effect. Experiment with the same spread on thin and thick type. body.label: Identify
body.text: Many early presets show faded blacks, warm color casts, and darkened corners. Some add pale borders or strong contrast, suggesting aged snapshots.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Digital presets remap pixel colors and brightness through tone curves and color adjustments. Added vignettes and borders imitate photographic artifacts without changing camera exposure or chemically developing film.

body.label: Example
body.text: Kevin Systrom: Photograph of a dog in Mexico, 2010.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Apply a vintage preset to a daylight photograph, then compare its darkest shadows, white surfaces, and corners with the original.

context: Instagram launched in 2010 with named filters that made repeatable photographic styles available through a simple selection. Early looks borrowed from instant prints, inexpensive cameras, and color photographs altered by age or processing. These were digital interpretations, not faithful simulations of one film stock. Tone curves could lift the darkest values, while separate color adjustments shifted shadows and highlights. Vignettes darkened the edges, and optional borders suggested physical prints. Combined with the platform’s original square format, these treatments helped establish a recognizable visual language for everyday mobile photography.
effects.distinction: Unlike chemical cross-processing, these filters alter digital image values rather than develop film in chemistry intended for another film type. Unlike simple sepia toning, many presets preserve several colors while changing their relationships.
effects.aftermath: The technique shows how repeatable color and tonal choices can make new photographs suggest an imagined photographic past.
effects.funFact: Kevin Systrom’s early dog photograph used the X-Pro II filter before Instagram’s public launch.

margin.note: Mappings that determine how original brightness values become new ones. They can brighten shadows without equally brightening highlights.
Gradual darkening toward an image’s edges or corners. Software can add this even when the lens produced even brightness.
A particular kind of photographic film, with its own sensitivity, grain, and color response.

context: Interlacing transmits the two line groups of a television image alternately. This saves transmission bandwidth at a higher temporal sampling rate than a full frame at the same frame rate. If two different phases of motion are shown simultaneously on a progressive display, comb edges can appear. The decade designation refers to early television history, while the illustration explicitly shows a current design approach. Adobe documents the correct processing of field order and deinterlacing.

effects.aftermath: A technical conversion error can become a distinct visual style.

effects.title: Isometric Pixel Graphics
effects.name: Isometric Pixel Graphics
effects.dating: 1990s, Maxis and Blizzard Entertainment PC games
effects.caption: Medieval Isometric Strategy Game Scene. A bustling medieval village with farms, buildings, and tiny soldiers is depicted from a high, angled vantage point.
effects.credit: Age of Empires · CC BY 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a three-dimensional world drawn on a flat grid without vanishing points. Objects remain the same size whether they are near or far away.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Artists draw scenes using parallel projection, typically rotated 45 degrees and tilted down. Every pixel line follows a rigid mathematical stepping pattern.

body.label: Example
body.text: Maxis: SimCity 2000, 1993.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a boxy object in an isometric game and notice that its parallel lines never meet or converge.

context: In the 1990s, computer hardware lacked the power to render complex 3D environments in real time. Developers solved this by pre-drawing 2D sprites and placing them on a diamond-shaped grid. True isometric projection uses a thirty-degree angle. However, digital artists used a two-to-one pixel stepping ratio instead. This created an angle of about 26.5 degrees. This specific ratio prevented jagged lines from appearing on low-resolution monitors. Players felt they were looking down into a deep, tactile miniature world. This allowed for vast, detailed strategy and role-playing games.
effects.distinction: Unlike true 3D graphics, isometric pixel art cannot rotate freely. The camera angle is permanently fixed by the artist's original drawings.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how technical constraints can create a beloved, timeless visual aesthetic.
effects.funFact: Isometric projection was first formalized in 1822 by Professor William Farish to draw accurate machine parts.

margin.note: A point on the horizon where parallel lines seem to meet. Isometric art completely avoids these points.
A drawing method where lines of sight remain parallel. Objects do not shrink as distance increases.
The specific arrangement of pixels used to draw lines. Isometric art usually moves two pixels horizontally for every vertical one.

context: JPEG compresses image information using a structured encoding. Strong quantization and corrupted encoded data can produce various artifacts. Artistic glitch practice explores these peculiarities rather than treating every error as a uniform pattern. effects.title: Jump Cut
effects.name: Jump Cut
effects.dating: 1960, Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless
effects.caption: AI illustration: Abrupt temporal shift in a taxi interior.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a sudden, jarring skip forward in time within the same scene. The subject appears to instantly teleport to a slightly different position.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An editor removes a middle section of a continuous film take. They then splice the remaining two pieces together.

body.label: Example
body.text: Jean-Luc Godard: Breathless (À bout de souffle), 1960.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Record a video of yourself talking, then delete a random two-second chunk from the middle and watch the jarring skip.

context: Early filmmakers like Georges Méliès used jump cuts to create magical illusions. However, classical Hollywood editing strictly avoided them to maintain a smooth flow of time. This changed in the late 1950s and 1960s with the French New Wave. Jean-Luc Godard famously embraced the technique in his 1960 film Breathless. To shorten scenes without losing pacing, he cut out sections of single takes. This broke traditional rules of spatial and temporal continuity. The jarring visual jumps reminded audiences they were watching a constructed movie. It shifted film editing from an invisible craft to a highly visible artistic tool.
effects.distinction: Unlike a standard cut between two different camera angles, a jump cut stays on the same framing. This makes the missing time obvious and visually jarring.
effects.aftermath: It proves that audiences can understand a story even when edits intentionally break the illusion of continuous time.
effects.funFact: Godard supposedly invented the technique because his producer demanded he shorten the movie's running time.

margin.note: A single continuous recorded shot from the moment the camera starts rolling until it stops.
A 1950s and 1960s film movement where young directors rejected traditional studio rules and experimented with visual style.
The illusion that a movie scene flows logically in an uninterrupted physical space and continuous timeframe.

context: David Brewster invented the optical kaleidoscope in 1816. The V&A Dundee displays a patent kaleidoscope from 1820; therefore, this optical precursor is at the beginning of this photographic journey. The mirrors inside multiply shapes into symmetrical patterns. Museum history also describes photography through a type of teleidoscope that transforms the external world instead of enclosed pieces of glass. A digital filter replaces the real optics with reflections and transformations of a section of the image. GIMP's documentation separates the number of mirrors, rotation, and center. In this exercise, change only one parameter at a time: This will reveal whether the pattern change originates from more segments, a new axis, or a different section of the image.
effects.distinction: Radial repetition differs from rectangular tiling and simple bilateral symmetry.
effects.aftermath: The effect combines optical history with contemporary VJ design. Radial symmetry can create strong ornamental structures even from an ordinary photograph.
effects.funFact: A teleidoscope transforms the outside world; a classic kaleidoscope often contains enclosed colored pieces.

margin.note: Arranged in repeating sections around a central point, like petals around a flower.
A mirror-based viewer that turns the outside scene into repeating patterns rather than using loose colored pieces inside a tube.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Early motion pictures showing limited but striking natural colours, mostly reds and greens. Fast movement sometimes creates noticeable red and green ghosting edges.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Black-and-white film frames are alternately photographed and projected through rotating red and green filters. The human eye blends these alternating frames into a single coloured image.

body.label: Example
body.text: Charles Urban: With Our King and Queen Through India, 1912.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Blink rapidly while watching a spinning multi-coloured object to see how alternating images blend together.

context: Kinemacolor was the first successful natural colour motion picture process. George Albert Smith invented it in England in 1908. It was an additive process relying on persistence of vision. A special camera exposed alternating frames of standard black-and-white film behind a rotating wheel with red and green filters. To see the colours, theatres needed a matching projector. It ran at thirty-two frames per second, twice the usual speed, to reduce flickering. While the colours were mostly warm reds and earthy greens, lacking true blues, audiences found the effect astonishing.
effects.distinction: Unlike later Technicolor which printed colours directly onto the film strip, Kinemacolor film itself was entirely black-and-white. The colour only existed during projection when light passed through external filters.
effects.aftermath: It proved that audiences wanted colour cinema, sparking a race to develop better natural colour technologies.
effects.funFact: Theatres had to hire strong projectionists to manually crank the heavy colour projectors at double speed.

margin.note: A method where different colours of light are mixed together to create new colours. Combining red and green light creates yellow.
An optical illusion where the human eye retains an image for a split second. This blends rapid separate flashes into smooth motion.

effects.title: Kinetic Typography
effects.name: Kinetic Typography
effects.dating: 1959, Saul Bass's title sequence for North by Northwest
effects.caption: Letters as Animated Characters. A colorful montage presents letters as faces, figures, and playful arrangements with varied orientations and proportions.
effects.credit: Simonsegni (Stefano Simonetti) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see written words moving, shrinking, or expanding across the screen. The text acts like a character, shifting to match the audio.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Animators manipulate individual text elements frame by frame on a film camera stand. They alter the position, scale, and rotation of cut-out letters over time.

body.label: Example
body.text: Saul Bass: North by Northwest title sequence, 1959.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a lyric video on mute. Try to guess the mood of the song based purely on how the words move.

context: Before the 1950s, film title sequences were mostly static cards shown to credit the cast and crew. Designers like Saul Bass changed this by treating text as a moving, expressive element. By moving paper cut-outs under a camera, they made words slide, stretch, and collide in rhythm with the musical score. This transformed opening credits from a boring necessity into an active part of the storytelling. Kinetic typography set the mood of the film before any actors appeared. The technique soon spread to television commercials and eventually digital animation.
effects.distinction: Kinetic typography involves moving text to express emotion or rhythm. This differs from standard subtitles, which stay still at the bottom of the screen just to translate dialogue.
effects.aftermath: It teaches us that how a word moves can be just as important as what the word actually means.
effects.funFact: Early kinetic typography often required moving heavy pieces of glass on large, multi-plane camera stands.

margin.note: A traditional animation technique where a scene is photographed one still picture at a time.
A specialized vertical rig used to photograph flat artwork or animation cels from above.

effects.title: Kirlian Photography
effects.name: Kirlian Photography
effects.dating: 1939, Semyon and Valentina Kirlian's experiments
effects.caption: Multicolored Corona Around an Oval. A dark oval is surrounded by a brilliant halo of green, pink, and blue light with finely radiating streaks.
effects.credit: Sérgio Valle Duarte .mw-parser-output .messagebox{margin:4px 0;width:auto;border-collap… · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see an object surrounded by a glowing, jagged halo of light against a dark background. Often, leaves or fingertips appear in high contrast with branching, electric sparks forming an aura.

body.label: Principle
body.text: High-voltage electrical currents pass through an object placed directly on photographic film or plates. This creates a corona discharge in the air, which exposes the film without using a camera lens.

body.label: Example
body.text: Semyon and Valentina Kirlian: Glowing leaf photographs, 1939.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Rub a balloon on your hair in a dark room and watch for tiny static sparks to visualize similar miniature electrical discharges.

context: In 1939, Russian inventor Semyon Kirlian and his wife Valentina accidentally discovered this technique. They noticed a visible flash when a patient received electrotherapy. They placed a photographic plate near electrodes and captured glowing silhouettes of hands and leaves. The images map the moisture and electrical conductivity of the subject. A moist leaf creates strong discharges, while a dry leaf produces a faint glow. Some people wrongly claimed these auras showed living energy or a soul. Actually, the glowing borders just show electrical sparks reacting to humidity and pressure changes.
effects.distinction: It differs from standard photograms. Photograms use external light to cast shadows. Kirlian photography uses electricity to generate light directly around the object.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how invisible physical variables like moisture and static electricity can create striking visual patterns on photographic film.
effects.funFact: A sweaty fingertip creates a much larger, brighter Kirlian aura than a perfectly dry one.

margin.note: A small electrical spark that happens when high voltage ionizes the surrounding air. It creates a faint glow.
A measure of how easily an electric current can flow through a specific material. Water usually increases this flow.
A medical treatment that uses electrical energy. It was popular in the early twentieth century for treating ailments.

effects.title: Kodachrome Color
effects.name: Kodachrome Color
effects.dating: 1935, Eastman Kodak
effects.caption: Portrait in an Embroidered Vest. A man wears a striped green cap and an embroidered dark vest over a bright white shirt.
effects.credit: Arthur Rothstein · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see rich, vivid colors with deep contrast and warm skin tones. Reds and yellows pop brilliantly. Shadows stay sharply defined.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The film holds three black-and-white emulsion layers sensitive to red, green, and blue light. Complex development adds color dyes chemically later.

body.label: Example
body.text: Steve McCurry: Afghan Girl, 1984.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Find a high-saturation digital filter. Compare its look to a vintage Kodachrome photo to spot true deep reds and crisp shadows.

context: Kodachrome was introduced in 1935 by Eastman Kodak. It was the first successful mass-market color film. The raw film itself contained no color dyes. It used a subtractive color process built on three layers of silver halide crystals. Each layer recorded a different primary color of light during exposure. The actual color dyes were chemically added during a highly complex development stage. Because the dyes were added later, the film layers were extremely thin. This thinness produced beautifully sharp images with almost invisible grain. Its unique chemical dyes also created incredible archival stability.
effects.distinction: Unlike Autochrome which used a mosaic of dyed potato starch, Kodachrome used a multi-layered subtractive process for much sharper images.
effects.aftermath: It teaches us that separating light recording from dye creation allows for sharper, more stable colored images.
effects.funFact: The inventors of Kodachrome, Leopold Mannes and Leopold Godowsky Jr., were professional classical musicians.

margin.note: This method creates colors by absorbing certain light wavelengths and reflecting others. It mixes cyan, magenta, and yellow dyes to absorb light.
These are light-sensitive chemical compounds used in photographic film. They capture the invisible image when exposed to light.
The chemical process that turns the invisible captured image into a visible photograph. For Kodachrome, this involved dozens of precise steps.

effects.title: L-System Plants
effects.name: L-System Plants
effects.dating: 1990 landmark publication; roots in Lindenmayer’s 1968 work
effects.caption: Branching Tree With Nested Foliage. An asymmetric rendered tree exposes angular limbs beneath rounded clusters of delicate green foliage.
effects.credit: Unknown author · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Plants display repeated branching patterns, nested sprays of leaves, and stems dividing at consistent angles. Some look diagrammatic; others resemble natural vegetation.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Parallel rewriting rules replace symbols across successive rounds, generating instructions for plant structure. A turtle interpretation converts those symbols into movements, turns, and branching paths.

body.label: Example
body.text: Przemyslaw Prusinkiewicz and Aristid Lindenmayer: The Algorithmic Beauty of Plants, 1990.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Trace one small branch in an L-system plant image, then find similar arrangements elsewhere in the plant.

context: Aristid Lindenmayer introduced L-systems in 1968 to describe biological development through formal rules. Their later use in computer graphics made plant structures visible as generated drawings and models. The Algorithmic Beauty of Plants brought this approach together in 1990. Symbols can represent plant components or drawing commands, depending on the model. Each rewriting round replaces symbols in parallel, rather than editing one branch at a time. Brackets can save and restore a drawing position and direction, allowing branches to emerge. Random choices and numerical parameters can introduce variation.
effects.distinction: Unlike a generic fractal tree, an L-system plant is defined by a symbol-rewriting process. Its branches need not repeat exactly at every scale.
effects.aftermath: L-system plants show how compact developmental rules can generate complex forms without specifying every twig separately.
effects.funFact: L-systems began as models of biological development, not as a method for drawing trees.

margin.note: All eligible symbols are replaced using the same starting string for that round. New symbols wait until the next round.
An imaginary drawing cursor follows commands to move and turn. In three dimensions, its orientation determines where each new segment goes.
Numbers attached to symbols can control properties such as segment length, branch angle, or age.

effects.title: Lantern Slide
effects.name: Lantern Slide
effects.dating: 1850s, Langenheim brothers' photographic glass slides
effects.caption: Hand-Coloured Lantern Slide of Lucea. A hand-coloured coastal view appears within a black slide mount inscribed “Lucea and Dolphin Head” and “Jamaica.” The coloured photographic positive exemplifies the luminous imagery carried by glass lantern slides.
effects.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a transparent glass rectangle showing a positive image. The image is often delicately hand-painted with vivid, translucent colours.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Light shines through a developed photographic emulsion on glass. A lens then projects this bright, enlarged positive image onto a screen.

body.label: Example
body.text: William and Frederick Langenheim: Hyalotype slides of American scenery, 1850.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Hold a piece of coloured transparent plastic up to a bright flashlight in a dark room to project its colours.

context: Magic lanterns existed long before photography, using fully hand-painted slides. In 1850, the Langenheim brothers invented the hyalotype. This allowed real photographic images to be printed on transparent glass. Photographic emulsions coated the glass plate, capturing fine details when exposed to a negative. After development, artists carefully tinted the black-and-white positive with translucent paints. An oil or limelight lantern then projected the glass slide. This created a massive, luminous image for large audiences in darkened rooms. These shows became incredibly popular for public education and evening entertainment.
effects.distinction: Unlike a daguerreotype, which is a unique opaque image viewed directly, a lantern slide is transparent and meant for projection.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how combining photographic images with light projection paved the way for modern cinema.
effects.funFact: Projectionists created intense light by burning oxygen and hydrogen on quicklime, which is the origin of the word 'limelight'.

margin.note: An image where the light and dark areas match human vision, rather than being inverted like a negative.
A light-sensitive chemical layer applied to a surface that reacts to light to capture an image.
An early photographic process that used egg whites (albumen) to bind light-sensitive chemicals to glass slides.

body.text: Faces become landscapes, architecture becomes organisms. New intermediate forms continuously change their meaning.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A model generates images along interpolated latent representations or parameters. Learned image structures replace simple pixel blending.

body.label: Example
body.text: Wang/Golland and DiffMorpher show different research approaches to image interpolation in 2023.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare dissolve, classic morphing, and generative interpolation between two motifs. Look for newly invented intermediate forms.

context: GAN prehistory in the 2010s; open diffusion experiments from 2022/2023.

It's not just finished pixels that are blended. A model generates intermediate states along interpolated latent representations, conditionings, or model parameters. The visible form can change semantically in the process.
Wang and Golland, Interpolating between Images with Diffusion Models (2023); DiffMorpher (2023) interpolates, among other things, LoRA parameters and latent noise states.

Regarding the illustration: Historical research example. Plausible new image states are created between two inputs, instead of simply blending pixels. The original research image shows portrait, architectural, and dog morphs.
effects.distinction: Frame interpolation fills in temporal intermediate frames of a movement. Generative image interpolation can switch between different image content. Not every AI zoom is a true latent morph. Latent interpolation predates the 2020s. In that decade, with the widespread use of image generators, it became a highly visible creative practice.
effects.aftermath: The transition itself became a search for images. Its intermediate forms can be more surprising than the two target images.
effects.funFact: In 2023, DiffMorpher not only interpolates image states, but also, among other things, adjusted model parameters.

margin.note: Compact numerical descriptions learned by a model. Changing them can alter the objects, shapes, or styles in a generated image.
Creating new images between two inputs using a trained model, rather than merely fading one picture into the other.

effects.title: LED Volume
effects.name: LED Volume
effects.dating: 2019, Industrial Light & Magic's StageCraft system
effects.caption: Performer Within an LED Virtual Interior. A seated performer occupies a stage enclosed by screens depicting a continuous purple architectural interior, with production monitors nearby.
effects.credit: Tim Sheerman-Chase · CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Actors and physical props appear naturally lit by complex, realistic backgrounds. Moving reflections on shiny armor exactly match the surrounding scenery.

body.label: Principle
body.text: High-resolution LED screens surround a physical stage to display real-time, 3D digital environments. The camera's tracking data updates the background perspective instantly.

body.label: Example
body.text: Industrial Light & Magic: The Mandalorian, 2019.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a behind-the-scenes video of a volume stage. Notice how the screen background shifts instantly when the camera moves.

context: In the late 2010s, filmmakers sought better ways to blend live actors with digital effects. Green screens caused colored light to spill onto sets. This required tedious digital corrections in post-production. The LED volume solved this by wrapping the set in massive video walls. Video game engines render the background in real time. As the physical camera moves, the digital scene shifts precisely to match its perspective. The LED panels also provide realistic lighting. Shiny props reflect the actual digital environment instantly. This allows actors to see the world they are acting in.
effects.distinction: Green screen relies on removing a solid color to add backgrounds later. An LED volume films the final background live on set.
effects.aftermath: It shows how real-time video game technology is fundamentally changing traditional cinematic lighting and photography.
effects.funFact: The video walls act as giant lamps, providing perfectly accurate colored lighting for the actors.

margin.note: Digital information that records the exact position, angle, and movement of the physical camera in the real world.
Software platforms originally built for gaming that can generate complex 3D graphics and lighting almost instantly.

effects.title: Lenticular Print
effects.name: Lenticular print
effects.dating: 1964: LOOK parallax panoramagram as a media example
effects.caption: Lenticular principle: Production illustration from Smithsonian Exhibits, 2020.
effects.credit: Smithsonian Exhibits, didactic illustration.

body.label: Identify
body.text: The image changes or appears spatial as you walk past it.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Rasterized image strips lie beneath a film of cylindrical lenses.

body.label: Example
body.text: Arthur Rothstein: LOOK-Parallax-Panoramagram, 1964.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Tilt a lenticular card; separate the illusion of movement from the illusion of depth.

context: Lenticular printing combines a pre-printed stripe pattern with a lens surface. Depending on the viewing angle, a different part of the nested images reaches the eye. This creates image changes, short animations, or different perspectives for a sense of depth. The Museum of Fine Arts Houston preserves Arthur Rothstein's LOOK parallax panoramagram from February 25, 1964; it serves as the specific historical reference point. Smithsonian Exhibits explains the same basic idea for contemporary exhibition graphics. It requires neither a screen nor electronic reproduction. The illustration explains the modern production process, not the historical LOOK object. When learning, always check whether multiple temporal states or multiple spatial views have been nested together.
effects.distinction: A single photograph of the print only partially shows its change in perspective.
effects.aftermath: Wobbly images and spatial lenticulars share an optical principle, but pursue different perceptual goals. Viewing angle and distance are part of the design.
effects.funFact: Lenticular lenses can convey movement or depth without electricity and without additional 3D glasses.

margin.note: Tiny lenses curved in one direction. Each directs a different image strip toward different viewing angles.
Narrow slices of several images arranged in a repeating pattern to line up with the lens sheet.

sources.label: Smithsonian Exhibits: Did That Graphic Just Change?

effects.title: Light Field Refocus
effects.name: Light Field Refocus
effects.dating: 2010s; Lytro's first consumer camera shipped in 2012
effects.caption: AI illustration: Shifting focus from foreground cup to background cafe.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: The plane of sharp focus shifts between foreground and background within the same captured scene. Soft blur surrounds whichever depth appears sharp.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A microlens array lets the sensor record both light position and light direction during exposure. Software combines these samples to reconstruct different focus distances after capture.

body.label: Example
body.text: Lytro: First-generation light-field camera, 2012.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Open an interactive light-field photograph and alternate between near and distant subjects, watching which details sharpen and which soften.

context: Light-field photography builds on older research into recording light from multiple directions. During the 2010s, Lytro brought this approach to consumer photography. Its first camera shipped in 2012 and let viewers choose focus after capture. A microlens array behind the main lens divided incoming light into small views on the sensor. Software aligned and combined those views to reconstruct a chosen focus distance. This exchanged some spatial resolution for directional information. Refocusing remained limited by the recorded data; it could not make every distance perfectly sharp.
effects.distinction: Unlike a rack focus, this changes the selected focus after exposure rather than moving lens focus during filming. Unlike ordinary blur filters, it uses recorded directional information.
effects.aftermath: It shows that a photograph can store information for several possible focus choices rather than one fixed rendering.
effects.funFact: The sensor records many tiny views, not simply one photograph with everything sharp.

margin.note: A grid of tiny lenses. Each lens directs light from different parts of the main lens onto different sensor locations.
The ability to distinguish fine image details. Recording light directions uses sensor capacity that could otherwise capture more scene detail.
Data about the directions from which light reaches the camera. This helps software determine how to combine samples for refocusing.

effects.title: Light Leaks
effects.name: Light leaks
effects.dating: 1990s Lomography; 2010 digital retro filters
effects.caption: Lomography: deliberate analog light incidence. Contemporary experiment.
effects.credit: Lomography / Community Photography; Credits on source page

body.label: Identify
body.text: Colored veils or light bands move from the edge into the picture.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Unwanted light further exposes the film.

body.label: Example
body.text: Analog light incidence from a Lomography experiment.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Place a faint veil of light at a believable edge of the image.

context: Light leakage occurs, for example, at leaky camera seals or during loading and unloading. The additional exposure overlays the actual subject. Experimental analog photography later consciously embraced such traces as chance and material signals. Digital retrofilters made the effect reproducible. The artistic use thus differs from the original technical goal of reliably protecting the film from extraneous light.
effects.distinction: A true light leak can ruin images and is not precisely controllable. For this exercise, a digital simulation is sufficient. Bright color gradients can also be artistic overlays and do not indicate a camera defect.
effects.aftermath: A flaw at the edge can make the entire image readable as analog material.
effects.funFact: Red light can appear when light hits the film from the back through the substrate.
highlights: Unwanted light further exposes the film

margin.note: Light-blocking strips or joints that prevent stray light from entering a camera.
Extra light reaching film on top of the intended photograph, potentially washing out or coloring parts of it.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Deliberately drawn light paths or moving lighting.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A moving light source creates a drawing during a long exposure.

body.label: Example
body.text: Contemporary light spheres on the Swan River.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Write a word in the air with a small lamp.

context: Man Ray's Space Writing from around 1935 is one of the early artistic examples of photographic light writing. The technique combines body movement, time, and the photographic image. Modern variations create spheres of light, writing, or object illumination using moving lamps. The photographer thus creates not just a view, but a sequence of events. Today's example vividly illustrates this logic without being presented as a historical original.
effects.distinction: Unlike random traffic patterns, light painting follows a creative choreography. You can draw the light source yourself or illuminate a subject sequentially. For a learning experiment, an LED or flashlight is sufficient; fire is not required.
effects.aftermath: The exposure becomes a small performance.
effects.funFact: Light painting can illuminate an object without the moving lamp itself appearing in the picture.

margin.note: Keeping the camera shutter open long enough to record movement as trails rather than a frozen instant.
Ball-shaped light trails made by moving a lamp repeatedly around a central point during an exposure.

effects.name: Light trails
effects.dating: 2016: Automated light trails in Nikon COOLPIX; long exposure is much older
effects.short: Light trails caused by long exposure
effects.caption: Nikon School: Nighttime light trails through long exposure. A contemporary teaching example.
effects.credit: Nikon School / Neil Freeman

body.label: Identify
body.text: Moving lamps become bright, continuous paths.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The open shutter collects light along the movement.

body.label: Example
body.text: Traffic lights in the Nikon night photography example.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Using a tripod, photograph the same stretch of road with exposure times of one and ten seconds.

context: Light trails are a special form of motion blur: The light source itself traces its path. The surroundings can remain sharp with a tripod. In 2016, Nikon introduced Multiple Exposure Lighten for several COOLPIX cameras: This function automatically combines images to create light trails. This is a dated digital approach to a much older image effect, not an invention of long exposure photography. A single long exposure and such an image series are different technical methods.
effects.distinction: The track shown is not a real, fixed line in space. It summarizes movement over the exposure time. A safe, stationary position away from traffic is required for the experiment; a digital exercise will also work.
effects.aftermath: A stationary picture frame can make moving time visible.
effects.funFact: A vehicle can almost disappear, while its lights leave a clearly visible trail.

margin.note: The camera mechanism or electronic timing that determines how long light is recorded.
The durations over which the camera gathers light. Longer times record more of a moving light’s path.

effects.title: Limited Animation
effects.name: Limited Animation
effects.dating: 1950s, especially UPA's stylised theatrical cartoons
effects.caption: Stylised Action in The Dover Boys. Angular cartoon figures collide in an exaggerated grouping inside a wooden room in The Dover Boys.
effects.credit: Chuck Jones · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Flat stylised shapes and held poses give scenes a graphic, poster-like appearance. Often, only a mouth, arm, or other isolated part moves.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Fewer unique drawings are needed because images are held across frames, movement cycles repeat, or separate layers isolate moving parts. Timing, editing, and sound help these selective movements communicate action.

body.label: Example
body.text: Robert Cannon: Gerald McBoing-Boing, 1950.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a short cartoon passage without sound. Count how long a body stays still while its mouth or eyes change.

context: Limited animation existed before the 1950s, but UPA made selective movement central to a distinctive modern graphic style. Its artists favoured simplified shapes, expressive poses, and backgrounds that did not need convincing depth. In cel animation, separate transparent sheets allowed a moving mouth to change while the body drawing remained unchanged. Holding drawings reduced drawing work without requiring a slower projection speed. Television studios later expanded these economies to meet tight budgets and schedules. However, UPA's approach also showed that fewer drawings could support deliberate artistic choices.
effects.distinction: Unlike full animation, limited animation concentrates changes in selected poses, parts, and moments rather than continuously redrawing movement. Flat design alone does not make animation limited.
effects.aftermath: It teaches that expressive motion depends on selecting meaningful changes, not simply increasing the number of drawings.
effects.funFact: Gerald McBoing-Boing won an Academy Award despite rejecting the rounded realism associated with many earlier Hollywood cartoons.

margin.note: Drawings on transparent sheets are photographed over backgrounds. Separate sheets let artists replace one part without replacing everything.
The rate at which film frames pass through a projector. This differs from how often the drawing changes.
Sequences of drawings reused to repeat an action, such as walking.

effects.title: Lippmann Interference Photography
effects.name: Lippmann interference photography
effects.dating: Introduced in 1891; a scientific milestone, not a mass production procedure
effects.caption: Richard Neuhauss: Parrot, circa 1899. Lippmann interference color photography.
effects.credit: Dr. Richard Neuhauss (1855-1915) / Public domain; Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Historical color images with strong angle-dependent viewing.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Standing light waves leave behind thin layers that reflect specific wavelengths.

body.label: Example
body.text: Richard Neuhauss: Parrot, around 1899.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Explain the difference between dyes and interference colors.

context: In 1891, Gabriel Lippmann presented his interference-based color photography. A reflective background creates standing waves during the exposure; the resulting fine structure reflects selected colors. Long exposures and demanding viewing requirements limited its practical application. In 1908, Lippmann received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this invention. This story broadens our understanding of color: it doesn't necessarily have to be stored using pigments or dyes.
effects.distinction: This process is a scientific milestone and was not a common everyday look. An ordinary screen photograph only indirectly conveys the original color reproduction. Lippmann plates should not be confused with lithographic photochrom prints.
effects.aftermath: Color can be stored as a physical structure.
effects.funFact: Lippmann received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1908 for his photographic color process.
highlights: thin layers that reflect specific wavelengths

margin.note: A stationary pattern of bright and dark zones formed when incoming and reflected light overlap. The photographic emulsion records this very fine pattern.
Colors produced by light waves reinforcing or canceling one another, rather than by colored dyes absorbing light.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Rounded translucent controls float above content, with bright edge highlights and warped backgrounds. Their shapes and apparent thickness change during interaction.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Real-time rendering combines background blur, simulated refraction, and moving highlights to suggest curved glass. Software alters displayed pixels rather than bending light through physical interface elements.

body.label: Example
body.text: Apple: iOS 26 Liquid Glass interface, 2025.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Scroll a detailed image beneath a translucent toolbar in iOS 26. Watch how background details blur and distort near its edges.

context: Apple introduced Liquid Glass in June 2025 as a shared design language across its operating systems. It followed earlier translucent interfaces, including Apple's own, but emphasized curved edges, distortion, and responsive movement. The design also drew on the spatial interface of visionOS. Its glass is a rendered material, not a transparent physical layer. Background content supplies colors and patterns that software filters and distorts beneath controls. Animated highlights suggest a changing surface as elements move or reshape. The result creates visual depth, but busy backgrounds can complicate contrast and readability.
effects.distinction: Frosted-glass interfaces mainly soften the background with blur and transparency. Liquid Glass also emphasizes simulated refraction, bright contours, and fluid shape changes.
effects.aftermath: It shows how simulated material behavior can suggest depth while creating new challenges for readable controls.
effects.funFact: The glass-like controls are drawn on an opaque screen; they are not physical glass objects.

margin.note: The device generates images quickly enough to respond as you scroll, tap, or move controls.
Software distorts background imagery to imitate light changing direction through a transparent material.
The difference in brightness or color between a control and its surroundings helps you distinguish them.

context: The Liquify tool makes spatial distortion directly controllable by hand. Adobe documents pushing, pulling, twisting, contracting, and inflating, as well as masks for freezing unchanged regions. The 2000s serve as a milestone in its retouching and filter culture, without claiming exclusive invention for these forms of image distortion. The effect can subtly correct or intentionally create an elastic, impossible image.
effects.distinction: Liquify is a local distortion and not an automatic identification of realistic body shapes. Adjacent lines often reveal where the image has been shifted.
effects.aftermath: Deformation limits and background reactions are just as important as the target region.
effects.funFact: A freeze mask can be used to protect part of an image during deformation.

effects.title: Lith Printing
effects.name: Lith Printing
effects.dating: 1980s, popularization by fine art photographers
effects.caption: AI illustration: Misty Railway Station Platform in Lith Print.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see gritty, peppery grain in the dark shadows. The lighter areas look smooth, featuring warm tones like peach or pink.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Photographers overexpose standard black-and-white paper, then develop it slowly in diluted lithographic chemicals. This triggers an explosive, localized reaction in the darkest areas.

body.label: Example
body.text: Anton Corbijn: Miles Davis portrait, 1989.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a vintage music portrait from the late 1980s. Compare the gritty black shadows to the smooth, softly tinted faces.

context: Lith printing relies on infectious development, a unique chemical process. Originally, printers used lithographic developers to create pure black-and-white text graphics. In the late twentieth century, artists used these highly diluted chemicals on standard photographic paper. Artists learned to heavily overexpose the paper under the enlarger. As the print developed, dark shadows suddenly accelerated, creating harsh, peppery grain. Meanwhile, the bright highlights developed very slowly. This difference created smooth, warm tones and coarse, dark tones. Photographers had to quickly snatch the print from the chemical bath.
effects.distinction: Unlike sepia toning, lith printing does not color the entire image uniformly. It creates contrasting dual tones and coarse grain during actual development.
effects.aftermath: It reveals how manipulating standard chemical processes can yield entirely new, expressive aesthetics.
effects.funFact: Prints must be snatched from the developer at the exact second before turning completely black.

margin.note: A chain reaction where developing silver particles rapidly accelerate the development of neighboring silver particles.
Giving the photographic paper more light than normal when projecting the negative image onto it.
An optical device used in a darkroom to project and magnify a photographic negative onto light-sensitive paper.

effects.title: Lithophane
effects.name: Lithophane
effects.dating: 1820s; patented in France by Paul de Bourgoing in 1827
effects.caption: Brass Enclosure with Lithophane Panels. A brass enclosure holds pale translucent panels depicting detailed figure scenes.
effects.credit: Detlef Dauer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: A thin porcelain plaque reveals a softly shaded picture when lit from behind. Under front lighting, the same surface looks like a shallow relief.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Variations in porcelain thickness control transmitted light: thinner areas appear brighter, while thicker areas appear darker. These differences create continuous tones without requiring painted shading.

body.label: Example
body.text: Unknown maker: The Last Supper (after Leonardo da Vinci), 19th century.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare a lithophane under front lighting and against a bright window; notice which raised areas become dark.

context: Lithophanes emerged in Europe during the 1820s, with a French patent granted to Paul de Bourgoing in 1827. Makers shaped an original model, often in wax, and used molds to reproduce its relief in porcelain. After firing, the thin ceramic remained translucent. Its varying thickness converted a sculpted surface into a shaded image when illuminated from behind. Portraits, landscapes, and scenes copied from paintings became popular subjects. Plaques appeared in window hangings, candle screens, and lampshades, placing pictures within everyday domestic lighting.
effects.distinction: Unlike a painted transparency, a lithophane forms its shading through material thickness rather than applied pigment. Unlike ordinary relief sculpture, its intended picture depends on transmitted light.
effects.aftermath: The lithophane shows how a three-dimensional surface can encode a two-dimensional image through controlled light transmission.
effects.funFact: The areas that project most can become the darkest parts of the backlit picture.

margin.note: A sculpted surface whose raised and recessed areas extend only slightly from a flat background.
Light that passes through a material before reaching your eyes.
Able to let light through, but not clear enough to see objects sharply through it.

context: In 1991, Viennese students discovered LOMO LC-A in Prague. This led to the founding of the Lomographic Society International in 1992. The manifesto and the ten golden rules encouraged spontaneous photography. Exhibitions with large canvases transformed many small prints into a shared experience. The movement helped to interpret the idiosyncrasies of analog photography as creative choices, while digital photography became increasingly controllable.
effects.distinction: Lomography is not a single filter and does not guarantee light leakage. Not all results show vignetting, saturation, or blurring. The movement combines camera culture, community, and experimentation; its visual language is correspondingly diverse.
effects.aftermath: An attitude towards the intake can be more important than a post-processing recipe.
effects.funFact: The Lomographic Society International was founded in Vienna in 1992, not in the birthplace of the Soviet camera.

effects.title: Long Exposure Water
effects.name: Long Exposure Water
effects.dating: 2000s, popularization of heavy ND filters in digital photography
effects.caption: Silken Cascades Beneath an Evening Sky. White cascades flow over layered rock shelves beneath a wooded hillside and warm evening sky.
effects.credit: Basile Morin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: The water looks like smooth, opaque fog or flowing silk. Stationary objects like rocks and trees remain perfectly sharp.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The camera sensor records light over seconds or minutes. Moving water blurs across the frame, averaging out into a uniform smoothness.

body.label: Example
body.text: Michael Kenna: 'Kussharo Lake Tree, Study 1', 2002.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Stand near a fast river. Squint your eyes to ignore individual splashes, observing the whole flow as one solid shape.

context: Long exposure water became a massive trend in digital photography during the 2000s. Early digital sensors were highly sensitive to light. This made long daytime exposures physically difficult. Photographers adopted strong Neutral Density (ND) filters. These dark pieces of glass block most light from entering the lens. This forces the camera to keep its shutter open much longer for a proper exposure. While the shutter remains open, still elements like stones stay sharp. Moving elements like ocean waves continuously change position. The sensor averages these moving reflections together. The result is a ghostly, flattened texture that human eyes cannot naturally see.
effects.distinction: In intentional camera movement (ICM), the entire frame blurs because the photographer moves the camera. Here, the camera is locked on a tripod, so only the moving subjects blur.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that cameras do not just capture instant moments, but can accumulate passing time into a single static image.
effects.funFact: Some extreme neutral density filters are so dark they resemble solid plates of welding glass.

margin.note: Pieces of dark glass that reduce incoming light without changing the color of the image.
The physical or electronic curtain in a camera that controls how long light hits the sensor.
The total amount of light that reaches the camera sensor to create a picture.

effects.title: Low Poly
effects.name: Low Poly
effects.dating: early 2010s, digital illustration trend
effects.caption: Faceted Polygon Portrait. A human face emerges from interlocking angular patches against a black background.
effects.credit: KenClarck11 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see an image made entirely of flat, interlocking geometric shapes, usually triangles. There are no smooth curves, only sharp angles and flat color facets.

body.label: Principle
body.text: 3D modeling software renders surfaces using a mesh of flat polygons. Artists intentionally reduce the polygon count and remove smooth shading to expose this underlying geometry.

body.label: Example
body.text: Timothy J. Reynolds: 3D Low Poly Landscapes, 2012.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Find a low poly portrait and notice how lighting is faked using distinctly different shades on adjacent flat triangles.

context: Early 3D video games used low polygon counts due to hardware limits. Characters looked blocky out of technical necessity. By the 2010s, hardware could render smooth, photorealistic graphics. However, artists began adopting low poly visuals as a deliberate stylistic choice. They stripped away detailed textures and smooth shading algorithms. Instead, they exposed the raw geometric mesh beneath. This process turned a 3D model into a faceted sculpture. Lighting calculates distinctly on each flat face, creating crisp shadows. It became a minimalist digital art movement. The style celebrates the basic building blocks of computer graphics rather than hiding them.
effects.distinction: Unlike pixel art, which uses a flat 2D grid of colored squares, low poly uses a 3D spatial mesh.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that technical limitations from the past often evolve into cherished artistic aesthetics in the future.
effects.funFact: The iconic original 1996 Tomb Raider character model of Lara Croft consisted of only 540 polygons.

margin.note: The total number of flat geometric shapes used to build a digital 3D model.
A digital lighting trick that blends colors across sharp angles to fake a rounded surface.
The invisible 3D wireframe structure made of connected points that defines an object's shape.

effects.title: Mandelbrot Set
effects.name: Mandelbrot Set
effects.dating: 1980, Benoit Mandelbrot's computer visualizations
effects.caption: Mandelbrot Set With Rainbow Escape Bands. A large black cardioid joins a circular bulb, with smaller satellite bulbs and rainbow bands tracing the intricate perimeter.
effects.credit: PantheraLeo1359531 · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a complex, swirling pattern built around a distinctive beetle-like black shape. As the image zooms in, miniature copies of this shape appear endlessly at smaller scales.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A computer repeatedly feeds the output of a mathematical equation back into itself. Pixels get different colors based on how quickly their calculated numbers grow toward infinity.

body.label: Example
body.text: Heinz-Otto Peitgen and Peter Richter: The Beauty of Fractals, 1986.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Search for a Mandelbrot zoom video online, pick a spiral, and watch how similar shapes keep reappearing as it zooms.

context: Benoit Mandelbrot defined this set in 1980 while working at IBM. He used powerful computers to calculate the boundaries of complex numbers. Early printouts were rough, low-resolution black-and-white plots. Soon, mathematicians added vibrant colors to show how rapidly points outside the shape grew. This visual breakthrough made abstract mathematical concepts visible and widely popular. The 1986 book The Beauty of Fractals turned these computer-generated images into cultural icons. People suddenly saw infinite, organic-looking complexity emerging from incredibly simple rules.
effects.distinction: Unlike hand-drawn psychedelic art, a Mandelbrot image contains strict mathematical self-similarity. Zooming into a normal drawing reveals blurry pixels, not infinitely sharp new structures.
effects.aftermath: It teaches us that incredibly complex, organic structures can arise from very simple, repetitive rules.
effects.funFact: The famous equation creating this infinite visual complexity is surprisingly simple: z equals z squared plus c.

margin.note: The central geometric boundary of the Mandelbrot set, famously compared to a bug or snowman.
A mathematical concept representing endlessness, having no limits or boundaries.
A number system combining real numbers with imaginary numbers, plotted on a 2D grid.

effects.title: Match Cut
effects.name: Match Cut
effects.dating: 1968, Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey
effects.caption: AI illustration: Bone and Spacecraft Continuity across Time.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see two consecutive shots where an object in the first shot is instantly replaced by a similar object. The two shapes share the same size, motion, or position on the screen.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An editor splices two pieces of film together at a precise frame. The visual composition of the outgoing shot aligns perfectly with the incoming shot.

body.label: Example
body.text: Stanley Kubrick: 2001: A Space Odyssey, 1968.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Hold a pen horizontally, then blink and imagine it instantly becoming an airplane in the sky.

context: A match cut connects two different scenes by linking similar shapes or actions. Editors use it to jump across time or space instantly. The technique requires careful planning during filming. A director must frame both objects in the exact same part of the camera lens. During editing, the two shots are spliced together. The viewer's eye remains fixed on the same screen location. This creates a smooth visual bridge between unrelated events. In 1968, Stanley Kubrick used this to skip millions of years. A falling bone becomes an orbiting satellite, summarizing human technological evolution in one edit.
effects.distinction: A match cut relies on visual similarity to link scenes. A jump cut disrupts time by skipping forward within the exact same shot.
effects.aftermath: It shows how visual repetition can connect completely different eras and locations.
effects.funFact: Some match cuts link sounds instead of images, like a screaming voice cutting to a train whistle.
highlights: instantly replaced by a similar object
splices two pieces of film together
aligns perfectly with the incoming shot

margin.note: A single still image on a strip of motion picture film.

effects.title: Matrix Digital Rain
effects.name: Matrix Digital Rain
effects.dating: 1999, The Matrix
effects.caption: Fine Green Digital Rain. Fine green character streams extend vertically across a dark computer display, with scattered brighter glyphs interrupting the dim columns.
effects.credit: Tassilo Mödl · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Falling green glyphs form vertical columns against black, with bright leading characters and fading trails. Symbols change as the streams descend at different speeds.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Computer animation updates character positions and brightness over time, creating apparent downward motion. Fading trails and added glow suggest luminous screen text rather than physical rainfall.

body.label: Example
body.text: The Wachowskis: The Matrix, 1999.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a digital rain animation while following one column. Notice whether individual symbols move downward or change within fixed positions.

context: The Matrix made falling green code a widely recognized image of a simulated world in 1999. Designer Simon Whiteley created the film’s code imagery using Japanese characters among its visual ingredients. The green lettering recalls older monochrome computer terminals, but its flowing arrangement is a designed animation, not ordinary program output. Columns differ in speed, length, and brightness, making a flat screen feel layered. Changing symbols keep the pattern active even where positions remain fixed. Bright characters and fading trails help viewers read the sequence as continuous downward movement.
effects.distinction: Unlike ordinary terminal scrolling, digital rain divides text into independently changing vertical streams. Unlike a long exposure, its trails are deliberately generated brightness patterns.
effects.aftermath: It shows how motion, repetition, and controlled brightness can turn unreadable symbols into a convincing visual language.
effects.funFact: Whiteley said Japanese sushi recipes supplied characters for the code’s design.

margin.note: Visible shapes representing characters, such as letters, numerals, or other written signs.
A sequence of computer-generated images whose changes create the impression of movement.

body.label: Identify
body.text: A model world appears life-size.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Small structures are filmed with a suitable camera, lighting, and speed.

body.label: Example
body.text: Metropolis, 1927; The Lord of the Rings, 2001–2003.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Film a model at the eye level of its characters.

context: Model trickery belongs to the practical prehistory of digital worlds. Film crews build miniature versions of architecture, vehicles, or landscapes and combine the footage with live action. Wētā Workshop documented miniatures as part of its work on The Lord of the Rings. Such models provide real materials and real light; the difficult task is to reconcile all size cues with the claimed scale.
effects.distinction: Water, fire, gravity, and insufficient depth of field can reveal the scale. A model doesn't automatically appear large just because the camera is close.
effects.aftermath: The model trick reduces the size of the set; conversely, the tilt-shift look makes reality appear like a model.
effects.funFact: Wētā also built miniatures for The Lord of the Rings, in addition to armor and weapons.

margin.note: The camera height corresponding to a character’s eyes. Using the miniature inhabitants’ eye level helps a model seem full-sized.
The rate at which frames are recorded. Adjusting it can help miniature movements resemble the weight and timing of full-sized objects.

effects.name: Miniature faking / tilt-shift
effects.dating: Late 2000s: Miniature look on the web. Optical precursors were older.

effects.credit: Keith Loutit. © Keith Loutit; Original video thumbnail

body.label: Identify
body.text: Real cities look like toys. A narrow strip of focus separates the blurred foreground from the background.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Selective focus imitates miniature images. Elevated viewpoints, vibrant colors, and time-lapse photography can enhance the impression of size.

body.label: Example
body.text: Keith Loutit: Bathtub III (2008) combines miniaturization with time-lapse photography.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Edit a street scene from above. Compare a simple focus strip and a depth-of-field mask.

context: Particularly visible on the web in the late 2000s; optical tilt methods are much older.

Only a narrow area of ​​the image remains sharp; the foreground and background become heavily blurred. Combined with an elevated viewpoint, more vibrant colors, and possibly time-lapse photography, a real scene resembles a filmed model landscape.
Keith Loutit, Bathtub III (2008) and his Little Sydney films: Miniature look meets time-lapse.

Regarding the image: Historical original / source image. A narrow depth of field and heavily blurred foreground/background create the miniature impression. The original video is supplemented with time-lapse footage.
effects.distinction: A true miniature is physically constructed. Miniature faking alters the perceived size of a real scene. Shift alone, for example, straightens building perspectives. Tilt and shift are different lens movements. For the miniature look, the precise focus plane is crucial; digitally, the look can be achieved entirely without a special lens.
effects.aftermath: A known reality can be reinterpreted into a different order of magnitude simply by distributing sharpness.
effects.funFact: Keith Loutit's Bathtub III transformed real places into apparent toys in 2008 through miniature effects and time-lapse photography.

margin.note: A map controlling which parts stay sharp and which become blurred to imitate focus at different distances.
Recording frames at long intervals and playing them faster, making slow activity appear rapid.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Image copies repeat themselves in the grid, sometimes mirrored against each other.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Tiles are reduced in size, offset, and mirrored along changing axes.

body.label: Example

body.label: Try it out

context: Rectangular repetition and mirroring is an older ornamental method. The digital reference point for this slide is the GIMP documentation: The Small Tiles page was revised as early as 2005 and describes image repetition as well as horizontal or vertical mirroring of selected tiles. This dates an available implementation and not the origin of the symmetry. In contrast to the kaleidoscope, a rectangular field is primarily created here, not a radial segmented circle. The illustration shows the basic repetition; mirroring is an additional option. The exercise with four tiles helps to read transitions precisely. Pay attention to whether motif edges meet appropriately or suddenly form double faces and unintended symmetrical figures.
effects.distinction: Seamless tiling and mirror repetition are different ways to connect image edges.
effects.aftermath: This technique is suitable for the desired jersey and textile patterns. A usable repeat and the desired direction of repetition are crucial.
effects.funFact: A three-by-three grid results in nine tiles, even if only the parameter three is entered.

margin.note: Repeated image units used to build a larger pattern.

margin.note: Each position is written as one complex number, combining horizontal and vertical coordinates. Here, z is the input, w the output, and a, b, c, d are adjustable constants.

effects.title: Mode 7
effects.name: Mode 7
effects.dating: 1990, Super Nintendo Entertainment System release
effects.caption: Perspective Grid on a Flat Ground Plane. A pixelated green ground plane divided by gray lanes and white borders recedes toward a blue horizon.
effects.credit: Anomie · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a flat, pixelated ground plane stretching into the distance. This floor can rotate and scale smoothly beneath the camera.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Hardware calculates grid transformations line-by-line during the screen drawing process. This stretches and squashes a 2D map to simulate 3D perspective.

body.label: Example
body.text: Nintendo EAD: Super Mario Kart, 1992.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch gameplay of F-Zero and notice how objects on the track look flat painted, rather than standing up.

context: Mode 7 was the seventh background graphics mode on the Super Nintendo. Standard game consoles of the era built 2D worlds using rigid tiles. Mode 7 instead allowed a single massive background layer to be scaled and rotated freely by the hardware. By changing the scaling factor on each horizontal scanline as the screen drew, programmers could create a fake 3D floor. The horizon line usually hid the fact that no actual 3D math was calculating depth. This breakthrough allowed high-speed racing and flying games to exist without requiring complex polygonal rendering chips.
effects.distinction: Unlike true 3D graphics, Mode 7 does not calculate XYZ coordinates for vertices. It only distorts a flat 2D image.
effects.aftermath: It shows how creative hardware tricks can simulate spatial depth using only 2D image distortion.
effects.funFact: Some games used Mode 7 for giant spinning bosses instead of floors.

margin.note: Mathematical operations that change the shape, size, or position of an image.
A single horizontal row of pixels drawn across a screen by a cathode-ray tube display.
Drawing true 3D objects using connected geometric shapes with calculated depth coordinates.
