effects.name: Moire pattern
effects.dating: 2010s: prominent topic of digital cameras without low-pass filters
effects.caption: Nikon: Overlaying two grids creates moiré.
effects.credit: Nikon USA, technical demonstration.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Large waves or bands of color over fine, regular patterns.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Similar grids overlap or meet the sensor grid.

body.label: Example
body.text: Fabric samples, screen photography and Op Art graphics.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Slowly rotate two transparent grid lines against each other.

context: Moiré predates digital photography. Its association with the 2010s here marks its renewed visibility as a camera issue, not the phenomenon's origin. Nikon explains the relationship between fine subject structures and the regular sensor grid, discussing it using digital cameras as an example. Two similar patterns create a new, much coarser visible structure. With digital color sensors, incorrect color bands can also appear. For experimental use, subtle rotations are particularly revealing: The underlying grid moves little, while the apparent wave moves significantly. Then photograph both grids. This adds a third scanning structure, allowing you to distinguish optical superposition of shooting errors.
effects.distinction: Geometric moiré and digital color aliases are related but different phenomena.
effects.aftermath: In controlled graphics, a distracting artifact becomes an impression of movement. Size and viewing distance strongly determine what remains visible.
effects.funFact: Two fine regular grids can combine to create a much coarser pattern.
highlights: Large waves or bands of color

margin.note: The regular arrangement of light-sensitive elements in a digital camera. Fine repeating subjects can interfere with this arrangement and create false patterns.
Art that uses repeated shapes and strong contrasts to create illusions of movement or depth.

effects.title: Mordançage
effects.name: Mordançage
effects.dating: 1960s, Jean-Pierre Sudre's darkroom experiments
effects.caption: Portrait Amid Lifted Emulsion Veils. A woman's portrait emerges among sweeping translucent folds, fine wrinkles, and ragged dark edges.
effects.credit: stacey svendsen from a little bit of everywhere · CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see black-and-white photographs with distorted, fluid, or torn areas. The darkest parts often look like floating veils or wrinkled skin.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A harsh chemical bath bleaches the print and softens the darkest gelatin emulsion. The photographer then physically lifts or rearranges these shadows.

body.label: Example
body.text: Jean-Pierre Sudre: Paysages Matériologiques, 1960s.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a mordançage print and try to spot where the dark emulsion has been pushed into 3D wrinkles.

context: Mordançage is a destructive darkroom process popularized by French photographer Jean-Pierre Sudre in the 1960s. It evolved from a late 19th-century reversal technique called etch-bleach. Sudre placed a fully developed silver gelatin print in a toxic mixture of copper chloride, hydrogen peroxide, and acetic acid. This solution acts proportionally, softening the gelatin where the most silver is present. The darkest shadows swell and detach from the paper base. The photographer can leave these veils hanging, brush them away completely, or reshape them. Finally, they redevelop the remaining image into new colors.
effects.distinction: Unlike solarization, which uses light to reverse tones, mordançage uses chemicals and physical manipulation. This alters the print's actual physical surface.
effects.aftermath: It shows that a photograph is a physical object made of fragile layers, not just a flat image.
effects.funFact: The French word 'mordançage' originally refers to etching or using a mordant in textile dyeing.

margin.note: A light-sensitive layer of animal protein and silver salts used to coat photographic paper.
An older photographic process used to remove dark areas of an emulsion to make printing plates.
A chemical compound used in this process to bleach the silver image back into a sensitive state.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Bright edge bands trace object boundaries and fine textures, while uniform areas stay dark.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Using a flat structuring element, dilation takes each neighborhood’s maximum brightness, while erosion takes its minimum. Subtracting erosion from dilation reveals local brightness differences rather than the direction of change.

body.label: Try it out

body.label: Classification
body.text: Calculated image processing result.

effects.funFact: Adding a constant brightness offset leaves the gradient unchanged, provided no values are clipped.

margin.note: A small shape selects the neighboring pixels used at each position. Flat means it adds no brightness offsets.

effects.title: Motion Blur
effects.name: Motion blur
effects.dating: 1911: Futuristic photodynamics as a historical reference
effects.caption: Radomianin: Train at Dundas Station, Toronto, 2008. Movement against a sharper background.
effects.credit: Radomianin / CC BY-SA 4.0; Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Moving shapes leave directed streaks.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Movement during exposure distributes subject information across multiple image areas.

body.label: Example
body.text: A passing train next to a sharper environment.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph the same movement at 1/500 and 1/15 of a second.

context: Anton Giulio and Arturo Bragaglia used long exposures of motion for their futuristic experiments. Instead of isolated phases of movement, they aimed to create a flowing impression of time. This distinguishes their photographic concept from systematic serial photography. Today, the same fundamental photographic logic applies to sports, dance, and street photography. The shutter speed, together with the direction and speed of movement, determines how far the trail extends in the image.
effects.distinction: Motion blur is not the same as incorrect focus. Camera movement blurs the entire scene; a moving person, on the other hand, can appear blurred against a sharp background. The everyday example shown is not a historical Bragaglia photograph.
effects.aftermath: A photograph can show duration instead of just a frozen moment.
effects.funFact: The futuristic Bragaglia brothers already studied the flow of movement photographically in 1911.

margin.note: The time during which the camera collects light for one image. Movement within that interval can spread detail into a streak.
Two shutter durations. The longer one records more movement during each image and therefore usually produces more motion blur.

context: Muybridge's successful motion studies of 1878; preceded by earlier experiments. Science, art, and precursors of cinema at the end of the 19th century. Detailed mechanism: Multiple cameras or rapidly successive shots break down a sequence of movements into phases. Time, like space, can be manipulated. This is not stop-motion puppet animation.
effects.distinction: Time can be shaped like space. This is not stop-motion puppet animation.
effects.aftermath: Contact sheets, multi-shot sports images, motion studies and loop animations.
effects.funFact: Muybridge's The Horse in Motion from 1878 broke down real movement into individual phases long before the cinema boom.
highlights: Multiple cameras or rapidly successive recordings

margin.note: Separate moments within a movement, such as takeoff, midair, and landing in a jump.
Images captured one after another in time, allowing changes in movement to be compared.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Dynamic flights of miniature spaceships appear as a single recording, even though multiple layers are combined.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Motors precisely repeat a camera path. This allows the model, light, and background to be captured separately and combined perfectly.

body.label: Example
body.text: ILM's Dykstraflex: Space battles and flybys in Star Wars (1977).

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare image planes with identical and differing movements. When does the spatial illusion break down?

context: Particularly consequential: Star Wars (1977), Dykstraflex.
Motors and computers store a camera path and repeatedly follow it identically. Model, light pass, background, and other elements can thus be captured separately and later perfectly aligned.
ILMs Dykstraflex for the space battles and flybys in Star Wars: A New Hope (1977).

Image: Historical original / source image. A camera robot films a TIE fighter model in front of a blue screen. The photo shows the production process; the composite light and model passes are created through precise repetition.
effects.distinction: Motion control moves the camera in a controlled manner; motion capture records the movement of a person or object as data. This is not an invention of every automatic camera. The milestone is the precise, repeatable camera movement for multiple effect layers.
effects.aftermath: Special effects shots gained the energy of a moving documentary camera; miniatures could be credibly combined with space and speed.
effects.funFact: In 1977, Dykstraflex repeated camera movements for Star Wars so that separate shots would align perfectly.
highlights: Motors precisely repeat a camera path

margin.note: A computer-controlled camera rig developed at Industrial Light & Magic for repeatable miniature photography on Star Wars.
Separate image layers, such as a model and a background, combined to suggest a single scene.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Shadow detail becomes clearer, while broad brightness differences shrink and local contrast grows.

body.label: Principle
body.text: At each scale, it subtracts the logarithm of a Gaussian-blurred image from the logarithm of the original image. It averages these differences across several blur scales to reduce illumination variation and emphasize local detail.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Vary the blur scales and watch shadow textures, bright edges, and possible halos.

body.label: Classification
body.text: Calculated image processing result.

effects.funFact: The name Retinex combines retina and cortex.

margin.note: A mathematical function that compresses large values more than small ones. Subtracting logarithms measures brightness ratios rather than simple brightness differences.
An image smoothed by averaging nearby pixels, with closer pixels receiving more weight. Here, it provides a rough estimate of illumination.

effects.title: Multiplane Camera
effects.name: Multiplane Camera
effects.dating: 1937, Walt Disney Studios' widespread use
effects.caption: AI illustration: Multiplane camera setup with forest landscape layers.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a two-dimensional animated scene where the background appears deep. Elements move at different speeds as the camera pushes forward.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Artwork is painted on separate glass panels spaced at different distances from the lens. Moving the camera creates realistic motion parallax.

body.label: Example
body.text: Walt Disney Studios: The Old Mill, 1937.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Hold one hand near your face and the other arm extended. Move your head sideways to see how they shift differently.

context: Early animation looked very flat. When characters moved across the screen, the background remained static and lacked natural depth. In the 1930s, animators needed a way to simulate a real, three-dimensional world. They built towering wooden or steel frames to hold several layers of glass artwork. The camera pointed downward from the top. Lights illuminated each layer independently to prevent unwanted shadows. By moving the glass panes at different speeds, operators created an illusion of depth called parallax. Walt Disney Studios popularized this massive machine with their 1937 short film. It revolutionized how audiences experienced animated spaces.
effects.distinction: Unlike a simple zoom that enlarges a flat image, a multiplane camera changes the relative spacing between objects. This mimics how our eyes naturally perceive distance.
effects.aftermath: It proves that separating flat visual elements into physical layers can trick the brain into seeing a deep, immersive world.
effects.funFact: An early version was built by animator Ub Iwerks using parts from an old Chevrolet car.

margin.note: A visual depth cue where things closer to you appear to move much faster than things far away.
Lacking movement or action. In early animation, the background was often a single, motionless painting.

effects.title: Neon Sign Glow
effects.name: Neon Sign Glow
effects.dating: 1910, Georges Claude’s neon demonstration at the Paris Motor Show
effects.caption: Texas Live Music Neon Sign. Blue live music lettering crowns red Texas lettering within a white outline of the state.
effects.credit: Carol M. Highsmith · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Bright tubular letters or outlines stand against dark surroundings, often with a soft halo. The luminous strokes have rounded bends and nearly uniform thickness.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An electric discharge excites atoms in low-pressure gas inside glass tubes, producing light as they release energy. Scattering in the eye or camera can spread this light into a soft halo beyond the tube.

body.label: Example
body.text: Georges Claude: Neon-tube demonstration at the Paris Motor Show, 1910.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph a working neon sign at several exposure settings; compare the tube’s visible shape with the apparent width of its halo.

context: Georges Claude demonstrated neon lighting at the Paris Motor Show in 1910. Commercial signs followed during the 1910s, turning bent glass tubes into illuminated lettering. Electrodes drive an electric discharge through gas sealed at low pressure. Neon itself produces orange-red light; other gases and fluorescent coatings provide other colors in signs commonly called neon. The tube emits light directly, rather than reflecting illumination from elsewhere. Its surrounding halo is not gas escaping into the air. Scattering, reflections, and photographic halation can enlarge the apparent glow.
effects.distinction: Unlike incandescent bulb lettering, neon can trace long, continuous strokes without rows of separate light points. LED imitations can resemble neon but use semiconductor emitters rather than a gas discharge.
effects.aftermath: Neon shows how a narrow light source can appear larger through scattering and the way an image records brightness.
effects.funFact: Neon gas itself produces orange-red light, not the full rainbow associated with neon signs.

margin.note: Electric current passing through gas can transfer energy to its atoms, making the gas emit light.
Conductive parts at the tube ends connect the gas discharge to the electrical supply.
Light can scatter or reflect within photographic film and its backing, creating halos around bright image areas.

effects.title: Neumorphism
effects.name: Neumorphism
effects.dating: Late 2019 emergence; widely discussed in 2020 interface design.
effects.caption: Soft Grey Neumorphic Interface Controls. Pale grey dials, sliders, switches, and rounded panels share a matching background, with blue accents marking selected controls.
effects.credit: Awesomecat · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Rounded controls resemble soft extrusions from a background of the same colour. Paired light and dark shadows make edges appear gently raised or pressed inward.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Opposing shadow offsets simulate directional lighting, while blurred edges suggest shallow depth. Inset shadows create recessed controls without changing the underlying flat screen.

body.label: Example
body.text: Alexander Plyuto: Skeuomorph Mobile Banking, 2019.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a pale grey rounded rectangle on matching grey, then add blurred white and dark shadows on opposite sides.

context: Neumorphism gained attention around 2020, following interface experiments shared online in late 2019. Alexander Plyuto’s banking concept became a widely cited example of the approach. It revived skeuomorphism’s suggestion of physical objects, but usually replaced detailed textures with smooth, nearly monochrome surfaces. Designers could construct the effect with CSS box shadows, placing a pale shadow opposite a darker one. The result suggested controls moulded from the surrounding panel rather than placed above it. However, weak boundary contrast could make controls and their states difficult to distinguish.
effects.distinction: Traditional skeuomorphism may imitate leather, metal, or other recognisable materials. Neumorphism usually suggests one continuous surface, unlike ordinary drop shadows beneath visibly separate cards.
effects.aftermath: It shows how small lighting cues can suggest depth, while revealing the accessibility costs of subtle control boundaries.
effects.funFact: The apparent highlight can be implemented as a white shadow rather than a separate lighting effect.

margin.note: Shapes that appear to project gently from a surface, with rounded transitions rather than sharp edges.
Shadows drawn inside a shape’s boundary. They can make its centre look lower than its surroundings.
Web styling instructions that draw shadows around or inside rectangular elements. Several shadows can be combined.

effects.title: Neural Radiance Fields
effects.name: Neural Radiance Fields
effects.dating: 2020, Ben Mildenhall et al. publication
effects.caption: AI illustration: Neural radiance field rendering of refractive glass objects.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a photorealistic, three-dimensional scene rendered from new camera angles. The view includes complex lighting, reflections, and translucent materials that shift naturally as you move.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A neural network analyzes multiple photographs to learn how light travels through a space. It calculates the color and density of light at every invisible point, generating new views.

body.label: Example
body.text: Ben Mildenhall et al.: "NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis", 2020.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a shiny object from different angles and notice how the reflections move; NeRF accurately simulates this exact shifting behavior.

context: Researchers at UC Berkeley, Google Research, and UC San Diego introduced NeRF in 2020. Before this, creating 3D computer graphics required building complex geometric meshes. NeRF took a radically different approach. Instead of polygons, it uses a massive mathematical formula—a neural network—to map a scene's volume. By feeding the network dozens of standard photographs along with their exact camera positions, the system learns the underlying light field. It deduces how dense objects are and how they scatter light. The result is a continuous volumetric scene that can render entirely new, highly realistic viewpoints.
effects.distinction: Unlike traditional photogrammetry, which creates a hollow 3D mesh wrapped in flat textures, NeRF calculates light and volume mathematically. This allows NeRF to perfectly recreate mirrors, glass, and complex shadows that confuse mesh-based systems.
effects.aftermath: It teaches that deep learning can translate 2D images into continuous volumetric light fields.
effects.funFact: Early NeRFs took days to compute, but modern versions render complex scenes in under a second.
highlights: complex lighting, reflections, and translucent materials

margin.note: A computing system inspired by the human brain that learns complex patterns directly from data.
A digital space where the entire internal volume is mapped mathematically, rather than just the outer surfaces of objects.

effects.title: Neural Relighting
effects.name: Neural Relighting
effects.dating: 2020s; Google’s Portrait Light introduced in 2020
effects.caption: AI illustration: Neural portrait relighting with warm directional source.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: A photographed face or scene gains redirected shadows, shifted highlights, or a new lighting color. The viewpoint stays fixed while the illumination appears to change.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A neural network predicts how image pixels should change under different lighting, using learned patterns of shape, materials, and illumination. Some methods estimate surface geometry explicitly; others generate the altered appearance directly.

body.label: Example
body.text: Google: Portrait Light, 2020.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Relight one portrait from opposite sides, then compare the nose shadow, cheek brightness, and reflections in the eyes.

context: Neural relighting became more accessible during the 2020s, building on earlier computational photography and computer graphics research. Google’s Portrait Light offered a prominent example in 2020, adding adjustable illumination to portraits after capture. Training can use photographs under controlled lights, rendered scenes, or other image collections. The central difficulty is separating surface reflectance from illumination: a dark patch might be paint, shadow, or both. A single photograph rarely provides enough evidence for a unique solution. The network therefore makes learned guesses, which can produce convincing but physically inconsistent results.
effects.distinction: Unlike a global exposure adjustment, neural relighting can change local shading according to inferred shape. It changes the image after capture, not the original exposure.
effects.aftermath: Neural relighting shows that convincing illumination can be synthesized without proving how the original scene was lit.
effects.funFact: A single dark patch can mean dark material, weak illumination, or a shadow.

margin.note: A computational model trained on examples to predict outputs from inputs.
The three-dimensional shape and orientation of visible surfaces. These influence where light falls and shadows form.
How a material reflects incoming light. This includes its color and whether its reflections are glossy or diffuse.

effects.title: Neural Style Transfer
effects.name: Neural Style Transfer
effects.dating: 2015, Leon Gatys's algorithm
effects.caption: Seated Portrait with Transferred Brushstrokes. A seated man's recognizable photographic portrait is overlaid with orange, gold, and green directional brushstrokes.
effects.credit: Kira Wales · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a photo altered to look like a painting. It keeps the original shapes but adopts another image's colors and brushstrokes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An artificial neural network separates an image's content from its style. It then combines the content mathematically with a new style.

body.label: Example
body.text: Leon Gatys, Alexander Ecker, and Matthias Bethge: A Neural Algorithm of Artistic Style, 2015.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Squint at a style-transferred image. Notice how the broad structural outlines remain recognizable, but the surface texture completely changes.

context: In 2015, researchers led by Leon Gatys published a breakthrough paper on image processing. They used convolutional neural networks, originally built to recognize objects in photos. The team discovered that different layers of the network process different image traits. Deep layers capture the spatial layout, or content. Shallow layers capture texture, color, and patterns, defining the style. By running a photo and a painting through the network, they extracted these elements. An algorithm then merged the photo's content with the painting's style. This digital technique sparked a massive wave of artificial intelligence art.
effects.distinction: Unlike simple digital photo filters, it does not just overlay a color tint or blur. It completely reconstructs the image using mathematically learned textures.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that artificial intelligence can mathematically isolate and manipulate the abstract concept of artistic style.
effects.funFact: The original 2015 algorithm took several minutes to process a single image on a powerful computer.

margin.note: A computing system inspired by biological brains, used to recognize patterns in data.
A specific type of artificial intelligence model that excels at analyzing visual imagery using mathematical filters.
The physical arrangement and proportions of objects within a scene.

effects.title: Night Vision
effects.name: Night vision / image intensifier look
effects.dating: 1990s: military visual culture; technology significantly older
effects.caption: Night vision with Astroscope: Northern Strike exercise, August 6, 2026.
effects.credit: Sgt. 1st Class Aaron Shuemake / West Virginia National Guard. Public domain.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Green, grainy image with bright noise and limited contrast.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Image intensifiers amplify available light; filters imitate the phosphor screen.

body.label: Example
body.text: Night vision recordings and subsequent surveillance aesthetics.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare the green hue alone with added grain and overexposure.

context: The classic green night vision impression originates from image intensifiers with a corresponding phosphor screen. It is not a natural color of darkness. The 1990s serve as a reference point for military perception and application; NASA documented human perception issues with such devices in 1991. The technology is older and has evolved. The US Army announced the switch from green to white phosphor tubes in 2019. Some modern devices combine image intensification with thermal information; this combination does not eliminate the fundamental difference. A green filter merely simulates the surface. The exercise therefore tests which additional characteristics, such as noise, resolution limits, and bright overexposure, actually contribute to the sensor impression.
effects.distinction: Night vision through light amplification and thermal heat vision are different sensor principles.
effects.aftermath: For music visuals, a deliberately stylized look is often sufficient. With documentary images, it must remain clear whether genuine sensor data or post-processing is used.
effects.funFact: Night vision doesn't have to be green: The US Army also describes devices with a white phosphor image.

margin.note: Devices that convert faint incoming light into electrons, amplify the signal, and turn it back into a visible image.
A surface that glows when struck by electrons, producing the visible image in an intensifier.

effects.caption: Normal Mapping: Comparison from the Blender manual.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Fine reliefs react to light, even though the basic shape remains simple.

body.label: Principle

body.label: Example
body.text: Blender: Normal map comparison.

body.label: Try it out

context: Appearance-Preserving Simplification by Cohen, Olano, and Manocha demonstrated in 1998 how color and normal textures can preserve details in simplified geometry. The practical result is a high degree of visible detail on comparatively simple models. Blender explains RGB-coded normals that must match the chosen coordinate space. The current documentation image illustrates the principle; it is not included as an image from the paper.
effects.distinction: A normal map does not typically model a new silhouette. Its RGB values ​​encode directions, not ordinary surface colors; the texture requires appropriate data settings.
effects.aftermath: Geometric complexity and perceived surface detail can be partially separated.
effects.funFact: The typical blue-violet of a normal map encodes directions instead of pigments.

margin.note: Directions perpendicular to a surface, used to calculate how light should shade it.
Red, green, and blue channels. In a normal map, they store direction information rather than ordinary surface color.

effects.title: NTSC Composite Artifacts
effects.name: NTSC composite artifacts
effects.dating: NTSC color television since the 1950s; later retro simulation.
effects.caption: NTSC look: current digital effect demonstration.
effects.credit: Digital effect demonstration; not a historical broadcast transfer.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Color flickering, wandering dot patterns, and frayed color edges.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Divided signal bandwidth creates crosstalk between color and brightness.

body.label: Example
body.text: Digital effect: NTSC signal simulation.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Experiment with fine stripes and rich color transitions.

context: This slide addresses the visible characteristics of a composite analog video signal. Fine image details can be misinterpreted as color, and conversely, color information can appear in the luminance signal. In 1993, Jim Blinn explained color coding and its consequences for computer graphics in his column "NTSC: Nice Technology, Super Color." Today's digital demonstration replicates the signal characteristics; it does not represent a historical fashion of the depicted subject.
effects.distinction: NTSC is a television system, not a synonym for every analog interference. Composite describes the shared transmission; separate signal paths can avoid some artifacts.
effects.aftermath: Signal errors explain why clean computer graphics look different on analog television.
effects.funFact: Fine black and white patterns can create false colors in the composite signal.

margin.note: The range of frequencies available to carry information. Limited space forces color and brightness information to share a crowded signal.
Unwanted interference between parts of a signal. Here, brightness detail can be mistaken for color, or color for brightness.

effects.title: Op Art
effects.name: Op Art
effects.dating: 1964, Time magazine coins the term
effects.caption: Optical Sphere in Repeated Lettering. Repeated black, white, and blue lettering swells into a large central sphere against a patterned ground.
effects.credit: Basile Morin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see high-contrast geometric patterns that seem to flicker, vibrate, or warp. The flat image creates a false illusion of movement or deep space.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Our eyes struggle to process sharp, repetitive contrasts like black and white lines. This visual overload triggers micro-movements in the eye, causing perceived motion.

body.label: Example
body.text: Bridget Riley: Movement in Squares, 1961.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Stare at a dense grid of black and white stripes for ten seconds and notice how the lines start to dance.

context: Op Art emerged in the 1960s as artists began exploring the science of human perception. Victor Vasarely and Bridget Riley painted precise, mathematical arrangements of lines, shapes, and colors. Their goal was not to show real objects, but to trigger active optical responses in the viewer's brain. The movement gained massive attention after the 1965 "The Responsive Eye" exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art. By stripping art down to stark geometry, these artists proved that still images could actively manipulate the human nervous system.
effects.distinction: Unlike Kinetic Art, which uses motors to physically move a sculpture, Op Art relies entirely on stationary patterns. The movement only happens inside your eyes and brain.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that seeing is an active, biological process where our brains constantly interpret and sometimes misread visual data.
effects.funFact: Fashion designers quickly copied Op Art, putting dizzying geometric patterns on 1960s mod dresses.

margin.note: This happens when the brain receives too much confusing optical information at once. It causes the eye to strain and misinterpret the image.
Our eyes constantly make tiny, involuntary shifts called saccades to keep vision sharp. In highly structured patterns, these tiny shifts make stationary lines seem to move.
This refers to the physiological reactions that occur in our eyes and brain when we look at specific light or color arrangements.

context: Optical Flow is an older field of research. In November 2015, Adobe introduced Optical Flow as an additional interpolation option in Premiere Pro; Pixel Motion and Timewarp in After Effects had earlier predecessors. The software analyzes adjacent frames and generates intermediate images based on estimated motion vectors. Timewarp is based on Foundry's Kronos. This slide discusses this specific interpolation principle without equating it with all AI video models. The crucial point is the comparison in motion.
effects.distinction: Optical flow reconstructs presumed motion, not actually captured intermediate frames. Occlusions, intersections, and rapid movements can introduce errors.
effects.aftermath: Intermediate images are a calculated interpretation of the recorded time sequence.

effects.title: Orton Effect
effects.name: Orton Effect
effects.dating: Mid-1980s, Michael Orton's landscape photography
effects.caption: Astronomical Clock with Soft Highlight Glow. An ornate astronomical clock displays softly glowing gold markings and pastel dial segments against dark carved stone.
effects.credit: Herr Kriss · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see an image that is both sharp and blurry at the same time. Bright areas glow softly while dark details remain clear.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A sharp, overexposed slide is physically layered over a blurry, overexposed slide of the exact same scene. The combined densities create normal contrast.

body.label: Example
body.text: Michael Orton: Trees, Beacon Hill Park, mid-1980s.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Duplicate a digital photo on your phone. Blur the top copy, make it semi-transparent, and increase the brightness of both layers.

context: In the 1980s, Canadian photographer Michael Orton sought to mimic watercolor paintings using a camera. He used slide film, which becomes lighter when overexposed. He took two photos of the same subject on a tripod. The first exposure was perfectly focused but heavily overexposed. The second exposure was out of focus and also overexposed. At a light table, he sandwiched these two slides together in a single mount. Because slide film creates a positive image, stacking two light images makes a properly exposed final picture. This analog process produced a distinct dreamy glow.
effects.distinction: Unlike simply taking an out-of-focus photograph, the Orton Effect retains sharp core details underneath the glow. It combines distinct clarity with ethereal blur.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how stacking multiple imperfect exposures can combine to create a properly exposed, textured final image.
effects.funFact: Digital editors often use the Multiply blend mode to mathematically replicate the physical stacking of transparent slides.

margin.note: Photographic film that produces a positive, transparent image directly on the strip. It is meant to be viewed using a projector.
A condition where photographic film receives too much light. On positive slide film, this makes the resulting image appear washed out and pale.
A small plastic or cardboard frame used to hold a piece of slide film flat. It allows the image to be easily handled or projected.

context: Ben Laposky photographed moving patterns on an oscilloscope screen and called the electronic compositions Oscillons. The Computer History Museum dates Oscillon 4 to approximately 1952 and cites the Sanford Museum as the source of the image. Early electronic imagery was thus made collectible and exhibitable through long-term photographic recording. Here, the decade refers to a documented example of art, not to the invention of mathematical curves.
effects.distinction: Lissajous curves are older than electronic displays. Not every oscilloscope artwork is a simple Lissajous figure; complex signals produce more complex shapes.
effects.aftermath: Sound and image can be two versions of the same signal.
effects.funFact: Laposky's early electronic images were captured with a camera.

margin.note: Repeated changes in an electrical signal. They can steer a screen’s light spot into looping patterns.

effects.title: Paik–Abe Video Synthesizer
effects.name: Paik–Abe Video Synthesizer

body.label: Identify
body.text: Faces and objects become patches of intense artificial colour, often layered into overlapping silhouettes. Abrupt colour boundaries replace natural shading.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Analogue circuits colourise and mix incoming video signals, turning brightness information into adjustable colour contributions. A colour television displays the result through additive colour mixing.

body.label: Example
body.text: Nam June Paik: Global Groove, 1973.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Apply a false-colour gradient to a grayscale video, then change the gradient while watching how faces separate into coloured regions.

context: Artist Nam June Paik and engineer Shuya Abe developed the synthesizer in 1969, working with Boston television station WGBH. It reached broadcast audiences in 1970 through Video Commune. The instrument let performers colourise and combine several video sources while images were running. Its analogue controls made television pictures something to play, rather than simply record. Colour came from electronic signal processing, not dyes or photographic development. Paik used this approach to challenge television’s familiar appearance and its usual separation between programme makers and viewers.
effects.distinction: Unlike optical filters, this system changes electrical image signals before display. Unlike realistic colour restoration, its colourisation deliberately need not match the original scene.
effects.aftermath: It shows how a recording medium can also become a live instrument for shaping colour and composition.
effects.funFact: Its broadcast debut, Video Commune, paired live video experimentation with Beatles music.

margin.note: Electronic components that process continuously varying electrical signals, rather than numerical pixel values.
Combining coloured light to make other colours. A colour television uses red, green and blue light.
Introduce colour into an image electronically. Here, those colours need not represent the subject’s actual appearance.

effects.title: Paint-on-Glass Animation
effects.name: Paint-on-Glass Animation
effects.dating: 1980s landmark: Aleksandr Petrov’s The Cow, 1989; the technique predates this film.
effects.caption: AI illustration: Animation stand with wet paint on glass.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Soft brush marks and luminous colours shift continuously, as figures emerge from painterly textures. Blurred edges and flowing transformations can make scenes resemble moving memories.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The animator alters wet paint on glass beneath a camera, photographing each stage as a separate frame. Sequential playback turns these small changes into movement; slow-drying oil paint allows repeated reshaping.

body.label: Example
body.text: Aleksandr Petrov: The Cow, 1989.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Spread washable paint on clear plastic, photograph it, then reshape and photograph it repeatedly; compare the images in sequence.

context: Paint-on-glass animation existed before the 1980s, but Petrov’s The Cow became a celebrated example at the decade’s end. The film uses oil paint on glass to create a world of shifting, textured images. Rather than preparing a separate drawing for every frame, the animator repeatedly changes the painting beneath the camera. Paint can be added, pushed aside, blended, or wiped away. Each photograph preserves a stage that later alterations may destroy. Lighting, paint thickness, and the background influence whether colours appear opaque or translucent.
effects.distinction: Unlike cel animation, which usually replaces separate drawings on transparent sheets, paint-on-glass animation often reworks the same painted surface. Its movement comes from successive photographs, not paint flowing during a continuous exposure.
effects.aftermath: It shows how changes to a material surface can create movement while preserving the visible traces of artistic gestures.
effects.funFact: A finished sequence may survive only in photographs because making the next frame changes the original painting.

margin.note: One still image within a moving sequence.
Showing recorded images one after another in order, fast enough to suggest movement.
Allowing some light through without being fully clear.

effects.title: Palette Cycling
effects.name: Palette Cycling
effects.dating: 1980s, indexed-colour computer graphics and Deluxe Paint
effects.caption: AI illustration: Waterfall movement through color index shifting.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Waterfalls stream, waves ripple, and lights pulse while their outlines stay fixed. Repeating bands of colour create apparent movement.

body.label: Principle
body.text: In indexed colour, each pixel stores a palette index rather than its own colour value. Rotating palette entries changes displayed colours without moving pixels.

body.label: Example
body.text: Mark Ferrari (background art): Loom, 1990.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a palette-cycling waterfall, tracking one edge: notice how its colours change while its shape stays still.

context: Palette cycling became a familiar animation technique on home computers during the 1980s. Deluxe Paint, first released in 1985, helped artists build pictures around cycling colour ranges. Artists arranged palette indices into spatial patterns, then rotated the colours assigned to those indices. This could suggest flowing water, flickering fire, or moving highlights without storing a separate picture for every frame. Different ranges could cycle at different speeds. Mark Ferrari became particularly associated with richly detailed scenes using this method, including waterfalls. The motion depended on careful painting, not simply changing arbitrary colours.
effects.distinction: Unlike frame-by-frame animation, palette cycling can leave the stored pixel indices unchanged. Unlike a uniform hue shift, it cycles selected palette entries.
effects.aftermath: Palette cycling shows how changing colour assignments can suggest motion without changing an image's geometry.
effects.funFact: One palette change can recolour thousands of scattered pixels at once.

margin.note: An image format where pixels refer to entries in a shared colour table.
A number identifying one entry in that colour table.
Selected groups of palette entries whose colours repeatedly exchange positions.

effects.title: Panning Shot
effects.name: Panning Shot
effects.dating: 2000s, popularization in digital sports and automotive photography
effects.caption: Bicycle Riders Crossing a Wet Street. A man pedals a red bicycle with a child seated behind him, crossing a wet street against streaked storefronts.
effects.credit: Md.Mijanur rahman Mijan · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a moving subject that appears mostly sharp and clearly defined. The background features long, horizontal streaks that convey a strong sense of high speed.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The photographer moves the camera to track a moving subject during a slightly long exposure. This keeps the subject fixed on the sensor while the stationary background blurs.

body.label: Example
body.text: Unknown Photographer: Digital automotive panning shots at Le Mans, 2000s.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Wave your hand in front of your face while tracking it with your eyes; notice how the background streaks while your hand remains clear.

context: Panning is an optical technique that grew massively in the 2000s thanks to digital photography. Before digital cameras, panning was highly unpredictable. Photographers had to wait for film development to see if they successfully matched the subject's speed. In the 2000s, digital screens provided instant visual feedback. This allowed photographers to adjust their shutter speed and tracking motion on the spot. Furthermore, the 2000s introduced optical image stabilization in camera lenses. Some lenses featured a specific panning mode that stabilized vertical shakes while allowing horizontal movement. This made sharp subjects against heavily blurred backgrounds much easier to achieve.
effects.distinction: In standard motion blur, the stationary camera captures a sharp background and a blurred subject. Panning reverses this entirely by moving the camera along with the fast subject.
effects.aftermath: It teaches how relative motion between the camera, subject, and background dictates what appears sharp or blurred in a photograph.
effects.funFact: Photographers often use shutter speeds as slow as half a second to create abstract color streaks.

margin.note: The electronic chip inside a digital camera that captures incoming light and converts it into a digital image.
The exact length of time a camera sensor is exposed to light while taking a photograph.
A physical mechanism inside a lens that shifts glass elements to counteract small hand movements during exposure.

effects.title: Panoramic Photography
effects.name: Panoramic Photography
effects.dating: 1840s-1850s, early multi-plate daguerreotypes
effects.caption: Waterfront Panorama on Adjoining Plates. A sequence of adjoining photographic plates presents a continuous waterfront with buildings, boats, and distant hills.
effects.credit: Charles H. Fontayne (1814–1901) and William Southgate Porter (1822–1889) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see an extremely wide landscape or cityscape image. The view spans a much broader horizontal angle than human vision.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Photographers exposed multiple overlapping plates by rotating the camera. Later, they used clockwork swing-lens cameras to expose one long curved negative.

body.label: Example
body.text: Charles Fontayne and William S. Porter: Panorama of Cincinnati, 1848.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Find a stitched multi-plate panorama and look for slight changes in lighting or moving subjects that get cut off at the seams.

context: Early lenses could not capture very wide angles without severe distortion. To photograph expansive cities or landscapes, photographers developed two clever solutions. The simplest method was taking sequential photos. They exposed a glass plate, rotated the camera slightly, and exposed another. These separate prints were then aligned and mounted side-by-side. Later inventors built specialized swing-lens cameras. Inside these devices, a clockwork mechanism rotated the lens across a wide arc. As the lens moved, a narrow slit exposed a curved strip of film. This swept the image onto the negative sequentially. Both techniques demanded perfect leveling to keep the horizon perfectly straight.
effects.distinction: Unlike wide-angle lenses which capture a broad view instantly, panoramas scan or stitch across time. This causes moving objects to warp, blur, or vanish.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that early photographers treated the camera not just as a static eye, but as a mechanical scanning apparatus.
effects.funFact: Some swing-lens cameras rotated a full 360 degrees, letting the same person appear twice at opposite ends.

margin.note: Separate photographic negatives taken from the same spot, shifted slightly so their edges share visual information.
Specialized cameras where the lens rotates during exposure, scanning the image sequentially across a curved film surface.

effects.title: Particle Systems
effects.name: Particle Systems
effects.dating: 1982, William Reeves's Genesis Effect
effects.caption: Particle Emitters and Collision Barrier. Two yellow emitters produce a soft white plume and a stream of red spheres that encounters an inclined barrier.
effects.credit: Holger Weihe · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a swarm of tiny, glowing dots or shapes moving together to form fuzzy, chaotic shapes. They often look like fire, smoke, sparks, or magic spells.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A computer program spawns hundreds of independent digital points and applies basic physics rules to them. These points live, move, and die over a set lifespan.

body.label: Example
body.text: William Reeves (Industrial Light & Magic): Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan, 1982.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Drop a handful of sand in the wind and watch how individual grains move together to form a fluid dust cloud.

context: Before the 1980s, computer graphics struggled to draw fuzzy or fluid things like fire. Traditional geometry relied on rigid polygons, which looked fake and blocky. In 1982, William Reeves at Industrial Light & Magic invented particle systems to solve this. Instead of drawing a solid shape, his code generated thousands of tiny graphical points. Each point followed basic rules for speed, gravity, and color before fading away. He first used this for the "Genesis Effect" in Star Trek II. The result was a stunning wall of fire spreading across a planet. This technique revolutionized how computers simulate natural chaos.
effects.distinction: Particle systems generate many independent points using math, unlike fluid simulations which calculate continuous flows on a 3D grid. Particle rendering is faster but less physically accurate.
effects.aftermath: It shows that complex natural phenomena can emerge from simple, repetitive mathematical rules.
effects.funFact: Reeves originally tested the effect by simulating digital fireworks against a simple black background.

margin.note: This means generating or creating a new digital object in the computer's memory.
These are flat, geometric shapes like triangles used to build 3D computer models.
The unpredictable, complex way things like smoke, water, and fire move in the real world.

effects.title: Pen Plotter Art
effects.name: Pen Plotter Art
effects.dating: 1960s; Georg Nees and Frieder Nake exhibited computer drawings in 1965.
effects.caption: Pen-Plotted Geometric Envelopes. A flatbed plotter holds a drawing of intersecting straight lines surrounding a broad curved opening.
effects.credit: Tomasz Sienicki [user: tsca, mail: tomasz.sienicki at gmail.com] · CC BY 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Fine ink lines form geometric grids, repeated shapes, and controlled irregularities on paper. Overlapping strokes create dense patches without continuous painted shading.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A computer sends movement commands to a mechanical plotter, which moves a pen relative to paper. Programmed rules and sometimes pseudorandom numbers determine the pen paths.

body.label: Example
body.text: Frieder Nake: Hommage à Paul Klee, 1965.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a grid of squares, using dice to choose each square's tilt; notice how fixed rules produce varied results.

context: In 1965, Georg Nees and Frieder Nake exhibited computer-generated drawings made with pen plotters in Germany. These machines also served engineering and technical drafting. Artists wrote programs that translated geometric rules into coordinates and drawing instructions. The plotter lowered its pen to draw and lifted it to move without marking. Repetition made the underlying system visible, while pseudorandom numbers introduced variation within chosen limits. Ink accumulated on paper through individual strokes, not photographic exposure. The artist designed the procedure rather than guiding every line by hand.
effects.distinction: Unlike raster printing, pen plotting traces paths with a moving drawing tool rather than building images from rows of dots. Not all plotter drawings use randomness.
effects.aftermath: Pen plotter art shows how an artist can shape an image by designing rules, constraints, and opportunities for variation.
effects.funFact: A plotter can move across a drawing without leaving a mark by lifting its pen.

margin.note: A machine that draws by moving a pen and paper relative to each other under automatic control.
Numbers generated by a repeatable calculation to behave like random choices.
Numbers that specify positions, such as distances across and up a sheet of paper.

context: This stage trick, which became popular in the 19th century, combines a visible stage with the reflection of a hidden area. Changes in lighting make the apparition appear or disappear. effects.distinction: The glass image is often called a hologram. However, it is created through reflection; viewing angle, darkness, and brightness levels are crucial.
effects.aftermath: New displays can spectacularly reuse very old principles.
effects.funFact: Kate Moss’ famous McQueen appearance in 2006 used a Victorian stage trick.

effects.title: Perlin Noise
effects.name: Perlin Noise

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see organic, flowing patterns that resemble clouds, marble, or swirling water. Unlike television static, it has smooth transitions between light and dark areas.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A computer algorithm generates random values at specific points on a grid. It then smoothly interpolates between them to create continuous gradients.

body.label: Example
body.text: Ken Perlin: Tron (visual effects), 1982.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at water ripples in an older video game. Try to spot the repeating, wavy gradients simulating nature.

context: In the early 1980s, computer graphics looked very flat and artificial. Ken Perlin worked on the movie Tron and wanted realistic digital surfaces. He invented a mathematical function to generate controlled randomness. This procedural texture method layered different sizes of visual noise together. It created complex natural looks without requiring massive amounts of memory. Instead of hand-drawing every detail, computers could calculate textures on the fly. Perlin won an Academy Award for this technical breakthrough. It remains a foundational tool in modern animation and video games.
effects.distinction: White noise places entirely random pixels next to each other, creating harsh static. Perlin noise mathematically connects nearby points to form smooth waves.
effects.aftermath: It shows how mathematical formulas can capture the structured randomness found in the natural world.
effects.funFact: Ken Perlin won a Technical Achievement Academy Award in 1997 for this exact algorithm.

margin.note: This means calculating intermediate values between two known points. It creates a smooth mathematical bridge instead of a sudden visual jump.
A surface pattern generated entirely by mathematical rules. It is calculated by the computer rather than being painted or photographed.
A specific set of step-by-step mathematical instructions. A computer follows these rules to solve a problem or create an image.

effects.title: Petzval Swirl Bokeh
effects.name: Petzval Swirl Bokeh
effects.dating: 1840, Josef Petzval's portrait objective
effects.caption: Garden Plaque Framed by Swirl Bokeh. A square rose-garden identification plaque sits sharply within a ring of blurred foliage.
effects.credit: Javier Perez Montes · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a sharp, central subject surrounded by a blurred background. The out-of-focus background highlights stretch into circular, swirling shapes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Optical vignetting blocks some light rays at the edges of the lens. This physically shapes the background highlights into angled, cat's-eye ovals.

body.label: Example
body.text: Julia Margaret Cameron: Portrait of Sir John Herschel, 1867.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at bright spots in a blurred photo background. Are they perfectly round, or do they look squashed near the edges?

context: In 1840, mathematician Josef Petzval designed the first fast portrait lens. Daguerreotypes required incredibly long exposure times in bright sunlight. Petzval's new lens gathered about sixteen times more light than earlier optics. Photographers could suddenly capture human subjects in mere seconds. However, this early mathematical design had a distinct flaw called field curvature. The focus plane was curved like a bowl rather than perfectly flat. To keep the subject sharp, the edges fell rapidly out of focus. Combined with the long lens barrel blocking angled light, this generated a strong, swirling blur. People eventually loved this optical defect.
effects.distinction: Radial blur is a digital filter that smears pixels outward. Petzval swirl is an optical artifact affecting only out-of-focus background light.
effects.aftermath: Technical flaws in early photographic tools often become beloved artistic choices later on.
effects.funFact: Josef Petzval never earned royalties from his famous lens because he failed to secure a comprehensive patent.

margin.note: The physical blocking of light rays entering a lens from an angle, causing darker or distorted image edges.
The squashed shape that round points of light take on when clipped by the edges of a camera lens barrel.
An optical flaw where a lens projects the sharp image onto a curved bowl shape instead of a flat sensor.

effects.title: Phenakistiscope Loop
effects.name: Phenakistiscope Loop
effects.dating: 1832, Joseph Plateau's spinning animation disc
effects.caption: Transforming Faces Phenakistiscope Disc. A circular disc presents a ring of caricatured heads with progressively changing facial proportions and narrow viewing slots near its rim.
effects.credit: Simon Stampfer · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a series of sequential drawings arranged in a circle on a flat disc. When viewed properly, these drawings merge into an endlessly repeating moving image.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Narrow radial slits block your vision while the disc spins, revealing each drawing only for a split second. This rapid replacement creates the illusion of continuous motion through persistence of vision.

body.label: Example
body.text: Joseph Plateau: Phénakisticope discs (published by Ackermann), 1833.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Stand in front of a mirror with a slotted paper disc, look through the slits, and spin it.

context: Belgian physicist Joseph Plateau introduced the phenakistiscope in 1832. It was the first device to create a fluid illusion of motion from static pictures. The device consists of a cardboard disc with equidistant radial slits. A sequence of slightly changing images is drawn around the disc's center. To use it, a person holds the disc facing a mirror and looks through the moving slits. As the disc spins, the slits act as a shutter. They prevent the images from blurring together. Your brain pieces these brief flashes together. This transforms a sequence of flat drawings into a looping animation.
effects.distinction: The zoetrope uses a spinning drum with slits on the side instead of a flat disc. This allows multiple people to view the animation at once.
effects.aftermath: It proves that our visual system requires brief moments of darkness between images to perceive smooth motion.
effects.funFact: Austrian professor Simon von Stampfer invented an identical device called the stroboscopic disc in the exact same year.

margin.note: Narrow cuts pointing outward from the center of the disc. They work as a simple shutter mechanism.
The optical phenomenon where an image briefly lingers in your visual system. It helps blend sequential frames into motion.
A device that quickly blocks and unblocks light. It prevents spinning drawings from looking like a smeared blur.

effects.title: Phong Shading
effects.name: Phong Shading
effects.dating: 1973, Bui Tuong Phong's illumination model
effects.caption: Flat, Gouraud, and Phong Shading Compared. Three blue spheres compare flat, Gouraud, and Phong shading, progressing from visible facets to a smooth surface with a compact highlight.

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see smooth, 3D computer models with tight, bright spots of reflected light. These shiny highlights curve naturally across the object's surface.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The computer calculates how light bounces for every single pixel. It interpolates the surface orientation across flat polygons to simulate curves.

body.label: Example
body.text: Martin Newell: Utah Teapot, 1975.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at a glossy plastic object like a computer mouse. Notice how the bright spot moves naturally as you turn it.

context: In the early 1970s, 3D computer graphics looked clunky and flat. Objects were made of flat geometric panels. Early methods softened the edges between panels, but objects still looked dull. In 1973, Bui Tuong Phong changed this while working at the University of Utah. He realized glossy materials needed sharp reflections of the light source. His math calculated the surface angle for every pixel. This allowed digital objects to look like shiny plastic. It revolutionized 3D graphics by adding realistic specular highlights.
effects.distinction: Gouraud shading only calculates light at polygon corners and blurs the colors inward. Phong shading calculates light for every pixel, allowing sharp reflections.
effects.aftermath: It teaches that calculating lighting per pixel creates much more realistic 3D materials than calculating per corner.
effects.funFact: Phong sadly passed away from leukemia in 1975, just two years after publishing his revolutionary shading method.

margin.note: To estimate unknown values that fall between known values. Here, it creates smooth numerical transitions between corners.
The exact 3D direction a specific point on an object faces, mathematically called a normal vector.
The bright, mirror-like reflections of a light source on a glossy or shiny surface.

effects.title: Photo Booth Strip
effects.name: Photo Booth Strip
effects.dating: 1925, Anatol Josepho's Photomaton in New York
effects.caption: Four Poses in a Photo Booth Strip. Four black-and-white portraits form a narrow vertical strip, showing a bespectacled man changing his pose and holding a round object near his eyes.
effects.credit: leafar · CC BY-SA 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: A narrow paper strip holds stacked portraits, commonly four frames, separated by pale borders. The fixed viewpoint makes changing expressions and small movements easy to compare.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Timed exposures record separate moments through one camera, while an automatic mechanism advances the photographic material. Chemical processing then produces visible, lasting pictures; exposure alone does not create the finished strip.

body.label: Example
body.text: Andy Warhol: Ethel Scull 36 Times, 1963.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Take four portraits from one fixed position, changing your expression each time; stack them vertically and compare the smallest differences.

context: Anatol Josepho opened his Photomaton in New York in 1925, making automatic portrait photography available without a photographer operating each exposure. His early machine produced eight pictures, rather than the four now commonly associated with booth strips. Inside, a camera recorded successive exposures, and machinery carried photographic material through chemical processing. The sitter received finished pictures after waiting several minutes. Enclosed booths encouraged playful expressions as well as practical identification portraits. Artists later reused booth photographs; Warhol's Ethel Scull 36 Times arranged portraits derived from a booth session into a larger artwork.
effects.distinction: A contact sheet displays images from negatives placed directly against photographic paper. A booth strip comes from successive automatic portraits, not necessarily contact printing.
effects.aftermath: The strip shows how a fixed camera and repeated framing can turn tiny changes into a visual sequence.
effects.funFact: Josepho's early Photomaton delivered eight pictures, not the familiar four.

margin.note: The camera admits light at scheduled intervals. Each exposure records one moment.
Chemical baths turn the recorded light pattern into a visible photograph and make it stable.
A light-sensitive surface, such as coated paper or film, records the camera's image.

effects.title: Photochrom
effects.name: Photochrom
effects.dating: Developed in the 1880s; peak period 1890s to early 1900s
effects.caption: Museum in Berlin, photochrom print, circa 1890–1905.
effects.credit: Library of Congress / Photochrom Print Collection / Public Domain

body.label: Identify
body.text: Photographic detail meets strikingly placed colors.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Black and white negatives provide the basis for several colored lithographic stones.

body.label: Example
body.text: View of a Berlin museum, around 1890–1905.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look for colors that seem to be interpreted rather than observed.

context: Hans Jakob Schmid developed the process in the 1880s for the Swiss company Orell Füssli. Licensees such as the Detroit Photographic Company disseminated the colored views from the 1890s onward. Photographic capture and lithographic color printing combined technical accuracy with sophisticated color design. Tourist views, in particular, made this hybrid form economically attractive before everyday color photography became readily available.
effects.distinction: Photochrom is neither an original color photograph nor simply a hand-painted print. The color information was created during the printing process. Therefore, colored historical images should not be uncritically interpreted as exact documents of the original object colors.
effects.aftermath: An image can be photographically precise and color-wise constructed.
effects.funFact: Many colored travel views from around 1900 are based on black and white negatives.

margin.note: Prepared stone surfaces used to print ink. Separate stones carry different colors that are aligned to build the final picture.
Images with reversed light and dark values. Here they supply photographic detail for a manually interpreted color printing process.

effects.title: Photocopy Aesthetic
effects.name: Photocopy aesthetic / Xerox look
effects.dating: 1970s–1990s: Copy Art, Zines and DIY publications

body.label: Identify
body.text: Harsh contrasts, toner spots, and lost intermediate tones.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Copying or thresholding plus noise reduces the image.

body.label: Example
body.text: Punk flyers and photocopied zines.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Make five copies; document the loss of detail.

context: Photocopying became a means of production in art, self-published magazines, and musical subcultures. MoMA's zine documentation has documented this publishing practice since the 1970s. The copy was not merely a cheaper reproduction: its contrast, blemishes, and deterioration upon recopying could be deliberately manipulated. A modern digital Xerox filter builds this effect from threshold and several noise components. The example is a contemporary simulation, not a historical punk flyer. In the exercise, compare the first and fifth generations: Which contours merge, and which disappear? Copying errors can combine image elements, thereby altering their meaning, not merely their surface.
effects.aftermath: This look is particularly suitable for your zines if a clear silhouette is maintained. Faces with a lot of detail require a more nuanced threshold.
effects.funFact: A copy of the copy further alters the motif; reproduction thus becomes a design step in itself.

margin.note: Fine powder used by many copiers to form the printed image. Uneven deposits can create spots and rough texture.

effects.title: Photodynamism
effects.name: Photodynamism
effects.dating: 1910s; Anton Giulio Bragaglia's experiments from 1911
effects.caption: Bragaglia's Saluting Figure in Motion. A man's bowed head and gesturing hands dissolve into overlapping contours and pale, flowing trails against a dark background.
effects.credit: Sebastiano Arturo Luciani · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Moving figures dissolve into flowing motion trails, overlapping contours, and translucent smears against a relatively still background. Sharper resting positions sometimes anchor the blurred movement.

body.label: Principle
body.text: During a long exposure, light from a moving subject reaches successive areas of the photographic surface. Continuous recording creates connected traces rather than isolated snapshots; the trails form during exposure, not development.

body.label: Example
body.text: Anton Giulio Bragaglia: The Typist, 1911.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Steady a camera for a one-second exposure and move your hand sideways, pausing briefly halfway; compare the pause with the flowing trace.

context: Anton Giulio Bragaglia developed photodynamism with his brother Arturo in the early 1910s, within the orbit of Italian Futurism. Their photographs explored movement as a continuous experience rather than a sequence of frozen poses. A stationary camera and prolonged exposure let gestures spread across the image. Pauses could leave stronger outlines, while faster passages appeared faint or blurred. Bragaglia wanted these traces to suggest the expressive energy of an action, not merely measure its path. Some Futurist painters resisted his claims for photography as a Futurist art.
effects.distinction: Chronophotography typically separates motion into successive recorded phases, sometimes within one image. Photodynamism instead emphasizes the continuous transitions between positions, using blur as its central expressive material.
effects.aftermath: Photodynamism teaches that a photograph can describe an interval of movement rather than a single frozen instant.
effects.funFact: Photodynamism provoked resistance from Futurist painters, despite sharing their fascination with movement.

margin.note: An exposure that records light long enough for movement to visibly affect the image.
Chemical processing that makes a recorded image visible in light-sensitive photographic material.
An artistic movement that celebrated speed, machines, and a break with inherited traditions.

effects.title: Photoelasticity
effects.name: Photoelasticity
effects.dating: 1930s engineering use; established in the nineteenth century
effects.caption: Stress Fringes in a Plastic Housing. Rainbow bands fill a transparent moulded plastic housing, bending around its ribs, compartments, and curved edges against black.
effects.credit: Colin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Transparent plastic shows rainbow fringes against a dark background when viewed between crossed polarisers. Curved bands crowd around holes, corners, and loaded contact points.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Stress-induced birefringence makes two perpendicular polarisation components travel at different speeds through the material. A second polariser lets these components interfere, producing coloured bands in white light.

body.label: Example
body.text: Ernest George Coker and Louis Napoleon George Filon: A Treatise on Photo-Elasticity, 1931.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: View a clear plastic ruler against a white LCD screen through polarised sunglasses; rotate the glasses, then gently bend the ruler.

context: Photoelasticity became an important engineering tool before computer stress analysis. Its optical basis was known in the nineteenth century, but transparent models supported increasingly systematic measurements. Coker and Filon's 1931 treatise helped consolidate the method. Engineers loaded models between polarisers to reveal patterns invisible in ordinary light. Stress changes how the material transmits different polarisations. In suitable flat models, fringe order measures the difference between principal stresses, provided thickness and material response are known. White light produces coloured fringes; monochromatic light produces alternating bright and dark bands.
effects.distinction: Unlike diffraction rainbows, these colours arise from stress-dependent birefringence, not light spreading around edges or through fine grooves. They are not pigments within the plastic.
effects.aftermath: Photoelasticity shows how an invisible mechanical state can become a visible optical pattern, but interpreting that pattern requires calibration.
effects.funFact: A plastic spoon can reveal stresses left behind during manufacture, even when nobody is bending it.

margin.note: Two polarising filters with transmission directions at right angles. Without an intervening material changing polarisation, they block most transmitted light.
Mechanical stress makes an otherwise optically uniform material transmit two perpendicular polarisations at different speeds.
Normal stresses along special directions where shear stress vanishes. Their difference controls the measured optical delay in a suitable flat model.

effects.title: Photogram
effects.name: Photogram / rayograph
effects.dating: 1921–1922: Man Ray's Rayographs turn the process into an avant-garde language.

body.label: Identify
body.text: White silhouettes and transparent grey areas appear on a dark background.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Objects block light on photographic paper. After development, their shadows and transparencies remain. A camera is not necessary for this.

body.label: Example
body.text: Man Ray: Rayograph, 1922.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Guess the objects. What different traces would a glass, a sheet of paper, and an opaque metal object leave behind?

context: Cameraless photographs date back to the early days of photography. 1921–1922: Man Ray's Rayographs transformed the process into an avant-garde language. Man Ray did not invent the photogram; Rayograph is his own name for his version.

Recognize: White silhouettes, transparent grey areas and dark background; often spatially enigmatic objects.
Mechanism: Objects are placed on light-sensitive paper and block the light completely or partially. After development, shadows and translucencies remain.
example: Man Ray: Rayograph, 1922.
Practice: First, guess the objects shown, then examine their transparency. Consider what trace a glass, a sheet of paper, and a metal object would each leave if light shone on them from above.

Objects lie on light-sensitive paper and block the light completely or partially. After development, shadows and translucencies remain.
White silhouettes, transparent grey areas and dark background; often spatially enigmatic objects.
First guess the objects shown, then examine their transparency.
Man Ray did not invent the photogram; rayograph is his own name for his version.
effects.distinction: Man Ray did not invent the photogram; rayograph is his own name for his version.
effects.aftermath: Analogous counterpart to masks, negative forms and scanner experiments.
effects.funFact: Man Ray called his photograms Rayographs; camera-less photographs already existed in the 19th century.
highlights: Objects block light on photographic paper

margin.note: Paper coated with light-sensitive chemicals. Exposed areas typically darken during development, while covered areas remain lighter.

effects.title: Photogrammetry
effects.name: Photogrammetry / structure from motion
effects.dating: 2018: Meshroom facilitates the open photogrammetry workflow; older methods
effects.caption: Meshroom: View of a reconstructed scene in the official user manual.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Photographic textures over reconstructed three-dimensional surfaces.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Many overlapping photos provide camera positions, depth, and a textured model.

body.label: Example
body.text: AliceVision Meshroom, first released in 2018.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph a matte object from all sides with strong overlaps.

context: Photogrammetry extracts geometry from photographs and has a long history predating digital creative tools. This slide anchors the more recent development to the first Meshroom release from August 2018. AliceVision describes its open pipeline of features, camera estimation, dense reconstruction, and texturing. The method requires recognizable image features across multiple shots. Glossy, transparent, or low-texture surfaces complicate this because views do not reliably match. Therefore, a matte, detailed object in even lighting is suitable for this exercise. The surface color is taken from the photographs; the shape is reconstructed computationally. Missing areas and torn edges can later be intentionally left visible as part of the scan aesthetic.
effects.distinction: Photogrammetry is a measurement and reconstruction method; the scan look is a possible aesthetic use.
effects.aftermath: A scan is not a neutral impression: the image cover, light and algorithm determine which parts are fully and stably reconstructed.
effects.funFact: Meshroom's first released binary version appeared on August 9, 2018.

margin.note: The locations and viewing directions from which photographs were taken. Recovering them helps reconstruct a scene in three dimensions.
