effects.title: Photographic Joiners
effects.name: Photographic Joiners
effects.dating: 1980s; David Hockney’s Polaroid and photographic print collages, beginning in 1982
effects.caption: AI illustration: Grid portrait of seated man using instant prints.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: A scene breaks into overlapping photographs or a grid of bordered prints, with visible seams and repeated details. Shifting viewpoints make faces, rooms, or landscapes seem fractured yet connected.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Separate exposures record different parts of a scene from different positions or moments. Arranging the developed photographs together creates multiple perspectives rather than one continuous camera view.

body.label: Example
body.text: David Hockney: Pearblossom Hwy., 1986.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph a chair from nine slightly different positions, then arrange small prints so some edges connect and others visibly disagree.

context: David Hockney began making his well-known photographic joiners in 1982, first using Polaroid pictures and then conventional photographic prints. Earlier artists had already explored photographic collage. His early Polaroid arrangements often retained a regular grid, while later print collages allowed freer overlaps and irregular outlines. Each photograph records its own viewpoint and moment, so the assembled scene can contain small contradictions. This recalls Cubism’s challenge to a single fixed viewpoint. The visible joins encourage viewers to scan the picture, discovering space through successive details rather than one unified projection.
effects.distinction: Unlike a stitched panorama, a joiner preserves mismatches instead of hiding them. Unlike multiple exposure, it assembles separate photographs rather than recording several exposures on one frame.
effects.aftermath: Joiners show how a picture can combine separate moments and viewpoints without pretending they belong to one instantaneous view.
effects.funFact: The white borders of Hockney’s Polaroids became visible parts of the finished pictures.

margin.note: Individual captures of light by photographic film or a digital sensor, made as distinct pictures.
Different views of the same subject combined in one picture.
An art movement that broke subjects into geometric forms and often combined different views.

effects.title: Photogravure
effects.name: Photogravure
effects.dating: 1879, Karl Klietsch's perfected process
effects.caption: Photogravure Portrait of a Mustached Man. A mounted portrait shows a mustached man in a striped suit, his softly illuminated face emerging from a dark background.
effects.credit: Alvin Langdon Coburn · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a photographic image with continuous tones, incredibly rich, velvety blacks, and subtle grays. Under magnification, the image is made of a random, microscopic grain pattern rather than regular dots.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Light exposure hardens a gelatin layer on a copper plate, dictating how deeply acid bites into the metal. Ink settles into these varying etched depths, transferring continuous tones to paper under heavy pressure.

body.label: Example
body.text: Peter Henry Emerson: Gathering Water Lilies, 1886.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at an old printed photograph with a strong magnifying glass. If you see a random dusting of pigment instead of a rigid grid, it might be a photogravure.

context: Photogravure bridges early photography and fine art printing. In 1879, Karl Klietsch combined photography with traditional intaglio printmaking. First, a copper plate is dusted with fine rosin powder and heated, creating a microscopic grain. Next, a light-sensitive gelatin tissue exposed to a film positive is transferred to the plate. Acid etches the copper, biting deeper where the gelatin is thinnest. This creates tiny pits of varying depths across the metal. A printer rubs ink into the plate and wipes the surface clean. Finally, a heavy press forces damp paper into the pits to pull out the ink.
effects.distinction: Unlike standard halftone prints, which use grids of tiny dots to fake grays, photogravure varies physical depth. This results in true continuous tones rather than an optical illusion.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how early photographers used complex printmaking chemistry to elevate their images to accepted fine art.
effects.funFact: Paper money is still printed using a modern, highly automated variation of this intaglio process.

margin.note: A smooth blend of shades from light to dark without breaking the image into visible artificial dots.
A printmaking technique where the image is incised or etched beneath the surface of the printing plate.
A natural resin from pine trees, melted onto the copper plate to create the necessary ink-holding grain.

effects.title: Photomicrography
effects.name: Photomicrography
effects.dating: 1840s, early work by Alfred Donné and William Henry Fox Talbot
effects.caption: Historical Tissue Section Photomicrograph. An enlarged tissue section fills a historical plate with branching dark masses, pale spaces, and anatomical reference letters.
effects.credit: National Museum of Health and Medicine · CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Tiny structures fill the frame: enlarged cells, insect scales, or mineral crystals reveal fine internal patterns. Some images retain a circular field with dark edges.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A microscope forms a magnified optical image, which exposes a light-sensitive surface or reaches an electronic sensor. Illumination, focus, and the resolving power of the optics determine which details become visible.

body.label: Example
body.text: Alfred Donné and Léon Foucault: Atlas du cours de microscopie, 1845.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph a prepared plant slide through a microscope eyepiece, then compare visible cell boundaries at two magnifications.

context: During the 1840s, experimenters joined photography to microscopy to record structures too small for unaided sight. Donné and Foucault made daguerreotypes through microscopes. Their 1845 atlas presented engraved reproductions based on these photographs, rather than photographs pasted into the book. Talbot also explored photographing microscopic subjects during photography’s early years. The microscope supplied the enlarged optical image; photographic exposure recorded it on a sensitive surface. Development and fixing made the record visible and stable. Careful lighting mattered because magnification alone could not reveal every structure.
effects.distinction: Photomicrography records subjects through a microscope; macro photography generally records small subjects with a camera lens alone. Microphotography instead makes extremely small photographs, such as microfilm records.
effects.aftermath: Photomicrography shows that greater image size does not automatically mean greater resolved detail.
effects.funFact: An early atlas shared microscope photographs as engravings, translating photographic evidence back into printed lines.

margin.note: The ability to distinguish nearby features as separate, rather than as one blurred shape.
Photographs made on silver-coated metal plates. Each camera image is a unique object, without a separate negative.
Development makes the recorded image visible. Fixing removes remaining light-sensitive material so further light does not keep changing it.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Photo fragments, foreign body parts, impossible proportions and typography visibly collide.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Cut-out images and texts are rescaled and reassembled. Their new juxtaposition changes the meaning.

body.label: Example
body.text: Hannah Höch: Dada-Rundschau, 1919. Berlin Dada Fair, 1920.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Create a new message from five press photos. Enlarge one fragment and observe how the effect changes.

context: Composite photographs existed in the 19th century; Berlin Dada radicalized the method around 1918–1920. 1920s: Dada, illustrated press, and political graphics. The 1920s designation refers to the artistic breakthrough, not the invention of composite photography.

Recognize: Visible breaks, foreign body parts, impossible proportions, and typography.
Mechanism: Photo fragments and text are cut out, rescaled, and assembled into a contradictory visual world.
example: Hannah Höch: Dada-Rundschau, 1919; Schnitt mit dem Küchenmesser, 1919, beachtet auf der Dada-Messe 1920.
Practice: Create a new statement from five press photos; examine how the combination changes the meaning. Pay particular attention to size relationships: A tiny body under a huge head immediately shifts the message of the image.

Visible breaks, foreign body parts, impossible proportions and typography.
Create a new statement from five press images; examine how the combination changes the meaning.
The year 1920 refers to the artistic breakthrough, not the invention of composite photography.

effects.aftermath: Remix culture, zines, memes and digital cut-and-paste aesthetics.
effects.funFact: Hannah Höch's famous cut with the kitchen knife was created in 1919 and was shown at the Dada Fair in 1920.

margin.note: Placing things next to each other so their contrast or relationship suggests a new meaning.
An early twentieth-century art movement that challenged conventional logic and taste, often using collage, absurdity, and political satire.

effects.title: Photorealistic CGI
effects.name: Photorealistic CGI
effects.dating: Jurassic Park 1993: Breakthrough for digital film creatures.
effects.caption: Jurassic Park, 1993: digital T. rex in a photographed space.
effects.credit: Industrial Light & Magic / Universal Pictures. © Universal Pictures; Source image by ILM

body.label: Identify
body.text: Digital creatures interact convincingly with recorded people and real-world environments. Their origin remains invisible.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Animated 3D models are given textures and lighting. Compositing adds appropriate shadows, motion blur, perspective, and ground contact.

body.label: Example
body.text: Jurassic Park (1993) combines ILM's digital dinosaurs with practical effects.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Check a photo montage for light direction, perspective, and ground contact. What deviations does it reveal?

context: Breakthrough in the blockbuster: Jurassic Park (1993).

A 3D model is given a skeleton, animation, surface textures, and lighting. Rendering creates a camera image; compositing combines it with the real-world recording, including shadows, motion blur, and camera movement.
Jurassic Park (1993): ILM's CG dinosaurs combined with Stan Winston's practical dinosaurs; the film was deliberately a hybrid.
Regarding the image: Historical original / source image. Surface, light, shadows, and camera are adjusted to the filmed location. The film production also combined CGI and practical animatronics.
effects.distinction: Photorealism is the goal, CGI the toolkit. Non-realistic 3D animation is also CGI. CGI existed long before 1993. The decisive change was the convincing integration of moving digital animals into live-action, along with practical effects.
effects.aftermath: A scene no longer needed to be fully executable by a physical being or model. Image production could be planned using digital bodies.
effects.funFact: Jurassic Park's dinosaurs from 1993 were partly digital, partly practical models: The breakthrough was a hybrid.

margin.note: Combining separately made images into one shot so they appear to share the same space.
The visual connection between an object and the surface beneath it, supported by placement and shadows.

effects.title: Photosculpture
effects.name: Photosculpture
effects.dating: 1860, François Willème’s process
effects.caption: Bressant Photosculpture with Cane. The statuette identified as Bressant presents a costumed actor holding a cane, with a broad hat, curled hair, and an ornamented cape.
effects.credit: Willème, Auguste François (Sedan, en 1830 - Roubaix, en 1905), sculpteur · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a three-dimensional portrait bust or statuette, with a recognizable pose and modeled clothing. Its solid surface resembles conventional sculpture, not a photograph.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Twenty-four cameras around a sitter record views whose silhouettes guide the sculpture’s shape. A pantograph transfers traced outlines to guide subtractive cutting into a clay blank, followed by hand finishing.

body.label: Example
body.text: François Willème: Self-Portrait, circa 1860.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph a stationary figurine from four sides; compare the outlines and notice which surface details they cannot describe.

context: François Willème introduced photosculpture in France in 1860, combining photography with mechanical tracing and sculpture. His studio arranged 24 cameras around a central platform to photograph a sitter from different directions. After development, the photographs supplied outlines for tracing. A pantograph linked the traced profiles to the shaping of a clay blank. Cutting established the main volume; hand finishing supplied details that silhouettes could not capture. The resulting model could then be molded and reproduced. Photography helped measure the subject, but it did not directly turn light into solid material.
effects.distinction: Unlike stereoscopic photography, photosculpture produces a physical object rather than an illusion of depth. Unlike additive 3D printing, its shaping stage removes material.
effects.aftermath: Photosculpture shows how multiple photographic viewpoints can guide physical reconstruction without recording every surface detail.
effects.funFact: Twenty-four evenly spaced cameras give viewpoints only 15 degrees apart.

margin.note: A linked mechanical device that copies a traced movement, sometimes at a different scale.
Shaping by removing material from a larger mass, rather than adding successive layers.
The outer shapes seen from particular viewpoints. They do not reveal all the detail inside those boundaries.

effects.title: Pinhole Photography
effects.name: Pinhole photography
effects.dating: 1890: George Davison's The Onion Field as a pictorialist reference
effects.caption: George Davison: The Onion Field, 1890. Lensless pinhole camera photography.
effects.credit: National Science and Media Museum / George Davison

body.label: Identify
body.text: Consistently soft details and frequently long exposures.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A tiny hole projects the image without a lens.

body.label: Example
body.text: George Davison: The Onion Field, 1890.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare uniform softness with selective lens blur.

context: The lensless projection principle was known long before light-sensitive photographic materials. Artists deliberately utilized its limited detail. George Davison's *The Onion Field* attracted attention in the 1890 debate on painterly photography. More recent pinhole camera images combine simple, homemade devices with color film or photographic paper. The historical reference here refers to a prominent artistic use, not an invention, of the pinhole camera principle.
effects.distinction: Pinhole cameras and soft-focus filters are not identical methods. A tiny hole does not produce arbitrarily high sharpness: diffraction and the size of the hole limit the image. The camera obscura is much older than photography.
effects.aftermath: A technical limitation can lead to an independent conception of the image.
effects.funFact: A functioning photographic camera can be built without a glass lens.

margin.note: Extended periods of light collection. A pinhole admits little light, so recording the image often takes much longer than with a lens.
Blur that leaves one distance sharp while other distances appear softer. Pinhole images generally have a more uniform softness instead.

sources.label: National Science and Media Museum: The Onion Field

effects.title: Pinscreen Animation
effects.name: Pinscreen Animation
effects.dating: 1933, Alexandre Alexeieff and Claire Parker's technique
effects.caption: Soft Oval Rendered in Pin Shadows. A close view reveals a softly glowing oval emerging from a dark field of regularly spaced pins.
effects.credit: Lëa-Kim Châteauneuf · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a textured, shifting image in black, white, and gray. The picture looks like a moving engraving or a fluid, shadowed drawing.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Thousands of sliding pins are pushed into a white board and lit from the side. Extended pins cast long dark shadows, while pushed-in pins leave the white board bright.

body.label: Example
body.text: Alexandre Alexeieff and Claire Parker: Night on Bald Mountain, 1933.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Shine a flashlight across a hairbrush or a bed of nails, noticing how shadows change as you tilt it.

context: In 1933, Alexandre Alexeieff and Claire Parker invented the pinscreen to bring engraving techniques into film. They built a large vertical board pierced by over a million tiny headless pins. Animators used special tools to push the pins in or pull them out. A light source placed at a sharp angle cast shadows from every protruding pin. By altering how far the pins stuck out, they created smooth gradients of gray. They took a photo of the board, changed the pins slightly, and took another photo. This stop-motion process was incredibly slow. It produced a uniquely haunting, dreamlike texture that no other medium could match.
effects.distinction: Pinscreen animation relies on physical shadows from movable pins to create tone. Sand animation uses loose grains manipulated on a glowing lightbox to form high-contrast silhouettes.
effects.aftermath: It proves that complex, fluid shading in animation can be achieved entirely through manipulating physical shadows.
effects.funFact: Only a handful of true pinscreens were ever built because they are incredibly difficult to manufacture.

margin.note: Methods of cutting lines into a hard surface to create prints, often using precise hatching for shading.
An animation method where objects are moved in tiny increments and photographed frame by frame.

effects.title: Pixel Art
effects.name: Pixel Art
effects.dating: 1980s, early arcade and console graphics
effects.caption: Pixel Circuit Playground. A computer, circuit paths, logic gates, and tiny figures form a playful technological scene on dark green.
effects.credit: Nodin Cutfeet · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see blocky, grid-based images made of distinct square dots. The artwork has sharp edges, stark colors, and visible stair-step lines.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Artists manually color individual pixels on a low-resolution grid to build recognizable shapes. A highly restricted color palette forces strategic color placement.

body.label: Example
body.text: Shigeru Miyamoto: Super Mario Bros. character sprite, 1985.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Zoom far into a small digital icon until you can count the individual square colored blocks making up its curved edges.

context: In the 1970s and 1980s, computer memory was extremely expensive and severely limited. Game developers could not store high-resolution images or complex curved shapes. Instead, they built small digital characters, called sprites, on tiny grids. Artists had to place every single pixel by hand to ensure clarity on blurry television screens. They used specific tricks like dithering, mixing two solid colors in a checkerboard pattern to simulate a third shade. As technology improved, this technical necessity evolved into a deliberate, nostalgic artistic style still popular today.
effects.distinction: Pixel art requires manual, intentional placement of every individual dot. In contrast, digital noise or low-resolution photographs randomly generate blocky artifacts.
effects.aftermath: It reveals how extreme technical limits often inspire highly creative visual abstraction.
effects.funFact: Early designers often drafted their pixel art on physical graph paper before typing the code.

margin.note: The smallest controllable elements of a digital display, usually tiny colored squares.
Small, independent two-dimensional images that can be moved across a computer screen, often used for video game characters.
A technique that alternates differently colored pixels in a pattern to create the illusion of a new blended color.

effects.title: Pixel Sorting
effects.name: Pixel sorting
effects.dating: Kim Asendorf's ASDF Pixel Sort, 2010; Net art of the 2010s.
effects.caption: Kim Asendorf: mountains_2.jpg, example from the ASDFPixelSort repository.
effects.credit: Kim Asendorf, original example of the publicly available Processing script.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Image parts diverge into ordered, colored stripes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Pixel segments are reordered according to brightness or color value.

body.label: Example
body.text: Kim Asendorf: ASDF PixelSort example.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Limit the sorting to light areas of a landscape.

context: Kim Asendorf's public processing script bears the date 2010. It sorts certain sections into columns and rows, while thresholds define where these sections begin and end. The visibly stretched forms arise from a deliberate algorithmic order. The effect has become a distinctive feature of digital net art; the slide replaces an unsubstantiated, sweeping narrative of invention with verifiable script evidence.
effects.distinction: Pixel sorting arranges existing pixels. It requires neither corrupted files nor video compression and is therefore not the same as data moshing.
effects.aftermath: Ordered data can appear visually more chaotic than unordered data.
effects.funFact: Asendorf's script is dated 2010 in his head.

margin.note: Groups of neighboring pixels selected for sorting, often bounded by a brightness rule.
A numerical measure of a pixel’s color, used as a sorting key rather than its original position.

effects.title: Pixelation
effects.name: Pixelation / mosaic
effects.dating: Desktop effects culture of the 1990s; earlier digital raster fundamentals.
effects.caption: Mosaic pixelation: current official Adobe demonstration.
effects.credit: Adobe, After Effects documentation; not a historical screen recording.

body.label: Identify
body.text: The motif breaks down into large, monochrome rectangles.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Individual image areas are combined into coarser color samples.

body.label: Example
body.text: Adobe: Mosaic demonstration.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Reduce the same motif to 80, 40 and 20 columns.

context: Mosaic is part of the classic digital toolkit for stylized low-resolution images, transitions, and blurring image parts. Adobe documents two variations: a field either adopts the central sample or the average color value of its area. The 1990s are presented here as a learning experience for desktop image editing, not as the first evidence of pixel graphics. When reducing the image size, large silhouettes remain legible longer than small details.
effects.distinction: Pixelation reduces spatial resolution; posterization reduces tonal values. Pixel art can be intentionally drawn and is not automatically a pixelated photograph.
effects.aftermath: Fewer pixels can make the composition clearer.
effects.funFact: A mosaic field can use the mean value or just the middle color sample.

margin.note: Color measurements taken from parts of an image. Each enlarged block represents one such measurement or average.
Containing relatively few pixels, so fine details cannot be represented clearly.

effects.title: Pixilation
effects.name: Pixilation
effects.dating: 1950s landmark: Norman McLaren’s Neighbours, 1952; earlier examples exist
effects.caption: AI illustration: Sequential frames of a man walking using pixilation.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Live actors move in abrupt steps, slide without walking, or hover above the ground. Ordinary bodies acquire puppet-like movement and impossible rhythms.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The camera records separate frames while performers change position between exposures. Playback turns these staged poses into apparent motion, without recording the movements connecting them.

body.label: Example
body.text: Norman McLaren: Neighbours, 1952.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Keep a camera fixed and photograph someone standing still at successive floor marks; play the photographs in sequence to reveal sliding.

context: Pixilation treats living performers as stop-motion subjects rather than continuously filmed actors. Earlier trick films explored this approach, including Segundo de Chomón’s El hotel eléctrico, released in 1908. Norman McLaren’s Neighbours brought it particular prominence in 1952 at the National Film Board of Canada. Its suburban conflict becomes physically strange through carefully staged movement. Performers hold poses or repeat actions while the camera records selected moments. For hovering, successive photographs can catch a performer airborne during separate jumps. The apparent continuity comes from playback, not from continuous action during filming.
effects.distinction: Unlike puppet stop-motion, pixilation animates living performers. It is unrelated to pixelation, which makes an image look blocky by exposing or enlarging its pixel structure.
effects.aftermath: Pixilation shows how selecting moments can construct movement that never happened continuously before the camera.
effects.funFact: A sequence of separate jumps can become one apparently sustained flight.

margin.note: Animation made by changing a subject’s position between individually recorded images.
Intervals when light reaches film or a camera sensor to record an image.
Movement perceived when still images appear in rapid sequence.

effects.title: Plasma Effect
effects.name: Plasma Effect
effects.dating: 1990s, PC and Amiga demoscene
effects.caption: Multicolored Fractal Plasma. Green, violet, and orange color clouds surround dark pools edged in vivid red.
effects.credit: Ben Taylor, who is the creator of TheArtProblem.com · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Flowing, psychedelic patterns of shifting colors. They look like liquid color blobs blending and swirling together.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Mathematical sine and cosine functions overlap to calculate color values. This creates smooth, oscillating waves of color.

body.label: Example
body.text: Future Crew: Second Reality, 1993.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Drop two pebbles into a still puddle of water. Watch how the overlapping circular ripples create complex, shifting interference patterns.

context: In the 1990s, programmers in the "demoscene" competed to create impressive visual art. Early computers lacked fast graphics chips. To overcome this, coders relied on clever math tricks. The plasma effect used simple sine wave equations combined with "color cycling." Instead of redrawing the whole screen, the program just shifted colors in the hardware palette. This allowed slow computers to display fast, smooth, liquid-like animations. The overlapping mathematical waves created complex interference patterns. These rolling waves of bright colors became a hallmark of early digital underground art.
effects.distinction: Unlike fractal noise which looks like random organic clouds, sine plasma has a predictable, repeating geometric rhythm.
effects.aftermath: It shows how combining simple mathematical functions can produce complex, organic-looking visual phenomena.
effects.funFact: Early coders used pre-calculated sine tables stored in memory because doing math in real-time was too slow.

margin.note: Mathematical formulas that describe smooth, repetitive oscillations, like sound waves or swinging pendulums.
A technique that animates images by shifting the colors assigned to specific values in a computer's memory palette.
A computer art subculture where programmers and artists compete to create visually impressive audio-visual presentations.

effects.title: Platinum Print
effects.name: Platinum print / platinotype
effects.dating: Patented in 1873; art photography around 1900
effects.caption: Peter Henry Emerson: Coming Home from the Marshes, 1886. Platinum print.
effects.credit: The J. Paul Getty Museum / Peter Henry Emerson / Public Domain

body.label: Identify
body.text: Matte surface and very fine shades of gray.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Iron compounds impart a permanent platinum image to the paper.

body.label: Example
body.text: Emerson: Coming Home from the Marshes, 1886.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare five adjacent shades of gray instead of just black and white.

context: William Willis patented the process in 1873. Around 1900, art photographers appreciated the understated surface and nuanced midtones. Rising platinum costs and the restrictions imposed during World War I altered its availability; palladium gained importance as a related metal used in photography. The look serves as a reminder that photographic effect also depends on reflection, paper fibers, and the presence of metal in the final image.
effects.distinction: A digital scan can only partially convey matte surfaces and subtle tonal gradations. Not every soft black and white image is a platinum print. Platinum printing refers to a material process, not simply a desaturated color adjustment.
effects.aftermath: Material luxury can have a subtle effect: rich tonal values ​​instead of brilliance.
effects.funFact: When platinum became scarce during the First World War, palladium gained importance as a photographic alternative.

margin.note: A precious metal that forms the image in this printing process. It resists many chemical changes, helping the image remain stable.
Iron-containing chemicals that respond to light and help turn platinum salts into the metal forming the image.

effects.title: Pochoir Stencil Print
effects.name: Pochoir Stencil Print
effects.dating: 1910s, high-end French fashion plates
effects.caption: Art Deco Illustration With Hand-Brushed Colors. This theatrical illustration features sharply delineated areas of flat, opaque color over crisp line work.
effects.credit: Rijksmuseum · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see vivid, solid blocks of color with sharp, distinct edges. Colors appear thick and matte, lacking the dotted patterns of commercial printing.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Artisans cut shapes out of thin metal or celluloid sheets. They hand-brush watercolor or gouache through these cutouts onto printed paper.

body.label: Example
body.text: George Barbier: Gazette du Bon Ton illustrations, 1912.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at an Art Deco fashion print to spot tiny overlaps where brushed colors slightly cross the stencil boundaries.

context: Pochoir is a highly refined stencil technique that reached its peak in Paris during the early twentieth century. Publishers used it to produce luxury fashion magazines and artist portfolios. Unlike mechanized color printing, pochoir relied entirely on skilled human hands. Workshops employed dozens of artisans, called coloristes, who applied layers of gouache or watercolor layer by layer. Each color required a separate, custom-cut stencil. This labor-intensive additive process created incredibly vibrant, textured images that machines could not replicate. The resulting prints defined the elegant, geometric aesthetic of the Art Deco era.
effects.distinction: Pochoir uses hand-brushed paints through cutouts, leaving thick, irregular paint deposits. Chromolithography uses chemical stone printing, producing flat, mechanically smooth ink layers.
effects.aftermath: It shows how intensive manual craftsmanship briefly outshined industrial mass production in defining modern luxury.
effects.funFact: Some complex pochoir prints required up to one hundred individual stencils for a single image.

margin.note: An opaque watercolor paint. It contains white pigment that makes it thicker and less transparent than regular watercolors.

context: A point cloud stores spatial samples, such as those from a scan. It can be displayed as a visible field of points or refined into a nearly closed surface. QSplat by Rusinkiewicz and Levoy, presented at SIGGRAPH 2000, combined a hierarchical data structure with point-based rendering for very large scan models. The rendering becomes coarser during movement, while the image can progressively become finer when stationary. The illustration therefore deliberately shows a coarse level of refinement, not damage to the model. In this exercise, gradually reduce the point value. effects.aftermath: The visible scan point later becomes a stylistic device itself. Geometric scanning and the finished photorealistic reconstruction are nevertheless different representations.

effects.title: Polaroid Manipulation

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a photograph where the subjects look melted, smeared, or painted. The colors swirl together like thick wet paint.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Artists applied pressure to the surface of a developing instant photo. This pushed the trapped chemical emulsion around before it hardened.

body.label: Example
body.text: Lucas Samaras: Photo-Transformation, 1973.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Press your finger firmly against a sealed plastic bag filled with thick liquid to see how pressure displaces the contents.

context: Polaroid introduced the SX-70 camera in 1972. It ejected a self-contained film packet holding both the negative and positive layers. Between these layers sat a paste-like chemical emulsion that developed the image in daylight. This emulsion remained soft and wet for minutes after ejection. Artists like Lucas Samaras quickly discovered they could alter the image. They used styluses, blunt tools, or fingers to rub the protective clear mylar surface. This physical pressure physically displaced the colored dyes inside. The resulting images blurred the line between photography and painting.
effects.distinction: This differs from emulsion transfer, which moves a completed image layer onto paper. Manipulation changes the wet image inside its original casing.
effects.aftermath: It shows how photographers can physically intervene in automated chemical processes to create unique artwork.
effects.funFact: Heating the photos slightly could keep the internal chemicals soft and workable for a longer time.

margin.note: A light-sensitive paste containing silver salts and colored dyes suspended in a gel.

body.label: Identify

context: Introduced in 1972, the Polaroid SX-70 was a folding single-lens reflex camera. It used a radically new format called integral instant film. This film pushed out of the camera immediately after exposure. The photograph developed in daylight with no waste to discard. The thick bottom margin held a tiny pod of chemicals. As the picture ejected, steel rollers squeezed this pod. The paste spread evenly across the internal layers. An opaque chemical temporarily blocked ambient light to protect the negative. Underneath, subtractive color dyes migrated upward to form the final visible image.
effects.distinction: Unlike earlier peel-apart film, integral film sealed all chemical layers inside one packet. There was no messy paper negative to discard.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how complex photochemistry can be engineered into a simple, self-contained consumer product.
effects.funFact: Photographers often manipulated the soft emulsion with hard tools while it developed, creating a painterly effect.

margin.note: A type of photographic film where all developing chemicals and sensitive layers are permanently sealed inside a single unit.

effects.title: Political Retouching
effects.name: Political Retouching
effects.dating: 1930s, Stalin's Great Purge photographs
effects.caption: Stalin's Companions Progressively Removed. Four versions of a group portrait progressively reduce Stalin's companions until he stands alone beside the table.
effects.credit: Unidentified Soviet photographer. · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a historical photograph where a person is missing, leaving an unnaturally empty space. Sometimes, background textures like walls or water look slightly smudged or painted over.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Technicians used scalpels to scrape away the emulsion on the negative to remove a figure. They then used an airbrush and ink to paint in a fake background.

body.label: Example
body.text: Soviet state censors: The Vanishing Commissar (Nikolai Yezhov removed from Stalin photo), circa 1940.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at the water or wall behind a dictator in a 1930s photo to spot blurry, painted textures.

context: During the 1930s, the Soviet government systematically altered photographs to rewrite history. When political figures fell out of favor, they were executed and erased from the visual record. Skilled retouchers worked directly on photographic negatives and prints. They used sharp tools to physically scrape away the image of the condemned person. Next, they carefully applied ink with an airbrush to reconstruct the missing background. This subtractive and additive process required immense skill to match the film grain. The altered photos were then re-photographed and published as the new official truth.
effects.distinction: Unlike double exposure which adds ghostly figures, political retouching subtracts real people to create a false reality. It leaves behind painted, opaque backgrounds rather than transparent overlaps.
effects.aftermath: It shows how photographic truth can be manipulated by those in power using manual darkroom techniques.
effects.funFact: Some Soviet citizens defaced their own family albums to avoid possessing photos of political enemies.

margin.note: The light-sensitive chemical layer on photographic film that holds the actual image.
A small, pen-like tool that sprays a fine mist of ink or paint using compressed air.

effects.title: Praxinoscope
effects.name: Praxinoscope
effects.dating: 1877, Émile Reynaud’s mirror animation device
effects.caption: Illuminated Praxinoscope with Figure Strip. A lamp-equipped praxinoscope displays sequential figure drawings around an open drum and their reflections in a faceted central mirror assembly.
effects.credit: Sukkoria · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: A small figure performs a repeating action inside a spinning drum. Its reflected image appears relatively steady, with bright colours and no viewing slits.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A central ring of mirrors turns with a strip of sequential drawings inside the drum. Successive reflections place the drawings in nearly the same position, allowing the viewer to perceive continuous movement.

body.label: Example
body.text: Émile Reynaud: Praxinoscope, 1877.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a working praxinoscope, comparing the moving paper strip with its reflections; notice where the action becomes readable.

context: Émile Reynaud introduced the praxinoscope in 1877 as an improvement on the zoetrope. A paper strip carried successive phases of an action around the drum’s inner wall. At the centre, a ring of flat mirrors rotated with the drum, each mirror corresponding to one drawing. Viewers looked directly at the reflections rather than through narrow slots. This arrangement gave a brighter view and reduced the interruptions caused by slots. The short sequence repeated with every turn. Reynaud later developed more elaborate devices for presenting animated scenes.
effects.distinction: A zoetrope separates views through narrow slits in its rotating wall. A praxinoscope instead uses central mirrors to present successive reflected images.
effects.aftermath: It shows how separate drawings can suggest movement when their successive views remain visually aligned.
effects.funFact: The drawings and mirrors rotate together; the apparently steady figure is a reflection.

margin.note: Pictures arranged in order, each showing a slightly different stage of an action.
A rotating drum with viewing slits and a strip of drawings inside. Looking through the slits makes the drawings appear animated.
Images seen when light from an object bounces off a surface, such as a mirror, toward your eyes.

effects.title: Psychedelic Poster Art
effects.name: Psychedelic Poster Art
effects.dating: 1960s; Wes Wilson’s Fillmore concert posters, 1966
effects.caption: The Tale of the Dog. Elongated yellow-and-red lettering arches above a raised-arm figure and a bulging yellow-and-white checkerboard.
effects.credit: MerleEllaPatsy · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Melting lettering fills tightly packed shapes, often making words look like pictures. Vibrating complementary colours surround swirling ornaments, distorted figures, and dense decorative borders.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Strong hue contrast with similar lightness can make neighbouring colours seem to shimmer along their edges. This perceptual effect involves simultaneous contrast; printed inks absorb selected wavelengths rather than emitting coloured light.

body.label: Example
body.text: Wes Wilson: The Association (BG-18), 1966.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Place saturated red and green paper strips together, then separate them with white paper; compare how steady their shared edges appear.

context: Psychedelic posters became closely associated with San Francisco’s rock concerts and counterculture during the 1960s. Wes Wilson’s 1966 Fillmore posters helped establish their swelling, tightly fitted lettering. Artists drew on Art Nouveau curves, historical lettering, and contemporary experiments with visual perception. Hand-drawn words could become patterns that rewarded slow reading rather than immediate recognition. Offset lithography reproduced these designs using subtractive colour: inks absorbed parts of the light reflected from paper. Closely matched lightness and strong colour differences could make boundaries appear unstable. The apparent movement belonged to perception, not the printed sheet.
effects.distinction: Op art often builds illusions from repeated geometric patterns, sometimes using only black and white. Psychedelic posters combine perceptual instability with expressive lettering, imagery, and concert information.
effects.aftermath: The style shows how colour relationships and letter shapes can turn practical information into a demanding visual experience.
effects.funFact: Wilson drew inspiration from lettering by Austrian designer Alfred Roller.

margin.note: A colour’s appearance changes depending on the colours beside it.
A printing process transfers an inked image from a plate through a rubber blanket onto paper.
Inks or pigments absorb some wavelengths of light. The remaining reflected light determines the colour you see.

effects.title: Pulfrich Effect
effects.name: Pulfrich Effect
effects.dating: 1922, Carl Pulfrich's description
effects.caption: Pulfrich Effect Sight Lines and Apparent Ellipse. Two eyes view colored positions along a horizontal motion path, with sight lines and a dashed ellipse marking the apparent trajectory.
effects.credit: Cmglee · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: With one eye darkened, sideways motion appears to curve through depth. A swinging pendulum seems to follow an elliptical path instead of moving within one plane.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Reduced brightness creates a processing delay in the darkened eye's visual pathway. During lateral motion, this timing difference produces binocular disparity, which the brain interprets as depth.

body.label: Example
body.text: BBC: Doctor Who — Dimensions in Time, 1993.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a pendulum swing sideways with both eyes open, holding one sunglass lens over one eye; then switch eyes.

context: Carl Pulfrich described this effect in 1922, linking unequal brightness between the eyes to an illusion of depth during motion. A dark filter reduces the light reaching one eye and delays its visual response. The brain therefore combines signals corresponding to slightly different positions of a moving object. It interprets this mismatch as depth, much as it interprets differences between ordinary binocular views. Later television productions used the effect with specially arranged movement and glasses containing one dark lens. A stationary photograph alone cannot demonstrate the defining motion-dependent illusion.
effects.distinction: Unlike anaglyph 3D, this technique does not separate two encoded views using different colored filters. Its depth illusion depends on motion and unequal visual timing.
effects.aftermath: The effect shows that perceived depth depends on the timing of visual signals, not just their spatial arrangement.
effects.funFact: Switching the dark lens to the other eye reverses the pendulum's apparent direction of rotation.

margin.note: A difference in an object's apparent position between the two eyes' views. The brain uses this difference to estimate depth.
A lag before a visual signal contributes to perception. Here, the darker eye's signal arrives effectively later.
An oval-shaped route. The pendulum appears to travel around this route, although its actual swing stays within one plane.

effects.title: Push Processing
effects.name: Push Processing
effects.dating: 1960s, popularization in photojournalism and cinema
effects.caption: Coastal Skyline in Coarse Grain. A bird crosses above a coastal city rendered in coarse monochrome grain, with white surf bordering a nearly black sea.
effects.credit: Sérgio Valle Duarte .mw-parser-output .messagebox{margin:4px 0;width:auto;border-collap… · CC BY 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see unusually prominent, coarse grain across the image. The picture also features stark contrast with harsh highlights and deep shadows.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Photographers deliberately underexpose the film in the camera. They then overdevelop it in the darkroom to compensate for the missing light.

body.label: Example
body.text: Don McCullin: Vietnam War photojournalism, 1968.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at an old newspaper photo taken in dark conditions. Notice how the flat grey areas look like tiny swarming dots instead of smooth tones.

context: Photographers often faced low-light environments where normal exposure required impossibly slow shutter speeds. To avoid blurry photos, they set their cameras to a higher film speed than the film's actual rating. This deliberately underexposed the film. To fix the dark image, technicians left the film in the developer chemical for much longer than standard times. This extended chemical reaction forced the faint latent image to appear. However, it also clumped the silver halide crystals together. This clumping created the signature coarse grain and high-contrast look that defined 1960s gritty photojournalism.
effects.distinction: Push processing happens during chemical development to fix underexposure. In contrast, dodging and burning happens during printing to adjust local brightness.
effects.aftermath: It shows that technical flaws like grain can become powerful aesthetic choices that convey raw realism.
effects.funFact: Pushing color film often causes unpredictable color shifts, turning shadows green or magenta.

margin.note: Leaving the film in the developer chemical longer than the manufacturer recommends.
A standardized number indicating how sensitive the photographic film is to light.
Light-sensitive compounds in the film emulsion that form the image when exposed and developed.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Soft airbrushed shading, saturated colours, and crisp cutout edges often appear together in television titles and illustrated backgrounds. These traits suggest a workflow, not proof that Paintbox made an image.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A stylus and graphics tablet controlled digital brushes that changed pixels in a frame store. Electronic colour blending produced smooth gradients without spraying pigment or exposing photographic material.

body.label: Example
body.text: David Hockney: Painting with Light (BBC television contribution), 1986.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a hard-edged shape in a digital painting tool, then shade inside it with a soft brush. Compare the boundaries.

context: British company Quantel introduced Paintbox in 1981 as a dedicated digital painting system for television production. Artists worked with a stylus and tablet while viewing their images on a monitor. A frame store held the picture electronically, allowing brushes and other tools to alter its pixels. Broadcast teams could combine painted marks, lettering, and captured imagery without photographing finished artwork. Soft shading and precise cutouts became familiar features of this workflow. Paintbox was equipment, however, rather than a single filter or a fixed visual style.
effects.distinction: Traditional airbrushing deposits pigment on a surface; Paintbox simulates soft marks by changing pixel values. Unlike vector drawing, its painted image is a pixel grid.
effects.aftermath: Paintbox shows how direct drawing tools helped bring electronic image manipulation into everyday television production.
effects.funFact: David Hockney explored Paintbox on BBC television in 1986.

margin.note: Electronic memory that holds a complete video image so equipment can display or modify it.

context: Focus shift directs attention without a cut. The audience discovers a detail or a figure as soon as the lens focuses on its distance. Cornell describes a striking example in The Graduate from 1967. The chronological position refers to this film, not to an undeniable invention. Modern cameras automate the process, but the timing, direction, and dramatic context remain artistic choices.

effects.funFact: Shifting the focus can redirect attention without moving the camera.

context: In 1984, Cindy Goral, Kenneth Torrance, Donald Greenberg, and Bennett Battaile published their seminal Cornell paper on diffuse light exchange. The original Cornell Box contained no obscuring objects because the exchange factors were calculated analytically. Only later versions expanded the test model. Cornell compares calculated images with a physically measured space: The well-known box is thus also an experiment for verifying simulations.
effects.distinction: Radiosity refers to a specific method for diffuse light exchange. Not every image with indirect light was calculated using a radiosity solver.
effects.aftermath: Color is not just part of materials; it travels with indirect light.
effects.funFact: The original Cornell Box from 1984 did not contain any interior objects.

margin.note: Scattered in many directions rather than reflected like a mirror. This lets a colored wall tint nearby surfaces.

effects.title: Raster Bars
effects.name: Raster Bars
effects.dating: 1980s, early demoscene and video games
effects.caption: AI illustration: Horizontal raster bars on a vintage personal computer.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see horizontal bands of bright, gradient colors moving up and down a computer screen. These thick lines often overlap or bounce smoothly behind text or graphics.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Programmers change the screen's background color palette at exact moments while the monitor's electron beam scans horizontally. This creates solid bands of color without using video memory for actual pixels.

body.label: Example
body.text: Red Sector Inc.: Megademo, 1989.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Slowly drag a colored physical ruler up and down behind a cut-out paper window to simulate the visual timing.

context: In the 1980s, early home computers lacked the processing power to draw large moving graphics. Programmers found a clever hardware trick. Monitors updated the screen line by line, from top to bottom. Coders wrote small routines that triggered an interrupt exactly as the electron beam finished a line. They instantly changed the background color for the next line. This bypassed the central processor and required almost no memory. On the Commodore Amiga, a special chip called the Copper handled this perfectly. This created smooth, bouncing rainbow gradients known as copper bars. These colorful bars became a proud signature of the demoscene.
effects.distinction: Raster bars are hardware-driven horizontal color changes tied directly to screen scanning. In contrast, standard gradient graphics are pre-drawn pixels stored heavily in video memory.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how early programmers manipulated physical hardware timings to surpass the theoretical limits of simple computers.
effects.funFact: The Amiga's famous Copper chip was named directly after its core hardware function: the Co-Processor.

margin.note: Older CRT monitors displayed images by rapidly sweeping a beam of electrons across a phosphor-coated glass screen.
This is a specialized storage area in a computer that holds the data for every visible pixel.
A hardware signal that briefly pauses a computer's current task to immediately run a high-priority function.

effects.title: Raycasting
effects.name: Raycasting
effects.dating: 1990s landmark: Wolfenstein 3D, 1992; raycasting predates the game.
effects.caption: From Room Plan to Raycast View. A tiled room plan and viewing cone accompany a first-person view of yellow walls beneath a blue ceiling.
effects.credit: Mewtow · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Blocky corridors show upright walls, sharp corners, and enlarged texture pixels nearby. Walls appear as vertical strips that shrink toward the distance.

body.label: Principle
body.text: In this method, a ray crosses a two-dimensional map for each screen column until it hits a wall. The perpendicular distance sets the height of a textured strip drawn in that column.

body.label: Example
body.text: id Software: Wolfenstein 3D, 1992.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: In a raycasting demonstration, approach a wall and watch its texture enlarge while its vertical edges remain upright.

context: Raycasting became widely recognized through early 1990s computer games, especially Wolfenstein 3D. Its walls came from a two-dimensional grid map, rather than a general three-dimensional polygon scene. Each screen column sampled the map along a viewing ray. The first wall hit supplied a texture position, while perpendicular distance controlled the strip’s height. This restriction made convincing movement through corridors practical on contemporary personal computers. Wolfenstein 3D used equal-height walls and flat-colored floors and ceilings. Enemies and many objects were separate sprites, not wall geometry. Other raycasting engines extended these limits.
effects.distinction: Unlike general ray tracing, this column-based method does not trace secondary rays for reflections or refraction. It exploits upright walls to render whole columns from individual map intersections.
effects.aftermath: Raycasting shows how carefully chosen geometric restrictions can create a convincing sense of space with relatively little computation.
effects.funFact: Wolfenstein 3D’s enemies were flat sprites, even though they seemed to occupy its corridors.

margin.note: Depth measured straight away from the viewing plane, rather than along a slanted ray.
An image sampled onto a surface to give it visible details, such as bricks.

effects.title: Reaction-Diffusion Patterns
effects.name: Reaction-Diffusion Patterns
effects.dating: 1990s computer graphics; Alan Turing’s 1952 theory; Greg Turk’s 1991 texture synthesis
effects.caption: Pattern Formation in Limbs and Fins. Anatomical drawings of limbs and fins appear beside grayscale fields of branching stripes and rounded spots.
effects.credit: Zhu, Jianfeng & Zhang, Yong-Tao & Alber, Mark & Newman, Stuart. · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Rounded spots, winding stripes, and branching mazes repeat with roughly consistent spacing. Their organic boundaries suggest animal markings, coral, or microscopic colonies.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A simulation couples local reactions with diffusion, which spreads substances or numerical concentrations across a surface. Under suitable conditions, these interactions amplify small disturbances into organized patterns.

body.label: Example
body.text: Greg Turk: Generating Textures on Arbitrary Surfaces Using Reaction-Diffusion, 1991.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: In a reaction-diffusion simulation, change one reaction rate and watch whether isolated spots merge into winding stripes.

context: Alan Turing described a chemical basis for biological pattern formation in 1952. His model showed how reacting substances with different diffusion rates could destabilize an initially uniform mixture. Small disturbances could then grow into spatial patterns. In 1991, Greg Turk applied reaction-diffusion systems to computer texture synthesis on arbitrary surfaces. This helped connect mathematical biology with digital graphics during the 1990s. The visible image maps simulated concentrations to colors or shades. Spots and stripes emerge through repeated local calculations, rather than being individually drawn or copied from photographs.
effects.distinction: Unlike marbling, reaction-diffusion patterns need no flowing liquid to stretch pigment into swirls. Unlike ordinary noise textures, they emerge from interacting reaction and diffusion processes.
effects.aftermath: The technique shows how simple local rules can generate complex visual order without a central design.
effects.funFact: Turing’s pattern theory appeared decades before computers could routinely render its results as detailed textures.

margin.note: The spreading of a substance from higher concentration toward lower concentration through random motion.
The computational creation of surface patterns, rather than simply photographing an existing surface.
Numbers representing how much of each modeled substance exists at each location.

effects.title: Recursive Ray Tracing
effects.name: Recursive ray tracing
effects.dating: Turner Whitted: groundbreaking publication 1979/1980.
effects.caption: Turner Whitted: Reflection and Refraction, Original Paper, 1980.
effects.credit: Turner Whitted / Communications of the ACM, 1980; Original illustrations, University of Utah Archives.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Reflections, refractions of glass and shadows correspond spatially.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Rays track visibility, reflection, and refraction through the scene.

body.label: Example
body.text: Turner Whitted: early bullet test scene.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare a glass ball against a patterned background.

context: Whitted's An Improved Illumination Model for Shaded Display was introduced in 1979 and published in Communications of the ACM in 1980. The recursive tracking of reflection and refraction rays provided a crucial step towards consistent specular and transparent surfaces. Earlier ray-tracking techniques preceded this; therefore, the slide does not claim to have invented all ray tracking in 1980. Modern renderers combine these fundamentals with more comprehensive light transport models.
effects.distinction: Ray tracing is a computational principle, not a uniform look. Simple recursive ray tracing does not automatically calculate every form of indirect lighting.
effects.aftermath: Light behavior can be systematically simulated instead of being faked for each surface individually.
effects.funFact: Ray tracing usually traces lines of sight from the camera into the scene.
highlights: reflection, and refraction through the scene

margin.note: The bending of light as it passes between materials, such as air and glass.
Imaginary paths used to calculate what a camera sees. At reflective or transparent surfaces, additional rays can be traced to determine reflections and transmitted light.

effects.dating: Early 2000s, Lomography community experiments
effects.caption: Waterfront Skyline Beneath an Orange Sky. A waterfront skyline and curving roadway lie beneath a dramatically orange clouded sky, with buildings and palms sinking into dark green shadows.
effects.credit: cliffchen1973 from Kaohsiung, Taiwan · CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Images show a strong color shift toward warm tones like red, orange, and yellow. Skies may appear green or dark yellow instead of blue.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The film is loaded backwards so light hits the back of the film first. It passes through the red-sensitive layer before reaching the green and blue layers.

body.label: Example
body.text: Lomography Society: Redscale XR film release, 2008.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look through a piece of dark orange cellophane to see how it filters and warms the colors of your surroundings.

context: Redscale emerged as a popular technique during the early 2000s analog photography revival. Photographers manually spooled color negative film backwards into empty canisters. Normally, light hits the blue-sensitive layer first, then green, then red. By reversing the film, light passes through the semi-opaque anti-halation layer and the red-sensitive layer first. This starves the blue and green layers of light. The result is a striking, unpredictable warm color cast. Commercial film companies eventually manufactured pre-reversed redscale film to meet the growing demand from experimental photographers.
effects.distinction: Unlike sepia toning which applies a uniform brown dye to monochrome prints, redscale alters how color film chemically records different wavelengths.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how altering the physical sequence of light exposure changes the entire chemical translation of a scene.
effects.funFact: Pushing light through the film base requires exposing it at lower ISO settings than normal.

margin.note: Standard photographic film designed to capture inverted colors that are later corrected during printing or scanning.
A dark coating on the back of film that prevents light from reflecting back through the emulsion.

body.label: Identify
body.text: The photograph takes on the reference image's palette, changing its overall colors and tones while keeping its spatial structure.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The algorithm converts both images to lαβ color space, which separates brightness from two color components. It shifts and scales each source channel to match the reference's mean and standard deviation, then converts back to RGB.

body.label: Classification
body.text: Calculated image processing result.

effects.funFact: Erik Reinhard and colleagues published the method in 2001.

margin.note: A way to represent colors using one brightness-related coordinate and two color coordinates. It is different from CIELAB, another common color space.
A measure of how widely values spread around their average. Matching it adjusts the variation within each channel.

Temporal effect: still image or image sequence.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Water recoils; destroyed things come together.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The order of the individual images is reversed.

body.label: Example
body.text: The Bathers, 1900; Coldplay: The Scientist, 2002.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Film falling paper and play the clip backwards.

context: Early animation discovered how easily cause and effect could be resolved by reversing the sequence of images. The BFI's *The Bathers* depicts bathers seemingly leaping out of the water, their clothes flying towards them. In music videos, such a reversal can structure entire narratives. The decade refers to early film use; a specific date of invention is not claimed.
effects.distinction: Reversing changes the order, not necessarily the speed. Natural gestures, hair, or smoke can give away the reversal; lip-syncing in reverse requires careful planning.
effects.aftermath: The image sequence itself is an effect tool.
effects.funFact: In the early animated film The Bathers, clothes appear to fly onto the body when walking backwards.

margin.note: The time sequence of frames in a clip. Playing them from last to first makes recorded actions run backward.
A short segment of moving-image footage that can be played or edited as a unit.

effects.title: RGB Split
effects.name: RGB split / chromatic glitch
effects.dating: Older predecessors. Customizable digital look of the 2010s.
effects.caption: Rosa Menkman: Glitch Art, 2011: digital color fringes and destroyed image structure.
effects.credit: Rosa Menkman. CC BY 2.0

body.label: Identify
body.text: Red-cyan double contours, shifted lines and image jumps indicate a damaged digital signal.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Color channels are shifted relative to each other. Line offsets and block errors simulate signal problems. Actual data manipulation can produce similar artifacts.

body.label: Example
body.text: Rosa Menkman: A Vernacular of File Formats (2010) examines digital artifacts.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Shift the red channel of a portrait. Add line errors. Test how little distortion is needed for the desired effect.

context: Older technical and artistic precursors; strongly present in the 2010s as a customizable effect and plug-in look.

The red, green, and blue channels are shifted relative to each other. Additional line offsets, block errors, noise, or image dropouts create a distorted signal aesthetic. True databending and a controlled filter can look similar.
Rosa Menkman, A Vernacular of File Formats (2010), as an important reference for the study of digital artifacts; not as the alleged invention of the RGB split filter.

Regarding the image: Historical original / source image. The authentic glitch artwork shows colorful channel/line distortions. It is an example of glitch art; not every visible distortion is identical to a simple RGB split filter.
effects.distinction: Optical chromatic aberration arises from wavelength-dependent lens behavior. RGB splitting is a freely configurable digital channel shift; Datamosh uses temporal compression. There is no single inventor and no reliable first trend year. The classification describes a stylistic trend, not the origin of the chromatic error.
effects.aftermath: Technical errors become a recognizable language for instability, networks, memory, and media friction.
effects.funFact: In 2010, Rosa Menkman investigated file formats as their own visual languages: Digital errors were deliberately made readable.

margin.note: Separate red, green, and blue components that combine to form a color image.
Visible features introduced by processing, encoding, or errors rather than by the original scene.

effects.title: Risograph
effects.name: Risograph / Riso print
effects.dating: 1980: first RISOGRAPH; later zine and design revival
effects.caption: Riso simulation: modern digital demonstration.
effects.credit: Digital effect demonstration.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Bright special colors, grainy surfaces and slight color variations.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Colors are applied separately using stencils and printing drums.

body.label: Example
body.text: Zines, art books, and multicolored small print runs.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Separate an image into two colors; move one section slightly.

context: RISO launched its first RISOGRAPH products in 1980. The manufacturer describes the process as a unique duplication technology. The attractive design, featuring separate colors, overprinting, and offset printing, gained further significance in artistic publishing. The decade here refers to the documented product launch, not the date of each subsequent production. Digitally, the visible properties can be simulated using separate color channels, paper texture, and offset separations. A digital image editor can produce a subtractive overprint simulation using scanned grain plates for this purpose. Pay particular attention to the overlaps: A third visible color can emerge from two printed colors. This is precisely what distinguishes overprinting from simply adjacent color fields.
effects.distinction: A risograph look on the screen does not replace paper or real spot colors.
effects.aftermath: Keep colors and print passes mentally separate. A small misalignment can create rhythm, a large one makes facial recognition and readability more difficult.
effects.funFact: The first RISOGRAPH appeared in 1980; its name refers to a specific printing technology.

margin.note: Thin sheets with openings that let ink pass through only where the image should print.
Printing one ink over another. Transparent inks can combine to create a third visible color.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Broad shading is reduced, making small bright details stand out against a more even background.

body.label: Principle

margin.note: A curved mathematical shape, not a physical object. Its radius controls which scales of brightness variation count as background.

effects.title: Rotoscoping
effects.name: Rotoscoping
effects.dating: Late 1910s–1920s: Out of the Inkwell. Later music video and digital VFX.
effects.caption:
Early rotoscope in the living room of the Fleischer family.
Temporal effect: still image or image sequence.
effects.credit: Fleischer Studios archive; Fleischer Studios web reproduction; no open license stated.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Drawn figures move in a strikingly human and fluid manner.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Real film movements are traced frame by frame. Digital rotoscoping can also create animated clipping masks.

body.label: Example
body.text: Max and Dave Fleischer: Out of the Inkwell, from 1918. Max developed the rotoscope in 1915.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Trace three consecutive body poses. Invent another figure with the same movement.

context: Max Fleischer developed the rotoscope in 1915; patent granted in 1917. Late 1910s–1920s: Out of the Inkwell; later, music video and digital VFX. The Fleischer website contains an obvious typo in the patent dates: 2015/2017; MoMA confirms 1915. This does not refer to automatic AI video transmission.

Recognize: Drawn figures move in a strikingly human and fluid manner.
Mechanism: Real film movements are traced frame by frame. In digital compositing, roto also refers to the manual animation of clipping masks.
Example: Max and Dave Fleischer: Out of the Inkwell, from 1918; later Cab Calloway's Dance in Snow-White, 1933.
Practice: Trace a person's posture in three consecutive video frames. Then invent a new character that could perform the exact same sequence of movements.

Real film movements are recreated frame by frame. In digital compositing, roto also refers to the manual animation of clipping masks.
The drawn figures move in a strikingly human and fluid way.
Trace the posture of a person in three consecutive video frames.
The Fleischer website contains an obvious typo in the patent data: 2015/2017; MoMA confirms 1915. This does not refer to automatic AI video transmission.
effects.distinction: The Fleischer website contains an obvious typographical error in the patent data, stating 2015/2017; MoMA confirms 1915. This does not refer to automatic AI video transmission.
effects.aftermath: Bridge between live-action and animation; basis for many cutout works.
effects.funFact: For early rotoscoping, Max Fleischer filmed his brother Dave in a clown costume and traced his movements.

margin.note: Working on each individual image in a film sequence rather than changing the whole clip at once.
Shapes that determine which parts of an image layer remain visible. Animated masks follow moving subjects over time.

effects.title: Rutt–Etra Scan Processing
effects.name: Rutt/Etra scan processing
effects.dating: Developed in 1973; visible in Vasulka's C-Trend in 1974.
effects.caption: Woody Vasulka: C-Trend, 1974. Original video still, EAI.
effects.credit: Woody Vasulka / Electronic Arts Intermix; copyright protected.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Bright areas of the image grow into curved, seemingly spatial linear landscapes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The image brightness controls the deflection of the electronic grid.

body.label: Example
body.text: Woody Vasulka: C-Trend, 1974.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Translate a portrait into height-modulated horizontal lines.

context: The Daniel Langlois Foundation documents Steve Rutt, Bill Etra, and Louise Etra as developers. The prototype was created in 1972–73, and the commercial version followed in 1975. Steina and Woody Vasulka researched the conversion of image brightness into grid deflection; their recordings made the signal visible as material. EAI also cites George Brown's Multikeyer and Eric Siegel's Colorizer for C-Trend.
effects.distinction: No digitally calculated wireframe geometry: The spatial effect arises from distorted grid lines of an analog video signal. Digital practice simulates this principle.
effects.aftermath: Precursor to today's height-based image distortions and audio-reactive raster visuals.
effects.funFact: Louise Etra was involved in all phases of development and construction.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Matte paper surface, soft details and visible fiber structure.

body.label: Principle

context: Talbot developed the salt paper print from his early experiments with light-sensitive paper. A negative is placed directly on the prepared sheet and printed using daylight. The image substance is embedded in the paper fibers, which is why the texture plays a more significant role than with a smooth egg white layer. In the 1850s, albumen paper increasingly replaced the process; later art photographers rediscovered its material properties.
effects.distinction: A salt print is the positive paper image. Calotype primarily refers to the process for the paper negative. Both can be related, but remain different stages of the photographic process.
effects.aftermath: The same negative can appear differently on different paper.
effects.funFact: The print was created using sunlight under the negative; an enlarger was not necessary.

margin.note: A silver-containing chemical used to prepare the paper. It reacts with salt to form light-sensitive silver chloride.
Egg white used as a coating to hold photographic chemicals on paper. Its smoother surface can retain finer detail than uncoated salted paper.

effects.title: Sand Animation
effects.name: Sand Animation
effects.dating: 1969, Caroline Leaf’s Sand, or Peter and the Wolf
effects.caption: Mounted Warrior in Backlit Sand. An armored rider on horseback crosses a mountainous landscape rendered in brown grains against a luminous ground.
effects.credit: Manas Sahoo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Grainy silhouettes shift across a glowing background, with soft edges and scattered specks. Figures seem to dissolve, stretch, and grow into new shapes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Sand on a lightbox blocks transmitted light, making thicker deposits darker and cleared areas brighter. Small changes photographed frame by frame create apparent movement during playback.

body.label: Example
body.text: Caroline Leaf: Sand, or Peter and the Wolf, 1969.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Spread fine sand on a clear tray above a cool light source; photograph five small changes and compare the resulting silhouettes.

context: Caroline Leaf made Sand, or Peter and the Wolf in 1969 while studying at Harvard. It became an important early example of sand animation. She manipulated sand on an illuminated surface and photographed successive arrangements. This stop-motion method turns loose grains into moving figures without requiring separate drawings for every frame. Adding sand blocks more light; removing it reveals the bright surface below. Thin, uneven layers produce intermediate tones and visible texture. Because each change alters the existing image, transformations can flow directly from one scene into another.
effects.distinction: Unlike live sand drawing, this technique builds movement from separately photographed arrangements rather than continuously filmed gestures. Unlike cel animation, it reshapes loose material instead of replacing drawings.
effects.aftermath: Sand animation shows how changing a material’s distribution can turn blocked light into expressive movement.
effects.funFact: A character can become its own scenery simply by redistributing the same grains.

margin.note: A shallow box with a lit, translucent top that spreads light beneath the working surface.
Light that passes through a material or surface, rather than bouncing off it.
Animation made by photographing physical material after each small adjustment.

context: Lee Harrison's Computer Image Corporation developed real-time animation systems based on ANIMAC. Scanimate dominated television logos, commercials, and program opening sequences in the 1970s. effects.aftermath: Real-time control and an operable image instrument combine early TV graphics with today's motion tools.
