effects.title: Scanning Electron Micrograph
effects.name: Scanning Electron Micrograph
effects.dating: 1960s; commercial Stereoscan introduced in 1965
effects.caption: Filaments Across a Cellular Surface. Bright green filaments weave across a blue, deeply folded cellular surface.
effects.credit: BernbaumJG · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Grey surfaces show deep focus, crisp textures, and a sculptural, three-dimensional appearance. Bright edges often stand against dark recesses; false colour may highlight selected structures.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A focused electron beam scans the specimen, while a detector measures signals such as secondary electrons emitted near its surface. Signal strength becomes image brightness; the beam’s narrow convergence angle provides a large depth of field.

body.label: Example
body.text: Janice Haney Carr: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), 2005.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare an SEM image of pollen with a light micrograph, noting which raised and recessed features remain sharp.

context: Scanning electron microscopy developed before the 1960s, but commercial instruments helped bring it into wider laboratory use. Cambridge Instruments introduced its Stereoscan in 1965. Unlike a camera, an SEM builds an image by scanning an electron beam across a specimen. Secondary electrons reveal surface detail, while detector position influences apparent shading. Conventional preparation often includes drying biological specimens and applying a thin conductive coating. These steps can alter delicate structures. The recorded signal has no inherent visible colour. Colour added afterward can separate structures or guide interpretation.
effects.distinction: Unlike transmission electron microscopy, which commonly reveals internal structure through thin specimens, SEM usually emphasizes surfaces. Its sculptural shading suggests depth, but a single image is not a three-dimensional measurement.
effects.aftermath: SEM images teach us that convincing depth and detail can arise from measured electron signals rather than reflected light.
effects.funFact: A biological specimen may receive a thin gold coating before imaging.

margin.note: Low-energy electrons released when the incoming beam interacts with the specimen. Those escaping near the surface help reveal fine detail.
The range of specimen heights that appear sharp at once.
A thin layer that lets electrical charge flow away. It helps prevent charge buildup from distorting the image.

effects.title: Schlieren Photography
effects.name: Schlieren Photography
effects.dating: 1864, August Toepler's optical experiments
effects.caption: Shock Waves Around a Supersonic Aircraft. Sweeping dark and light bands surround a slender aircraft, with a narrow wake trailing below it.
effects.credit: NASA & US Air Force: J.T. Heineck / Ed Schairer / Maj. Jonathan Orso / Maj. Jeremy Vand… · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see transparent air currents rendered as visible, swirling shadows. Heat waves, sound waves, or gases look like dark and light ripples.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Light passes through varying air densities, bending the rays slightly. A sharp physical edge blocks the bent rays, creating visible shadows.

body.label: Example
body.text: August Toepler: Schlieren images of sound waves, 1866.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look over a hot toaster against a plain wall; watch the air shimmer and distort the background.

context: In 1864, German physicist August Toepler invented this method to see the invisible. He wanted to observe sound waves moving through air. Air density changes when it heats up or when sound travels through it. Different densities bend light at different angles. This bending is called refraction. Toepler used lenses and a precisely placed knife edge. The edge blocks light rays that bend away from their normal path. This transforms invisible density changes into high-contrast images. Scientists later used it heavily in aerodynamics to study supersonic airflow.
effects.distinction: Shadowgraphs project light through fluid onto a screen without blocking rays. Schlieren uses a knife edge to achieve much higher sensitivity.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that even empty air contains dynamic, structured fluid mechanics.
effects.funFact: The word Schlieren means streaks in German, originally referring to visual flaws inside window glass.

margin.note: The bending of light as it passes from one transparent substance into another. This happens because light slightly changes speed.
A physical barrier placed at the focal point of the lens. It intercepts deflected light to create image contrast.

context: In the early 1920s, Eugen Schüfftan and Ernst Kunstmann developed a mirror technique for creating gigantic-looking sets. A tilted mirror reflects the small model; exposed sections allow a direct view of the actors. A composite image is created during the filming process. The technique became famous through the film Metropolis. Filmportal documents both their collaboration and the development of the technique prior to this film.
effects.distinction: The camera and mirror must be precisely aligned. This differentiates this recording process from a freely movable digital collage; imprecise transitions betray the combination.
effects.aftermath: Early compositing can already occur in the camera.
effects.funFact: Ernst Kunstmann also worked on the Schüfftan process.
highlights: combines model reflection and real performers

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see an image that is mostly black-and-white. A single object or area retains its bright, natural color.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Film editors use digital masks to isolate a specific item. They then desaturate the rest of the image into grayscale.

body.label: Example
body.text: Steven Spielberg: Schindler's List, 1993.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a colorful photo and squint until only the brightest red or yellow object stands out from the background.

context: Selective color creates stark contrast to guide the viewer's eye. Early filmmakers hand-painted dyes onto black-and-white film frames. The 1990s introduced digital compositing instead. Editors scanned film into computers and mathematically removed color data from unselected pixels. By drawing a digital boundary around an object, they preserved its original hues. This process turns normal color footage into black-and-white, except for the masked area. The technique highlights narrative importance. It famously marked innocence amidst a black-and-white tragedy.
effects.distinction: Selective color digitally removes surrounding hues from an original color image. Hand-tinting physically adds colored dye to a black-and-white image.
effects.aftermath: It teaches how stark contrast isolates subjects and forces audiences to notice specific narrative details.
effects.funFact: Some digital cameras now have built-in sensors that isolate specific color wavelengths in real time.

margin.note: This means reducing the intensity of colors. If taken to the extreme, it leaves only shades of gray.
This is the practice of combining multiple visual elements from separate sources into a single digital image.
These are the smallest individual points of light or data that make up a digital display.

context: 1890s, 19th century; later, a universal nostalgia look.

Sepia toning is part of the history of chemical post-processing of photographic prints. Sulfide toning produces brown tones and can improve the durability of a silver print. Later, photo editing software adopted the color scheme as a symbol of memory and the past. The decade-based association marks the historical brown look, not a clearly datable invention.
effects.distinction: Brown historical images can also result from their printing process or aging. The hue alone does not identify sepia toning. Digital tinting replicates the visible look; it does not automatically possess the same material properties.
effects.aftermath: Read color association and material history separately.
effects.funFact: Sepia toning could improve not only the color change but also the durability of a silver print.

margin.note: A compound of silver and sulfur that can replace metallic silver during sepia toning, producing brown tones.
A chemical treatment that changes the material forming a photographic image, altering its color and sometimes improving its stability.

effects.title: Shaky Cam
effects.name: Shaky Cam
effects.dating: 1990s prominence; handheld roots in earlier documentary filmmaking
effects.caption: Camera Shake on a Night Street. Illuminated façades and a church spire rise above a wet street, with stationary architectural details visibly smeared and doubled.
effects.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: The frame shows irregular jolts, drifting horizons, and abrupt reframing rather than smooth camera travel. Moving details may smear briefly.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Unstabilized camera movement changes the viewpoint and framing during recording. Movement during each exposure can also produce motion blur, depending on exposure time.

body.label: Example
body.text: Daniel Myrick and Eduardo Sánchez: The Blair Witch Project, 1999.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Record the same short walk with stabilization off and on, if available. Compare horizon movement and how easily you follow objects.

context: Shaky cam became especially visible in 1990s fiction, but handheld documentary practice long predates that decade. Lightweight cameras let operators follow events without fixed supports. Their footsteps, breathing, and corrections could become visible in the frame. Fiction filmmakers borrowed these signs to suggest urgency, uncertainty, or eyewitness access. The Blair Witch Project made unstable footage part of its story: characters were recording their own frightening experience. In the following decade, Paul Greengrass's Bourne films combined handheld movement with rapid editing for action. Camera shake and editing remained separate techniques.
effects.distinction: Shaky cam changes framing within a shot; rapid cutting switches between shots. Motion blur can accompany shake, but either can occur without the other.
effects.aftermath: Shaky cam teaches how imperfect framing can suggest eyewitness authenticity without proving that an event is real.
effects.funFact: The Blair Witch Project mixes black-and-white 16 mm film with color video.

margin.note: A sudden change in what the picture includes or where subjects sit within it.
The duration during which film or a sensor gathers light for one image.
Frequent cuts between shots. This can intensify action even when each camera remains steady.

effects.title: Silhouette Animation
effects.name: Silhouette Animation
effects.dating: 1920s, Lotte Reiniger's feature films
effects.caption: Silhouette Figures Against Layered Scenery. Two elaborately outlined black figures exchange a gesture before a softly illuminated, patterned background.
effects.credit: Lotte Reiniger/Primrose Productions · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see stark black figures moving against brightly lit, detailed backgrounds. The characters lack internal details like eyes or clothing patterns.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Jointed paper or metal cut-outs are placed on a glass table. A camera above photographs them while lights shine from below.

body.label: Example
body.text: Lotte Reiniger: The Adventures of Prince Achmed, 1926.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Hold a cardboard shape flat against a sunny window and notice how all surface details disappear into a solid black shadow.

context: Silhouette animation adapts the ancient art of shadow puppetry into stop-motion film. Lotte Reiniger pioneered this technique in the 1920s. She meticulously cut characters from black cardboard and thin lead. To allow movement, she connected their limbs with wire hinges. These figures rested on a multi-plane camera stand consisting of glass layers. This setup created depth between the sharp black foreground and softly glowing tissue-paper backgrounds. Animators moved the figures slightly between each frame. Backlighting from underneath ensured the characters remained completely opaque. This intense contrast forced viewers to focus entirely on outline and movement rather than texture.
effects.distinction: Unlike traditional cel animation, characters are opaque physical cut-outs rather than drawings. Traditional shadow puppetry happens live, whereas this is filmed frame-by-frame.
effects.aftermath: It shows how expressive character emotion can be conveyed entirely through body language and precise outlines.
effects.funFact: Reiniger cut over 300,000 individual frames by hand for her most famous animated feature film.

margin.note: An animation technique where objects are moved in small increments. They are photographed once per movement to create continuous motion.
A device holding artwork on multiple separate layers of glass. It creates an illusion of three-dimensional depth in flat animation.
Lighting that originates from behind the subject. In this technique, it washes out front details to create a solid silhouette.

effects.title: Silkscreen Print
effects.name: Silkscreen Print
effects.dating: 1962, Andy Warhol's Pop Art
effects.caption: Red Ink Applied to a Printing Screen. A hand spreads thick red ink across a framed screen containing a masked graphic design.
effects.credit: Manolis Angelakis · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see flat, bold areas of vivid color separated by stark photographic outlines. Colors often overlap or miss their outlines entirely.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Ink is pushed through a porous mesh stencil onto paper or canvas. Misaligned stencils cause colors to slip outside their boundaries.

body.label: Example
body.text: Andy Warhol: Marilyn Diptych, 1962.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Cut a paper stencil, place it over another drawing, and dab paint through it to see how misalignment alters the image.

context: Silkscreen printing began as a commercial method for making signs and advertisements. In the 1960s, Pop artists adopted it to mass-produce art. The process relies on a tight mesh screen coated with a light-sensitive emulsion. A photographic positive blocks UV light, leaving specific areas of the emulsion soft. When washed, these areas create open pores. A squeegee forces ink through these open pores onto a canvas. To print multiple colors, artists use a different screen for each hue. If the screens do not align perfectly, colorful gaps and overlaps appear.
effects.distinction: Unlike a woodcut print where raised wood stamps ink onto paper, silkscreen forces ink through open holes in a flat mesh.
effects.aftermath: It reveals how industrial manufacturing errors can be embraced as a distinctive artistic style.
effects.funFact: Early screens were made of real silk threads, but modern versions use woven polyester or nylon.

margin.note: A thick, light-sensitive liquid spread across the printing screen. It hardens under UV light to block ink from passing through.
A tool with a flat rubber blade used to drag and press ink evenly across the screen.
A template with cut-out or blocked shapes. It controls exactly where ink is allowed to reach the final surface.

effects.title: Skeuomorphic Interface
effects.name: Skeuomorphic Interface
effects.dating: 2000s prominence; Apple's iPhone launched in 2007
effects.caption: AI illustration: Mobile calendar with leather and paper textures.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Controls resemble physical objects, with raised buttons, simulated materials, and familiar details such as stitching or ruled paper. Leather, wood grain, and green felt can turn screens into desks, shelves, or gaming tables.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Digital textures, gradients, and shadows simulate surface materials and depth on a flat display. These visual metaphors connect software functions with familiar objects, without requiring their physical construction.

body.label: Example
body.text: Apple: iPhone Notes, 2007.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Study an early iPhone Notes screenshot, then separate useful notebook cues from decorative details that cannot affect digital writing.

context: Skeuomorphic interfaces predate smartphones, drawing on earlier desktop metaphors and software that imitated physical equipment. The 2007 iPhone brought familiar objects into touch interaction, including a Notes application resembling a yellow notepad. Leather, wooden shelves, and felt appeared across Apple's interfaces in subsequent years, not all in the original iPhone. Designers used bitmap textures, gradients, highlights, and shadows to suggest tangible surfaces. These cues could help users recognize controls, but decoration sometimes competed with content. The approach became especially visible as touchscreens reached wider audiences.

context: Variable camera speeds predate digital editing software. However, in digital post-production, speed changes can be precisely controlled using keyframes and curves. Action films and music videos made the combination of acceleration and drawn-out climaxes particularly noticeable. Adobe's guide explains the smooth transitions as a re-imposition of time. The 2000s represent a popular phase for this look, not the first technical possibility.
effects.distinction: Speed ​​ramping is not constant slow motion and not simply a cut between speeds. For significantly slowed-down sections, appropriate frame rates or calculated intermediate frames are required.
effects.aftermath: The timing of an effect can be shaped like its spatial form.
effects.funFact: A speed ramp changes the speed within a clip.

effects.title: Spirit Duplicator
effects.name: Spirit Duplicator
effects.dating: 1923, Wilhelm Ritzerfeld's spirit duplicator
effects.caption: Violet Chemistry Worksheets. Overlapping chemistry worksheets bear violet lettering on pale paper, with handwritten marks added in red.
effects.credit: Richard Masoner · CC BY-SA 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Purple lettering and line drawings sit on pale paper, often with soft edges and uneven density. Later copies can look noticeably weaker.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An alcohol-based solvent dissolves small amounts of aniline dye from a master and transfers them onto paper. The master gradually loses dye, producing progressively paler copies.

body.label: Example
body.text: Wilhelm Ritzerfeld: Spirit duplicator, 1923.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare several surviving copies of one ditto sheet, looking for changes in purple density and the disappearance of fine lines.

context: Introduced in 1923, the spirit duplicator became familiar in schools, offices, and small publishing operations. Typing or drawing pressed a waxy dye coating from a backing sheet onto the master's reverse. This created a mirror image of the original marks. During duplication, paper moistened with an alcohol-based fluid contacted that image, picking up a little dissolved dye. Purple was common, though other colors existed. The process required neither photographic exposure nor development. Its limited dye supply suited short runs, while repeated copying gradually weakened the printed image.
effects.distinction: Mimeographs force ink through openings in a stencil; spirit duplicators dissolve dye from a master. Gelatin hectographs also transfer dye, but use a gelatin surface rather than this alcohol-moistened paper process.
effects.aftermath: Spirit duplication shows how a finite supply of color can make the copying process visible in its results.
effects.funFact: The word “spirit” refers to alcohol, not ghosts.

margin.note: A historical term for synthetic dyes associated with aniline chemistry. These dyes supplied the color rather than an ink reservoir.
The prepared sheet carrying the image used to make multiple copies.
An image reversed left to right. Transferring it onto another sheet restores the readable orientation.

effects.title: Spirit Photography
effects.name: Spirit Photography
effects.dating: 1861, William Mumler's portraits
effects.caption: Seated Woman with Translucent Male Apparition. A seated woman in a dark dress is overlapped by a large, pale male apparition and flowing translucent forms.
effects.credit: Buguet (Paris) · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a standard 19th-century portrait with a faint, translucent figure standing nearby. The background often shows right through the faded ghost.

body.label: Principle
body.text: This is an additive process created through double exposure. The photographer exposes the same glass plate twice before developing it chemically.

body.label: Example
body.text: William Mumler: Portrait of Mary Todd Lincoln with the ghost of Abraham Lincoln, roughly 1869.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a window reflection at night. Notice how your reflected image overlaps additively with the darker objects outside.

context: In the 1860s, the American Civil War left countless families grieving. Simultaneously, the Spiritualist movement convinced many that the dead could communicate. William Mumler capitalized on this by producing the first spirit photographs in Boston in 1861. He secretly used previously prepared glass plates that already held a faint, underexposed image. When he took a portrait of a living client, the two exposures added light together. Because photography was new, many clients believed these translucent figures were genuine spirits. They trusted the camera's mechanical eye implicitly.
effects.distinction: Unlike a simple motion blur, which smears a moving subject, double exposure freezes two distinct moments in time onto one surface.
effects.aftermath: It shows how easily technical novelty can be weaponized to exploit human grief and trust.
effects.funFact: Mumler was tried for fraud in 1869, and famous showman P. T. Barnum testified against him.

margin.note: A method where multiple layers of light are added together, making the overlapping areas brighter.
The act of letting light hit a photographic surface twice before applying chemicals to reveal the final image.
Early cameras used heavy sheets of glass coated with light-sensitive chemicals to capture images, rather than modern film.

effects.title: Spirograph
effects.name: Spirograph
effects.dating: 1965, Denys Fisher’s Spirograph drawing toy
effects.caption: Multicolored Spirograph Pattern Studies. Two study sheets display multicolored circular rosettes, interlaced rings, and angular loop patterns.
effects.credit: Rev. Daniel Elis Axelrod · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Fine lines form looping rosettes, with repeated petals arranged around a shared center. Overlapping curves create dense woven bands and open, star-shaped spaces.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A pen sits off-center in a toothed wheel that rolls around a fixed gear or ring. Rolling inside a circular ring produces hypotrochoid curves; rolling outside a circular gear produces epitrochoid curves.

body.label: Example
body.text: Denys Fisher: Spirograph, 1965.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw twice with the same wheel and ring, changing only the pen hole; compare the depth of the loops.

context: British engineer Denys Fisher introduced Spirograph in 1965, turning gear-guided drawing into a widely recognized toy. Its mathematics was much older than the plastic kit. A small toothed wheel rolls against a stationary ring, while a pen follows a hole away from the wheel’s center. The gear teeth prevent slipping and keep the motion regular. Tooth counts determine how the rotations repeat, while the pen’s offset changes the curve’s shape. Changing ink colors or starting positions builds layered patterns without changing the underlying mechanical rule.
effects.distinction: A harmonograph draws looping patterns using swinging pendulums rather than meshing gears. Spirograph’s regularity comes from gear ratios, not the timing and decay of pendulum motion.
effects.aftermath: Spirograph shows how simple mechanical constraints can generate intricate, predictable visual patterns.
effects.funFact: Some gear combinations need several trips around the ring before the pen closes the curve.

margin.note: Paths traced by a point attached to a circle rolling inside another circle without slipping.
Paths traced by a point attached to a circle rolling around the outside of another circle without slipping.
The distance between the pen hole and the moving wheel’s center.

effects.title: Split Screen
effects.name: Split screen
effects.dating: 1920s: avant-garde experiments; later telephone and action montage
effects.caption:
Pillow Talk (1959): two rooms simultaneously in a split image.
Temporal effect: still image or image sequence.
effects.credit: © Universal; Educational clip, Columbia Film Language Glossary.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Multiple views simultaneously share the same image area.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Separate recordings are spatially composed side by side.

body.label: Example
body.text: Napoleon, 1927; Pillow Talk, 1959.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Show the same action from two contradictory perspectives.

context: Split screen has been used since early film experiments to create multiple settings and subjective comparisons. Abel Gance's Napoléon made monumental multiple images famous in 1927. Columbia also shows the telephone montage of Pillow Talk and the quadruple image of Timecode. The effect differs from parallel editing: The audience sees the views simultaneously, rather than switching between individual, full-screen shots.
effects.distinction: Images visible at the same time do not necessarily represent events recorded simultaneously. The division can suggest proximity, make comparisons, or emphasize differences.
effects.aftermath: Simultaneity is a design statement, not automatically documentary evidence.
effects.funFact: Timecode (2000) tells its story in four simultaneously visible camera images.

margin.note: Arranged in different regions of the frame, rather than shown one after another in time.
Different viewpoints on the same subject. Split screen can show them together for direct comparison.

effects.title: Split Toning
effects.name: Split toning
effects.dating: 2010s preset culture; chemical precursors significantly older
effects.caption: Adobe tutorial example: digital split toning with separate highlight and shadow colors.
effects.credit: Adobe / Teaching example; not a historical recording

body.label: Identify
body.text: Lights and shadows have different color tones.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Two color areas are colored separately according to image brightness.

body.label: Example
body.text: Cool shadows meet warm lights.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Create three moods using the same two color controls.

context: Analog toning could alter shadows and highlights differently. Digital programs made this logic easily repeatable as a combination of sliders. Lightroom long offered separate shadow and highlight colors for this purpose; in 2020, Adobe expanded the principle with color grading that included additional midtones. A good learning objective is to guide the mood with subtle color shifts and to consciously control skin tones.
effects.distinction: Split toning refers to two differently tinted brightness ranges and is not a selective object coloring. The presence of multiple colors in an image does not prove this technique. The decade mark indicates the digital learning and preset context, not the origin of chemical split toning.
effects.aftermath: Color can structure brightness instead of changing the color of objects.
effects.funFact: In 2020, Adobe's Color Grading expanded the previous split-toning control with additional options.
highlights: colored separately according to image brightness

margin.note: How light or dark each image area is, used here to determine which tint it receives.

effects.title: Split-Field Diopter
effects.name: Split-field diopter
effects.dating: 1970s–1990s: frequently used cinematic look
effects.caption: Star Trek: The Motion Picture (1979): near and far faces in sharp focus at the same time.
effects.credit: © Paramount; Film frame in American Cinematographer.

body.label: Identify
body.text: A near and a distant subject are in focus simultaneously.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A half close-up lens only changes part of the image.

body.label: Example
body.text: Jaws, 1975; Star Trek: The Motion Picture, 1979.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look for the hidden transition zone in the image.

context: ASC describes the split diopter as a halved optical attachment. One part of the image uses the close-up lens, the other only the main camera lens. This allows a close face and a distant object to be kept in focus simultaneously. The dividing line is often hidden along a door frame or other structure. This distinctive arrangement was particularly common between the 1970s and 1990s.
effects.distinction: This does not automatically mean continuous depth of field. Two separate zones of focus may be separated by a blurry or distorted seam; the close-up lens does not simply increase the depth of field everywhere.
effects.aftermath: Simultaneous sharpness can result from multiple optical zones.
effects.funFact: The transition edge can be hidden, for example, in a door frame.

margin.note: An extra lens placed in front of the main lens to bring nearby objects into focus.
The boundary between the lens-assisted and unassisted parts of the image, which can reveal the effect unless concealed.

effects.title: Sprite Scaling
effects.name: Sprite Scaling
effects.dating: 1980s arcade graphics; Sega's Hang-On, 1985
effects.caption: AI illustration: Receding palm tree sprites in a motorcycle game.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Cars, trees, and signs grow rapidly as they approach, creating an illusion of forward motion. Their flat bitmap shapes retain crisp edges or visible pixel steps as their size changes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Graphics hardware resamples bitmap sprites at different sizes, making flat images suggest changing distance. Coordinated screen positions and drawing order strengthen the impression of depth.

body.label: Example
body.text: Sega: Out Run, 1986.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch Out Run footage and track one roadside tree: notice how its size and screen position change together.

context: Sprite scaling became a defining feature of Sega's 1980s arcade racing and action games. Hang-On appeared in 1985, followed by Out Run in 1986. Sega's Super Scaler hardware family made large numbers of changing sprite sizes practical during play. Stored bitmap artwork supplied vehicles, scenery, and other objects. Hardware sampled that artwork to produce different displayed sizes. Position, overlap, and size changes suggested movement through depth without constructing every object from polygons. Separate road graphics helped complete the scene. The result combined flat pictures with a convincing sense of speed.
effects.distinction: Unlike polygon rendering, sprite scaling does not reveal new surfaces when an object turns; different views generally require different artwork. Unlike scrolling, it changes displayed size, not just position.
effects.aftermath: Sprite scaling shows how coordinated size, position, and overlap can suggest depth without fully three-dimensional objects.
effects.funFact: Some Hang-On cabinets let players lean a motorcycle-shaped seat to steer.

margin.note: Separate game objects drawn from stored grids of colored pixels.
Selects pixels from a source image to create an output image at a different size.
The sequence used to place objects on screen. Objects drawn later can cover those drawn earlier.

effects.title: Star Filter
effects.name: Star Filter
effects.dating: 1960s, popularized in television entertainment and glamour photography
effects.caption: Starburst Lamps Along the Waterfront. A curving row of waterfront lamps forms golden stars above dark water.
effects.credit: Flocci Nivis · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see bright points of light radiating symmetrical, needle-like lines. These luminous streaks transform ordinary glare into distinct, multi-pointed stars.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A glass or plastic filter is etched with a fine grid of intersecting lines. This physical grid bends incoming light through diffraction, spreading point sources into visible rays.

body.label: Example
body.text: Harry Stradling Sr. (Cinematographer): Funny Girl, 1968.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a distant streetlamp through a finely woven window screen at night to see a similar geometric ray effect.

context: Photographers and television operators in the 1960s sought new ways to make scenes look glamorous. They placed specialized glass filters in front of their lenses. These filters had microscopic patterns etched into their surfaces. The etched lines scattered intense light sources into dramatic starbursts. Four-point, six-point, and eight-point variations were created by changing the grid pattern. The technique became a staple of music variety shows and romantic film close-ups. It turned reflections on jewelry, stage lights, and wet streets into dazzling spectacles. The effect peaked in the 1970s disco era before declining.
effects.distinction: Unlike lens flares caused by internal glass reflections, star filters are created deliberately by exterior grids. Star filters always produce highly symmetrical, evenly spaced rays from light sources.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how microscopic physical modifications to a lens surface can radically reshape captured light.
effects.funFact: You can make a functional DIY star filter by tightly stretching sheer pantyhose over a camera lens.

margin.note: The physical bending and spreading of light waves as they pass around an edge or through a gap.
Carved or scratched into a hard surface like glass to create a permanent physical pattern.

effects.title: Steadicam Float
effects.name: Steadicam Float
effects.dating: 1975, Garrett Brown's invention
effects.caption: Steadicam Operator Following a Cyclist. A harnessed camera operator films a cyclist balancing on a raised stone platform in a city square.
effects.credit: Pattymooney · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a smooth, gliding camera movement that follows a subject perfectly. The shot feels unhurried and floating, even over rough ground.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A mechanical harness isolates the camera from the operator's body movements. Springs and counterweights absorb steps and bumps to keep the lens level.

body.label: Example
body.text: Stanley Kubrick: The Shining, 1980.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Walk briskly while holding a cup filled to the brim with water; notice how your elbow acts like a shock absorber.

context: Before 1975, filmmakers had two main choices for moving the camera. They could push a heavy dolly on metal tracks, or they could hold the camera by hand. Tracks were smooth but took hours to build. Handheld shots were fast but shaky. Inventor Garrett Brown solved this by creating a body-mounted harness with an articulated arm. This system used heavy counterweights and springs to separate the operator's footsteps from the camera. The result was a device that let a person run up stairs or through forests while keeping the shot perfectly stable.
effects.distinction: Unlike a dolly shot which moves in fixed straight lines, a Steadicam can turn freely and fit through tight doorways. Unlike handheld shots, it does not jitter when the operator walks.
effects.aftermath: It teaches us how isolating the camera's center of gravity unlocks absolute physical filming freedom.
effects.funFact: The first movie to use the Steadicam was the 1976 Woody Guthrie biopic Bound for Glory.

margin.note: A wearable vest that attaches to the operator's body to carry heavy camera equipment securely.
Heavy objects placed at the bottom of the camera rig to lower the center of gravity and maintain balance.
A wheeled cart used to create smooth horizontal camera movements, usually running on laid tracks.

effects.title: Steel Engraving
effects.name: Steel Engraving
effects.dating: 1820s onwards, steel-plate book illustrations
effects.caption: Walt Whitman in Hat and Work Clothes. Walt Whitman stands in a broad-brimmed hat and open-necked shirt, with one hand resting on his hip.
effects.credit: Samuel Hollyer (1826-1919) of a daguerreotype by Gabriel Harrison (1818-1902)(original … · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Extremely fine parallel lines build delicate skies, crisp architecture, and detailed landscapes. Close inspection reveals crosshatched shadows and tiny strokes rather than continuous gray washes.

body.label: Principle
body.text: In this intaglio process, ink fills incised lines in a steel plate while the surface is wiped clean. Printing pressure pushes damp paper into these grooves, transferring ink onto the sheet.

body.label: Example
body.text: Samuel Rogers: Italy (illustrated edition), 1830.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Magnify a steel-engraved landscape, then step back to see separate lines merge visually into gray tones.

context: Steel engraving became important for illustrated books during the 1820s. Engravers translated paintings and drawings into networks of lines, sometimes combining acid etching with cuts made using a burin. Plates could be softened for working and hardened for printing. Hardened steel resisted wear better than copper, supporting larger editions while retaining fine detail. Publishers used these durable plates for landscapes, portraits, travel books, and literary annuals. The resulting gray tones depend on line spacing and thickness, not a continuous layer of gray ink.
effects.distinction: Copperplate engraving uses the same basic intaglio principle, but copper generally wears faster. Fine lines alone cannot reliably identify the plate metal.
effects.aftermath: Steel engraving shows how durable printing surfaces and carefully spaced lines made detailed images available to larger audiences.
effects.funFact: Many illustrations called steel engravings combine acid-etched lines with lines cut directly by hand.

margin.note: Printing from recessed marks that hold ink, rather than from raised surfaces.
A sharp engraving tool pushed through metal to cut a groove.
Acid bites exposed metal through openings in a protective coating, creating recessed lines.

effects.title: Stencil Coloring
effects.name: Stencil Coloring
effects.dating: 1903, Pathé Frères introduced an automated stencil system
effects.caption: Stencil-Colored Annunciation Scene. A kneeling woman in pale blue faces a winged angel in pink, framed by brown architecture and a green pastoral backdrop.
effects.credit: Lucien Nonguet / Ferdinand Zecca · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see black-and-white moving pictures where specific objects are brightly colored. The colors often jitter or pulse slightly between frames.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Workers cut specific shapes out of a film strip to make a stencil. Dye was brushed through these holes onto a matching print.

body.label: Example
body.text: Pathé Frères: The Life and Passion of Jesus Christ, 1903.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Watch a digitally restored stencil-colored film and track one colored object, noticing how the color edges shift slightly.

context: In the earliest days of cinema, films were often colored by hand, frame by frame. Because this was slow and expensive, Pathé Frères industrialized the process in the 1900s. They used a pantograph machine to carefully trace and cut out specific areas across sequential frames. These cut frames became a stencil roll. A machine then pressed this stencil against a fresh projection print. Velvet rollers applied dye through the cutouts onto the film below. Up to six colors could be added by using a different stencil roll for each dye.
effects.distinction: Hand-coloring involves painting directly onto each frame with a brush, causing wild variations. Stencil coloring applies flat dye through precise cutouts.
effects.aftermath: It highlights early cinema's intense labor and the desire for color long before photographic color film existed.
effects.funFact: Pathé's stencil factory employed hundreds of young women who specialized in cutting and dyeing film strips.

margin.note: A mechanical linkage tool used to trace and scale movements. In film, it guided a needle to cut the stencils.
A positive copy of a film meant to be shown in a theater. This is the strip that received the dye.

effects.title: Stereo Day-Night Tissue
effects.name: Stereo Day-Night Tissue
effects.dating: 1850s onward, French tissue stereoviews.
effects.caption: AI illustration: Parisian Boulevard in Day and Night Stereoview.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: In front light, paired photographs show an ordinary daylight scene with stereoscopic depth. With backlighting, hidden colours emerge, windows glow, and tiny points of light suggest lamps, stars, or fireworks.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Thin photographic prints, coloured backing tissue, and selective pinholes control transmitted light. Colouring filters the backlight subtractively, while pierced areas transmit brighter light; the paired views supply depth.

body.label: Example
body.text: Pierre Hennetier and Louis Habert (sculptors): Diableries, series begun 1867.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Compare front lighting and backlighting on a paper reproduction backed with coloured tissue; never pierce or alter an original.

context: French tissue stereoviews combined photography, hand colouring, and paper construction in a small theatrical object. They appeared in the 1850s and remained popular later in the century. A stereoscope presented a slightly different view to each eye, creating apparent depth. Thin photographic prints carried colouring behind them, often with a tissue backing. Front lighting largely concealed these additions. Backlighting revealed colour and made pierced details shine, suggesting night illumination rather than simply darkening the scene. The transformation happened during viewing, not through another exposure or chemical development.
effects.distinction: Unlike an ordinary coloured stereograph, a tissue view changes markedly with the direction of illumination. Unlike a double exposure, it needs no second photographed scene.
effects.aftermath: It shows how a photograph’s physical layers and viewing light can change its apparent time, atmosphere, and meaning.
effects.funFact: Some Diableries tissue views give their skeletons glowing eyes when illuminated from behind.

margin.note: Apparent depth produced when each eye sees a slightly different photograph of the same scene.
Light that passes through an object, rather than bouncing off its front surface.
By absorbing some wavelengths of light. The colouring removes parts of the backlight rather than adding coloured light.

body.label: Identify

body.label: Principle
body.text: A real object is moved minimally between individual photographs. The sequence of images creates the illusion of independent movement.

context: Precursors existed before 1900; object animation by the 1900s at the latest. Pixilation animates living people using the same frame-by-frame principle.

Recognize: Three-dimensional, tangible figures; often with deliberately slightly jerky movements.

effects.title: Stroboscopic Photography
effects.name: Stroboscopic Photography
effects.dating: 1931, Harold Edgerton's high-speed flashes
effects.caption: Milk Drop Crown. A milk splash forms a delicate crown, with rounded droplets suspended above a red surface.
effects.credit: Harold Edgerton · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a single image showing multiple overlapping stages of a fast movement. Alternatively, you see a frozen moment in absolute detail.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The camera shutter stays open in a dark room. A rapidly pulsing electronic flash exposes the moving subject multiple times onto one film frame.

body.label: Example
body.text: Harold Edgerton: Golfer (Densmore Shute), 1938.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Wave your hand under a flickering fluorescent tube to see continuous motion break into separate steps.

context: Before the 1930s, freezing high-speed motion was nearly impossible. Mechanical shutters could not open and close fast enough to stop a speeding bullet. Harold Edgerton, an electrical engineer at MIT, solved this problem with light. He invented a gas-filled tube that fired brilliant, microscopic bursts of light. By leaving the camera shutter open in the dark, only the brief flashes recorded onto the film. Each flash acted as a tiny, precise exposure. This allowed photographers to capture bullets shattering apples or multiple stages of an athlete's swing on a single frame.
effects.distinction: Chronophotography uses multiple cameras or a spinning disc to create a series of separate images. Stroboscopic photography uses one camera and flashing light to layer multiple exposures on one frame.
effects.aftermath: It reveals that continuous motion is made of countless unseen, distinct phases.
effects.funFact: Edgerton's strobe light flashes could last for just one millionth of a second.

margin.note: A device that produces a highly intense, brief burst of artificial light to illuminate a subject.
A sealed glass cylinder containing a noble gas that glows brightly when an electric current passes through it.
The exact amount of light reaching the photographic film, determined in this case by the ultra-short duration of the flash.

context: In 2001, Henrik Wann Jensen, Steve Marschner, Marc Levoy, and Pat Hanrahan presented a practical model for light transport under surfaces. Their deliberately simple facial model uses few triangles, minimal texture, and only one light source to clearly illustrate the difference between the light models.

effects.title: Teal and Orange
effects.name: Teal and orange color grading
effects.dating: 2000s–2010s: widespread cinema and video look
effects.caption: Exposure Software: Orange and Teal Grading, 2017.
effects.credit: Exposure Software / Jimmy Beech, official tutorial example.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Cool shadows and warm skin or lights.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Color correction shifts tonal ranges to complementary color families.

body.label: Example
body.text: Complementary grading in cinema, advertising and travel videos.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Show the same scene subtly and exaggeratedly; compare skin tones.

context: Orange and teal formed a common contrast in digital color grading of the early 21st century. Adobe explicitly describes this look as a popular video aesthetic of that time. Its effect is based on separating warm skin tones or light colors from a cooler background. This can be achieved by shifting shadows towards blue-green and highlights towards orange. This isn't a universal rule for all people or lighting conditions. For this learning exercise, keep the same recording: First, change only the shadows, then the highlights. Afterward, check neutral objects and faces. This will help you recognize when color separation enhances readability and when it appears unnatural.
effects.distinction: Skin tone and lighting logic require more attention than a general LUT.
effects.funFact: Many skin tones lie in the orange spectrum; cool backgrounds can make them stand out more.

margin.note: Groups of brightness values, such as shadows, midtones, and highlights.
Color groups on opposite sides of a color wheel. Blue-green and orange create a strong cool–warm contrast.

effects.title: Teletext Graphics
effects.name: Teletext Graphics
effects.dating: 1974, BBC Ceefax launch
effects.caption: RTL Teletext Index. An RTL teletext index displays German headlines, page numbers, and advertisements in bright horizontal bands.
effects.credit: Gabidgjtx · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see chunky, grid-based images built from colored rectangles and simple text characters. They appear on black backgrounds in bright, saturated colors.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Broadcasters hid digital text data within the invisible lines of an analog television signal. A decoding chip inside the TV translated this data into visual blocks.

body.label: Example
body.text: BBC: Ceefax weather maps, 1974.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a picture using only a 40 by 24 grid of colored sticky notes to understand the resolution limits.

context: Teletext was invented in the United Kingdom to send text information to televisions. Engineers realized the standard TV signal had hidden gaps called the vertical blanking interval. They inserted digital data into these blank lines. A special decoder inside the television read the data. It displayed this information as pages of text and crude graphics. The graphics relied on block mosaic characters, dividing a single text space into smaller squares. Because memory was expensive in the 1970s, teletext stored an entire screen using only one kilobyte of data.
effects.distinction: Teletext graphics are generated by the TV using character codes. This differs from raster graphics, which store data for every individual pixel.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates how tight hardware limits can create a distinct and lasting visual aesthetic.
effects.funFact: Teletext pages could be downloaded as computer software by recording the TV audio to a cassette tape.

margin.note: This is a brief pause in a television signal. It allows the electron gun to return to the top.
These are specialized text symbols. They look like small grids instead of regular alphabet letters.
This is a small electronic component inside the TV. It translates the hidden digital data back into readable text.

effects.title: Text-to-Image Generation
effects.name: Text-to-Image Generation
effects.dating: 2021, public introduction of DALL-E
effects.caption: Théâtre D’opéra Spatial. Figures in elaborate gowns occupy a monumental hall dominated by a luminous circular opening.
effects.credit: Left intentionally blank · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see highly detailed pictures that match a written description. Early examples often feature visual errors like mangled fingers or nonsensical text.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Software gradually refines a field of random digital noise into a coherent picture. It relies on mathematical models trained on massive datasets.

body.label: Example
body.text: Jason Allen: Théâtre D'opéra Spatial, 2022.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at the hands, background text, and repeating patterns in an AI-generated image to find structural flaws.

context: Text-to-image generation surged into public view in the early 2020s. The dominant method uses a mathematical process called diffusion. The software starts with pure, static-like noise. Over many small steps, it subtracts this noise to reveal an image. A user's written prompt guides this subtractive process. The system understands concepts because it analyzed massive datasets of existing images and captions. Early tools struggled with complex human anatomy and spatial logic. However, the technology improved rapidly. It sparked intense debates about copyright, artistic intent, and visual authenticity.
effects.distinction: Unlike traditional 3D rendering where an artist builds virtual geometry, this process statistically predicts pixels based on linguistic patterns.
effects.aftermath: It demonstrates that human visual logic and computational pattern recognition are fundamentally different.
effects.funFact: Early AI generators often placed strange, unreadable text on signs because they recognized letters but could not spell.

margin.note: A mathematical process that creates data by gradually removing artificial noise, step by step.
Randomly colored or grayscale pixels that look like television static, serving as the starting material.
Vast collections of existing images and paired text used to teach the software pattern recognition.

effects.title: Thaumatrope
effects.name: Thaumatrope
effects.dating: 1825, popularized by John Ayrton Paris
effects.caption: Birdcage Thaumatrope on Cords. A white disc bearing a black birdcage hangs between two posts on red cords.
effects.credit: Marcin Wichary from San Francisco, U.S.A. · CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a single composite image that flickers slightly. It is formed by visually blending two separate pictures located on opposite sides of a spinning disc.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Rapid rotation causes the viewer's eyes to retain the image of each side for a fraction of a second. This biological quirk fuses the two alternating views into one combined scene.

body.label: Example
body.text: John Ayrton Paris: A bird and a cage thaumatrope, 1825.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a jar on one side of a card and a bug on the back, then spin it quickly.

context: The thaumatrope was the first popular philosophical toy to demonstrate persistence of vision. Physicians like John Ayrton Paris used it in the 1820s to teach optical principles to children. The device consists of a simple cardboard disc with strings attached to the edges. One side might show a bare tree, while the reverse shows green leaves. When you twist the strings tightly and pull them, the disc rapidly twirls. The viewer's brain holds onto both images simultaneously, superimposing them. This parlor trick laid early conceptual groundwork for future motion pictures.
effects.distinction: Unlike a zoetrope, which creates the illusion of continuous motion from sequential frames, a thaumatrope only merges two static images.
effects.aftermath: It proves that our visual system actively constructs reality by bridging tiny gaps in time.
effects.funFact: The name combines the ancient Greek words for 'wonder' and 'turning,' literally meaning 'wonder-turner.'

margin.note: The slight delay in how our retinas and brain process light, often referred to historically as persistence of vision.
Placing one image directly over another so that both are seen at the exact same time.
A 19th-century term for playthings created to demonstrate scientific principles, particularly those involving human optics.

effects.title: Thermal False Color
effects.name: Thermal false-color look
effects.dating: 2020s: Filter revival of an older sensor aesthetic
effects.caption: Thermal false colors: modern digital simulation, not thermal imaging measurement.
effects.credit: Digital effect demonstration.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Rainbow-like color zones suggest heat distributions.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An image filter replaces visible brightness values with a false color palette.

body.label: Example
body.text: Sensor looks in music videos and experimental portraits.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Color the same image using two contrasting temperature palettes.

context: True thermography measures radiation in a suitable infrared spectral range and often displays measurements using a false-color palette. This slide, however, deals with the graphical thermal look of an ordinary photo or video. A digital filter assigns visible image values ​​and does not detect heat or temperature. The placement in the 2020s describes this current filter application, not the invention of thermal imaging devices. This distinction is particularly instructive: The same person can appear hot or cold depending on the palette, even though only the display has changed. Therefore, when viewing sensor images, always check what data was actually recorded.
effects.distinction: A thermal filter on a normal photograph does not measure temperature and does not detect heat radiation.
effects.funFact: The thermal palette of a normal photo filter shows brightness, not measured body temperature.

margin.note: A chosen set of colors used to represent numerical values rather than natural surface colors. Here it maps brightness, not measured temperature.
Color scales associated with hotter and colder values. Applied to an ordinary photograph, they suggest heat without actually measuring it.

context: A time displacement map determines which point in time of a clip becomes visible at a specific position in the frame. Adobe documented the effect in the 2012 After Effects CS6 manual, describing a neutral gray value as well as negative and positive time offsets. A smooth gradient creates continuous distortions; stepped maps divide the image into time segments. The year 2012 serves as a verifiable documentation reference point, not a purported invention. The similarity to slit scanning aids understanding but does not replace the historical distinction.
effects.distinction: Unlike spatial displacement scanning, this method shifts the scanning time. It is digitally programmable; a physical slot camera is not required.
effects.aftermath: Time is treated like a spatially paintable material.
effects.funFact: A map can display different points in time within the same single image.
highlights: simultaneously in different phases of movement

margin.note: An image whose light and dark values control which moment of the video each region displays.

effects.title: Two-Color Technicolor
effects.name: Two-Color Technicolor
effects.dating: 1922, The Toll of the Sea
effects.caption: Art Deco Stage Scene In Limited Color. A stage scene from an early color film is depicted with a limited palette dominated by warm, golden-orange hues and teal shadows.
effects.credit: Harry Beaumont / John Arnold · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Flesh tones appear unusually warm, often leaning toward orange or peach. Skies look cyan or greenish instead of deep blue. True yellows are entirely missing.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A custom camera exposes two consecutive frames simultaneously through red and green filters using a beam splitter. Prints are made on thin film, dyed red-orange and cyan, and cemented back-to-back.

body.label: Example
body.text: Chester M. Franklin: The Toll of the Sea, 1922.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look closely at a 1920s color film and try to find anything bright yellow; you will only see muddy browns or pale oranges.

context: Technicolor introduced its Process 2 in 1922 to solve flickering issues in earlier color systems. Instead of projecting through colored glass, this subtractive method embedded color directly into the film. A prism inside the camera split light to expose red and green records simultaneously. Laboratories printed these records onto half-thickness film stocks. Technicians dyed the red record cyan and the green record magenta-red. Finally, they cemented the two thin strips back-to-back. This created a single projectable print displaying a limited but vivid color spectrum.
effects.distinction: Unlike Three-Strip Technicolor, Process 2 entirely lacked a blue record. Unlike Kinemacolor, Process 2 prints could play on standard projectors without spinning color wheels.
effects.aftermath: It proved that audiences desired color films, paving the way for full-spectrum cinematography in the 1930s.
effects.funFact: The cementing process often caused the film prints to cup or warp from hot theater projector lamps.

margin.note: An optical device, usually a prism, that divides a single beam of light into two or more separate paths.
A color process that uses dyes or pigments to absorb certain colors of light, letting the remaining colors pass through.
A blue-green color used as a primary dye in photographic printing to control the amount of red light.

effects.title: Ultraviolet Photography
effects.name: Ultraviolet Photography
effects.dating: 1910s, Robert W. Wood's UV landscape and floral images

effects.credit: Callophrys rubi · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Familiar flowers or landscapes appear starkly different. Dark patches emerge on flower petals, and foliage looks unnervingly dark.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A special filter blocks visible light but lets invisible ultraviolet rays pass through. The photographic emulsion records these normally unseen wavelengths.

body.label: Example
body.text: Robert W. Wood: 'Ultraviolet photograph of a Potentilla flower', 1910.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Use an inexpensive blacklight in a dark room to reveal invisible fluorescent security features on modern currency or passports.

context: Robert W. Wood pioneered this technique around 1910 by inventing a special barium-sodium-silicate filter. This material, later called Wood's glass, blocked visible light entirely. It only allowed invisible ultraviolet light to reach the photographic plate. By photographing common plants, Wood revealed a completely hidden visual world. He discovered that many flower petals have intricate UV-absorbing patterns. These unseen markings act as landing guides for pollinating insects. Bees and other insects can naturally see these ultraviolet wavelengths. His experiments laid the groundwork for modern forensic science and astronomy.
effects.distinction: Unlike infrared photography, which often makes foliage appear snowy white, ultraviolet photography renders leaves very dark. It captures shorter, highly energetic wavelengths.
effects.aftermath: It visually proves that human eyes perceive only a tiny fraction of the broader electromagnetic spectrum.
effects.funFact: Wood's glass is still widely used today in modern blacklights for forensics and theatrical stage lighting.

margin.note: A light-sensitive chemical coating on photographic film or plates. It captures the image when exposed to incoming radiation.
Invisible waves of electromagnetic radiation. They are shorter than visible violet light but longer than X-rays.
A specialized dark glass filter invented by Robert W. Wood. It absorbs visible light but transmits ultraviolet wavelengths.

effects.dating: Silent film comedy; later action and deliberate stylization
effects.caption:
Parallel Exit / Ben Model (2020): practical comparison of different recording frequencies.
Temporal effect: still image or image sequence.
effects.credit: © Ben Model / Parallel Exit; comparison image by the copyright holder.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Movements appear accelerated and often more energetic.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Capture fewer images per second than you will play back later.

body.label: Example
body.text: Ben Model: Undercranking tests with parallel exit, 2020.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Record at 12 fps and play it back at 24 fps.

context: 1920s silent film comedy; later action and deliberate stylization

When cranking a film camera, the frame rate controls the perceived time effect. Fewer frames per second, projected later at a higher frequency, accelerate the action. Silent film expert and researcher Ben Model demonstrates this technique with contemporary actors and smartphone footage. Unlike reverse motion, the frame sequence remains the same; unlike long interval time-lapse, the camera typically films a continuous movement.
effects.distinction: Not every seemingly fast-paced silent film recording was intentionally undercranked. Variable historical projection frequencies and modern transfers can alter speeds. Undercranking refers to a deliberate shooting decision.
effects.aftermath: Time tricks become clearer when sequence, recording frequency and playback are considered separately.
effects.funFact: The term originates from the hand-cranked film cameras of the past.

margin.note: Recording fewer frames per second than the playback rate. The resulting action appears faster when projected or played normally.
Twelve frames captured each second. Playing them at 24 frames per second doubles the apparent speed of the action.

effects.title: Van Dyke Brown Print
effects.name: Van Dyke Brown Print
effects.dating: 1889, W. J. Nicol's Kallitype patent
effects.caption: Feather on Hand-Coated Brown Print. A pale feather emerges from a deep brown field surrounded by irregular brush marks on white paper.
effects.credit: Petr Vodička · CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a photograph with rich, deep brown tones and a matte finish. The image looks embedded directly in the paper fibers.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Ultraviolet light reduces light-sensitive ferric iron into ferrous iron. This new iron compound then reduces silver nitrate into solid metallic silver.

body.label: Example
body.text: W. J. Nicol: Early Kallitype and Vandyke brown tests, 1889.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Examine the shadow areas of a historical brown print under a magnifying glass to see exposed paper fibers.

context: Invented by W. J. Nicol in 1889, this technique is named after the Flemish painter Anthony van Dyck. The resulting rich, deep brown tones closely resembled the painter's favorite oil color. A photographer coats paper with ferric ammonium citrate, tartaric acid, and silver nitrate. After drying, a negative is placed directly on the paper. They expose this contact sandwich to bright sunlight or ultraviolet light. The light causes the iron salts to chemically react. This reaction converts the silver nitrate into visible metallic silver. Finally, the print is washed in water and fixed with sodium thiosulfate. This makes the deep brown image permanent.
effects.distinction: Unlike glossy albumen prints that use an egg-white binder, Vandyke prints lack a surface emulsion layer. Their matte image rests directly inside the paper fibers.
effects.aftermath: It proved that combining iron and silver chemistry could produce beautiful, accessible photographs without complex darkroom development.
effects.funFact: You only need plain water to initially develop the image before making it permanent with a fixer.

margin.note: A chemical form of iron that changes its state when exposed to ultraviolet light.
A light-sensitive chemical compound used heavily in historic photography to create silver-based images.
A chemical fixer that stops the photographic process by washing away unexposed silver.

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a digital collage of pastel neon colors, mostly pink and cyan. It features 1980s computer graphics, wireframe grids, classical busts, and Japanese text.

body.label: Principle
body.text: This visual style relies on digital image manipulation and sampling. Artists use graphic software to overlay glitch effects, VHS artifacts, and retro 3D renders.

body.label: Example
body.text: Macintosh Plus: Floral Shoppe (album cover), 2011.

body.label: Try it out

context: Vaporwave began as an electronic music microgenre in the early 2010s. It sampled 1980s and 1990s elevator music, corporate lounge tracks, and smooth jazz. Visually, it ironizes early internet culture and consumer capitalism. The aesthetic mixes outdated computer graphics with pristine classical marble statues. Artists heavily use neon pastels to mimic faded VHS tapes and CRT monitors. This nostalgic visual language reflects a sense of lost optimism about technology and globalized commerce.
effects.distinction: Vaporwave is often confused with Synthwave. Synthwave focuses on dark neon grids and 1980s action movie tropes, while Vaporwave uses soft pastels and surreal corporate imagery.
effects.aftermath: It reveals how internet communities recycle outdated technology to critique modern digital culture.
effects.funFact: The name "vaporwave" mocks "vaporware," which is software announced but never actually released.

margin.note: Sampling is the act of taking a portion of an existing media recording and reusing it in a new creation.
These are visual flaws like tracking lines, static, or distorted colors caused by the magnetic tape used in older video cassettes.

effects.title: Vector Display Graphics
effects.name: Vector Display Graphics
effects.dating: 1970s, arcade games like Asteroids
effects.caption: Luminous Vector Platforms and Ladder. Bright blue geometric platforms and a ladder glow across a Vectrex screen beneath a colored overlay.
effects.credit: RetroEditor · CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see crisp, glowing lines forming geometric shapes on a black background. The lines have no jagged pixels. Their intersections glow intensely.

body.label: Principle
body.text: An electron beam is drawn directly from point to point across a phosphor screen. This continuous movement creates perfectly smooth, unbroken lines.

body.label: Example
body.text: Atari, Inc.: Asteroids, 1979.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Draw a star without lifting your pen. Notice how ink pools at the points where lines cross, resembling glowing vector intersections.

context: In the 1970s, computer memory was very expensive. Raster screens wasted memory by storing every blank background pixel. Vector displays solved this by only processing coordinates for the actual shapes. An electron gun physically moved its beam between these X and Y coordinates. This stroke technique traced lines directly onto the glowing screen. Arcade makers loved this because it allowed fast, complex motion without heavy computing power. Games like Asteroids and Tempest used this hardware for smooth space combat. The technology faded when memory chips became cheaper.
effects.distinction: Unlike raster graphics which build images row by row using square pixels, vector monitors draw lines continuously like a pen.
effects.aftermath: It reveals how early hardware constraints inspired elegant engineering solutions for real-time graphics.
effects.funFact: Some vector monitors could physically catch fire if a software bug stopped the electron beam from moving.
highlights: drawn directly from point to point

margin.note: A layer of chemical compounds inside a monitor that emits light when struck by energetic particles.
Displays that render images by scanning horizontal rows of tiny dots, common in modern televisions.
A component inside older televisions and monitors that fires a targeted stream of charged particles.

context: Experimental since the 1960s; formative wave of video art in the 1970s.

effects.funFact: Skip Sweeney combined video feedback with Moog and Vidium synthesizers in 1975.

effects.title: Volumetric Light
effects.name: Volumetric Light
effects.dating: 2007, Crytek's implementation in Crysis
effects.caption: Sun Shaft Illuminating a Cave Interior. A massive, glowing shaft of sunlight pierces the darkness of a cave, illuminating the rocky interior and a standing figure.
effects.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see distinct shafts of light shining through an environment. Dust, fog, or smoke seems to glow within the bright beams.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A computer algorithm simulates light scattering through tiny particles suspended in the air. It calculates which parts of the 3D atmosphere are illuminated.

body.label: Example
body.text: Crytek: Crysis, 2007.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a window in a dusty or smoky room when direct sunlight streams in.

context: In the real world, light is invisible until it hits an object. "God rays" occur when sunlight reflects off atmospheric particles like dust or water vapor. In early 3D computer graphics, lights only illuminated solid surfaces. During the 2000s, developers created clever mathematical shortcuts to render glowing atmospheres in real time. A popular technique called "screen-space sun shafts" was adopted after the game Crysis released. It blurred bright light sources across the screen based on depth data. This created the illusion of complex 3D light shafts using very little processing power.
effects.distinction: Volumetric lighting simulates light scattering inside an atmosphere. Lens flares only simulate light bouncing inside a camera lens.
effects.aftermath: It shows how replicating atmospheric imperfections dramatically increases the realism of virtual spaces.
effects.funFact: Real-time volumetric light often relies on 2D image blurring rather than true 3D particle physics.

margin.note: A set of step-by-step instructions that a computer follows to solve a specific problem.
A visual trick that calculates light effects based only on the flat 2D image currently visible on the screen.

effects.title: Vortograph
effects.name: Vortograph
effects.dating: 1917, Alvin Langdon Coburn's abstract photographs
effects.caption: AI illustration: Kaleidoscopic deconstruction of glass objects.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Angular fragments and repeated reflections form an abstract pattern of overlapping triangles, bright planes, and deep shadows. Recognizable objects often disappear into kaleidoscopic geometry.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Three mirrors arranged as a triangular tube reflect the subject along multiple paths before light enters the camera lens. The pattern forms optically during exposure, rather than through chemical development or assembled prints.

body.label: Example
body.text: Alvin Langdon Coburn: Vortograph, 1917.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Arrange three small mirrors into a triangular tube, reflective sides inward, and look through it at crumpled paper under side lighting.

context: In 1917, Alvin Langdon Coburn made abstract photographs using a mirror attachment called a vortoscope. Its name connected the pictures with Vorticism, a modern art movement associated with angular forms and dynamic compositions. Three inward-facing mirrors formed a triangular tube in front of the camera lens. Their reflections broke ordinary subjects into intersecting shapes and repeated fragments. This was a mirror system, not a solid glass prism splitting light into colors. Coburn's vortographs explored whether photography could create an independent visual composition rather than simply describe recognizable objects.
effects.distinction: Unlike multiple exposure, a vortograph can record its overlapping forms in a single exposure. Unlike a refracting prism, its mirror attachment redirects light by reflection.
effects.aftermath: The vortograph shows how changing the light path before exposure can turn descriptive photography toward abstraction.
effects.funFact: Coburn gave his mirror attachment its own name: the vortoscope.

margin.note: Coburn's mirror attachment, placed before the camera lens to create fragmented, repeated views.
A British modern art movement that emphasized angular geometry and the energy of modern life.
The period when light reaches photographic film or another light-sensitive surface and records an image.

effects.title: Voxel Graphics
effects.name: Voxel Graphics
effects.dating: 1992, NovaLogic's Comanche: Maximum Overkill
effects.caption: Highlighted Voxel in a Cubic Volume. An isometric arrangement of gray cubes forms a stepped volume, with one cube highlighted in red.
effects.credit: Vossman; M. W. Toews; cmglee · CC BY-SA 2.5 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see 3D landscapes made of tiny stacked cubes rather than flat surfaces. The terrain looks dense, chunky, and naturally bumpy instead of sharply geometric.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The image is built from volumetric pixels, which are 3D data points with color. A rendering engine casts rays to draw these points on the screen.

body.label: Example
body.text: NovaLogic: Comanche: Maximum Overkill, 1992.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Look at a Minecraft landscape and notice how curved hills are actually stepped grids of solid blocks.

context: In the early 1990s, standard computers struggled to process complex 3D polygons quickly. Voxel graphics offered a clever shortcut for rendering outdoor environments. Instead of calculating flat geometric shapes, programmers used heightmaps. These maps told the computer how high to stack colored dots at any specific coordinate. The game engine then traced lines across the screen to quickly draw these points. This created incredibly detailed, rolling terrain that looked much more realistic than early polygon graphics. However, animating moving objects with voxels proved too heavy for computer memory, limiting its use.
effects.distinction: Unlike polygons, which form empty mathematical shells, voxels represent solid volume in 3D space. Think of polygons as origami and voxels as Lego bricks.
effects.aftermath: It teaches that representing solid volume can create rich textures that flat surfaces simply cannot achieve.
effects.funFact: Medical MRI scans still rely entirely on voxel data to build 3D models of human organs.

margin.note: The software program that calculates how 3D data should look when drawn as a 2D image.
A 2D image where the brightness of each pixel tells the computer how tall the terrain should be.
The core software framework that manages the rules, graphics, and memory of a video game.

effects.dating: Introduced in 1851; influential until the 1880s
effects.caption: Ludwig Bickell: Marburg, 1882–86. Original collodion glass negative.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Sharp glass negatives; hand-cast edges may remain visible.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The light-sensitive collodion layer is exposed and developed while still wet.

body.label: Example
body.text: Ludwig Bickell: Marburg, 1882–86, glass negative.

body.label: Try it out

context: Frederick Scott Archer published the wet plate process in 1851. The glass base allows for finer details than a paper negative. Coating, sensitization, exposure, and development had to be closely timed; therefore, a darkroom was part of the equipment when traveling. The historical negative shown illustrates that the camera image is not yet the final positive view.
effects.distinction: Irregular edges are possible traces of the working process, not a necessary characteristic of every collodion photograph. The negative should not be confused with the albumen print produced from it. Digital scratches alone do not reconstruct the process.
effects.aftermath: Process traces can make material and workflow visible.
effects.funFact: For outdoor shots, the darkroom had to travel along because the plate was still processed wet.
highlights: exposed and developed while still wet

margin.note: A syrupy solution of cellulose nitrate in solvents. It forms a thin film on glass that carries the light-sensitive chemicals.
An image on glass with light and dark reversed. It can be used to make positive paper prints.
