effects.title: Williams Process
effects.name: Williams Process
effects.dating: 1918, Frank D. Williams's travelling-matte patent
effects.caption: AI illustration: Walking figure composited against coastal waves.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Moving figures appear inside a separately filmed setting, with their outlines preserved as they cross the frame. Dark fringes or pale halos sometimes reveal the join.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Filming against a black backing supplies the contrast needed to make complementary masks through high-contrast copying. These travelling mattes control exposure during printing, combining foreground and background without simply overlaying both images.

body.label: Example
body.text: James Whale: The Invisible Man, 1933.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Pause a composite shot in The Lost World (1925), then advance several frames while watching the dinosaur's outline.

context: Frank D. Williams patented his process in 1918, helping filmmakers combine moving subjects with separately photographed scenery. A subject was lit against a black backing, which recorded little light. High-contrast copying produced masks that separated the subject's shape from its surroundings. Complementary masks protected different areas of the receiving film during successive printing exposures. Unlike a fixed mask, each travelling matte followed the subject from frame to frame. Careful alignment was essential: mismatched edges could produce visible outlines. Dark subject details could also disappear into the backing, complicating separation.
effects.distinction: Unlike simple double exposure, the Williams Process reserves space for the foreground instead of letting the background show through it. Unlike blue-screen separation, it relies on brightness contrast rather than color differences.
effects.aftermath: It shows how controlling where light reaches film can make separately photographed actions share one convincing space.
effects.funFact: Black velvet helped make a visible actor disappear in The Invisible Man.

margin.note: Masks whose shapes change across successive film frames to follow a moving subject.
Rephotographing film to emphasize clear and opaque areas while suppressing intermediate tones.
A matched pair of masks that block opposite areas. Together, they let separate images occupy different parts of one frame.

body.label: Identify
body.text: A shifting boundary replaces one attitude with another.

body.label: Principle
body.text: A moving mask reveals the next image.

body.label: Example
body.text: Scrooge, 1901; Flying Down to Rio, 1933.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Create a wipe using a passing person.

context: Columbia references Robert Paul's 1901 film Scrooge and a transition resembling a falling theater curtain. Early wipes often required complex laboratory production. Studios were able to use them more easily in the 1930s with the advent of their own optical printers. Later films also used them deliberately for nostalgic effect, such as The Sting. The direction and shape of the boundary influence the tempo and rhythm.
effects.distinction: The moving edge is part of the effect; it is not an additional decorative line. A wipe indicates a change in the image space and is much more noticeable than a hard cut.
effects.aftermath: A boundary in the image can itself become a narrative event.
effects.funFact: Early wipe transitions were more expensive than hard cuts or crossfades.

margin.note: A shape that controls which parts of an image are visible. Moving it progressively reveals the incoming shot.
A transition where a moving edge replaces one shot with another, rather than blending them across the whole frame.

context: Digital wire removal makes physical stunts and puppet movements invisible. In Foundry's example, RotoPaint uses masks and copied image areas; tracking keeps the repair in place as the camera moves. effects.title: Woodburytype
effects.name: Woodburytype
effects.dating: 1864, Walter Bentley Woodbury's patent
effects.caption: Woodburytype Book Illustration. This book spread features a tipped-in photographic print depicting men putting up street advertisements.
effects.credit: Rijksmuseum · CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a photographic print with rich, continuous tones and absolutely no dot pattern. The dark areas are slightly raised, giving the image a faint physical relief.

body.label: Principle
body.text: It relies on variable thickness of pigmented gelatin to create shades. A metal mold presses gelatin onto paper, leaving thicker ink for shadows.

body.label: Example
body.text: John Thomson: Street Life in London, 1877.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Tilt a Woodburytype near a light source to spot the slight physical texture mapping exactly to the dark shadows.

context: Walter Bentley Woodbury patented this method to mass-produce photographs without fading. It bridged the gap between photography and mechanical printing. First, light exposed a layer of light-sensitive gelatin, hardening it based on the image's brightness. The unhardened gelatin washed away, leaving a three-dimensional gelatin relief. A hydraulic press then crushed this fragile gelatin into a sheet of soft lead. This created a durable metal mold. Finally, printers filled this mold with pigmented gelatin and pressed paper onto it. The varying depth of the mold created perfect continuous tones, unlike dot grids used in later printing.
effects.distinction: Unlike half-tone prints that rely on grids of tiny dots to simulate shades, Woodburytypes use actual varying thicknesses of ink.
effects.aftermath: It shows how early inventors used physical depth to perfectly replicate photographic lighting.
effects.funFact: The hydraulic presses used to make the lead molds applied up to five tons of pressure.

margin.note: Smooth transitions between light and dark shades without being broken up into artificial dots or lines.
A mixture of animal protein and permanent colored dye used as the actual physical ink for the print.
A processed layer of gelatin that varies in physical thickness based on how much light exposed and hardened it.

effects.title: WordArt
effects.name: WordArt
effects.dating: 1990s, Microsoft Office decorative lettering
effects.caption: Ornate Lettering with Layered Outlines. Ornate blue lettering carries red and pale outlines, with soft shadows beneath its curling forms.

body.label: Identify
body.text: Large letters form curved lines or stretched shapes, often with rainbow gradients, heavy outlines, and simulated extrusion. Shadows and shiny highlights make flat lettering resemble solid objects.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Software transforms letter outlines and applies color fills, outlines, shadows, and depth effects. Gradients vary color across each shape; simulated extrusion adds visible sides without requiring a physical object.

body.label: Example
body.text: Microsoft: Word 97 WordArt gallery, 1997.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Style one word with a curve, gradient, and depth effect; remove each treatment separately to see what changes.

context: WordArt brought decorative display lettering into everyday office documents during the 1990s. Users could turn ordinary words into graphic objects rather than arrange individual letters by hand. Presets combined shaped text with outlines, fills, and other treatments, although available features changed between versions. Curving or stretching altered the lettering’s geometry. Gradients supplied changing color, while shadows and simulated sides suggested depth on a flat page. These accessible controls made elaborate headings practical for school assignments, flyers, and presentations. The recognizable look came from combinations of treatments, not one particular typeface.
effects.distinction: WordArt is not a font: the same typeface can receive many different treatments. Unlike physical extruded lettering, its apparent depth remains an image.
effects.aftermath: WordArt shows how reusable software presets can make decorative lettering recognizable across otherwise unrelated documents.
effects.funFact: The lettering could look sculptural while remaining editable as words.

margin.note: Drawn sides make a flat letter appear to extend backward into space.
The boundaries defining each letter’s shape, including holes inside letters such as O.
Saved combinations of settings that users can apply without adjusting every control separately.

effects.title: X-Ray Radiograph
effects.name: X-Ray Radiograph
effects.dating: 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen's first medical x-ray
effects.caption: Historic X-Ray of Hand with Ring. This historic image displays the skeletal structure of a hand, complete with a prominent silhouette of a ring on one finger.
effects.credit: Wilhelm Röntgen · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: You see a high-contrast, ghostly image where dense objects like bones appear white. Softer tissues appear as dark, transparent shadows.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Invisible electromagnetic rays pass through soft materials but are absorbed by dense matter. Unabsorbed rays expose a photographic plate, creating a shadow.

body.label: Example
body.text: Wilhelm Röntgen: Hand mit Ringen (Hand with Rings), 1895.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Hold your hand over a bright flashlight in a dark room to see how light passes through flesh but not bone.

context: In late 1895, physicist Wilhelm Röntgen was experimenting with a cathode-ray tube in a darkened room. He noticed a nearby fluorescent screen glowing. He discovered a new kind of invisible ray was escaping the tube. These "X-rays" could pass through cardboard, wood, and human flesh. He soon placed his wife Anna Bertha's hand between the tube and a photographic plate. After development, the plate revealed her bones and wedding ring. This subtractive shadow-casting proved that different materials absorb radiation at different rates. The discovery revolutionized medicine and physics immediately.
effects.distinction: Unlike a standard photograph that captures reflected visible light, a radiograph captures a shadow map of interior density. Surface colors and textures remain invisible.
effects.aftermath: It teaches that human vision captures only a tiny fraction of the electromagnetic spectrum.
effects.funFact: Early shoe stores used live X-ray machines to measure feet, exposing customers to high radiation doses.

margin.note: This is a type of energy that travels in waves. Visible light, radio waves, and X-rays are all part of this continuous spectrum.
Before flexible film rolls, photographers used flat sheets of glass coated with light-sensitive chemicals to capture images.
This is a sealed glass vacuum tube containing electrical electrodes. It produces invisible beams of electrons when high voltage is applied.

effects.name: Xerographic Animation
effects.dating: 1960s; Disney’s One Hundred and One Dalmatians, 1961
effects.caption: AI illustration: Animation cel showing raw xerographic line work.
effects.credit: Illustration generated for the Atlas (AI)

body.label: Identify
body.text: Sketchy black outlines surround flat painted colors, with rough edges and occasional stray pencil marks. The characters retain a visibly drawn texture rather than uniformly smooth ink contours.

body.label: Principle
body.text: Light exposure creates an electrostatic image, which toner develops into a visible powder image. The toner image is transferred and fixed onto transparent cels, preserving pencil marks without hand tracing.

body.label: Example
body.text: Walt Disney Productions: One Hundred and One Dalmatians, 1961.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Pause a close-up in One Hundred and One Dalmatians; compare the uneven black contours with the smooth painted areas.

context: Disney adopted xerography to transfer animation drawings onto cels, reducing the labor of tracing outlines by hand. Ub Iwerks helped adapt the process for animation production. One Hundred and One Dalmatians made its graphic possibilities especially visible in 1961. Light exposure formed an electrostatic image; toner development made that image visible before transfer to the cel. Artists still painted the colors, usually on the reverse side. The process preserved much of the drawing’s character, including irregular contours. Its early black outlines became a defining feature of Disney’s 1960s animation.
effects.distinction: Unlike hand-inked cel animation, xerography transfers the drawn contours instead of having an artist retrace them. It is not rotoscoping, which uses filmed movement as a drawing reference.
effects.aftermath: Xerographic animation shows how a labor-saving reproduction process can also change a film’s visual style.
effects.funFact: The familiar black outlines are toner, not hand-traced ink.

margin.note: A pattern of electrical charge that attracts toner in selected areas.
Fine powder used to develop the electrical image into visible marks.
Transparent sheets carrying drawings and paint. They were photographed over backgrounds to make animation frames.

sources.label: Wikipedia: One Hundred and One Dalmatians

effects.title: Zoetrope
effects.name: Zoetrope
effects.dating: 1834, William George Horner's device; popular in the 1860s
effects.caption: Blue Zoetrope with Dancing Figures. A blue hand-cranked drum has narrow vertical slits above an inner strip of figures in successive poses.
effects.credit: Runner1616 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Through a spinning drum's narrow slits, drawings appear to perform a repeating movement. The picture strip shows successive poses, often of people or animals.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The slits provide brief glimpses of successive drawings, reducing the blur that continuous viewing would produce. Apparent motion links these separate views into perceived movement.

body.label: Example
body.text: William George Horner: Daedaleum, 1834.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Spin a zoetrope and compare looking through its slits with looking over its rim: notice when the drawings become readable.

context: William George Horner described his rotating drum device in 1834, calling it the Daedaleum. It became widely popular as the zoetrope in the 1860s. A paper strip lines the drum's inner wall, with drawings arranged in sequence below the viewing slits. Looking through the passing slits reveals successive drawings across the drum. Each opening briefly interrupts the otherwise blurred view. Several people can watch from different sides without a mirror. The sequence usually forms a loop, returning smoothly from its last pose to its first.
effects.distinction: A phenakistiscope usually uses a slotted disc viewed in a mirror. A zoetrope uses a drum and needs no mirror.
effects.aftermath: The zoetrope shows how separate still images can produce perceived movement when their presentation is carefully timed.
effects.funFact: Several viewers can watch the same drum at once, each seeing the animation from a different position.

margin.note: Movement perceived when separate images appear in succession, although no depicted figure actually moves.
Horner's original name for his drum device, later widely known as the zoetrope.
A sequence that repeats, with its ending leading back into its beginning.

effects.title: Zone System
effects.name: Zone System
effects.dating: 1939–1940, developed by Ansel Adams and Fred Archer
effects.caption: The Tetons and the Snake River. The Snake River winds through wooded flats beneath the snow-streaked Tetons and a luminous, cloud-filled sky.
effects.credit: Ansel Adams · Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

body.label: Identify
body.text: Typical black-and-white prints show deep blacks, luminous whites, and carefully separated gray tones. Important shadows and highlights retain texture, though appearance alone cannot confirm the method.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The system maps measured scene brightness onto eleven zones, from black to white. With black-and-white negative film, exposure establishes shadow detail, while development adjusts contrast, especially in highlights.

body.label: Example
body.text: Ansel Adams: The Tetons and the Snake River, 1942.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Photograph a white towel beside dark fabric at three exposures; compare which versions preserve texture in each material.

context: Adams and Archer developed the Zone System around 1939–1940, building on established photographic sensitometry. It helped photographers predict a finished print before exposing the negative. Zones run from 0, representing black, to X, representing white. Adjacent zones correspond to one stop of exposure, not equal steps in printed brightness. Photographers meter selected areas and choose where their tones should fall. Exposure secures needed shadow information; development changes negative contrast to suit the scene and printing paper. Printing remains essential, and not every photograph needs the full tonal scale.
effects.distinction: Unlike simply increasing contrast, the Zone System plans tonal placement before exposure and coordinates development with printing. Strong contrast alone does not demonstrate its use.
effects.aftermath: It teaches that scene brightness, recorded information, and final print tones are related but distinct.
effects.funFact: Its eleven zones are numbered 0 through X, mixing zero with Roman numerals.

margin.note: The measurement of how photographic materials respond to light exposure and processing.
A doubling or halving of exposure.
The difference in density between lighter and darker areas of a negative.

effects.title: Zoom Blur
effects.name: Zoom blur / zoom burst
effects.dating: 2010s: documented filter and photographic practice; optical history older
effects.caption: Joost J. Bakker: Zoom blur (2010), photographic zoom tracks.
effects.credit: Joost J. Bakker, CC BY 2.0; via Wikimedia Commons. Reduced. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0

body.label: Identify
body.text: Radiating traces extend outwards from the subject.

body.label: Principle
body.text: The focal length changes during exposure; filters simulate this.

body.label: Example
body.text: Joost J. Bakker: Zoom blur, 2010.

body.label: Try it out
body.text: Zoom in on a light source during a long exposure.

context: The zoom effect is created photographically by rotating the zoom ring during a longer exposure. Points of light or high-contrast contours trace radial paths. Digital filters extend this optical principle and allow for a freely selectable center point. The 2010s refer to the use documented here in photography guides and software, not the origin of the technique itself. The crucial factor is the change in magnification, not simply a blurred focus setting.
effects.distinction: A real zoom blur changes the image scale during exposure. A digital zoom blur is a simulation; a dolly zoom, on the other hand, combines camera movement and focal length changes with a different effect.
effects.aftermath: Similarly sounding zoom terms describe different image mechanisms.
effects.funFact: The center point of the digital zoom blur does not have to be in the center of the image.

margin.note: A lens property that determines magnification and angle of view. Zooming changes it during the shot.
Recording light for an extended time, allowing motion or changing magnification to leave visible traces.
